This Universal Registration Document has been filed on March 18, 2025, with the Autorité des marchés financiers (the “AMF”) as the competent
authority under Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, without prior approval pursuant to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129.
This Universal Registration Document may be used for the purposes of an offer to the public of securities or admission of securities to trading
on a regulated market if completed by a securities note and, if applicable, a summary and all amendments to the Universal Registration
Document. The combined document is approved by the AMF in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2017/1129.
This Universal Registration Document is a reproduction in PDF format, translated into English, of the official version of the Universal Registration
Document issued in French in the xHTML format, filed with the AMF on March 18, 2025 and available on the AMF website (www.amf‑france.org). This
translation is available on our website (www.axa.com).
This Universal Registration Document (which we also refer to as this “Document” or “Annual Report”) includes (i) the Annual Financial Report
(Rapport Financier Annuel) referred to in paragraph I of Article L.451‑1‑2 of the French Monetary and Financial Code (Code monétaire et financier) as
well as in Article 222‑3 of the AMF General Regulation (Règlement Général de l’AMF) (the relevant Sections of this Document corresponding to such
required disclosures are referred to in the cross‑reference table in Appendix VII - Cross reference table of the Annual Financial Report), (ii) the
management report (rapport de gestion) of the Board of Directors to be presented at AXA’s Shareholders’ Meeting to be held on April 24, 2025,
prepared pursuant to Articles L.225‑100 et seq., L.232‑1 et seq. and L.22‑10‑35 et seq. of the French Commercial Code (Code de commerce) (the
relevant Sections of this Document corresponding to such required disclosures are referred to in the cross‑reference table in Appendix V - Cross
reference table of the Board of Directors' management report (including the corporate governance report)); and (iii) the corporate governance report
(rapport sur le gouvernement d'entreprise) established pursuant to Articles L.225‑37 et seq. and L.22‑10‑8 et seq. of the French Commercial Code (the
relevant sections of this Document corresponding to such required disclosures are referred to in the cross‑reference table in Appendix V - Cross
reference table of the Board of Directors' management report (including the corporate governance report)). The cross‑reference table in Appendix VI
- Cross reference tables - EU regulation indicates the items of Annexes 1 and 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/980 to which the information
contained herein corresponds.

Certain preliminary information about this Document
In this Document, unless provided otherwise, (i) the “Company”, “AXA”
and “AXA SA” refer to AXA, a société anonyme (a public limited
company) organized under the laws of France, which is the publicly
traded parent company of the AXA Group, and (ii) the “AXA Group”, the
“Group” and “we” refer to AXA SA together with its direct and indirect
consolidated subsidiaries.
The Company’s ordinary shares are referred to in this Document as
“shares”, “ordinary shares”, “AXA shares” or “AXA ordinary shares”. The
principal trading market for AXA’s ordinary shares is the regulated
market Euronext in Paris (Compartment A), which we refer to in this
Document as “Euronext Paris”.
The Group’s consolidated financial statements and related notes are
prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting
Standards (IFRS) (the “Consolidated Financial Statements”) and
published in Euro (“Euro”, “euro”, “EUR” or “€”), as are all other
amounts in this Document, with applicable foreign exchange rates
presented in Section 2.2.1.3 - Exchange rates, and presented in million

for convenience. Such amounts may have been rounded. Rounding
differences may exist, including for percentages.
In this Document, unless provided otherwise, “restated” refers to the
comparative period that was restated following (i) the termination in
May 2024 of the sale agreement of a closed life and pensions portfolio
at AXA Germany, classified as held for sale in 2023 and (ii) the
announcement on August 1, 2024, that AXA had entered into an
exclusive negotiation to sell its asset manager AXA Investment
Managers (“AXA IM”) to BNP Paribas, leading to classify it as a
discontinued operation in the Consolidated Financial Statements.
Where reference is made to a website in this Document, the contents
of such website do not form part of this Document. No information,
document or material from the website of the Company
(www.axa.com) or any other source shall form part of this Document,
unless such information, document or material is expressly
incorporated by reference into this Document.

responsibility including by offering adapted products and services
designed to facilitate the climate transition by enhancing protection
and insurability. Beyond supporting the transition to a lower carbon
economy, we are also focused on fostering positive societal impact
through inclusive insurance solutions for vulnerable populations and
community and workforce engagement, notably through the AXA Hearts
in Action initiatives.

2024 was a year of significant change and uncertainty marked by
geopolitical tensions, divergent economic performance across
geographies and climate change challenges. Amidst these challenges,
the rapid pace of technological innovation is opening new avenues
for innovation, offering the potential to enhance efficiency, improve
decision-making, and create tailored solutions that better meet the
evolving needs of consumers and businesses.

The “Unlock the Future” strategy is off to a strong start. The Group
reported an 8% increase in topline growth with revenues reaching €110
billion, while our underlying earnings per share also rose by 8%. We have
delivered a 15% return on equity while maintaining a strong balance
sheet with a Solvency II ratio of 216%.

In a world characterized by volatility, uncertainty, and evolving risks,
there is an urgent need for robust risk management solutions. The value
of insurance has never been more relevant. For businesses, insurance
provides the essential protection that allows them to continue their
operations with confidence, safeguarding against unforeseen events
that could disrupt their activities and financial stability. For individuals,
insurance offers peace of mind by ensuring that their assets are protected,
their health is covered, and their retirement is secure. Insurance fosters
resilience, enabling both businesses and individuals to thrive in an
uncertain world. At AXA, we remain committed to addressing the needs
of our customers, ensuring they have access to the coverage they require
in an uncertain world.
Our business model, which is balanced between commercial and retail
insurance, with leading positions in our markets, continues to thrive.
With strong distribution and product capabilities, we are well placed to
meet the evolving needs of our customers and capitalize on the growth
opportunities that we see in our markets. We remain agile to respond to
changing market dynamics.
Our business model is delivering consistent results for our shareholders.
In 2024, AXA successfully launched its new Strategic Plan, “Unlock
the Future”, aimed at growing and strengthening the core insurance
business. The plan is focused on driving higher organic growth and
scaling technical and operational excellence across the Group. At the
same time, we affirm our long-standing commitment to corporate social

In 2024, we also made a strategic decision to further simplify our
business profile through the sale of AXA Investment Managers (IM) to
BNP Paribas. This transaction will pave the way for the creation of a
leading and scaled European asset manager with whom we plan to
maintain a strong relationship in the years ahead. This partnership will
give our clients access to a broader range of investment solutions and our
colleagues at AXA IM a scaled platform to grow. As part of our ambition
to strengthen our insurance franchise in our markets, we also announced
the acquisition of Nobis in Italy last summer.
In 2025, AXA will celebrate its 40th anniversary. This is an occasion
to celebrate and an opportunity to draw inspiration from AXA’s past
successes. As we move forward, we remain focused on meeting the
evolving needs of our customers, driving profitable growth, while also
delivering value to our shareholders.
Finally, this performance is a collective success, and we would like
to acknowledge the exceptional work of our employees, agents, and
partners. We are extremely grateful for their unwavering commitment to
serving our customers.

Strategics Orientations
In 2024, the insurance industry faced a complex landscape shaped by
various macroeconomic factors:
■ Geopolitical and climate challenges: (i) High geopolitical tensions,
including the ongoing war in Ukraine and instability in the Middle
East, continued to pose significant global risks. (ii) The escalating
competition between the US and China, along with the rise of populism
in Europe, increased the likelihood of disruptive policy changes. (iii)
Climate change remained a critical concern, with more frequent and
severe natural disasters impacting the industry.
■ Insurance industry dynamics: (i) The sector benefited from
a favorable cycle in Property & Casualty (P&C), driving premium
growth, while higher interest rates supported a recovery in the Life
& Health (L&H) segment. Claims cost showed signs of stabilization
amid moderating general inflation. (ii) Regulators continue to focus
on consumer protection, emphasizing transparency. (iii) Rapid
technological advancements prompted insurers to modernize
operations and enhance customer experience.
■ Growth opportunities: (i) High interest rates spurred demand for
Life insurance, particularly savings and retirement products. (ii) The
demand for Health and Protection rose, driven by demographic shifts
and protection gaps. (iii) Significant potential emerged to leverage
data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance operational
excellence in underwriting, pricing, and claims management.
AXA’s strong market position enabled it to navigate this challenging
environment and drive strong growth, particularly in the first year
of executing its 2024-2026 strategic plan, “Unlock the Future”.
■ Driving profitable organic growth: (i) P&C Commercial lines
experienced robust revenue growth, with premiums increasing by
+6% to EUR 34.9 billion. (ii) In Personal lines, premiums rose by 7%,
reflecting disciplined pricing actions, notably in the UK and Germany.
(iii) Short-term Life & Health premiums reached EUR 16 billion with
continued margin expansion. In the UK, we made significant progress
in claims pathway management to help customers find the right care.
Laya, a leader in the Irish health market, was successfully integrated
into the Group and met its 2024 business objectives. (iv) Our highquality L&S portfolio demonstrated strong growth dynamics in UnitLinked following successful sales campaigns;

■ Expanding AXA’s social role: (i) Our inclusive insurance unit, AXA
EssentiALL, is addressing the significant protection gap for low-tomiddle-income households and small businesses in emerging markets,
expanding its geographical reach into European markets. In 2024, we
launched a pan-European flagship product for microentrepreneurs
and tailored offers for the retail segment. (ii) The Group continues to
set targets to reduce carbon emissions and maintain its commitment
to climate transition.
We remain focused on simplifying our business profile and
strengthening our positions in core markets: (i) The acquisition of
Nobis (pending regulatory approval) is expected to enhance our position
in the Italian P&C market, adding scale and diversified distribution
capabilities. (ii) Partnering with the Spanish postal service, Correos,
should extend our reach to new customers. (iii) The sale of AXA
Investment Managers (AXA IM) to BNP Paribas aligns with our strategy to
focus on our core insurance business. As part of this planned transaction,
AXA and BNP Paribas would establish a long-term strategic partnership,
providing AXA a broader range of products and strategies.
In 2025, AXA intends to maintain its focus on executing its “Unlock
the Future” strategic plan. In P&C, we aim to deliver disciplined growth
and better customer retention while benefiting from the earn-through
of higher pricing. In Life & Health, we intend to sustain the growth
momentum in short-term business, particularly Employee Benefits, and
focus on improving net flows in our savings business.
As we pursue profitable organic growth, we will continue to scale
technical excellence and drive operational improvements across the
Group, including through the deployment of technology and AI. We
expect to remain on track to meet the key financial targets outlined in
AXA’s strategic plan.

■ Boosting technical excellence: (i) Our P&C combined ratio improved
to 91.0%, reflecting underwriting measures taken in the UK & Ireland
and Germany in response to higher frequency in Motor in 2023, and
continued improvement in Commercial lines. (ii) We continued to
enhance technical excellence in Health by leveraging proprietary assets
for pricing and claims management;
■ Enhancing operational excellence: (i) AXA’s offshore locations in
India, Poland, and Morocco saw continuous growth, increasing the
share of high-value services in technology, data, AI, and industrial
automation. (ii) We scaled over 17 high-value data and AI use cases
across entities, in addition to our disciplined execution of automation
initiatives that continue to yield benefits as planned. (iii) The number
of generative AI use cases increased throughout 2024 in alignment with
our strategic objectives; and

The AXA Group
1.2 Business overview

1.2

Business overview

AXA operates in five hubs (France, Europe, AXA XL, Asia, Africa &
EME‑LATAM, and AXA IM) and offers a broad range of Property &
Casualty, Life & Health, and Asset Management products and
expertise. AXA and its subsidiaries have established branches
across various jurisdictions to support their operations. For
additional information on the Group’s main subsidiaries, see
Note 2 of Chapter 6.6.
The nature and level of competition vary among the countries
where AXA operates. AXA competes with insurance companies
along with banks, asset management companies, investment
advisors and other financial institutions.
The principal competitive factors are as follows:
●

size, strength and quality of the distribution channels, in
particular the quality of advisors;

range of product lines and product quality, feature
functionality and innovation;

●

●

price;

●

quality of service;

●

investment management performance;
historical level of bonuses with respect to participating
contracts;

●

●

crediting rates on General Account products;

●

reputation, visibility and recognition of brand; and

●

ratings for financial strength and claims‑paying ability.

For additional information on markets, see Section 2.2 “Market
environment - Market conditions” of this Document.

1.2.1 France
1.2.1.1

Products and services

AXA offers in France a full range of insurance products,
including Property & Casualty, and Life & Health. Its offering
covers a broad range of products including Motor, Household,
Property and general liability insurance, Banking, savings, and
other investment‑based products for both Retail/Individual and
Commercial/Group customers, as well as Health, Protection,
and retirement products for individual and professional
customers.
In addition, leveraging on its product and distribution
expertise, AXA France has developed an Employee Benefit offer
internationally to individuals, corporates, and other
institutions.

1.2.1.2

New product initiatives

In Life & Health, AXA France has expanded its financial offering
in the context of the Green Industry Law and its product
offering in the context of the Shared Value Law. AXA France has
consequently renewed its offers of Mandate Management
(Wealth Management), Managed Investments (for the general
public), and Horizon Management (Retirement Savings
Enterprise products). In these latter offerings, three non‑listed
assets funds (financing of the real economy and environmental
and social transitions) are now available, including private
debt, a new asset class, since 2024. Simultaneously, AXA France
has reaffirmed its commitment to society and its clients (e.g.,
strengthening of guarantees and financial education services)
while continuing its innovation in structured products. This
commitment is also evident in the Protection sector with the
launch of the “Family Assistance” guarantee, included for all
new subscriptions.

the claims management process to better support our

add‑on to our MPPI products in France.

Products and services

●

●

insurance, with a broad range of coverages, including

1.2.4 Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM
The Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM market includes AXA’s operations
in more than 15 countries, notably in Japan, Hong Kong, China,
Thailand, Indonesia, Mexico, Colombia, Türkiye, and Morocco.
Asia includes (i) the subsidiaries in Japan, Hong Kong, China
(AXA Tianping), and South Korea which are fully consolidated,
(ii) the Property & Casualty entity in Thailand, and the
non‑bancassurance Life & Health entity in Indonesia which are
fully consolidated, as well as (iii) the joint ventures in China
(Life & Health), Philippines (Property & Casualty and Life &
Health), Thailand (Life & Health), and Indonesia (Life & Health)
which are consolidated under the equity method and do not
contribute to Gross Written Premiums and Other Revenues.
Africa & EME‑LATAM includes (i) Mexico, Colombia, Brazil,
Türkiye, Morocco, Egypt and Nigeria which are fully
consolidated, combined with (ii) Russia (Reso) that is
consolidated under the equity method and does not contribute
to Gross Written Premiums and Other Revenues.
Further details on the scope of market activities are defined in
the Glossary set forth in Appendix IV of this Document.

1.4 Dividends and dividend policy

1.4

Dividends and dividend policy

The Company pays dividends in Euro.
AXA’s dividend policy is based on Underlying Earnings Per
Share. AXA targets, in line with its “Unlock the Future” strategic
plan announced on February 22, 2024, to (i) pay a dividend per
share of 60% of the Group’s Underlying Earnings Per Share, and
(ii) adhere to a dividend per share floor whereby the proposed
dividend per share in any given year is targeted to be at least
equal to the dividend per share paid in the prior year (subject
to the absence of a significant capital event, i.e. an event which
significantly deteriorates the Group’s solvency). The Board of
Directors has full discretion to determine the dividend to be
proposed at the applicable Shareholders’ Meeting, taking into

account a variety of factors, including AXA’s earnings, financial
condition, applicable capital and solvency requirements,
prevailing operating and financial market conditions and the
general economic environment.
A dividend of €2.15 per share for the 2024 fiscal year will be
proposed to the Shareholders’ Meeting to be held on April 24,
2025.
The Company’s dividend policy is part of a wider capital
management policy which targets an aggregate payout ratio
(based on dividend payouts and share buy‑backs) of 75% of the
Group’s Underlying Earnings Per Share (see Section 2.4.5 Group capital management objectives of this Document).

1.5 Ratings

The Group is rated by recognized rating agencies which assess
the financial strength and the creditworthiness of the Company
and certain of its insurance subsidiaries. The ratings set forth
below are subject to revision or withdrawal at any time by the
assigning rating agency in its sole discretion. Credit ratings are
intended to reflect the ability of AXA to meet its payment
obligations and may not reflect the potential impact of all risks
on the value of AXA’s securities. A rating is not a
recommendation to buy, sell or hold securities. None of these
ratings should be construed as an indication or forecast of the

historical or potential performance of AXA’s securities nor
should any such rating be relied upon for the purpose of
making an investment decision with respect to any of the
Company’s securities. The Company does not undertake to
maintain its ratings, nor publish press releases relating
specifically to its ratings, and in no event shall the Company be
responsible for the accuracy or reliability of any of the ratings
set forth below. The significance and the meaning of individual
ratings vary from agency to agency.

including the corresponding share buyback, was expected to
have a ca. -1 point impact on AXA Group’s Solvency II ratio (10).

Activity Report and Capital Management
2.1 Operating highlights

AXA entered into an exclusive negotiation to
sell AXA Investment Managers to BNP Paribas
On August 1, 2024, AXA announced that it had entered into an
exclusive negotiation to sell its asset manager AXA Investment
Managers (“AXA IM”) to BNP Paribas for cash proceeds (1) of
€5.1 billion. In addition, AXA would receive €0.3 billion
consideration from the sale of Select (2) to AXA IM prior to the
closing of the proposed transaction. The total estimated
transaction value was expected to be €5.4 billion, representing
a multiple of 15x 2023 earnings. Under the terms of the
proposed transaction, AXA and BNP Paribas would also enter
into a long‑term strategic partnership under which BNP Paribas
would provide investment management services to AXA. The
combination of AXA Investment Managers and BNP Paribas
would create a leading European asset manager, with total
assets under management of €1.5 trillion (3).
Following the completion of the information‑consultation
procedure with the employee representative bodies of both
AXA and BNP Paribas, AXA announced on December 21, 2024,
that it had entered into a Share Purchase Agreement with BNP
Paribas in relation to the transaction. The completion of the
transaction is subject to customary closing conditions,
including the receipt of regulatory approvals, and is expected
to take place around the end of the second quarter of 2025.
In FY24, AXA IM has been classified as “discontinued
operations” in AXA’s Consolidated Financial Statements and
AXA will continue to account for the contribution of AXA IM to
the Group’s Underlying Earnings until the expected completion
of the sale. Upon completion, the transaction is expected to
result in (i) a reduction in Underlying Earnings of ca. €0.4 billion
on an annualized basis for the Group and (ii) an estimated
one‑off Net income gain of €2.2 billion. AXA intends to offset

the earnings dilution from the transaction with a share buyback
of €3.8 billion, to be launched following the closing of the
transaction. The transaction and the associated share buyback
are expected to have a neutral impact on AXA’s Solvency II ratio.
The transaction is expected to have no material impact on the
key financial targets (4) that were communicated as part of the
“Unlock the Future” plan.

AXA expands its Retail P&C operations in Italy
with the acquisition of Nobis Group
On August 1, 2024, AXA announced that it had entered into an
agreement to acquire Gruppo Nobis (“Nobis”). Nobis is a
predominantly Retail P&C insurance company in Italy,
benefiting from a well‑diversified distribution network, that
includes multi‑tied agents and car dealer partnerships. Nobis
reported (5) €0.5 billion of gross written premiums and net
income of €35 million in 2023. Under the terms of the
transaction, the upfront consideration for the acquisition would
amount to €423 million, with a potential earn‑out (6) of up to
€55 million. Based on the full consideration, the
price‑to‑earnings multiple was ca. 11x, including expected
synergies. Upon closing, the transaction was expected to result
in an impact of -1 point on AXA Group’s Solvency II ratio. The
acquisition would further diversify AXA’s distribution channels,
particularly through long‑term agreements with car dealerships
within the Nobis network, supporting profitable growth. By
leveraging Nobis’ network and expertise, AXA Italy expected to
improve its market position in P&C from #5 to #4, gaining
ca. 1 point of market share.
The completion of the transaction is subject to customary
closing conditions, including the receipt of regulatory
approvals, and is expected to take place before the end of the
first half of 2025.

2.1.3 Capital/debt operations
AXA announced the successful placement
of €1.5 billion Restricted Tier 1 Notes
On January 10, 2024, AXA announced that it had successfully
completed the placement of €1.5 billion of Reg S perpetual
deeply subordinated notes (the “Notes”) with institutional
investors. The Notes qualify as Restricted Tier 1 capital under
Solvency II. Investor demand for the issuance was strong with a
book subscribed more than 5 times.
The initial fixed rate was set at 6.375% per annum until the end
of a 6‑month call window period (ending on January 16, 2034),
when the interest rate will reset every five years thereafter at the
prevailing Euro 5‑year Mid Swap rate plus a margin of
384.1 basis points. In line with the Solvency II requirements, the
Notes feature a loss absorption mechanism in the form of a
write‑down (1) of the nominal amount of the Notes if one of the
solvency‑related triggers (2) is breached (3). Interest payments
are at the full discretion of AXA unless they are mandatorily
prohibited.
The Notes were rated BBB+ by Standard & Poor’s and
Baa1(hyb) by Moody’s. They are eligible to be treated as capital
from a regulatory and rating agencies’ perspective within
applicable limits.
This issuance was part of AXA Group’s funding plan for 2024
and the proceeds were to be used for general corporate
purposes, including the refinancing of part of AXA Group’s
outstanding debt.
The settlement of the Notes took place on January 16, 2024.

Despite ongoing geopolitical uncertainty, global equity markets
continued to benefit from strong momentum in 2024,
supported by strong corporate earnings, decreasing inflation
and loosening of monetary policies, although the performance
was uneven across geographies.
The MSCI global equity index posted another strong year of
gains with an increase of 17%, following a 22% increase in the
previous year.
In the United States, the S&P 500 index witnessed another
strong year posting a growth of 23%. The year saw some sector
rotation, but technology stocks continued to perform strongly.
Moreover, the appreciation was broadly even across the year
and further gains occurred after the presidential elections.

2.2.1.2

In Europe, markets rose in early 2024, but flatlined from Q2 as
economic growth slowed down. The Eurostoxx 50 index posted
gains of just 8% over the year compared to a 19% in 2023. In
France, the CAC 40 underperformed other markets as stocks
suffered from the political and fiscal uncertainty following the
mid‑year elections. The French index fell by 2% by end of 2024
compared to the 17% gain in 2023. In the United Kingdom, the
FTSE 100 index rose by 6% compared to a 4% in 2023 following
the election of the new Labour government which introduced a
new budget marked by fiscal loosening.
In Asia, Japan’s stock markets posted gains of 19% across 2024
boosted by the sharp depreciation of the Yen, which increased
overseas sales and earnings.

2.2 Market environment

Bond markets have had different yield evolutions over 2024
across the United States, Europe, and Asia.
In the United States, yields dipped to a low of 3.62% following a
50 bps rate cut in September. However, the combination of a
stronger economy, inflation and the results of November’s
presidential elections saw yields rise, finishing the year at
4.57%.
In Europe, German yields softened in early H2 2024, reflecting
an economic contraction. However, this was reversed later in
the year as a result of political uncertainty, finishing the year at
2.37% up 34 bps. This occurred despite the expectations of an
accelerated monetary policy easing by the European Central
Bank. French OAT yields rose by 64 bps to 3.20% in response to

2.2.1.3

political and fiscal uncertainty, while Italian BTP yields fell by
18 bps to 3.52%. The UK gilt yields rose by 103 bps to 4.57% by
year‑end due to fiscal uncertainty.
In Japan, increasing confidence that the country has overcome
its deflationary battle saw the Bank of Japan raise the policy
rate and signal further tightening ahead. Hence, the Japanese
10‑year rose by 49 bps, finishing the year at 1.10%.
Corporate spreads continued to tighten through 2024 across
jurisdictions. In the United States, spreads have continued to
narrow to their tightest levels since 2007, below post‑pandemic
levels. European credit spreads have also narrowed sharply
following a significant correction last year.

The US Dollar had been relatively steady against a basket of
currencies through most of 2024. However, starting at the end
of September, it posted significant gains against most
currencies thanks to a combination of a resilient economic
momentum, a revision of interest rate expectations and the
presidential elections.
The Euro came under pressure as weaker growth and fading
inflation allowed the ECB to ease policy at a faster pace. The

Euro fell by 6% and closed 2024 at USD 1.04. It also fell by 5%
against the British Pound Sterling (to GBB 0.83), which
remained supported by expectations of reduced monetary
loosening from the Bank of England. However, it gained 4%
against the Japanese Yen (to JPY 163), which remained weak
given expectations of only limited rate hikes from the Bank of
Japan.

2.2 Market environment

2.2.2 Market Conditions
2.2.2.1

Insurance activities

Main developed markets
In France, the savings insurance market was up by 14%
compared to the previous year, with premiums reaching
€173 billion. This growth was fueled by a positive trend in both
Unit‑Linked (+8%) and General Account (+17%) products. The
share of Unit‑Linked products slightly decreased compared to
the previous year, standing at +38% (40% in 2023). In a context
of economic, fiscal and political uncertainty as well as a
stagnant real estate market, the saving ratio increased,
supporting net flows in the Life insurance market. The level of
surrenders decreased compared to the previous year in General
Account funds, despite the “Livret A” rate being maintained at
3%, partially offset by an increase in Unit‑Linked surrenders.
The Protection and complementary Health insurance market
witnessed medical inflation that the market partly absorbed
through an average tariff increase of 8% in 2024. The rising cost
and frequency of claims have both been accentuated. In
addition, political uncertainty around the budget for the French
welfare system (the Sécurité Sociale) led some insurers to
foresee that the decrease in the share of medical expenses
reimbursed by the Sécurité Sociale would result in further tariff
increases. In 2024, the Property & Casualty market witnessed an
increase in claims in the Motor business notably due to driver
behavior as well as repair costs. Several natural catastrophes
marked the year, such as overseas cyclones Belal (c.
€0.1 billion) and Chido (c. €0.65 - €0.8 billion), as well as
numerous floods (c. €0.35 - €0.42 billion), including those
resulting from the Kirk depression.
In Europe (excluding France), Property & Casualty insurance
markets faced economic challenges such as rising repair costs
supported by persistent but moderating inflation along with
evolving risks such as climate change. Insurance markets have
been impacted by less severe but multiple weather events
mainly from hailstorms and floods across most geographies.
Insurers are responding by implementing pricing measures and
reshaping product offerings as well as risk management
practices. In Life & Savings, European markets are recovering
from last year’s challenging macroeconomic environment but
are still affected by modest growth as well as economic and
political uncertainties. In Health, European private insurers are
facing an ageing population, claims cost inflation and strains

30

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

on national healthcare systems, leading to the implementation
of progressive price increases. In the meantime, private health
insurance providers are focusing on digital transformation,
including care pathway management and developing wellness
benefits to meet changing consumer expectations.
In Japan, the Life insurance market grew by 5% in terms of
gross written premium, mainly from strong sales of traditional
GA savings products as policyholders benefited from higher
guarantees being offered as a result of the increase in interest
rates in Japan. The net income of major insurers was driven by
a better investment income from a favorable Japanese equity
market performance. The Property & Casualty insurance
market improved by 3% in terms of gross written
premiums, driven by price increases in Motor and Fire
insurance.
In Hong Kong, Life gross written premiums increased by
8%. New business recorded significant growth of 16% derived
from non‑Linked individual business. New business from
Mainland China Visitors slightly decreased compared with 2023,
representing 28% of total Individual business. The Property &
Casualty insurance market remained stable.
The United States Property insurance market rates have
risen, although at a slower pace in 2024, with strict
underwriting across capacity deployment, risk selection, and
terms and conditions. However, the increased frequency of Nat
Cat events, particularly secondary perils, along with rising
reinsurance costs and economic inflation that drove up
construction costs, have adversely impacted the market.
Overall, the United States Casualty insurance market
continues to experience rate increases due to loss trends.
However, elevated casualty claims due to social inflation have
impacted underwriting margins and reserves.
The Reinsurance market remains well‑capitalized, with
companies successfully raising capital to support growth
initiatives. The property reinsurance market has experienced
increased rates and attachment points, resulting in improved
margins. The realignment of property catastrophe risk has
allowed reinsurers to limit their losses despite active weather
patterns. Strong underwriting performance along with
improved Investment returns have helped mitigate adverse
prior year reserves development reported in US casualty
business.

2.2 Market environment

Main emerging markets

In Other Emerging Markets:

In Asia Emerging Markets, the Property & Casualty insurance
markets benefited from growth across most geographies. The
market grew notably thanks to Motor business in China and the
Philippines, as well as Property in Thailand and the Philippines.
The Life insurance market continues showing good trends. In
Thailand, new business volumes grew by 3% driven by higher
sales of G/A Saving products benefiting from higher yields.
Philippines volumes grew by 16% mainly driven by single
premium products sales in main channels. China observed the
continued expansion of Health. Life insurance markets
continued to mature, shifting away from pricing wars to focus
on customer needs with rapid development of participating
products, while governments and regulatory authorities have
also issued a series of policies to guide market players into
reducing costs and increasing efficiency. Indonesia observed
low persistency in Unit‑Linked products, partially offset by the
launch of new Endowment and Protection products.

●

●

●

the Mexican insurance market saw 18% growth, where
Property & Casualty benefited from market‑wide price
increases in Motor to mitigate inflation. Life insurance
growth was driven by sales of Unit‑Linked products while
Health insurance growth was mainly driven by price
increases;
in Türkiye, the Property & Casualty market grew by 67%,
mainly driven by high 44% inflation. Excluding inflation, the
growth was mainly linked to higher volumes in the Motor
business. The Health segment grew by 97% driven by
significant price increases driven by strong inflation as well
as higher volumes following increased awareness; and
the Colombian insurance market grew by 8%, primarily from
mandatory accident insurance in P&C Protection business,
Individual Life insurance, and Workers’ Compensation,
despite a slowdown of the banking sector, partly offset by
the Motor business due to lower new car sales.

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

Activity Report and Capital Management
2.2 Market environment

2.2.2.2

Asset Management activities

In 2024, after battling inflation for two years, major central
banks began lowering interest rates. Although inflation was still
above target, the expectation of lower rates boosted equity
markets and attracted more investment in equity ETFs. Growing
excitement around artificial intelligence also contributed to this
success, with the S&P 500 rising 23% by the end of the year.
However, confidence in significant rate cuts from the US
Federal Reserve decreased due to resilient growth and sticky
inflation. Meanwhile, the European Central Bank’s lower rate
strategy remained steady, resulting in strong investments in
euro credit. This positive economic environment and
moderating inflation also boosted interest in high yield
investments. The credit asset class performed well too, with
most sectors yielding better returns than government bonds.
High yield credit was particularly strong, achieving over 8%
returns in both US dollar and Euro markets.

Private debt remains a notable alternative strategy within the
alternative assets sphere, continuing to provide appealing
returns for investors. Conversely, the real estate and
infrastructure markets continued to experience value
adjustments during the first half of 2024 – in line with their
usual valuation lag; however, the more accommodative central
bank policy allowed for values to stabilize in the second half of
the year.

Property & Casualty gross written premiums were up 7%
(or €+3,511 million) on a comparable basis to
€56,514 million:
●

●

●

Commercial lines grew by 6% (or €+2,029 million) primarily
driven by (i) AXA XL Insurance (+5%) mainly from strong
price increases across all lines except US Professional and
Cyber, along with volume growth and strong retention
mostly driven by Property, Casualty as well as the renewal of
a multi‑year fronting deal, (ii) Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM
(+24%) mainly driven by Türkiye mostly from higher average
premiums in Property and Motor in a hyperinflationary
context, along with favorable volume and price effects most
notably in Mexico and Brazil, (iii) Europe (+4%) from price
increases in all lines of business, and (iv) France (+4%)
reflecting price increases, notably in Property and Motor;
Personal lines grew by 7% (or €+1,246 million) driven by
(i) Motor (+6%), in particular in France (+14%) from strong
price increases combined with new business growth, in Asia,
Africa & EME‑LATAM (+9%) mainly driven by Türkiye mostly
from higher average premiums in a hyperinflationary
context, along with favourable volume effects, and by
Mexico, and in Europe (+3%) driven by strong price effects,
partly offset by lower volumes and a change in business mix,
reflecting measures to restore profitability in United
Kingdom & Ireland as well as in Germany, (ii) Non‑Motor
(+8%) primarily in Europe (+6%) mostly in Germany, United
Kingdom & Ireland and Spain from strong price increases,
partly offset by lower volumes with a focus on profitability,
in France (+7%) stemming from price increases as well as
business growth, and in Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM (+25%)
notably in Colombia from higher volumes and price effects
in Compulsory accident insurance, and Türkiye from higher
average premiums in Property;
AXA XL Reinsurance increased by 10% (or €+235 million)
driven by volume increases especially in Property and
Specialty combined with price increases in Property and in
Casualty.

Life & Health gross written premiums were up 8%
(or €+4,089 million) on a comparable basis to
€51,983 million.

€+2,797 million) on a comparable basis to €34,497 million:
●

●

●

‑
(i) Europe (+26%) primarily from the launch of a new
product in Italy, as well as (ii) France (+12%) from successful
commercial campaigns in Individual savings;
General Account savings increased by 12% (or €
+1,115 million) mainly driven by (i) Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM
(+92%) reflecting elevated sales of a capital‑light Single
Premium Whole Life product in Japan, and (ii) Europe
(+12%) notably from the successful launch of capital‑light
products in Italy and Belgium;
Protection grew by 3% (or €+450 million) mainly driven by
(i) Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM (+5%) from continued growth in
Japan, and (ii) Europe (+2%) mainly from Switzerland, with
a higher share of Protection with Unit‑Linked business.

Health gross written premiums were up 8% (or
€+1,292 million) on a comparable basis to €17,486 million:
●

●

Group business increased by 11% (or €+815 million), driven
by strong price increases and higher volumes mostly in
France (+13%), in Asia, Africa & EME‑LATAM (+21%) mainly in
Mexico and Hong Kong, and in Europe (+8%) notably in
United Kingdom & Ireland;
Individual business grew by 5% (or €+476 million),
primarily from price increases, driven by Asia, Africa &
EME‑LATAM (+10%) mostly in Mexico and Türkiye, and in
France (+14%).

on a comparable basis to €1,701 million mainly driven by
higher management fees (€+89 million) from higher Average
Assets under Management and higher performance fees (€
+12 million).
Average Assets under Management increased by 3% (or
€+24 billion) on a comparable basis to €759 billion mainly
driven by favorable market effects, combined with business
growth in AXA IM Alts.
Banking revenues increased by 26% (or €+25 million) on a
comparable basis to €118 million mainly due to improvement
of funding costs in the context of interest rates decrease.

business mix in France.

2.3.3 Alternative Performance Measures
Underlying Earnings, Underlying Earnings Per Share, Combined
Ratio, Underlying Return On Equity and Debt Gearing are
Alternative Performance Measures (“APMs”) as defined in
ESMA’s guidelines and the AMF’s related position statement
issued in 2015. A reconciliation from Underlying Earnings and
Combined Ratio to the most directly reconcilable line item,
subtotal, or total in the Consolidated Financial Statements of

the corresponding period is provided in the above tables.
Underlying Return On Equity and Underlying Earnings Per
Share are reconciled to the Consolidated Financial Statements
in the table set forth on Section 2.3.7 “Shareholder value” of
this document. For further information on any of the
above‑mentioned APMs, please see the definitions and the
Glossary on Appendix IV of this document.

Activity Report and Capital Management
2.4 Liquidity and capital resources

2.4

Liquidity and capital resources

Information in this section should be read in conjunction with
Note 4 “Financial and insurance Risk Management” in Chapter 6
“Consolidated Financial Statements” of this Document.
Liquidity management is a core part of the Group’s financial
planning and includes the management of our debt and the
maturities of our debt instruments and, more generally, the
Group’s capital allocation strategy. Our liquidity resources mainly
come from our insurance and asset management operations,
capital‑raising activities and committed bank credit facilities.

Over the past several years, the Group has expanded its core
operations through organic growth, direct investments, and
acquisitions. This expansion has been funded primarily through (i)
dividends from operating subsidiaries, (ii) proceeds from debt
instruments and intra‑group borrowings, (iii) issuance of shares,
and (iv) proceeds from the sale of non‑core businesses and assets.
The liquidity and financing needs of the Group must be managed
in compliance with regulatory constraints, including minimum
solvency ratios.

2.4.1 Liquidity sources and needs for Group operating entities
Each major operating subsidiary of the Group is responsible for
managing its own liquidity position in coordination with the
Company, which, as the holding company, coordinates funding
and liquidity management, and participates in financing the
operations of certain of its subsidiaries. The principal sources of
liquidity for the Group’s (re)insurance subsidiaries and the
Company’s reinsurance activities are premiums, investment
income, and proceeds from sales of invested assets. These funds
are mainly used to pay policyholder benefits, claims, policy
surrenders and operating expenses, purchase financial assets, and
meet potential collateral obligations related to derivatives. The
liquidity of the Group’s insurance operations is affected by the
quality of its investments and its ability to timely liquidate financial
assets to meet policyholder benefits and claims. The Group
regularly reviews asset quality to ensure adequate liquidity in
stress scenarios.
Information on projected payments and surrenders related to Life
& Health and Property & Casualty insurance contracts is disclosed
in Note 12.1.9 “Liquidity risk arising from contracts within the
scope of IFRS 17” in Chapter 6 of the Consolidated financial
statements in this Document.
Information in this section should be read in conjunction with the
Chapters 5.1.1.1 “Market‑related risks”, 5.1.2.1 “Insurance and
reinsurance pricing and underwriting‑related risks”, and 5.1.2.2
“Operational risks” in Chapter 5.1 “Risk factors” of this Document.

2.4.1.1

Property & Casualty
(including reinsurance)

Liquidity needs of Property & Casualty activities can be affected
by actual claims experience. These insurance activities' net
cash flows are generally positive but can be negative in the
event of exceptional losses or poor portfolio profitability. A
portion of these cash flows is invested in liquid, short‑term
bonds and other listed securities to manage liquidity risk.

2.4.1.2

Life & Health

Liquidity needs of Life & Health activities can be affected by
fluctuations in surrenders, withdrawals, maturities, and
guarantees to policyholders.
AXA’s Life & Health subsidiaries design their investment strategy
to match the return and maturity profile of their investments
with expected cash flows from insurance contracts. Entities
regularly monitor the valuation, duration, and performance of
their financial assets. Financial market performance can affect
surrenders and withdrawals on life insurance policies and
actual and projected cash needs. Group entities adjust their
investment portfolios accordingly.

2.4.1.3

Asset Management

The principal sources of liquidity for AXA’s Asset Management
subsidiaries are operating cash flows, repurchase agreements,
borrowings from credit institutions, and drawings on credit
facilities.
The financing needs of Asset Management subsidiaries arise
principally from their activities, requiring working capital to
constitute seed money for new funds at AXA IM (1).

(1) On December 21, 2024, AXA announced that it has entered into a Share Purchase Agreement with BNP Paribas Cardif for the sale of AXA IM.

2.4 Liquidity and capital resources

2.4.2 Liquidity position
In 2024, AXA continued to follow a prudent approach to
managing its liquidity risk. At year‑end 2024, the Group had:
●

●

●

a significant cash position across all business lines, with
cash and cash equivalents of €18.1 billion, net of bank
overdrafts of €0.9 billion;
broad access to various markets via standardized debt
programs, including a maximum capacity of €6.0 billion of
French Negotiable European Commercial Paper, $2.0 billion
of US commercial paper, €20.0 billion under a Euro Medium
Term Note program (with €17.3 billion already issued), and
€1.5 billion of French Negotiable European Medium Term
Notes;
a debt profile characterized by mostly subordinated debt
with a long maturity profile. In 2024, AXA SA reimbursed
€0.1 billion of debt (net of issuances), resulting in
consolidated debt of €19.2 billion at year‑end. Debt
gearing (1) increased by 0.2 points to 20.6% at year‑end 2024,
(compared to 20.3% at year‑end 2023), driven by other
comprehensive income (OCI) decrease due to decrease in
swap rates and government bond spreads widening.

AXA has a robust liquidity Risk Management framework,
reviewed regularly through quarterly monitoring of liquidity
and solvency requirements in stressed scenarios at both local
and Group levels. For additional information, refer to Chapter
5.2 “Internal control and Risk Management - Consolidated
Financial Statements” (2) and Chapter 5.5 “Liquidity risk” (3) of
this Document.
In 2024, the Liquidity Risk Management framework has been
reshaped to take into account the resilience to several stress
scenarios, with time horizons ranging from 1 week to 12
months, including an extreme short‑term scenario, whereby
entities must ensure they can sustain a very quick and severe
financial stress on collateral needs arising from derivatives and
repo transactions. Each major operating subsidiary of the
Group is responsible for monitoring short term liquidity risk,

leveraging on a weekly Liquidity dashboard, detailing available
eligible collateral before and after the extreme scenario. Excess
of liquidity can then be monetized by implementing term
lending transactions, generating additional investment income.
At year‑end 2024, Group entities held more than €181 billion of
government and related bonds, including €103 billion issued by
diverse Eurozone countries, to address local liquidity needs
through highly liquid assets. AXA SA maintained liquid
resources consisting of cash, money market instruments, highly
liquid fixed income investments, and a portfolio of investments
backing its statutory reinsurance liabilities. AXA SA also
maintained available credit facilities of €7.9 billion at year‑end
2024. Its liquidity requirements primarily arise from solvency
needs of entities under severe stress scenarios, its central
reinsurance activities, the remuneration of its shareholders and
its portfolio of collateralized derivatives.
For additional information on the currencies in which our cash
and cash equivalents are held, refer to Chapter “5.3.3.2
Exchange‑rate risk related to the operating activities of group
subsidiaries” of this Document. For information on borrowings,
refer to Note 11.1.1, Note 15, and Note 16.2 in Chapter 6
“Consolidated Financial Statements” of this Document.
For additional information on the use of financial instruments for
hedging purposes, refer to Note 18 “Derivative instruments” in
Chapter 6 “Consolidated Financial Statements” of this
Document.
As part of its risk control framework, the Company is vigilant
regarding contractual provisions that may give lenders,
securityholders or other counterparties the right to accelerate
repayment, demand collateral or seek other similar remedies
under circumstances that could have a material adverse effect
on the Group’s consolidated financial position. At year‑end
2024, AXA had no rating triggers and no financial covenants in
its credit facilities.

2.4 Liquidity and capital resources

2.4.4 Impact of regulatory requirements
The Group’s operations are subject to a wide variety of
(re)insurance and other laws and regulations in the
jurisdictions in which it operates, including regulatory capital
and solvency requirements.
For additional information, refer to Chapter 7.3 “Regulation and
Supervision” (1) of this Document.

2.4.4.1

Regulatory capital requirements

The Group’s operating (re)insurance entities (including AXA SA
as a reinsurance company) are subject to local regulatory
capital requirements designed to protect policyholders and
monitor capital adequacy.
If the Group or any of its (re)insurance entities fail to meet
minimum regulatory capital requirements, regulators would
have broad authority to take various actions. Such a failure or
severe deterioration of solvency may necessitate to inject
significant new capital in the relevant Group's entities, which
could adversely affect the Group’s liquidity. For additional
information, refer to “The Group’s or its insurance or
reinsurance entities’ failure to meet their solvency and capital
adequacy requirements” in Chapter 5.1 “Risk Factors” of this
Document.
The Group and AXA SA maintained Eligible Own Funds in
excess of their Solvency Capital Requirement (“SCR”) at all
times during 2024 and monitor compliance with this
requirement continuously.
If the Group’s Solvency II ratio were to deteriorate excessively,
the AXA Group may take measures to improve it, such as being
more selective on growth initiatives, increasing reinsurance,
reducing its investment risk appetite or reducing its dividend.
AXA’s approach is to maintain its Group Solvency II ratio above
the risk appetite limit of 140%.

2.4.4.2

Tiering analysis of capital

Solvency II Eligible Own Funds relate to the Group’s and AXA
SA’s (on a solo basis) available capital resources before tiering
eligibility restrictions and after considering the potential
non‑availability of certain capital elements.
Eligible Own Funds are split into three tiers as defined under
Solvency II regulations. The classification depends upon the
extent to which the own fund item is immediately available to
absorb losses including in case of a winding‑up (permanent
availability) and subordinated to all other obligations including
towards policyholders and beneficiaries. The highest‑quality
capital elements are classified in Tier 1. Eligibility limits apply to
these components to cover the Group’s and AXA SA’s (on a solo
basis) SCR.
For compliance with the SCR, the following quantitative limits
apply: (a) the eligible amount of Tier 1 items must be at least
50% of the SCR, (b) the eligible amount of Tier 3 items must not
exceed 15% of the SCR, and (c) the sum of the eligible amounts
of Tier 2 and Tier 3 items must not exceed 50% of the SCR.
Hybrid debt instruments eligible for Tier 1 must not exceed 20%
of the total Tier 1 capital.

2.4.4.3

Dated and undated subordinated
debt description

Dated and undated subordinated notes issued by the Company
qualify as Eligible Own Funds.
Subordinated notes issued by the Company since January 18,
2015, are structured to be eligible as own funds under
Solvency II regulations. Subordinated notes issued before
January 17, 2015, mostly benefit from transitional provisions in
Directive 2014/51/EU (Omnibus II), as they were eligible under
the Solvency I regime and issued prior to the entry into force of
Delegated Regulation EU 2015/35 of October 10, 2014. Such
transitional provisions are ending on January 1, 2026.
The Company has issued dated subordinated notes (“TSR”),
undated subordinated notes (“TSDI”), and undated deeply
subordinated notes (“TSS”), which include provisions designed
to allow the Company to ensure continuity of activities if its
financial position deteriorates.

2.4 Liquidity and capital resources

Certain TSR include clauses that permit or force the Company
to defer interest payments. Additionally, redemption at
maturity requires (i) prior approval by the ACPR and (ii) the
absence of any event (a) causing the Company’s and/or the
Group’s own funds to be below regulatory capital
requirements, (b) triggering a requirement for the Company to
take specific action regarding payments under the notes due to
its financial condition, or (c) having an adverse effect on its
insurance subsidiaries’ ability to pay claims.

Under its TSS issued under the Solvency II regime, the
Company is required to cancel interest payments in certain
circumstances, including when the Company and/or the Group
does not meet (or would not meet, as a result of making such
payment) its regulatory capital requirement, or when the
Company distributable items are insufficient, as defined under
the terms and conditions of such TSS. Furthermore, the
Company has full discretion to cancel payment of interest in
respect of such TSS.

Under the terms and conditions of AXA’s TSDI, the Company
may, and in certain circumstances must, defer interest
payment. Deferred interest payment may become due in
specified cases (e.g., payment of a dividend, end of a regulatory
demand to restore solvency, liquidation of the Company, or
redemption of the TSDI).

2.4.4.4

Most of the Company’s TSS and all TSS issued under the
Solvency II regime (Restricted Tier 1) include loss absorption
mechanisms which provide that under certain circumstances
where the Company and/or the Group does not meet its
regulatory capital requirements, the principal amount of each
of the relevant TSS will be written down. In such event, interest
will become payable on the reduced principal amount only.
The principal may be reinstated when the Company and/or the
Group returns to financial health, as defined under the terms
and conditions of the TSS.
For most of the Company’s TSS issued under the Solvency I
regime, the Company is required to defer interest payments
upon certain events related to consolidated net earnings and
shareholders’ equity.
Under its TSS issued under the Solvency I regime, the Company
can cancel interest payments upon the deterioration of its
financial position, unless certain events occurred in the
preceding year, such as a dividend payment, interest payment
on any TSS, share buy‑back outside the Company's share
repurchase program, or a repurchase or redemption of any TSS.

Fungibility of Group capital

In assessing whether fungibility restrictions on capital held by
AXA's subsidiaries may limit coverage of the Group SCR, the
Group considers whether:
●

●

●

legal or regulatory requirements restrict the ability of own
funds items to absorb all types of losses anywhere in the
Group;
legal or regulatory requirements restrict the transferability
of assets to another insurance or reinsurance entity; and
making those own funds available for covering the Group
SCR is possible within 9 months.

Own funds not deemed available at Group level are included in
the Group’s own funds if they are eligible for covering the SCR
of the entity which holds them. However, subordinated debt
instruments issued by Group subsidiaries are not deemed
available at Group level if they cannot cover the Group’s SCR,
despite being eligible for the issuing entity’s SCR. Currently,
no subordinated debt instrument issued by a Group subsidiary
is deemed available at Group level.
The ACPR currently considers that AXA SA is not subject to
financial conglomerate requirements.

2.4.5 Group capital management objectives
Following the announcement of its “Unlock the Future” strategic

●

●

●

●

52

AXA intends to pay annual dividends representing a payout

AXA intends to buy back shares annually in an amount
corresponding to 15% of the Group’s UEPS, representing a

the share buy‑back component may be canceled by the

of annual share buy‑backs, (iii) and investment in inorganic

2.6 Outlook

Outlook

AXA is focused on executing its “Unlock the Future” plan over
2024‑2026, which is based on delivering profitable organic
growth and scaling technical excellence across each of its
businesses, while driving operational excellence across the
organization.
In P&C Personal lines, the Group aims at further accelerating
volume growth while higher pricing is expected to continue to
earn through. In P&C Commercial lines, pricing remains favorable
in SME and mid‑market, while continuing to moderate in Large
Commercial lines with conditions varying by lines. The Group will
remain disciplined to ensure good cycle management and
expects to maintain margins including through efficiency gains.
The Group’s natural catastrophe (1) load of ca. 4.5 points of
combined ratio for 2025 is maintained. This includes the Group’s
current estimated losses from California wildfires of €0.1 billion,
before tax and net of reinsurance (2). In Life & Health, in the
near‑term, earnings growth should come from the Short‑Term
Business reflecting attractive growth opportunities, notably from
Employee Benefits, as well as continued margin expansion. New
business volumes combined with improved persistency are

expected to drive higher normalized CSM growth over time.
Results in Holdings reflect investments in technology and growth
initiatives and are expected to remain at a similar level in 2025.
Considering the strong overall operating performance delivered
in 2024, and assuming current operating conditions persist,
Management believes AXA is on track to deliver the main
financial targets of AXA’s “Unlock the Future” plan: (i) Underlying
Earnings Per Share growth of 6‑8% CAGR (3) target range
between 2023 and 2026E, (ii) underlying Return On Equity
between 14% and 16% between 2024 and 2026E, and
(iii) cumulative organic cash upstream in excess of €21 billion for
2024‑2026. The Group is committed to its capital management
policy (4), targeting a total payout ratio of 75% (5), comprising a
60% dividend payout ratio and an additional 15% from annual
share buy‑backs (6).

(1) Natural Catastrophe charges include natural catastrophe losses regardless of event size.
(2) Preliminary estimates, subject to change.
(3) Compounded Annual Growth Rate; period‑to‑period results may vary.
(4) Subject to Board and Shareholders’ Annual General Meeting approvals and absent (i) for share buy‑backs, any significant earnings event (i.e., significant
deviation in the Group’s Underlying Earnings) and (ii) for dividends, the occurrence of a significant capital event (i.e., event that significantly deteriorates
Group solvency). Board discretion includes taking into account AXA’s earnings, financial condition, applicable capital and solvency requirements,
prevailing operating and financial market conditions and the general economic environment.
(5) Payout ratio is calculated based on Underlying Earnings Per Share.
(6) Annual share buy‑backs exclude share buy‑backs related to the neutralization of earnings dilution from disposal and in‑force management transactions,
as well as the dilutive effect relating to employee share offerings and stock‑based compensation.

3.1.1 Governance principles and applicable corporate
governance code
Since 2008, the Company has adhered to the French corporate
governance code for listed companies published by Afep and
Medef (the “Afep‑Medef Code”), available on the following
websites www.afep.com and www.medef.com.
The Board of Directors considers that AXA’s corporate
governance practices comply with the recommendations of the
Afep‑Medef Code (revised in December 2022) as well as its
implementation guidelines. The Board also takes into

consideration the evolution of governance practices, both
nationally and internationally, as well as the recommendations
and standards of shareholders, regulators, the High Committee
on Corporate Governance (Haut Comité de Gouvernement
d’Entreprise), proxy advisors, rating agencies, and other
stakeholders in setting its governance.

Corporate Governance
3.1 AXA's governance

3.1.2.1

Separation of the roles of Chairman
of the Board of Directors and Chief
Executive Officer

Since 2016, the roles of Chairman of the Board of Directors (the
“Chairman”) and Chief Executive Officer (the “CEO”) have been
separated. This decision is in line with the ACPR’s
recommendations, best governance practices, and the
expectations of many shareholders, and is considered the most
suitable for the Group’s current situation and challenges.
Thomas Buberl was appointed as CEO in 2016, at the same
time as Denis Duverne, who became non‑independent
Chairman. In 2022, whereas the mandate of Thomas Buberl as
CEO was renewed, the Board decided to maintain this
separated governance model and to appoint Antoine
Gosset‑Grainville as independent Chairman, replacing Denis
Duverne.
In 2024, following the renewal of his mandate as director by the
Shareholders’ Meeting, the Board of Directors confirmed
Antoine Gosset‑Grainville as Chairman.
These decisions were taken in light of the complementary
profiles and experiences of Antoine Gosset‑Grainville and
Thomas Buberl, as well as the quality of governance in place
both within the Board of Directors and during interactions with
Management, as notably illustrated by the results of the annual
assessment of the Board carried out in 2023.

3.1.2.2

Chairman of the Board of Directors

In accordance with French law, the Chairman organizes and
oversees the work of the Board of Directors. In this context, he
notably (i) sets the agenda for Board meetings, (ii) maintains
regular discussions with the CEO and directors, (iii) ensures
that directors are able to carry out their duties, and (iv)
organizes training programs for the directors.
Given his experience, expertise and in‑depth knowledge of the
Group, the Board has entrusted the following duties to its
Chairman:
●

●

he contributes to the promotion of the Company’s values
and culture and protects its reputation, using his best
endeavors to promote the actions undertaken by the Group,
in particular in relation to corporate responsibility and
ethics and professional deontology;
he regularly consults with the CEO and, on his initiative, on
all major topics and events relating to the Company
(including the Company’s strategy, major acquisition or
divestment projects, significant financial transactions,
major community endeavors or the appointment of the
principal executives of the Group);

●

●

upon invitation from the CEO, he takes part in internal
meetings with the Group’s executives and teams to provide
his opinion on strategic issues. The Chairman reports to the
Board of Directors on such consultations and meetings;
and
upon request by the CEO, he represents the Company in its
relations, on a national and international level, in particular
with public bodies, institutions, regulators and shareholders
as well as the Company’s main strategic partners and
stakeholders.

As a general rule, the Chairman of the Board provides
assistance and advice to the CEO and organizes his time to
ensure that he is available and puts his experience to the
service of the Group. His responsibilities are contributory and
do not carry any executive authority. For any responsibilities
that are entrusted to him other than by law, the Chairman acts
in close collaboration with the CEO who is solely responsible
for the Company’s operational leadership and management.
In this context, in 2024, the Chairman participated in:
●

national and international events where he represented the
Company;

●

events with individual shareholders;

●

internal meetings, at the CEO's request; and

●

governance roadshows with institutional shareholders of
the Company, in particular prior to the Shareholders'
Meeting, to discuss governance, compensation and
sustainability.

3.1.2.3

Chief Executive Officer

The CEO is entrusted with the most extensive powers to act on
behalf of the Company in all circumstances and represents the
Company in its dealings vis-à-vis third parties, within the limits
of the corporate purpose and subject to the powers attributed
to the Shareholders' Meetings and the Board of Directors.
However, the Terms of Reference of the Board of Directors (the
“Board's Terms of Reference”) provide for specific limitations to
the CEO’s powers. Prior authorization of the Board is for
instance required to perform certain transactions as set out in
Section 3.3.1.3 - Powers of the Board of Directors of this
Document.

3.1.2.4

Management Committee

The CEO is supported by a Management Committee to assist
him in steering the operational management of the Group.
The Management Committee meets regularly to notably
discuss the Group’s strategic, financial, operational and
sustainability matters.
The Management Committee has no formal decision‑making
power.

3.2 Composition of the Board of Directors and its Committees

3.2.3 Board of Directors’ diversity policy
3.2.3.1

Policy statement

The Board of Directors is committed to achieving a balanced
composition in terms of gender, tenure, age, independence,
skills, expertise and experience. It also strives to reflect a
diversity of nationalities and cultures, given the Group’s
international profile. A source of creativity and performance,
this diversity is essential to the Board of Directors' smooth
functioning, providing an opportunity to examine issues from
different perspectives.

The Board of Directors, assisted by its Compensation,
Governance & Sustainability Committee, regularly reviews the
balance of its composition and that of its Committees. Each year,
the Board measures progress made against the objectives set.

3.2.5 Directors’ independence
In accordance with the Afep‑Medef Code, a director is
independent if he or she has no relationship of any kind
whatsoever with the Company, its Group or its management
that may interfere with his or her freedom of judgment.
Accordingly, a director is qualified as independent when he or
she meets the following criteria:
●

●

●

●

●

Criterion 1 - Employee or executive officer during the
previous five years: not to be, or have been during the
previous five years: an employee or executive officer of AXA;
an employee, executive officer or director of a company
consolidated within AXA or an employee, executive officer or
director of AXA or a company consolidated within AXA;
Criterion 2 Cross‑mandates: not to be an executive
‑
officer of a company in which AXA directly or indirectly holds
a directorship or in which an employee appointed as such
or an executive officer of AXA (currently in office or having
held such office within the last five years) holds a mandate;
Criterion 3 - Significant business relationships: not to be
a customer, supplier, commercial banker, investment
banker, or consultant that is significant for AXA or the Group
or for which AXA represents a significant portion of its
activity;
Criterion 4 - Family ties: not to be related by close family
ties to a corporate officer of AXA;
Criterion 5 - Statutory Auditor: not to have been a
statutory auditor of AXA within the previous five years;

●

●

●

Criterion 6 - Term of office exceeding 12 years: not to
have been an AXA director for more than twelve years;
Criterion 7 - Status of
non‑executive corporate officer: a
‑
non‑executive officer cannot be considered independent if
he/she receives variable compensation in cash or in the
form of securities or any compensation linked to the
performance of AXA or the Group;
Criterion 8 - Status of major shareholder: directors
representing major shareholders of AXA may be considered
independent, provided those shareholders do not take part
in the control of AXA. Nevertheless, beyond a 10% threshold
in capital or voting rights, the Board, upon report from the
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee,
should systematically review the qualification of a director
as independent taking into account the composition of
AXA's share capital and potential conflicts of interest.

During its meeting held on February 26, 2025, the Board
assessed the independence of each of its directors (excluding
the members representing the employees and the employee
shareholders, i.e. Martine Bièvre, Bettina Cramm and
Helen Browne) on December 31, 2024 according to the
Afep‑Medef Code criteria.
The Board noted that four members do not meet all the
Afep‑Medef Code criteria: Thomas Buberl, Gérald Harlin,
Ramon de Oliveira and Angelien Kemna.

3.2 Composition of the Board of Directors and its Committees

Regarding the specific situation of Angelien Kemna, the fact
that she sits on the Board of AXA Investment Managers as
non‑executive director was a point for consideration by the
Board as part of its overall assessment. After discussion and in
line with its previous assessments, the Board has concluded
that this situation neither prevents Angelien Kemna from
exercising her mandate as a director of AXA with complete
independence nor impairs her independence under the
Afep‑Medef Code given her past performance as a director as
well as her independent mindset. This conclusion was further
supported by the fact that AXA Investment Managers is a 97%owned unlisted subsidiary of the Group and that any potential
conflict could be resolved by Angelien Kemna abstaining from
any discussion and/or vote on the relevant subject, in
accordance with the Board’s Terms of Reference.
In addition, considering Angelien Kemna’s experience and
knowledge of the asset management business, this position
provides the Board with valuable insight into the strategy,
operational activities, processes, and teams of AXA Investment
Managers, and more broadly into the Group’s asset
management strategy and activities. These skills have been
particularly useful to the Board in recent years in a context in
which the asset management sector has undergone significant
changes and in which the Board has discussed the strategic
positioning, risks, and opportunities for AXA Investment
Managers on numerous occasions. Due to this, procedures that
involve a regular review of the situation have been put in place
to manage potential conflicts of interest that could arise from
Angelien Kemna’s mandate at AXA Investment Managers. The
Board considered that Angelien Kemna was not in a position of
conflict of interest during the preliminary discussions. However,

it was concluded that Angelien Kemna should abstain from
participating in any deliberation and vote related to the sale of
AXA Investment Managers to BNP Paribas and the conclusion of
a long‑term strategic agreement in which BNP Paribas would
provide investment management services to AXA.
The Board also specifically assessed the business relationships
between independent directors and the Group. To this end, the
Board (1) reviewed the annual disclosures submitted by
directors detailing any business relationships with the Group
during the past year and confirming that these are not likely to
create a conflict of interest, and if applicable, (2) qualitatively
and quantitatively analyzed each business relationship, taking
into account; (i) the director’s position within the entity with a
business relationship with the Group, the existence of direct
decision‑making power over the relationship, or any
compensation received by the director relating to the
relationship; and (ii) the significance of the relationship,
ensuring that the business relationships do not represent a
significant portion of the Group’s overall business in terms of
revenues, nor create any potential economic dependency or
exclusivity. The Board concluded that none of the independent
directors had significant business relationships with the
Company or the Group that could compromise their
independence.
In light of the foregoing, the Board of Directors concluded that
nine out of twelve (1) directors should be considered
independent according to the Afep‑Medef Code criteria:
Clotilde Delbos, Rachel Duan, Guillaume Faury, Ramon
Fernandez, Antoine Gosset‑Grainville, Isabel Hudson, Angelien
Kemna, Rachel Picard and Marie‑France Tschudin.

Change within the Board since January 1, 2025

Based on the analysis of its Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee, the Board of Directors concluded that
Ewout Steenbergen, who meets all the Afep‑Medef Code criteria mentioned above, can be considered independent in light of the
Afep‑Medef Code criteria.

(1) Excluding directors representing the employees and the director representing the employee shareholders, in accordance with the Afep‑Medef Code.

Antoine Gosset‑Grainville
Chairman of the AXA Board of Directors (independent)
Partner at BDGS Associés, Law Firm
Expertise and experience
Antoine Gosset‑Grainville is a graduate of the Institut d’études politiques of Paris and holds a
“DESS” (postgraduate degree) in banking and finance from the University of Paris IX Dauphine. He was admitted
to the Paris Bar (2002) and the Brussels Bar (2002). After graduating from the French École nationale
d’administration, he began his career, in 1993, at the Inspection Générale des Finances, before taking the position
of Deputy General Secretary of the Economic and Financial Committee of the European Union in 1997. From
1999 to 2002, he was advisor for Economic and Industry Affairs in the office of the European Commissioner in
charge of Trade. In 2002, he became partner at Gide (law firm), where he managed the Brussels office for five
years before becoming Deputy Director of the Cabinet of the French Prime Minister in 2007, in charge of
economic and financial issues and the management of the French State’s investment portfolio. In 2010, he was
appointed Deputy Chief Executive Officer (Directeur Général Adjoint) of the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations in
charge of finance, strategy, investments and international operations and interim Chief Executive Officer of the
Caisse des Dépôts group from February to July 2012. In April 2013, he co‑founded BDGS Associés (law firm). On
April 28, 2022, Antoine Gosset‑Grainville was appointed Chairman of the Board of Directors of AXA.
