3.2.9 Other information relating to corporate officers
3.2.9.1

Absence of family ties between
corporate officers

To the Company’s knowledge, there are no family ties between
directors or with members of Executive Management.

3.2.9.2

Absence of conviction or
incrimination of corporate officers

To the Company’s knowledge, no director has, in the past five
years, (i) been convicted of fraud or been subject to any official
public accusation and/or sanction by statutory or regulatory
authorities (including designated professional bodies),
(ii) been disqualified by a court from serving as a member of a
governing body, management, or supervisory board of an
issuer or from participating in the management or conduct of
the affairs of an issuer, or (iii) been associated, as a corporate
officer or executive, with a bankruptcy, receivership,
liquidation, or placement of a company under judicial
administration, except to the extent that AXA may have in the
past disposed of, terminated, and/or restructured certain of its
activities and, as a result, voluntarily liquidated Group entities
engaged in such activities, and some of AXA’s directors may
have been involved in such voluntary liquidation or similar
operations concerning entities outside the AXA Group.

3.2.9.3

Absence of potential conflicts
of interest between the corporate
officers’ duties to AXA and their
private interests and/or other
duties

Neither the Chairman of the Board of Directors nor the CEO
currently holds any professional activity or corporate positions
outside the Group that the Board considers likely to
substantially restrict either person's availability to the Group
and its activities. However, some directors serve as corporate
officers and/or managers in companies that may have
contracts or agreements with the AXA Group, in the context of
transactions such as the granting of credit, the purchase of
securities (for own account or on behalf of third parties) and/or
the placement of financial instruments and/or the provision of
products or services. To the extent that such contracts or
agreements are generally subject to negotiation and are

entered into on arms' length terms, AXA considers that none of
these contracts or agreements gives rise to conflicts of interest
between (i) the directors’ obligations towards AXA and (ii) their
private interests and/or other obligations (see Section 3.2.5 Directors’ independence of this Document).
To the Company’s knowledge, there is no arrangement or
agreement with the main shareholders, customers, suppliers or
others, pursuant to which a director has been selected, with the
exception of Gérald Harlin who was appointed to the Board of
Directors at the Shareholders’ Meeting of April 28, 2022, as a
representative of the Mutuelles AXA (AXA Assurances IARD
Mutuelle and AXA Assurances Vie Mutuelle), together holding
15.40% of the share capital and 25.99% of the voting rights of
the Company on December 31, 2024.

3.3 Organization and activities of the Board of Directors and its Committees

3.3

Organization and activities of the Board
of Directors and its Committees

3.3.1 Operating framework

The Board’s Terms of Reference detail the role and
responsibilities of the Board and its Committees, as well as the
decisions falling within the Board's exclusive competence.

In addition, to promote the alignment of the directors’ personal
interests with those of the Company, directors (excluding
directors representing the employees) shall be shareholders of
the Company and are required to hold a number of shares
equal to at least one year's compensation as valued each year
on December 31.

3.3.1.1

3.3.1.2

The Board of Directors is supported by three Committees: the
Audit Committee, the Finance & Risk Committee and the
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee.

Ethics

Directors shall act in all circumstances in the corporate interest
(intérêt social) of the Company and its shareholders and shall
avoid carrying out activities or transactions which could give
rise to a conflict of interest with the Company.
Each director has the obligation to inform the Chairman and/or
the Senior Independent Director, if any, of any personal
situation likely to give rise to a conflict of interest with the
Company or with Group companies and to abstain from
engaging in discussion or voting in relation to any such
potential conflict of interest.
Directors must comply with the following obligations:
●

●

●

●

●

a general obligation of secrecy, confidentiality and
discretion;
observing the rules aimed at limiting the number of
mandates held in other companies in order to be able to
devote the necessary time and attention to their role;
having the integrity required to perform their duties,
enabling them to contribute to a sound and prudent
management of the Company;
complying in particular with the AXA Compliance & Ethics
Code, notably on trading (including black‑out periods) and
conflicts of interest; and

Information and training

Directors are informed by the CEO by any means and on a
regular basis of the Company's financial situation, cash flows
and commitments, together with any significant events or
transactions relating to the Company. At least quarterly, the
CEO shall report to the Board of Directors on the activities and
operations of the Company. In addition, each director may
request any documents that he/she deems useful for
performing his/her responsibilities.
Upon his/her appointment, each director receives training
related to the Company’s businesses, activities, the risks and
challenges it faces in terms of sustainability, including
climate‑related issues. Any director may also receive further
training if he/she deems it appropriate.
The Board collectively receives regular training adapted to the
challenges facing the Company. For further information, please
refer to Section 3.3.2.3 - Training of this Document.
Directors representing the employees and the director
representing the employee shareholders may also receive
customized training.
In addition, each director may attend meetings of the Audit
Committee or the Finance & Risk Committee, even if he/she is
not a member of that Committee.

reporting to the AMF and the Company any transactions
they may have performed on AXA securities (for transactions
declared in 2024, please refer to Section 3.2.9.5 Transactions reported in 2024 by directors and closely
associated persons involving the Company’s securities of
this Document).

3.3 Organization and activities of the Board of Directors and its Committees

3.3.1.3

Powers of the Board of Directors

The Board of Directors exercises the powers vested in it by
applicable laws and acts at all times in the corporate interest of
the Company.
The Board endeavors to promote long‑term value creation by
considering the interests of the Company’s various
stakeholders and its social and environmental impacts.
It notably has the power to:
●

●

●

●

●

●

●

84

choose the Company’s governance model;
appoint and dismiss the Chairman, any Senior Independent
Director, the CEO and, upon the CEO’s proposal, any Deputy
CEOs and the persons who effectively run the Company;
determine the strategic orientations of the Company’s
activities and ensure their implementation; notably the
multi‑year strategic orientations in terms of social and
environmental responsibility. In conjunction with these
strategic orientations, it regularly monitors opportunities
and risks such as financial, legal, operational, social and
environmental risks as well as measures taken in relation
thereto;
prepare the Company’s annual financial statements, the
Group’s consolidated financial statements and half‑year
financial statements, and the management report, including
in particular sustainability‑related information;
convene Shareholders’ Meetings and present a report on
corporate governance to the shareholders;
fulfill its obligations under applicable laws and regulations
(including Solvency II and the Digital Operational Resilience
Act (DORA));
set the risk appetite and overall risk tolerance limits for the
Company;

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

●

●

determine the compensation of the corporate officers and
the granting of long term incentives;
authorize regulated agreements (conventions réglementées).

In addition, certain significant transactions are subject to the
prior authorization of the Board, including in particular:
●

●

●

●

●

disposals or acquisitions (exceeding €500 million per
transaction or €2 billion in aggregate over one year);
reinsurance transactions entered into with a third party and
resulting in a transfer of reserves for €10 billion or more;
share buy‑backs other than those intended to hedge
employee shareholding and share allocations to employees
or corporate officers;
sureties, guarantees, endorsements or warranties provided
in favor of third parties (exceeding €200 million per
transaction executed in order to guarantee obligations of
the Company’s subsidiaries or sureties put up to guarantee
its own obligations, or €100 million for other guarantees,
endorsements and warranties, and, up to a limit of €1 billion
in aggregate over one year); and
financial transactions that may substantially change the
Company’s financial structure or fall outside the strategy
previously announced by the Company.

3.3 Organization and activities of the Board of Directors and its Committees

In accordance with the Board's Terms of Reference, the
Chairman convenes the directors at least once a year without
the presence of the CEO.
In addition, the Chair of the Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee shall convene the members of the
Board of Directors, at least once a year, without the presence of
the Chairman of the Board of Directors and Executive
Management. These meetings are an opportunity to assess the
performance of the Chairman of the Board of Directors, to
review his/her compensation and prepare his/her succession
plan.
In 2024, the directors met three times without the presence of
the CEO to discuss, in particular, the evaluation of his
performance, his compensation and his succession.
The Board also met once without the presence of the Chairman
(and the CEO) to discuss his performance in the context of the
Board assessment, as well as his compensation and
succession.

3.3.2.3

Training

In 2024, directors received training on the CSRD, the double
materiality assessment and ESRS (European Sustainability
Reporting Standards).
Directors received training on the reduction of the carbon
intensity of the Group's investments, the decarbonization of the
Group's own operations and the alignment with Group
incentives. Prior to this training, the directors were also invited
to take the “Low carbon transition” course on the AXA Climate
platform dedicated to the Board.
The Board of Directors received a presentation on sustainable
and responsible forest management during its visit to one of
the forests managed by the Group.

composition, the organization and activity of the Board,
executive compensation and the Group’s sustainability
strategy. The Chairman of the Board took part in a number of
these meetings, alongside representatives of the relevant
teams of the Company.
The main questions and comments from investors and proxy
advisors as well as a proposed action plan were presented to

3.3 Organization and activities of the Board of Directors and its Committees

3.3.3.4

Joint sessions of the Committees

In 2024, several joint sessions between Board Committees were
organized.
Joint sessions of the Audit Committee and the Compensation,
Governance & Sustainability Committee were held on three
occasions, notably to discuss (i) SNFP, (ii) the climate and
biodiversity reports, (iii) the double materiality assessment and
(iv) the structure of the future Sustainability Statement.

Joint sessions of the Audit Committee and the Finance & Risk
Committee were also held on three occasions, notably to
review: (i) the risk sections of the financial statements and
management report, as well as the main off‑balance sheet
commitments, (ii) the Group and Company ORSA, SFCR, and
RSR reports, (iii) the Group and Company reinsurance strategy
and (iv) the Solvency II policies.

3.3.4 Assessment of the Board of Directors and its Committees
In accordance with the recommendations of the Afep‑Medef
Code, the Board of Directors assesses and discusses its
composition, organization, and activities, as well as those of its
Committees, on an annual basis. In 2023, the Board’s
assessment was carried out by an external consultant (Russell
Reynolds Associates), under the supervision of the
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee. This
consultant was selected from among several providers
following a tender process, based notably on the following
criteria: (i) experience in Board assessments, (ii) independence,
(iii) knowledge of the industry, etc.
Each director completed an online questionnaire, and then met
with the external consultant to assess, in particular (i) the
progress made compared to the conclusions of the 2022
self‑assessment, (ii) the composition and the organization of

the Board and its Committees, (iii) the role of the Chairman,
(iv) the relationship between the Board and Management and
(v) the alignment of the Board with the Group strategy,
particularly in terms of sustainability. During the individual
interviews, the directors were also asked to comment on other
members’ individual contributions to the Board’s work.
All results were anonymous, and the directors received
individual feedback from the Chairman of the Board on their
respective contributions.
In 2024, the assessment exercise was conducted internally. In
December 2024,
the
Compensation,
Governance
&
Sustainability Committee conducted a review of the results of
this assessment before submitting its conclusions to the Board
of Directors, including identified areas for improvement and a
proposed action plan.

Assessment procedure Each director (with the exception of the Chairman of the Board):
implemented in 2024 1. replied in writing to an anonymized questionnaire;

2. met with the Chairman of the Board to give his/her opinion on the composition, organization and
activities of the Board as well as the other members' individual contribution to the Board’s work. Each
director then received an individual feedback from the Chairman on his/her contribution;
3. met with the Chairman of the Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee to assess the
Chairman’s contribution to the Board's work.

Results

The assessment highlighted the positive perception by directors of the composition and organization of
the Board and its Committees.
The directors noted the progress made in those areas of improvement identified in the previous
assessment, which notably led to (i) the appointment of Ewout Steenbergen, (ii) the implementation of a
work plan including regular deep dives on business topics, (iii) the review of the M&A approval process
and the succession processes, (iv) the review of the Board's Terms of Reference, and (v) the organization
of several joint sessions of the Committees.
The directors confirmed that, both individually and collectively, the Board of Directors had the relevant
skills, expertise and experience to carry out its duties.

Areas for
improvement

The Board identified several areas for improvement, in particular:
1. continue to operationalize the division of responsibilities for sustainability between the Committees
and the Board;
2. discuss more regularly the competitive environment in which AXA operates and the risks to which the
Group is exposed;
3. continue to refine the M&A process;
4. further discuss human resources developments and strategy at the Board;
5. provide more information on upcoming regulatory changes and their potential implications for the
Group.

3.4 Agreements

3.4

Agreements

3.4.1 Regulated agreements
During the financial year ended December 31, 2024, the Company did not enter into any agreements falling within the scope of
“regulated agreements” (conventions réglementées) pursuant to French law which would require shareholder approval.

3.4.2 Assessment procedure for ordinary agreements entered into
on arm's length terms and conditions
The Board adopted a procedure to assess on a regular basis
whether agreements relating to ordinary agreements entered
into on arm’s length terms and conditions actually meet these
conditions.
This procedure, which is reviewed by the Board annually,
involves promptly informing the Group Legal Department
before entering into any agreement falling within the scope of
Article L.225‑38 of the French Commercial Code, regardless of
the ordinary nature of the transaction or its arm’s length terms.
The Group Legal Department conducts a preliminary review of
the agreement to determine whether it should be subject to the
“regulated agreements" procedure set out in Articles L.225‑38
et seq. of the French Commercial Code, or if it is exempt. For
this purpose, the Group Legal Department may seek the
opinion of other relevant departments within the AXA Group
and of the Statutory Auditors.

Furthermore, the Group Legal Department annually assesses, in
cooperation with AXA Group’s relevant departments, and with
the Statutory Auditors where necessary, whether the ongoing
agreements entered into on arm’s length terms and conditions
continue to meet the conditions for such qualification. If the
Group Legal Department considers that an agreement initially
qualified as ordinary and entered into on arm’s length terms
and conditions constitutes a “regulated agreement", it will
inform the Chairman of the Board. The Board will then decide
on the qualification of the said agreement and on the actions
to be taken in relation thereto according to the qualification
adopted.
This procedure was reviewed by the Board during its meeting
of February 26, 2025.

3.5 Executive compensation and share ownership

3.5

Executive compensation and share ownership

Guiding principles of AXA's compensation policy
AXA's compensation policy is designed to attract, develop and
motivate critical skills and talents, encourage superior
performance and align compensation levels with the results of
the Company.
To align the interests of the Group's executives and employees
with those of the Company and its shareholders, the
compensation policy is based on a pay‑for‑performance
approach that (i) requires the achievement of challenging
financial and operational targets that are defined and aligned
with the Group's strategy, (ii) promotes long‑term sustainable
performance while incorporating risk adjustment measures in
performance metrics and (iii) determines the effective of the
actual individual compensation on the basis of financial and
extra‑financial results.
Thus, AXA's policy on executive compensation focuses on the
variable part of compensation at risk for beneficiaries and
encourages both individual and collective performance over
the short, medium and long term while ensuring compliance
with regulatory requirements.
It follows four main guiding principles:

●

●

●

●

competitiveness and market consistency of the
remuneration practices while avoiding potential conflicts of
interest that may lead to undue risk taking for short‑term
gain;
fairness based on individual and collective performance, in
order to ensure remuneration is reflecting employees’
individual quantitative and qualitative achievements and
impact;
internal equity based on remuneration policies and
procedures designed to ensure that employees are paid
equitably based on objective and justifiable professional
criteria (such as, but not limited to, role, skills, contribution
or impact), and do not discriminate on the basis of factors
irrelevant to duties of the role; and
achievement of the Group’s overall financial and
extra‑financial, as well as operational objectives over the
short, medium, and long term and execution against
medium and long‑term strategic objectives as a
prerequisite to fund any mid‑to‑long term award.

The requirements set out in AXA’s compensation policy may be
supplemented in order to comply with local regulatory
requirements. The Policy is reviewed and updated annually to
mirror, as the case may be, changes in the internal organization
and the nature, scale and complexity of the risks inherent to
AXA’s business.

3.5.1 Compensation policy for the Company's corporate officers
(submitted to the Shareholders' Meeting on April 24, 2025)
This policy was prepared in accordance with articles L.22‑10‑8
and R.22‑10‑14 of the French Commercial Code and presents
the principles and criteria for determination, distribution, and
allocation of all elements of compensation of the corporate
officers (mandataires sociaux, i.e. Chief Executive Officer,
Chairman of the Board and other directors) of the Company as
approved by the Board of Directors on February 26, 2025, after
recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee.
AXA regularly engages with its shareholders to discuss
governance, compensation and sustainability matters.
Following the 2024 Shareholders’ Meeting and after having
analyzed investors’ feedback and the results of the votes, the
Board of Directors has decided to maintain the main terms of
the compensation policy approved by shareholders on April 23,
2024, which were considered appropriate, fair and balanced. As

part of the continuous shareholder engagement approach, the
Board of Directors will keep monitoring investors’ and proxy
advisors’ expectations, along with market practices.
The Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee,
which is mainly composed of independent members in
accordance with the Afep‑Medef Code, is responsible for
formulating proposals to the Board on the compensation and
principles for the Company's corporate officers. The Committee
meets frequently with the Group executives and the
departments of the Company including Group human
resources, Group Legal and Group Sustainability. It may also
work with a compensation‑consulting firm in order to benefit
from external technical expertise and an independent overview
in order to compare AXA’s variable compensation practices with
market’s.

3.5.1.1

Compensation policy for the Chief Executive Officer

Amount, structure and criteria for
determining the compensation of the Chief
Executive Officer
The Chief Executive Officer's compensation policy is based on
practices of AXA's main European and international
competitors (insurance, reinsurance companies and banks)
and other CAC 40 companies. It is also in line with the
recommendations of the Afep‑Medef Code, the G20, the
European Commission and the Financial Stability Board (FSB).
The overall amount, structure and criteria of the Chief Executive
Officer's compensation are determined in accordance with the
guiding principles of AXA's compensation policy described
above.

In application of the pay‑for‑performance approach, the at‑risk
portion of the CEO's total compensation (variable cash
compensation and share‑based compensation) represents a
significant component of his compensation structure to align
his compensation with the operation strategy of the Group and
the interests of shareholders.
Upon the renewal of Thomas Buberl's term as Chief Executive
Officer in 2022, the Board of Directors, following the
recommendation of the Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee, decided that his total compensation
would remain unchanged for the duration of his term of office,
i.e. until 2026.
The Board of Directors has decided to maintain this
compensation for 2025.

Annual fixed compensation of the Chief Executive
Officer
The determination of the amount of the Chief Executive
Officer’s annual fixed compensation, in 2022, was notably
based on an in‑depth analysis of market practices carried out
by an independent external advisory firm (Willis Towers
Watson) as well as applicable regulations. It also took into
consideration experience, skills, as well as the criticality and
scarcity of such skills, and the Group’s fairness principles or the
individual’s compensation history.
Upon recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee, the Board confirmed that the Chief
Executive Officer’s annual fixed compensation, set in 2022, at
€1.65 million will be maintained for 2025.

Annual variable compensation of the Chief Executive
Officer
When it determined the Chief Executive Officer’s target annual
variable compensation, in 2022, following a comparative review
of national, European, international and industry practices, the
Board of Directors sought to establish a balanced structure
between the fixed part and the variable part of his cash
compensation.
Upon recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee, the Board confirmed that the Chief
Executive Officer’s target annual variable compensation, set
in 2022, at €1.75 million (i.e. 106% of the amount of his annual
fixed compensation) will be maintained for 2025 and would
continue to be subject in its entirety to challenging
performance conditions and closely aligned with the Group’s
strategy.
No minimum payment is guaranteed to the Chief Executive
Officer and his total effective variable compensation may not
exceed 130% of his target variable compensation (i.e. 142% of
his annual fixed compensation).
The evaluation of the Chief Executive Officer's annual
performance for the 2025 financial year will be based on the
following two components, each capped at a 130%
achievement rate:
●

The Group’s performance, evaluated on the basis of
(i) Underlying Earnings per share, (ii) cash remittance,
(iii) the reduction in Group carbon footprint in General
Account assets, and (iv) the Net Promoter Score (customer
recommendation index). The relative weight of each
indicator will remain unchanged (i.e. 45%, 25%, 15% and
15% respectively).
The financial and extra‑financial indicators chosen to
measure the Group performance are directly linked to the
Group’s strategic orientations for growth, capital
management, sustainability and customer proximity and
rely on the achievement of a predefined budget or target
defined by the Board of Directors. Each of the indicators is
associated with a floor threshold below which the
performance condition is considered not to be met and will
be capped at a 130% achievement rate.
Some of these indicators (Underlying Earnings per share,
cash remittance and the reduction in Group carbon

●

The Individual performance, based on (i) various
indicators and qualitative and quantifiable objectives
determined by the Board of Directors in a target letter
drawn up at the beginning of the year, and
(ii) demonstrated leadership abilities by the Chief Executive
Officer. The target letter includes detailed objectives related
to the Group’s progress in the implementation of its
strategic plan as well as other performance indicators and
objectives assessing the achievement of global strategic
initiatives or related to certain geographic areas, as well as
progress on investments that are expected to contribute to
the development of the Group’s operations. Each of the
indicators will be capped at a 130% achievement rate.

With respect to 2025, the Board of Directors, upon
recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee, set the five following objectives and
their respective weights: (i) successfully deliver on the second
year of the strategic plan, especially on the financial targets
(30%), (ii) further assess strategic opportunities and initiatives
(20%), (iii) portfolio management: develop and decide M&A
strategy and successfully close AXA investment Managers' sale
(15%), (iv) begin reflection on the key challenges for the next
strategic plan (2027‑2029) (10%), and (v) people: successfully
drive the efficiency and cohesion of the Management
Committee, and further develop the solid succession plans
(25%).
With respect to 2025, the determination of the actual amount
of variable compensation to be paid to the Chief Executive
Officer will continue to be based on the addition of two
components: the Group performance for 70% and the
individual performance for 30%. Each of these two
components will be evaluated separately so that the Chief
Executive Officer’s overall variable pay‑out reflects his
performance against two distinct components assessed
independently.
To ensure that AXA remains aligned with current market
practice and regulations within the financial industry, both in
France and abroad, the Board of Directors decided to continue
to use a deferral mechanism with respect to the Chief Executive
Officer’s annual variable compensation.
Under this mechanism, the payment of 30% of his actual
annual variable compensation will be deferred over a
three‑year period paid out in three equal tranches and will
remain subject to performance conditions. The deferred
amount effectively paid out for each tranche will vary
accordingly depending on the performance of the AXA share
price over the deferral period within the limit of a cap at 130%
of the deferred amount but without a floor. No deferred
variable compensation would be paid (i) in the event that the
Group’s Underlying Earnings are negative for the year ending
immediately prior to the year of the scheduled payout, or (ii) in
case of resignation or dismissal, for gross or willful misconduct
prior to the payout date.

Each year, the Board of Directors, upon recommendation from

decides to grant Long‑Term Incentives (LTI) to the Chief

To give the Chief Executive Officer a stake in long‑term value
creation, these performance shares represent an important
part of his compensation. However, the value of the
performance shares granted to the Chief Executive Officer, as
determined in accordance with the IFRS standards, may not in
any event exceed half of his total compensation.
The Board of Directors also decided that the number of LTI
granted to the Company’s executive corporate officers,
including the Chief Executive Officer, may not exceed 10% of
the total number of LTI granted to all beneficiaries within the
Group.
The performance shares granted to the Chief Executive Officer are

3.5 Executive compensation and share ownership

Exceptional compensation of the Chief Executive
Officer
The Board of Directors does not contemplate granting any
exceptional compensation to the Chief Executive Officer.

Directors’ compensation of the Chief Executive Officer
The Chief Executive Officer, who is also a member of the Board
of Directors of the Company, is not entitled to payment of any
directors’ compensation from the Company.

Benefits in kind granted to the Chief Executive Officer
The Chief Executive Officer benefits from the use of a company
car.
The Chief Executive Officer also benefits from social benefits
(health expenses, provident funds, etc.) on terms equivalent to
those of all other AXA Group management executives in France.

Compensation elements related to the retirement
of the Chief Executive Officer
The Chief Executive Officer does not participate in any pension
schemes with defined benefits.
As all other executives of AXA Group entities in France, he
participates in the retirement performance share plan, under
which grants are made on an annual basis.
The retirement performance shares granted under such plans
are subject to (i) an acquisition period of three years, and
(ii) an undertaking not to sell the retirement performance
shares before the date on which the beneficiary retires, subject
to the option offered to the beneficiaries, for diversification
purposes, to sell their shares (after the end of the acquisition
period of three years) as long as the proceeds of such sale are
invested in a long‑term savings plan until the beneficiary
retires.
The acquisition of the retirement performance shares is subject
to the satisfaction of a performance condition (the details of
which are set out in Section 3.5 - Executive compensation and
share ownership of this Document), linked to the average AXA
Group Solvency II ratio calculated over the performance period.
No minimum grant or gain is guaranteed to the Chief Executive
Officer under this scheme.
The Board of Directors, upon recommendation from its
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee,
decided that the total value of the retirement performance
shares to be granted to the Chief Executive Officer during 2025
shall not exceed 15% of his fixed and cash annual variable
compensation.
As all other employees of AXA Group entities in France, the
Chief Executive Officer participates in a mandatory and
collective supplementary pension scheme with defined
contributions (collective insurance contract – contrat
d’assurance de Groupe as defined in article L.141‑1 of the
French Insurance Code). This AXA pension fund was
implemented in 2011 and benefits to the employees of AXA
Group entities in France falling within the Scope of the
Collective Agreement of December 18, 2009. The individual

employer contribution rate is set at 0.75% of the total gross
compensation, which is not capped. The contribution base is
the same as the one used for contributions related to the Social
Security General Scheme. Contributions are subject to 9.7%
social charges (9.2% for CSG and 0.5% for CRDS).

Commitments made to the Chief Executive Officer
upon termination of service
In accordance with the recommendations of the Afep‑Medef
Code, Thomas Buberl has decided to renounce his
employment contract as of the date of his appointment as
Chief Executive Officer.
In connection with this decision, the Board of Directors upon
recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee undertook a review of the
consequences of this renunciation including with respect to the
continuity of the social benefits (Health insurance, Life
insurance, Disability insurance, etc.) to which Thomas Buberl
was entitled as an employee. In this context, the Board of
Directors was concerned that the decision of Thomas Buberl to
renounce his employment contract in accordance with the
recommendations of the Afep‑Medef Code would jeopardize
the continuity of his accrued and future social benefits.
As a result, on August 2, 2016, the Board of Directors decided to
maintain social benefits and provide a contractual severance
benefit for Thomas Buberl, in case of termination of service,
designed to replicate the benefits to which he would have been
entitled as AXA employee under the 1993 collective agreement
covering director‑level employees of the insurance sector, but
with the addition of performance conditions. A severance
benefit would be applicable, except in the case of gross or
willful misconduct, solely in the event of dismissal or
non‑renewal further to the Board of Directors’ decision. The
payment of the severance benefit would be subject to the three
following performance conditions as determined by the Board
of Directors: (i) achievement, for at least 2 of the 3 preceding
fiscal years, of the objectives set for the beneficiary’s variable
compensation and corresponding to the payment of at least
60% of his variable compensation target, (ii) evolution of the
AXA share price at least equal to the stock reference index of the
insurance sector (SXIP) (in percentage) over a 3‑year period
preceding the termination of the term of office, and (iii) the
average consolidated adjusted ROE over the 3 preceding years
higher than or equal to 5%.
The amount of severance benefit to be paid to the beneficiary
would be adjusted in accordance with the level of achievement
against these performance conditions: 100% of the severance
benefit will be paid if at least two of the three performance
conditions are met; 40% of the severance benefit will be paid if
only one performance condition is met; and no severance
benefit shall be paid if none of the performance conditions are
met. Notwithstanding the foregoing, if only two of the three
performance conditions are met, the amount of severance
benefit will be reduced by 50% if performance condition
(i) above is not met or if AXA’s consolidated net income for the
preceding fiscal year is negative.

3.5.1.2

Compensation policy of the
Chairman of the Board of Directors

Structure and criteria for determining
the Chairman of the Board of Directors’
compensation
The Board of Directors, upon recommendation from its
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee, and in
accordance with the recommendations of the Afep‑Medef
Code, has determined that the most appropriate compensation
structure for the Chairman of the Board of Directors consists
exclusively of fixed compensation.
In determining the annual fixed compensation of its Chairman,
the Board of Directors consulted an independent advisory firm
(Willis Towers Watson) in 2022 to identify compensation
practices for similar functions among a sample of CAC 40
companies and major European companies in the financial
sector.
It also considered Antoine Gosset‑Grainville's experience and
expertise, as well as the extensive duties assigned to him as
Chairman of the Board of Directors. These are detailed in the
Terms of Reference of the Board of Directors and exceed the
duties assigned to the Chairman of the Board under French
law. This duties are detailed in Section 3.1 - AXA's
governance of this Document.
Accordingly, the Board of Directors, upon recommendation
from its Compensation, Governance & Sustainability
Committee, decided to maintain the Chairman's annual fixed
compensation unchanged at €925,000 for 2025.

3.5.2.1

Compensation of the Chief
Executive Officer
on December 31, 2024

The target level and structure of executives’ compensation are
based on a detailed analysis of market practices, applicable
regulations, equity principles within the Group and the
executive's previous compensation level.
Each year, AXA, with the assistance of specialized firms,
conducts compensation reviews to ensure the competitiveness
and consistency of executives’ compensation. Three markets
are used as a reference:
●

●

●

a first market composed of 12 companies in the French
CAC 40 index (companies selected to form the panel, which
may vary from year‑to‑year, which are comparable to AXA in
terms of stock capitalization, revenues, sector, number of
employees and/or geographic coverage);
a second market composed of international financial
companies comparable in size and Scope to the AXA Group
(mainly insurance, reinsurance companies and banks)
principally based in the main European markets (France,
Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Spain
and Switzerland);
a third market composed of international financial
companies comparable in size and Scope to the AXA Group
(mainly insurance and reinsurance companies and banks)
principally based in the United States and Asia.

Annual cash compensation
Total target compensation

The annual fixed compensation of the Chief Executive Officer

Annual variable compensation
and performance conditions

●

(i) Underlying Earnings Per Share, (ii) cash remittance, (iii) a

in General Account assets), and (iv) the Net Promoter Score

130%), which defines the threshold above which the

To evaluate Thomas Buberl’s individual performance in respect

objectives set in his target letter:
●

Finalizing and launching
(achievement rate: 125%)

the

strategic

●

plan

The Group finalized and successfully launched its new strategic
plan including financial targets and a new capital management
policy.
The plan was well received by the market as shown by AXA’s
share price which outperformed the market following the
Investor Day, and which increased by 24% (dividends
reinvested) in 2024.
●

The Group developed and began implementing priority
Artificial Intelligence (AI) use cases as part of its Tech, Data and
Operation (TDO) program.

Implementing the strategic plan and delivering 2024
performance (achievement rate: 120%)

Despite difficult political headwinds, the Group delivered a
strong performance in 2024 (Revenue at +8%, Underlying
Earnings (UE) reached €8.1bn, up 8% and UEPS +8% and
Solvency II ratio at 216%) and is well on track to deliver on its
key financial plan targets.
Moody’s upgraded AXA’s rating outlook to positive.
The impact of hurricanes Helene and Milton has been limited
and the Group ended 2024 below the CAT budget, which
demonstrates the impact of the portfolio re‑underwriting
discipline undertaken over the past years.
Significant turnarounds have been completed in the three
businesses that faced difficulties in 2023 (UK Health, UK Motor,
Germany Retail).
On Technical Excellence, the new Group Underwriting function
had been implemented and has successfully supported local
teams.
The Group began implementing a new Health business unit
and strategy.
The Group executed the rollout of Secure GPT across the
Group.

Managing continued stability in Management
Committee, with solid succession plans and strong
collaboration while continuing to drive progress on
diversity and inclusion amongst leadership teams
(achievement rate: 105%)

Management has built a solid succession pipeline for each
member of the Management Committee.
Management continued to focus on gender diversity, and the
Group continued to compare favorably with its peers in the
insurance industry and other CAC 40 companies. In 2024, the
Group maintained gender diversity at all levels: the
Management Committee (38% women), the Partners Group
(48% women), and the “Global Leadership Network” (GLN)
(41% women). Progress has also been made among executives
(Top 2000) with an increase from 35.4% women in 2023 to
37.5%.
Across the Group’s global employee population, engagement
remains at a high level. The most recent Pulse results show that
engagement remained strong at 85%. Since 2017, the Group
has observed a steady increase in employee engagement levels
and this trend appears to be continuing.
●

Navigating the Group through political, regulatory, and
reputation risks in the context of a turbulent political
and geopolitical environment (achievement rate: 100%)

The Group executed the first year of its plan and achieved
strong results overall in spite of the political uncertainties
across several of its core European markets, uncertainties
stemming from the US election, the continuing impact of the
Ukraine war and increased regulatory / reporting obligations
across many of its markets.
●

Continuing to assess opportunities to optimize the
perimeter of the Group (achievement rate: 125%)

The Group took the strategic decision to exit Asset
Management and to enter into a long‑term investment
management partnership with BNP Paribas in line with its
strategy to focus on insurance business: Life & Savings,
Property & Casualty and Health.
The Group announced the acquisition of Nobis in Italy. This
acquisition will further diversify the Group distribution
channels, through long‑term agreements with car dealerships.
Each of these two metrics (Group Performance and Individual
Performance) is evaluated separately so that the overall
variable payout reflects performance against two distinct
components assessed independently. Each of these two
metrics is in any case capped at a 130% achievement rate.

3.5 Executive compensation and share ownership

The actual amount of variable compensation for the Chief
Executive Officer is determined using the formula: Variable
compensation due = target Annual Variable compensation x
(70% Group Performance +30% Individual Performance).
Since the 2020 performance year, the weight of the Group
Performance within the variable compensation assessment has
increased to 70% (from 50% previously) reducing the Individual

Performance weight to 30%. The Board of Directors, upon
recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee, aimed to strengthen the formulaic/
quantitative component of the Chief Executive Officer’s variable
compensation, aligning with market practices and institutional
investors' feedback. Transparency for each Group Performance
indicator has also been improved to show the target, floor, cap
and actual payout for each criterion.

As of 2022, the Board of Directors, upon recommendation from
its Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee,
decided to extend the deferral period from two years to three
years to align executive officers’ variable compensation with
shareholder interests. The Board of Directors also decided to
(i) eliminate the payout floor (previously set at 80% of the
deferred amount) to emphasize the “at risk” nature of this
component, and (ii) increase the payout cap (from 120% to
130%) in the event of superior share price performance.

Their fixed remuneration is completed by a total variable
compensation consisting of the annual cash variable
compensation and the annual Long Term Incentive grant (AXA
Performance Shares).

Under this mechanism, the Chief Executive Officer's deferred
amount of actual annual variable compensation for the 2024
fiscal year will be paid in three tranches, in 2026, 2027 and 2028.
Each tranche will be subject to performance conditions as
described in Section 3.5.1.1.

mechanical business performance score subject to a possible
Individual Performance modifier while remaining overall
capped at 130%. The business performance score is calculated
as follows:

Annual grant of Long‑Term Incentive (LTI)
In 2024, the Board of Directors, upon recommendation from its
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee,
granted Long‑Term Incentives (LTI) to the Chief Executive
Officer in the form of performance shares. They ensured that
the Performance Shares valued in accordance with IFRS
standards are not disproportionate compared to the aggregate
compensation granted (as described in following tables).
The Performance Shares granted to the Chief Executive Officer
are acquired at the end of a three‑year acquisition period, with
the entirety of the acquired shares restricted from sale during a
two‑year holding period. These Performance Shares are
integrally subject to performance conditions as described in
Section 3.5.3. and therefore do not guarantee any grant or
minimal gain.

to compensation has been designed for the other members of
the Management Committee to deliver strong financial and
non‑financial performance.

3.5.3 Shares subject to performance conditions (Performance
shares and international performance shares, restricted
shares and international restricted shares)
Shares subject to performance conditions are designed to
recognize and motivate the Group’s best talents and core skills
by aligning the individuals’ interests with the overall
performance of the AXA Group, and the corresponding
operational entity/business unit as well as with the stock
performance of the AXA share over the medium‑long term.
Shares subject to performance conditions generally result in
low shareholder dilution due to the possibility to deliver
existing shares, this choice being the one made up to this date.
Since 2022, the Board of Directors, upon recommendation from
its Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee,
may grant Performance Shares to Senior Management (1),
including members of the Management Committee and
Restricted Shares to other beneficiaries.
Performance Shares and Restricted Shares are usually granted
to beneficiaries residing in France, while International
Performance Shares and International Restricted Shares are
generally granted to beneficiaries residing outside of France.

3.5.3.1

Grant procedure

Within the multi‑annual cap authorized by the Shareholders’
Meeting, the Board of Directors approves all programs of shares
subject to performance conditions prior to their
implementation.
Each year, the Board of Directors, acting upon
recommendation from its Compensation, Governance &
Sustainability Committee, approves a pool of global
performance shares to be granted subject to performance.
The recommendations for grants of shares subject to
performance conditions are made by the management of each
operating business and by the Group’s functional department
heads. These recommendations are reviewed by the Executive
Management to ensure a global coherence and respect of the
Group’s internal equity principles. The amount and nature of
individual share grants (in the form of Performance Shares or
Restricted Shares) subject to performance conditions are then
decided by the Board of Directors, provided that individual

grants to the Chief Executive Officer and other members of the
Management Committee are preceded by a proposal of the
Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee of the
Board of Directors, taking into consideration their aggregate
compensation elements as well as the market studies carried
out by the Group together with an independent
compensation‑consulting firm. Furthermore, the grant to AXA
executive officers shall depend on the level of achievement of
the strategic objectives previously defined by the Board of
Directors.
The Company, in line with market best practices, applies a
regular and consistent formula to determine the number of
shares to be granted each year to the beneficiaries.
The Board of Directors also decided that the total number of
performance shares granted to the Company’s executive
officers each year may not exceed 10% of the aggregate
number of shares subject to performance conditions
(Performance Shares and Restricted Shares) granted during the
same year, to avoid an excessive concentration of performance
shares granted to the executive officers.
Since 2020, the annual grant of shares subject to performance
conditions occurs in March in order to simplify the structure of
the senior executives’ total variable compensation, so that they
are granted (i) a variable compensation in the form of cash
(annual bonus), and (ii) shares during the same month.

3.5.3.2

Rules regarding shares subject
to performance conditions

Each beneficiary receives an initial preliminary allocation of
shares subject to performance conditions (Performance Shares
or Restricted Shares) which is then used as a reference to
calculate the number of shares that will be definitely granted at
the end of a 3‑year performance period.
During the performance period, all shares subject to
performance conditions initially granted are integrally subject
to performance criteria regardless of the beneficiary’s status.

(1) Performance Shares are granted to approximately 250 senior managers as well as employees who are subject to specific local regulations on the date of
grant.

For the Performance Shares granted in 2024, the Board of
Directors, upon recommendation from its Compensation,
Governance & Sustainability Committee, reviewed the nature of
the performance conditions and the relative weight of each
with the objectives of strengthening alignment with the Group’s
strategic orientations and maintaining a balance between
financial and extra‑financial criteria, while taking into
consideration market practices observed in France and abroad
as well as feedback from certain institutional investors.

intensity in General Account assets) +10% sustainability
strategy (operations carbon emission) +10% sustainability
strategy (Inclusion and Diversity – proportion of women within
the Group’s executive population (1)), all capped at 130%.

It has thus been decided to (i) replace the relative criterion
linked to the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment

carbon intensity in General Account assets, also accounting for

3.5 Executive compensation and share ownership

The Performance Shares and International Performance Shares
granted to the Management Committee members (except for
the Chief Executive Officer) will be acquired after a three‑year
acquisition period, and 50% of the shares acquired will be
subject to a further two‑year holding period. The Performance
Shares granted to the Chief Executive Officer will remain
acquired at the end of a three‑year acquisition period, with the
entirety of the acquired shares restricted from sale during a
two‑year holding period.

75th percentile. Should AXA’s average score, calculated over the
performance period, be equal to the 50th percentile, only half of
the shares initially granted would be acquired. Finally, should
AXA’s average score, calculated over the performance period,
be lower than the 50th percentile, no shares would be granted.
This scheme does not guarantee a minimum gain to the
beneficiaries. Among the different performance levels, the
number of shares definitively granted is calculated on a linear
basis depending on the achieved performance.

The amounts corresponding to International Performance
Shares and International Restricted Shares are operating
expenses during the vesting period. They do not create any
dilution for shareholders as no new shares are issued. The
payment is made in shares. Should this type of payment not be
possible for legal, tax or any other reason, the payment could
be made in cash.

For Performance Shares and Restricted Shares, the
achievement rate of the performance criterion (performance
rate) is used to determine the number of AXA shares that will be
definitively acquired by the beneficiaries at the end of the
acquisition period, under the condition that the beneficiary is
still employed by the AXA Group. The number of AXA shares
definitively granted shall therefore be equal to the number of
rights to AXA shares initially granted multiplied by the
performance rate, which may not exceed 130% for the
Performance Shares and 100% for the Restricted Shares.
Furthermore, for the Performances Shares and Restricted
Shares, should no dividend be proposed for payment (outside
regulatory constraints) by the Board of Directors to the
Company shareholders for any of the fiscal years of the
performance period, the number of shares definitively acquired
would be automatically divided by two.

achievement of an average result of AXA’s score in the S&P
Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (DJSI), calculated

The fair value of shares subject to performance conditions
(Performances Shares and Restricted Shares) is determined in
accordance with IFRS standards. It corresponds to a historical
value at the date of grant, calculated for accounting purposes
as described in section 6.6, Note 23.3 “Share‑based
compensation". This value does not represent a current market
value, a current valuation of these performance shares or the
actual proceeds if and when the shares subject to performance
conditions are acquired.

Under the AXA Group Compliance & Ethics Code, all employees
(including the executive officers of the Company) are
prohibited from engaging in any transaction designed to hedge
the value of equity‑based compensation awards (shares
subject to performance conditions) granted under any plan or
arrangement maintained by AXA or any of its subsidiaries. This
restriction applies from the date of grant until such time as the
beneficiary receives the securities underlying the award upon,
for example, the lapse of restrictions on shares subject to
performance conditions or similar events. In accordance with
the recommendations of the Afep‑Medef Code, the executive
officers of the Company make a formal commitment to not
resort to such hedging transactions.

3.5.4 Stock options
From 1989 to 2018, AXA granted stock options to its corporate
officers and its employees in France and abroad. The purpose
of these grants was to associate them with AXA’s share price
performance and encourage their performance over the long
term. In 2019, after having progressively reduced the number of
stock options beneficiaries over the past few years, AXA’s Board
of Directors, upon recommendation from its Compensation,
Governance & Sustainability Committee, in order to simplify
AXA’s compensation policy and in line with market practice and
feedback received from a number of institutional investors,
decided to cease awarding stock options to corporate officers
and AXA employees.

Performance conditions
All options granted to all members of the Management
Committee until 2018 were subject to a performance condition.
This performance condition also applied to the last tranche of
each option grant (i.e., the last third of the options granted) for
all other beneficiaries of options.

Previous plans are still valid until their expiration (maximum
duration period of 10 years). They were granted at market
value, with no discount, and become exercisable by tranches,
generally in thirds between 3 and 5 years following the grant
date.

Pursuant to this performance condition, the options become
fully exercisable only if the AXA share price outperformed the
stock reference index of the insurance sector (1). No option
subject to such performance condition can be exercised as
long as this criterion has not been reached. This external
performance condition subjects the acquisition of the right to
exercise the options to the achievement of a fully objective and
public performance and allows the measure of the relative
performance of AXA compared to its main European
competitors over a period of at least three years.

Pursuant to the stock option plan rules, beneficiaries who
resign from the Group lose the right to exercise their options.

If the performance condition has not been met at the expiry
date of the options, these options are automatically cancelled.

On December 31, 2024, 68 AXA employees held a total of
2,475,227 outstanding options, representing 0.11% of the
Company’s share capital on the same date.

Furthermore, the Board of Directors decided that a second
performance condition would apply to all options granted
in 2017 and 2018, pursuant to which beneficiaries would not be
able to exercise their stock options in the event the net income
of the Group is negative, and for as long as it remains so.

(1) SXIP index (STOXX Insurance Index): a capitalization‑weighted index, which includes European companies that are involved in the insurance sector. As at
December 31, 2024, the index included 31 companies of the sector.

3.5.5 Share ownership policy for executives of the Group
AXA implemented a shareholding policy for the main senior
executives of the Group. This policy requires each executive to
hold, during the entire duration of his/her functions, a
minimum number of AXA shares (the “Minimum Shareholding
Requirement”) representing a multiple of their annual fixed
compensation during their tenure:
●

●

●

The Chief Executive Officer is required to hold shares
equivalent to three times his annual fixed compensation ;

Pursuant to articles L.22‑10‑59 II and L.22‑10‑57 of the French
Commercial Code, the Board of Directors has decided that,
until the Chief Executive Officer meets his Minimum
Shareholding Requirement, all Stock Options and Performance
Shares granted to him will be subject to the following
restrictions:
●

Management Committee members are required to hold
shares equivalent to two times their annual fixed
compensation ;
Partners Group members are required to hold shares
equivalent to their annual fixed compensation.

AXA shares, ADS AXA or shares of listed Group subsidiaries, held
directly or indirectly through Mutual funds or similar
investment vehicles, regardless of their acquisition procedure,
are considered for calculating the Minimum Shareholding
Requirement.
Each concerned senior executive must meet the Minimum
Shareholding Requirement within a period of 5 years as from
the date of their first appointment.

For Performance Shares, the Chief Executive Officer must, at

3.5.6 Retirement Commitments
Since December 2016, AXA has implemented a retirement
performance shares plan which benefits all executive
employees (directeurs) of AXA Group entities in France
including the Chief Executive Officer, Thomas Buberl.
It provides beneficiaries with portable pension benefits until
retirement in line with Directive 2014/50/UE/of the European
Parliament and of the Council of April 16, 2014, on enhancing
worker mobility by improving the acquisition and preservation
of supplementary pension rights.
These performance shares are subject to (i) a three‑year
acquisition period, and (ii) an obligation to hold the shares
until retirement. Beneficiaries may sell their shares for
diversification purposes after the three‑year period), provided
the sale proceeds are invested in a long‑term savings plan until
retirement.
The definitive acquisition of these performance shares is
subject to (i) the beneficiary’s presence in the AXA Group on
December 31 of the year during which the grant is decided, and
(ii) the achievement of a performance condition related to the
average AXA Group Solvency II ratio during the performance
period.
To acquire the totality of performance shares initially granted,
the average AXA Group Solvency II ratio during the performance
period must be at least 170%. However, if the average ratio is
150%, only half of the shares initially granted will be acquired.
No shares will be acquired if the average ratio is below 150%.
No minimum number of shares is guaranteed.
Between these performance levels, the number of shares
acquired is calculated on a linear basis depending on the
achieved performance.
In the event that no dividend would be proposed for payment
(outside regulatory constraint) by the Board of Directors to the

Company shareholders for any of the fiscal years of the
performance period, the number of shares acquired shall be
automatically divided by two.
The Board of Directors also decided that no more than 10% of
the total number of shares granted in any fiscal year should be
granted to AXA’s executive officers, to avoid an excessive
concentration of retirement performance shares amongst
them.
On December 11, 2024, the Board of Directors approved a grant
of retirement performance shares. Accordingly, 520,615
retirement performance shares were granted to 482 officers,
representing 0.024% of the outstanding share capital on the
date of the grant, of which 16,433 retirement performance
shares were granted to AXA’s Chief Executive Officer
representing 3.156% of the total grant.
All retirement performance shares granted are subject to the
performance conditions described above and calculated over a
three‑year period beginning on January 1, 2024 and ending on
December 31, 2026.
In addition, Group’s executives, as well as all other employees
of AXA Group entities in France, participate in a mandatory and
collective supplementary pension scheme with defined
contributions (collective insurance contract – contrat
d’assurance de Groupe as defined in article L.141‑1 of the
French Insurance Code). This AXA pension fund was
implemented in 2011 and benefits to the employees of AXA
Group entities in France falling within the scope of the
Collective Agreement of December 18, 2009. The individual
employer contribution rate is set at 0.75% of the total gross
compensation, which is not capped. The contribution base is
the same as the one used for contributions related to the Social
Security General Scheme. Monthly contributions are subject to
9.7% social charges (9.2% for CSG and 0.5% for CRDS).

published in the French official journal on December 7, 2023,

disclosures regarding the impacts, risks and opportunities
(“IRO”) related to environmental, social and governance (“ESG”)
sustainability matters that are material to the Group's activities
and operations. AXA has identified the material IROs through a
double‑materiality assessment (“DMA”) of its risks and
opportunities (i.e. an outside‑in perspective) and its positive
and negative impacts (i.e. an inside‑out perspective) based on
the ESRS.

in Section 4.1.3.2 - AXA’s material impacts, risks and
opportunities.

4.1.2 Sustainability strategy and business model
4.1.2.1

Sustainability strategy

AXA’s stated purpose is to “act for human progress by
protecting what matters”, which embodies the social purpose
deeply embedded in AXAs core business of insurance
(mutualizing risk to protect its customers which underpins
commerce and promotes economic development) and its
ambition to create sustainable value for the environment and
for society. As society and the economy are undergoing
significant transitions driven by demographics, technology and
climate change, our customers and the communities we
operate in are facing new threats and challenges, raising the
fundamental question of the insurability of these new risks. In
the face of multiple crises, AXA's sustainability strategy aims to
align and leverage AXA's assets to serve the purpose of
protection and insurability. These assets include: its ability to
invest in the global economy and to provide protection and
prevention services to individual and corporate customers; its
expertise in improving resilience against risks; but also the
responsible management of its different stakeholders’ interests.
AXA leverages its understanding of risks to help better protect
the basic needs of individuals and communities, such as
environmental protection, access to healthcare, prosperity, and
quality of life.

Employees
AXA’s own workforce is another group of relevant stakeholders.
Social dialogue at the local and Group level has always been
considered as essential to AXA's culture. At Group level, the
European Works Council (“EWC”) serves as an important forum
to engage with employee representatives. It meets twice a year
in plenary sessions chaired by the Group CEO, and seven times
in bureau sessions, which are more restricted. Together,
members of the EWC serve as representatives of employees’
views and interests. The Group’s sustainability strategy and
sustainability‑related initiatives are presented at least once a
year to employee representatives at the European level. These
exchanges are helping to roll out successful initiatives more
broadly across the Group, as illustrated by the Group's
commitment to enhancing the role of senior employees.
To effectively engage with all employees, AXA conducts regular,
voluntary and anonymous surveys to collect feedback about
their working experience at AXA. The results of the Pulse and
Inclusion surveys described below contribute to the
development of the People strategy and, consequently, are
leveraged to adapt human resources (HR) policies, such as
“Smart Working”, inclusive recruitment guidelines and action
plans related to multigeneration management and disability
inclusion.
AXA’s Global Pulse surveys are short and focused employee
surveys that measure a few components at a time to evaluate
the impact of AXA's strategy and business model on its own
workforce and facilitate the identification of areas for
improvement. These surveys are conducted biannually and
address topics relevant to AXA's cultural and organizational
strategy to check how employees feel about AXA – both its
business and its corporate culture. For example, the surveys
measure how confident employees are in AXA’s strategic
direction, and how connected they feel to their teams. A range
of key metrics, notably covering participation, engagement,
strategic alignment and team connection, have been measured
over time, allowing monitoring of historical trends over the past
five years. With the launch of AXA's new 2024‑2026 strategic
plan “Unlock the Future” and its People strategy: Care & Dare,
Pulse surveys have been enhanced in order to reflect
up‑to‑date market practices for assessing employee
satisfaction.
AXA believes that employees should feel welcomed and fairly
treated. To learn about the experiences of its employees and
seek ways to continuously improve, AXA conducts the Inclusion
survey
annually.

survey

optional
self‑identification questions on age, disability, gender, sexual
orientation, ethnicity minority and socio‑economic background
to help AXA track progress, spot patterns and identify
challenges faced by these specific groups. This enables the

and well‑being.

4.1 General information

4.1.3.2

AXA’s material impacts, risks
and opportunities

The following section gives an overview of the methodologies,
assumptions, and key steps involved in identifying and
assessing the material IROs that AXA has included in this
Sustainability Statement.

Methodologies and assumptions
This Sustainability Statement reports on sustainability matters
based on the double materiality principle and this is the first
year that such a statement has been prepared. In the absence
of specific judgement or guidance AXA has exercised its
judgement based on its own facts and circumstances. As this is
the first year of reporting for the Sustainability Statement, there
can be no comparison with prior reporting years. The DMA
process follows the ESRS and the guidance provided by the
European Financial Reporting Advisory Group (“EFRAG”). The
assessment considers both impact materiality and financial
materiality, focusing on potential and actual impacts on people
and the environment and the financial risks and opportunities
arising from sustainability issues.
AXA adopted a phased approach to identify material IROs
related to sustainability matters. This approach involved
breaking down the process into manageable stages, ensuring a
consistent identification of material IROs. This enabled AXA to
prioritize and focus on the most significant matters in its
sustainability reporting. Data sources include internal
reporting, external research, and engagement with affected
stakeholders. The DMA covered all of AXA's operations, that is
its own operations as well as upstream and downstream value
chains.

Identification of IROs related
to sustainability matters
As a first step, the assessment involved gaining a
comprehensive understanding of AXA's business activities,
business relationships, and key affected stakeholders, which
set the foundation for the subsequent analysis. Building on the
five main categories of stakeholders introduced previously (see
Section 4.1.3.1), and considering distinctly insurance and
investment activities, eleven groups of key affected
stakeholders have been mapped across AXA’s activities and
business relationships, which are depicted in the chart in
Section 4.1.2.2.

Then, AXA identified 16 relevant sustainability matters by
considering ESRS guidance, previous sustainability risk
assessments, and stakeholder engagement. A macro‑level
analysis of each topic was carried out and documented.
The analysis and the subsequent steps of the assessment were
supported by external publications and reports from
international organizations (such as the United Nations
Environmental Program or the World Health Organization),
European Union agencies (such as the European Environment
Agency or the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions
Authority), global research organizations (such as the World
Resources Institute or the Global Real Estate Sustainability
Benchmark), data providers (such as MSCI or ENCORE
Partnership) and other organizations (such as the WWF or the
Banque de France).
The relevance of the sustainability matters was evaluated
during a consultation phase that mobilized 125 internal experts
across various functions and entities, as well as 11 external
stakeholders using individual interviews and collective
workshops. The analysis eventually helped to confirm the list of
relevant sustainability matters to be assessed and more
specifically the 98 sustainability subtopics which required
further analysis.
The internal experts consulted were selected based on their
experience and ties to certain stakeholder groups, as well as
their expertise on sustainability issues. This allowed for a broad
and representative coverage of the Group's activities and the
integration of perspectives from entities that are more
specifically exposed to certain issues or stakeholders.
Employees from the following entities of the Group were also
consulted in the process: AXA XL, AXA Banque, AXA Partners,
AXA Japan, AXA China, AXA IM, AXA Climate, AXA Group
Operations, AXA Next, AXA European Markets, AXA Emerging
Customers, AXA International Markets, ALHIS, Healthanea, One
Health, Keralty, AXA France, AXA UK&I, AXA Switzerland, AXA
Spain and AXA GIE.
In parallel, a representative and diverse selection of external
stakeholders was interviewed to obtain their respective views
on the material impacts of AXA. The consultation sought to
gather insights from institutional investors, distributors,
corporate
and
individual
clients,
suppliers
and
non‑governmental organizations.

4.4.1 - Business Conduct impacts

AXA has mapped relevant sustainability topics to key affected
stakeholder groups and value chains to identify actual and
potential IROs. AXA then assessed impacts deriving from its
operations and business relationships.
Leveraging information gathered through the previous steps
and information about key stakeholders' areas of priority, AXA
initially identified 1,030 individual IROs relevant to the
materiality assessment. The review process focused on specific
activities, business relationships, geographies, and factors that
give rise to heightened risk of adverse impacts.
The long list of individual IROs was then reduced to 128
aggregated IROs after verifying that the grouping of
stakeholders and/or sustainability topics would not obscure
the conclusions of the detailed assessment.

Assessment and determination of the material
impacts related to sustainability matters
To determine the material impacts, AXA assessed their severity,
likelihood, and connection, while also considering the time
horizon. In the absence of specific guidance and
benchmarking, AXA exercised judgment based on its own facts
and circumstances and its own evaluation of the identified
impacts in relation to each other. As the information available
at this stage is insufficient and at times inconclusive to set
specific quantitative thresholds, the approach followed was to
rank the various impacts on each of the dimensions of the
analysis. Positive and negative impacts were analyzed
according to their scale and scope. In addition, negative
impacts were assessed according to their irremediable
character. Five‑point scales were systematically used to assess
the different criteria.
The overall impact materiality score was calculated as the
average of the scores related to the severity, the likelihood,
time‑horizon and the connection with the impact. Based on the
results of the initial phase of the DMA, the significance of a
matter and its priority for AXA also impacted the scoring.
Where a score was equal to or above 4, the materiality
assessment concluded that the impact is material. After
grouping, 10 positive impacts and 13 negative impacts have
been identified as material.

136

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

Sustainability
4.1 General information

Assessment and determination of the material
risks and opportunities related to
sustainability matters
The detailed assessment and scoring process for financial
materiality focused on evaluating the risks and opportunities
related to sustainability matters, but followed a similar
approach to the one used for the assessment of impact
materiality. In this case, the objective was to understand how
these factors may affect the financial performance of the
organization.
For financial materiality, it was necessary to assess the
magnitude of potential financial impacts and the likelihood of
these risks or opportunities occurring. The assessment also
took into consideration the time‑horizon. Judgement was
applied to assess how significantly the risks and opportunities
would affect the organization’s performance, including
financial, operational, and reputational aspects.
Similarly to its assessment of impact materiality, AXA exercised
judgment based on its own facts and circumstances, evaluating
the risks and opportunities in relation to each other, due to the
lack of specific guidance and benchmarks. The approach also
involved ranking the various risks and opportunities on each of
the dimensions of the analysis and systematically positioning
them on five‑point scales, with comments to support the
ratings.
The overall financial materiality score was calculated as an
average of the scores in relation to magnitude, likelihood and
time‑horizon. Based on the results of the initial phase of the
DMA, the significance of the risk or opportunity to AXA also
affected the scoring.
Whenever the score was equal to or above four, the risk or the
opportunity was deemed material, resulting in six individual
material risks and two individual material opportunities. AXA
determined it was appropriate to aggregate several risks for
purposes of the financial materiality assessment, resulting in
two material risks and two material opportunities.

Decision‑making process and internal
control procedures
In the context of the first implementation of CSRD reporting
requirements, the DMA was conducted in project mode,
overseen by a Steering Committee. The sponsor and the
project director regularly updated the Role in Society Steering
Committee (“RISSC”), the Audit, Risk and Compliance
Committee (“ARCC”), the Group Audit Committee (“GAC” or
“Audit Committee”) and the Compensation, Governance and
Sustainability Committee (“CGSC”) on the progress and the
results of the DMA. The final results of the DMA were reviewed
by the RISSC and the ARCC, before the GAC and the CGSC
jointly recommended them to the Board of Directors for
approval, together with this Sustainability Statement.
An internal control procedure was implemented to confirm that
the DMA had been prepared pursuant to ESRS requirements
and was approved by the relevant internal stakeholders. See
section 4.1.4.3 - Risk Management and Internal Control over
sustainability reporting.

Integration with Risk Management
and overall management processes
With the close involvement of Group Risk Management, the
DMA process was integrated into AXA's overall risk management
process, enabling AXA to evaluate its overall risk profile and risk
management processes. AXA management was consulted to
review and confirm risk prioritization. Additionally, the process
for identifying and managing material opportunities was
integrated into the overall management process thanks to the
engagement of Group Investments & ALM and Group
Underwriting Office.
For further information about AXA's risks factors and Risk
Management, refer to Sections 5.1 - Risk factors and 5.2 Internal control and Risk Management.

Since 2022, the Board of Directors has been conducting a
comprehensive review of its governance on sustainability
matters in an effort to clarify the duties of each Committee and
ensure that sustainability matters are regularly included in the
meeting agendas of the Board and its Committees. As a result
of this work, the Board of Directors notably decided to rename
the “Compensation & Governance Committee” the
“Compensation, Governance & Sustainability Committee” in
order to emphasize its role on sustainability matters, and
specify each Committee’s duties in respect of these matters.
In 2024, the Board's Terms of Reference were further amended,
notably to take into consideration the requirements of CSRD
and further clarify how duties among the Committees in
connection with sustainability matters, including sustainability
reporting, are allocated.
