The Management Committee is supported by the Role in
Society Steering Committee (“RISSC”). The RISSC is charged
with developing and overseeing the operational
implementation of the Group’s sustainability strategy and
reviewing material sustainability‑related issues faced by the
Group as well as monitoring material sustainability‑related
initiatives across the Group. The RISSC oversees the setting of
targets on key sustainability matters, including material IROs,
and is regularly updated on their progress. The RISSC meets
monthly and is co‑chaired by the Group Chief Underwriting and
Pricing Officer, Group Chief Investment Officer, and Group Chief
Communication, Brand and Sustainability Officer. The RISSC
reports back to the Management Committee on a regular basis
concerning material sustainability‑related decisions taken or to
be taken and issues considered in respect of which
Management Committee guidance and/or decisions are
needed.
Furthermore, the Audit Risk and Compliance Committee
(“ARCC”) is charged with reviewing all material audit, risk
(including sustainability‑related risks) and compliance issues
faced by the Group. The ARCC also reviews mandatory
sustainability reporting (including this Chapter 4). The ARCC
meets monthly and is chaired by the Group General Counsel,
and reports back to the Management Committee on a regular
basis on such topics. For more information, please refer to
Section 5.2 - Internal control and Risk Management.
Core elements of due diligence

investment and sustainable underwriting strategies
respectively. For more information, please refer to Section 4.2.1
- Climate change.

4.1 General information

4.1.4.3

Risk Management and Internal Control over sustainability reporting

AXA regularly communicates information related to its
sustainability strategy, objectives and risks notably through
Annual Reports and updates, whether prepared to comply with
regulatory requirements (such as this Sustainability Statement)
or on a voluntary basis (e.g.: Climate & Biodiversity Report). The
extra‑financial reports involve several professional families and
benefit from risk management and internal control frameworks
that were primarily designed for financial reporting. The
preparation of this Sustainability Statement follows the same
approach and diligence process, as further described below.
The governance framework applicable to external reporting is
set by the Group Standards, as supplemented by internal
guidelines, manual and procedures. Regular trainings are
available to staff in charge of reporting across the Group. As the
level of non‑financial disclosures increases and evolves, AXA
regularly updates the controls and processes applicable to
non‑financial reporting.
The guidelines and procedures are designed to mitigate risks
related to data collection and reporting and securing data
accuracy, coherence, and consistency. These measures of
control also aim to reduce the compliance risk (e.g.: liability risk
related to sustainability information disclosure) which is also
subject to the operational risk management framework. This
framework is deployed throughout the Group and the main
risks identified are regularly presented to the management via
established governance structures. For more details on Risk
Management and Internal Control framework, please refer to
respectively Section 5.2 - Internal control and Risk
Management and Section 5.7 - Operational risks .

144

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

From an operational standpoint, sustainability statements must
be prepared on an annual basis and are coordinated by the
Planning, Budget, Results, Central (“PBRC”) Department. Given
this Sustainability Statement was the inaugural publication, a
special operational governance framework was established,
which included a dedicated steering committee that was
co‑chaired by Group Finance and Group Sustainability teams to
coordinate and supervise contributions from all professional
families across the Group. Professional families also developed
and maintained a list of manuals (e.g.: the Sustainability
Reporting Manual, the Environmental reporting Methodology &
Process Handbook, the Digital Sustainability Environmental
Reporting Protocol and the Social Data Reporting (SDR) User
Guide) and controls to support the contributors across AXA's
entities. The respective heads of departments signed off on
their contributions before this Sustainability Statement was
presented to the ARCC, GAC, CGSC and Board of Directors. In
addition, during the preparation of this first Sustainability
Statement, PBRC organized a dry‑run exercise and regularly
presented outputs of their controls (e.g.: inconsistency or
incoherences in preliminary data) and related action plans via
established governance structures.
Prior to its communication to the Board of Directors or external
stakeholders (e.g.: communication to administrative or
supervisory bodies) this Sustainability Statement, which is
included in the Board's Management Report, was reviewed by
the ARCC and by the GAC and the CGSC during a joint meeting.
The overall Risk Management and Internal Control frameworks
contribute to providing the Group’s Senior Management and
Board of Directors with reliable sustainability reporting.

AXA for Progress Index: Strategic Key Performance Indicators
Since 2021, AXA has implemented a set of strategic key performance indicators, the “AXA for Progress Index”, to measure the impact and track
progress of AXA’s role in society. This tool is designed to: (i) integrate sustainability into the Group's activities as an investor, insurer and
company; and (ii) monitor AXA's sustainability strategy at the Group level. During its 2024 Annual Shareholders’ Meeting, AXA presented the
second edition of the “AXA for Progress Index”, highlighting (i) a new set of strategic targets aligned with the 2024‑2026 Group strategic plan
“Unlock the Future”, (ii) its commitment to meeting its 2030 decarbonization targets which are set in line with industry standards (1); and (iii)
AXA’s extra‑financial performance leveraging S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (2), an internationally recognized methodology.

General basis for preparation

Reporting scope
The scope of this Sustainability Statement includes all the
entities included in the Group’s Consolidated Financial
Statements (1) and, in addition, all controlled entities excluded
from the financial consolidation scope for materiality reasons
which are material from the sustainability‑related standpoint.
The metrics disclosed in this report are measured on this
scope, unless otherwise indicated.
The following subsidiaries are included in this Sustainability
Statement for the purposes of article 19a(9) and/or article
29a(8) (as the case may be) of CSRD:

Frameworks used
This Sustainability Statement follows the requirements set out
in the CSRD and is in line with the ESRS.
To develop its sustainability strategy and this Sustainability
Statement, AXA voluntarily uses certain international
benchmarks, as described in this chapter. These include, for
example, the Greenhouse Gas (“GHG”) Protocol (https://
ghgprotocol.org) for the calculation of CO2 emissions.
In particular, the concept of Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 as
part of the computation of the Group's GHG emissions is key to
understanding the information presented in the Sustainability
Statement.

Scope 1 refers to emissions related to fuel combustion on
the Group’s sites (e.g. gas, heating oil…) as well as fuel
combustion by vehicle fleet.
Scope 2 refers to emissions from combustion of fuels to
generate electricity, steam, heating and cooling purchased
and consumed by the Group's buildings and data centers.
Scope 3 refers to emissions from business travel,
Information Technologies (IT) equipment manufacturing
and purchased services, and emissions related to the
production of fuels and energy purchased and consumed
by the Group as well as emissions related to investments.

It should be noted that, as of December 31, 2024, Spain and
Germany had not yet transposed the CSRD into national law.
AXA subsidiaries Roland Rechtsschutz Versicherungs‑AG and
AXA Seguros Generales S.A. are nevertheless included in this
Sustainability Statement. XL Catlin Services SE is also included
in the scope of this Sustainability Statement (2).

In addition, AXA refers to the Science Based Target Initiative
(“SBTi”) (https://sciencebasedtargets.org) for the reduction
taregt setting of its own operation carbon footprint and to the
Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials ("PCAF") for the
calculation of its underwriting and investment carbon
footprint.

The DMA performed by AXA covers the full value chain of the
Group including upstream, downstream activities and its own
operations. The scope of AXA’s information disclosed in this
Sustainability Statement covers AXA’s own operations and,
where relevant, value chain information (see Sections 4.1.2.2 Business model and value chain and 4.1.3.2 - AXA’s material
impacts, risks and opportunities for more details).

Other benchmarks and frameworks are highlighted in the
relevant notes or presented in Section 4.5.2 - Reporting
methodologies.

Time horizons
As part of the DMA performed by the Group, the time horizons
that were considered when identifying actual or potential IROs
are aligned with the ESRS requirements: (i) short term horizon
is defined as equal to or less than one year, (ii) medium term as
between one and five years and (iii) long term as over five
years.

4.2

Environmental information

AXA is committed to addressing the environmental challenges
facing the planet. The aim of this section is to provide a
complete overview of AXA's environmental performance and
commitments, demonstrating its efforts to contribute to a more
sustainable and resilient future. The section first covers AXA's

approach to managing climate risks and seizing opportunities
to support climate transition, as well as its efforts to reduce its
carbon footprint. The section also addresses AXA's approach to
other significant environmental challenges, such as biodiversity
loss, pollution, and resource use.

4.2.1 Climate change
As a result of the DMA, AXA has identified 13 IROs on climate
change. AXA has developed policies and defined key
performance indicators to track progress in reducing the
adverse impacts associated with these IROs.
As an insurer, an investor and a company, AXA’s overall
sustainability strategy aims to fulfill two main goals: to act
against climate change and to develop health and protection
activities as an inclusive insurer.
In 2024, the Group presented the main priorities of its new
strategic plan “Unlock the Future.” The pillar “Expanding AXA’s
role in society” focuses on the Group’s role and actions in
supporting major transitions and protecting people from new
risks. These new strategic guidelines build on ongoing actions
to address climate change, and biodiversity loss and help
society adapt to the already visible effects of global warming.
The following section presents AXA's Climate Transition Plan
(“CTP”) (see Sections 4.2.1.2 to 4.2.1.5) followed by its policies,
actions and targets related to climate change adaptation and

mitigation across (i) its investment activities, (ii) its insurance
activities, and (iii) its activities as a company. The Group's
climate resilience analysis is presented in Section 4.2.1.6 Addressing climate change risks. AXA's CTP should be
considered partial and will be further enhanced. AXA further
acknowledges that this CTP does not yet include all
ESRS‑required information for a CTP due to its unavailability as
of the date of this Sustainability Report. This includes, for
example, the quantification of GHG emissions reduction per
key levers and the quantification of funding for the CTP
implementation. AXA is working to produce this information for
subsequent reporting periods.
For information on how climate considerations are integrated
into Group's governance, see Section 4.1.4.1 - Sustainability
governance at AXA.
Definitions, methodologies and, where applicable, the
associated margins of uncertainty are specified for the relevant
indicators in Section 4.5.2.1 - Environmental methodologies.

AXA has identified transition risks, in respect of its investment
portfolio, and physical climate risks, in respect of its insurance
portfolio:
●

●

physical risk refers to the direct impacts of climate change
on people (life and health) and property, such as those
arising from rising temperatures, an increased frequency
and severity of extreme weather events, fires and rising sea
levels, and changes in exposure to vector‑borne diseases.
transition risk refers to the risks linked to the transition to a
low‑carbon economy, including those related to changes in
the behavior and strategies of industrial actors, market
participants and customers in response to climate change
as well as related policy, regulatory and technological
developments including cross‑sectoral structural changes
stemming from the transition towards a low‑carbon
economy. Transition risk can impair the value of
investments held by insurers and reinsurers.

4.2.1.2

Developing AXA's Climate
Transition Plan

AXA’s CTP is embedded in and aligned with AXA’s overall
business strategy and financial planning. It is integrated at the
highest level with the Group strategic plan “Unlock the Future”
featuring a pillar “Expanding AXA’s role in society”. One focus of
this pillar is “Climate Transition” in order to: (i) expand
prevention and consulting services for adaptation, and (ii)
increase transition underwriting in core activities. The CTP
decarbonization targets, key levers and actions cover AXA's
investment, underwriting, and operational activities (1), and
were approved by the Board on March 12, 2025.

AXA's climate change disclosures are organized into three
subsections reflecting AXA's activities: as an insurer, as an
investor and as a company. Each subsection addresses certain
ESRS E1 disclosure requirements.

AXA's CTP decarbonization targets
As an investor, upon joining the NZAOA in 2019, AXA engaged in
transitioning its investment portfolio to net‑zero GHG
emissions by 2050 through investment‑related intermediate
targets set every five years. After an initial intermediate
decarbonization target for 2025, AXA announced in June 2023 a
second target (2) aiming for a 50% reduction in carbon intensity
of its General Account by 2030 compared to 2019. The target
encompasses listed corporate debt, equity, and real estate
equity (3), covering investee's Scopes 1 and 2 GHG emissions
according to the GHG Protocol, and is based on carbon
intensity per Enterprise Value including Cash (“EVIC”) for listed
corporate assets and carbon intensity per Gross Asset Value
(“GAV”) for real estate equity. This target on AXA's investment
emissions (Scope 3.15) has been determined on a bottom‑up
approach relying on investment opportunities assumptions
and portfolio composition and constraints and is in line with
NZAOA (4) recommendation and interpretation from the IPCC
Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) for a +1.5°C pathways.
As an insurer, in 2023, AXA extended its decarbonization
commitments to its insurance business by announcing three
underwriting portfolio decarbonization targets (5) on AXA's
insured emissions: (i) reducing the Insurance‑Associated
Emissions (“IAE”) for AXA’s largest corporate clients (6) by 30% in
absolute value by 2030 compared to 2021. This target is in line
with the modelled scenarios from the IPCC Sixth Assessment
Report (AR6) WGIII for the +1.5°C pathway with no or limited
overshoot (7); (ii) reducing IAE intensity (8) for all other corporate
clients within AXA’s largest markets by 20% by 2030 compared
to 2021; and (iii) reducing the IAE intensity (9) for retail motor
vehicles insured within AXA’s largest markets by 20% by 2030
compared to 2019.

(1) This coverage pertains only to specific aspects of investment, underwriting, and our own operations, and does not encompass all activities
(2) As of end of 2024, the target has not been externally assured.
(3) Representing €165 billion as of end of 2024, equivalent to 36% of AXA's General Account
(4) https://www.unepfi.org/industries/target‑setting‑protocol‑fourth‑edition/
(5) As of end of 2024, the targets have not been externally assured.
(6) Consists of 88 clients, detailed in 4.2.1.4 Addressing climate change as an insurer.
(7) The target is in line with the IPCC AR6 2021/2022 WGIII C1 Category that limits warming to 1.5°C in 2100 with a likelihood of greater than 50%, and reach or

4.2 Environmental information

As a company, AXA set in 2024 a decarbonization target for its
own operations to reduce by 50% its GHG emissions related to
energy, car fleet (Scopes 1 and 2) and business travel (Scope
3.6) by 2030 compared to 2019. The targets are science‑based
and set in accordance with SBTi guidelines, applying the
“Absolute Contraction Approach” in alignment with the Paris
Agreement. The target is in line with SBTi criteria (1) for a 1.5°C
pathway for AXA's GHG Scopes 1 and 2 emissions reduction,
and with a well‑below 2°C pathway for its GHG Scope 3.6
business travel emissions reduction.

AXA's CTP decarbonization targets are on a gross basis. For
further information on decarbonization targets please refer to
Sections 4.2.1.3 - Addressing climate change as an
investor, 4.2.1.4 - Addressing climate change as an insurer, and
4.2.1.5 - Addressing climate change as a company.

AXA's CTP key levers and actions
AXA's CTP actions contributing to its decarbonization efforts are articulated around two key levers: (i) the “climate change mitigation”
lever associated with the GHG emissions reduction that results from actions that are within its control, and (ii) the “supporting the
transition” lever associated with the complementary GHG emissions reduction that results from actions that depend partly on the
actions and decisions of AXA's value chain stakeholders – such as clients, investees, and suppliers –, with AXA playing a support role.

AXA has set a target to decrease the carbon intensity of its
General Account assets. This target covers the listed corporate
debt and equities, and real estate equity assets (3) from AXA
Group's General Account. The selection of 2019 as the baseline
year allows for the exclusion of impacts resulting from the
COVID‑19 pandemic and ensures a coherent representation of
investment portfolios, particularly following the integration of
AXA XL. From 2019 to 2024, the carbon intensity was reduced by
50%, from 64.5 tCO2 eq/€m to 32.4 tCO2 eq/€m. This reduction
is largely due to active portfolio management and investment
selection, including assets financing climate transition.
Consequently, AXA has already reached the 50% reduction in
carbon intensity and is on track to meet the 2030
decarbonization target. The Group is currently developing an
updated target. For more information on the Group's existing
target, refer to Section 4.2.1.2 - Developing AXA's Climate
Transition Plan, and for sectoral and geographical analysis,
refer to Section 4.5.3.6 - Other tables.

AXA also measures the carbon intensity of its sovereign
debt (4) portfolio in accordance with the accounting
methodology recommended by NZAOA, which is based on the
current version of the PCAF’s Global GHG Accounting and
Reporting Standard (5). Covering such asset class for AXA is key
since it represents an important part of AXA’s General Account
assets, with €127 billion at the end of 2024, constituting 27% of
AXA’s General Account. AXA has not set a target for sovereign
debt given the dependence on each sovereign’s
implementation of its national climate action plan (or
Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)) as well as
liquidity constraints on AXA's portfolio. The carbon intensity of
these sovereign assets is 150 tCO2 eq/€m and covers 100% of
AXA's sovereign debt issuers. Additionally, the carbon intensity
of a fraction of AXA's private assets, which is also currently
outside of the boundaries of the decarbonization target, is 67
tCO2 eq/€m, with a carbon intensity coverage of 93.6%, with
€42 billion at the end of 2024 (6), constituting 9% of AXA’s
General Account.

Mitigating climate change
AXA's investment policy
AXA has defined the AXA 2023 Energy Policy (6) to manage the
material IROs within its investment portfolio. Over time, AXA
has put in place restrictions to address certain activities in
sectors that may pose certain risks to AXA as an investor, such
as the risk of having an investment portfolio not adapted to
climate change and exposed to both physical and transition
risks. AXA also aims to contribute to the transition toward a
more sustainable and less carbon‑intensive economy. Since
2015 AXA has implemented several fossil fuel‑related
restrictions, including restrictions on investments in thermal
coal and oil & gas. An updated version of these restrictions is
part of a global Energy Policy published in 2023. The overall
objectives of the policy are to progressively align with net‑zero
trajectories and to limit negative impacts on the environment
by restricting investments in the fossil fuel industry.

4.2 Environmental information

With regards to AXA’s contribution to climate‑change mitigation
through its investment activities, AXA believes it is critical to
accelerate the transition of the energy sector towards a more
sustainable model, consistent with net‑zero trajectories. This
transition can only happen through regular engagement with
companies to implement ambitious climate transition plans.
AXA’s ambition, as an investor, is to focus its support for
companies engaged in the climate‑transition path.
The Responsible Investment Committee (“RIC”) defines,
implements and monitors AXA's Energy Policy applicable to all
investment decisions. This policy is made available to
stakeholders, including investment managers, and is
communicated through AXA’s investment guidelines, regular
stakeholder meetings, and published on the AXA website to
facilitate accessibility and implementation across all
investment‑related activities.
To support the implementation of this policy, AXA takes the
following actions for General Account and in Unit‑Linked assets
with controlled mandates:

On thermal coal,
AXA prohibits investments in companies that have the following
characteristics:
●

●

●

mining companies with a coal revenue share exceeding 15%
or with an annual coal production over 20 million tons or
engaged in thermal coal exploration or planning to develop
new thermal coal mines;
power generation companies with a coal share of power
production (energy mix) exceeding 15% or with over 10 GW
of coal‑based power installed capacity or planning to
develop new thermal coal‑fired power capacity;
certain coal industry partners, defined as manufacturers
(e.g. equipment suppliers) and infrastructure players (e.g.
port terminals, dedicated railways) developing significant
new coal assets.

In addition, AXA is committed to a long‑term “exit” strategy of
reducing exposure to the thermal coal industry to zero by 2030
in respect of companies established or operating primarily in
the European Union and OECD countries, and by 2040 in
respect of companies in the rest of the world, as recommended
by certain climate scenarios (such as the IEA “Beyond +2°C”
scenario).

With respect to this long‑term exit target from the thermal coal
industry, AXA has achieved the following performance: As at the
end of 2024, the Group’s General Account exposure to coal
assets (1) amounted to €1.2 billion, representing 0.3% of the
General Account. Exposure to coal decreased by 35% in 2024
and by 74% compared to the end of 2019. In line with the AXA
2023 Energy Policy, the remaining exposure is mostly
concentrated on corporates with a low share of coal in their
activities, i.e. below the Group's current 15% exclusion
threshold.

Use of the environmental criteria related to climate
change in AXA's investment decisions
While carbon‑efficient technologies and low‑carbon products
can provide alternative growth opportunities to transition to a
low‑carbon economy, this transition may materially impact
financial performance, especially for entities reliant on
carbon‑intensive operations and products. Indeed, several
industries, particularly capital‑intensive businesses with low
geographical diversification are exposed to material physical
risks, which may lead to reduced demand, increased
compliance costs and lower returns on investments. Climate
change also poses increasing risks associated with physical
risks which can damage physical assets and disrupt business
operations.
Based on an overall assessment of environmental materiality,
AXA’s Credit Research Team assesses which issuers are eligible
for Fixed Income investments (5), assigns internal credit ratings
(ICRs) along with investment maturity constraints, and
classifies industries into three Resilience categories - high,
medium, or low. This assessment is also performed on the
social and governance pillars; For more information, please
refer to Section 4.3.2.2 - AXA's impact as an investor.

Supporting the transition
Financing the transition, including the development of
renewable energy sector
Aligning with net‑zero goals requires significant investments.
AXA is capitalizing on climate transition investment
opportunities to redirect its investments toward low‑carbon
and transition activities.
AXA established a transition financing target starting in 2024.
The objective consists of investing at least €5 billion per year
through 2030 in climate transition initiatives. This target
encompasses all asset classes from AXA’s General Account,
including green and transition bonds, as well as capital
expenditures that facilitate the transition with respect to real
estate assets. This target, part of the “AXA for Progress Index”,
was validated by the RISSC and RIC. This objective is based on
ESG market opportunities and assumptions on AXA's
investment capacity. Additionally, the RIC monitors this target
on a monthly basis.

Engage with companies to encourage them to adopt
ambitious climate strategies
As an investor, AXA aims to conduct yearly outreach with top
management of issuers in its investment portfolio. These
meetings provide an opportunity to discuss long‑term strategy,
risk appetite and ESG commitments. In the context of
transitioning its investment portfolio to net‑zero (“NZ”) GHG
emissions by 2050, AXA Group has specifically initiated
engagement with the largest contributors to its investment
portfolio carbon footprint since 2023. The NZ engagement
objectives include assessing issuers’ commitments, strategy,
and performance in achieving their 2030 and 2050 NZ targets,
as well as aligning the Group’s investments with its
intermediate and 2050 NZ targets. The engagement outcomes
are presented on a yearly basis to the RIC. Based on these
recommendations, AXA can decide to restrict or ban
investments on issuers deemed unaligned with AXA's
ambitions.
In the context of its NZ engagement, AXA selected 59 issuers in
2024, representing roughly half of its listed corporate portfolio’s
carbon footprint (1). Most issuers are part of the utilities, energy,

Following its engagement in 2024, AXA has drawn conclusions

transition, with leading companies embracing new business.
Key strategic drivers include coal exit, investments in low

Addressing climate change as an insurer
In 2024, following the identification of material IROs as part of
the DMA, AXA announced Transition Insurance objectives,
replacing the Green Business ambition and expanding the 2023
net‑zero ambition for renewable energy (2).

As an insurer, AXA supports individual and commercial insureds
with risk transfer products and accompanying services to
address and adapt to the impacts of climate change.
In 2021, AXA Group developed a Green Business Program to
deploy Property and Casualty (P&C) products (insurance
coverage or services) that contribute to climate change
mitigation, climate change adaptation, transition to a circular
economy and limitation of biodiversity loss and pollution.
Please refer to the Green Business Report (1) for more details
and examples.

AXA organized its sustainability action under three pillars of
focus for the P&C Underwriting businesses: climate change
mitigation, climate change adaptation and supporting the
climate transition. The efforts are viewed in terms of both
“what” AXA insures, i.e. the activities and assets which
contribute to sustainability objectives, and “how” AXA insures,
i.e. the insurance products and services which support
customers sustainable behaviors and choices.

In 2023, AXA published targets to drive the decarbonization of
some P&C insurance portfolios as part of a net‑zero ambition.

Target setting and monitoring
Extending the Group
net‑zero ambition to its
‑
insurance portfolio
To mitigate the negative impact of significant GHG emissions
from insurance underwriting activities, AXA extended its
investment target of net‑zero to its insurance business in June
2023 by announcing the first underwriting portfolio near‑term
decarbonization targets. The specific portfolio targets are
complemented by concrete actions to support the transition,
with new services, insurance products, and sustainable claims
options for insureds (specified in 2023 for retail motor claims),
and specific engagement targets with AXA’s largest commercial
clients (set at 200 of AXA's largest clients to encourage insured
transition efforts).
AXA used the following methodologies, protocols, and
frameworks at the time of the target setting development in
2022 and 2023:
●

●

●

Methodology for associating insured emissions to insurers
developed by the PCAF, namely the PCAF Standard Part
C (2) published
in
2023
which
outlines
the
Insurance‑Associated Emissions ("IAE") methodologies for
most, but not all, Commercial lines of business and for the
retail motor line of business;
Target Setting Protocol version 1 (3) developed by the former
net‑zero Insurance Alliance and published in 2023; and
EU Taxonomy Environmental Objectives, to classify
sustainability aligned activities and assets.

The initial decarbonization targets were based on calculation
methodologies developed by the insurance sector. AXA expects
these methodologies to evolve with sector usage and
refinement, with the application of various global regulatory
definitions and requirements, and as data availability improves.
These initial decarbonization targets are a first step to better
steer the carbon footprint of AXA’s insurance portfolios.
The emissions scope coverage of the IAE targets for the
Commercial lines calculation is Scopes 1 & 2 of commercial
insureds. Following the PCAF recommendation regarding
Scope 3, AXA will consider the inclusion of Scope 3 emissions of
commercial insureds where significant and data allows. AXA
will continue to monitor the availability and quality of Scope 3
emissions of the largest insureds, for future inclusion. The retail
motor calculation follows the boundary of emissions of the
PCAF methodology, which considers the insurance influence to
be only during the use of the vehicle.
As mentioned above, the initial decarbonization targets, in both
absolute and intensity values, have been set on AXA's most
material underwriting portfolios both in terms of Gross Written
Premium and the related IAE values. Specifically,
●

the Commercial lines IAE targets represent 24% of the total
Commercial primary GWP (excluding reinsurance) of the
three specific entities for the year 2024. The in‑scope
premium versus AXA total Commercial GWP is 16%; and

This in‑scope subset was thus initially focused on the portfolios
within France, Germany, and further AXA XL portfolios within
the US, Canada, Australia, and UK and the industry sectors of
agriculture (2), transport, manufacturing (heavy), manufacturing
(chemicals), utilities, and mining. The target setting process
involved the use of industry sector decarbonization
pathways (3) within the in‑scope territories, projections of
energy decarbonization trends for the in‑scope nation states,
and assumptions about changes to the underlying portfolios (4).
A baseline year of 2021 was chosen due to greater availability of
quality emissions and revenue information for use in the
calculation.

The retail Motor decarbonization target setting exercise
followed a similar approach, namely: the retail motor portfolios
most significant to AXA on a GWP basis were chosen, these
being in France, Germany, Switzerland, and the UK. And
decarbonization pathways for individual motor transport for
the in‑scope geographies along with expected changes to the
underlying retail motor portfolios were then used to perform
the target setting exercise. A baseline year of 2019 was chosen
as the best representation of the underlying portfolios
compositions and driving behaviors pre‑pandemic as driving
distances declined significantly during the pandemic.
Progress on the 2030 targets is expected to be monitored
annually at Group level. Given the long‑term nature of the
decarbonization targets and the possibility for changes that
impact the chosen scenarios or alter the pathways (e.g.
geopolitical risks, pandemic, etc.), and may invalidate
assumptions made for the purposes of future projections (e.g.
introduction of a new technology, failure of a nascent
technology, etc.), and/or business decisions that differ from
assumptions (e.g. acquisition or sale of a business unit, etc.),
year over year changes will serve as a monitoring opportunity,
with progress evaluated on a three- or five‑year timescale from
the baseline year. Any re‑baselining or modifications to the
target would therefore also be done on this timescale, the first
opportunity being after 2026 reporting for the Commercial lines
target and after 2024 reporting for the retail motor target.

Thermal coal restrictions
To support the implementation of the AXA Group Energy Policy
and to achieve the objective of reducing exposure to the
thermal coal industry, AXA has taken, and planned to take,
certain actions described below.
In 2019, AXA updated its thermal coal exclusions requiring its
entities to cease renewing existing business and to avoid
underwriting new business under the following restrictions:
●

●

●

for mining: companies developing new thermal coal mines,
clients extracting more than 20MT thermal coal per year,
standalone thermal coal mines;

for industry partners: any company who derives more than

is developing new coal assets. This specific exclusion only
applies to infrastructure owners or operators (port terminals
and railways), exporters and traders.

and facultative reinsurance (excluding Employee Benefits
and treaty reinsurance) for greenfield Ultra‑Deep‑Water oil &
gas exploration and development projects licensed after
December 31, 2021 (defined as drilling at least 1,500 meters
below sea level); and
Shale oil and gas: as of January 1, 2024, AXA no longer
provides insurance coverage (either for new or existing
businesses) for shale oil and gas projects carried out by
companies deriving more than 30% of their total oil and gas
production from shale oil and gas. In addition, AXA does not
provide new stand‑alone, site‑specific insurance policies for
shale oil & gas projects for new and existing clients.

With the implementation of policies described above, AXA
continues to reduce its thermal coal exposure, in line with the
2030 target in OECD countries and 2040 target in outside OECD
countries.
To determine thermal coal exposure, AXA is supported by
third‑party data sources such as the Global Coal Exit List (GCEL)
from Urgewald. For its 2024 reporting, AXA used the 2023 GCEL
list. For its 2025 reporting, AXA will use the 2024 GCEL list, as
Urgewald releases the list for the year before (N‑1) at the end of
the following year (N). AXA may diverge from that database on a
case‑by‑case basis when more up to date or relevant data is
identified.
More than half of the remaining thermal coal exposure relates
to companies located outside Europe. AXA France and AXA
Spain, for instance do not have any thermal coal exposure. 70%
of remaining coal exposure belongs to companies that have
thermal coal share power production between 10% and 30% and have credible transition plans to replace their thermal coal
assets.
All companies that have a coal share power production above
30%, have been assessed to verify their climate transition plan,
full exit coal commitments aligned with AXA and with very near
terms goals to reach AXA Energy policy criteria.

Supporting the transition
As mentioned above, AXA organized the sustainability action
under three pillars of focus for the P&C Underwriting
businesses: climate change mitigation, climate change
adaptation and supporting the climate transition. To support
insureds with their transition efforts and consequently aid AXA
underwriting portfolio decarbonization, accompanying the

decarbonization targets are targets for engagement and
support to the transition with sustainable insurance solutions,
namely sustainable retail motor claims.

Engaging with corporate clients
The initial engagement target was set for 200 of AXA's largest
corporate insureds, with an objective to engage and support
them with their transition and mitigation efforts between 2023
and 2026. AXA implemented a comprehensive strategy in 2023
to identify engagement leads for each of the original targeted
clients, define the types of engagements possible (1), and train
all engagement leads for the engagement conversation. The
first set of engagements began in 2024 with 15 of the original
200 participating in at least one form of the qualifying
engagement activities. After introduction in 2024, the program
was extended to clients not among the original 200, a reflection
of the value of the dialogues. An additional 52 Commercial
lines clients participated in climate transition engagements in
2024 at AXA for a total of 67 engagements.
The Group as an insurance underwriter aims to play a role in
accelerating the transition to a resilient, net‑zero emissions
economy, and engagement with insureds is one of the efforts
deployed. The Group P&C Underwriting has also structured the
client engagement process based on three types of
engagement:
1. Sustainability dialogue: specific meetings with corporate
clients focusing on Decarbonization and Biodiversity &
Nature strategy;
2. Engagement with objectives, firstly engagement with
incentives to encourage behavioral change;
3. Engagement with objectives linked with AXA's sustainability
underwriting policies.

Transition insurance
While the original transition insurance target focused narrowly
on support for renewable energies, as part of its new strategic
plan, “Unlock the Future”, AXA introduced a transition objective
to reach a cumulative €6 billion GWP from 2024 to 2026 that
encompasses assets and activities beyond renewable energy.
AXA intends to develop a range of insurance products
contributing to environmental objectives such as climate
change mitigation, circular economy, pollution prevention and
protection of biodiversity and nature, including nature‑based
solutions. In 2021, AXA developed a Green Business Program to
encourage P&C products (insurance coverage or services) that
contribute to these environmental objectives (for example,
low‑emission energy infrastructure/vehicles, environmental
risks insurance, and pay‑how‑you‑drive programs).
In 2024, AXA announced transition insurance objectives for the
P&C business that contribute to one of the environmental
objectives as listed above (to replace the Green Business
Program), for both “how we insure", meaning the risk transfer
product and accompanying coverage terms, and “what we
insure”, as in the ”assets" or “activities” of the insured. For
example:
●

climate change mitigation – by enabling or encouraging the
reduction of GHG emissions, e.g. low‑emission energy
infrastructure and vehicles and pay‑how‑you‑drive
insurance programs;

limitation of biodiversity loss and pollution – by protecting

insurance in case of an accidental pollution.

Adaptation to climate change
Helping our clients with adaptation solutions
A fundamental role of insurers is to help insureds adapt to the
effects of climate change through pre‑event education and risk
mitigation, and post‑event recovery through indemnification
and crisis support. As part of AXA’s ambition on climate
adaptation, a goal of providing 9,000 solutions and services to
commercial insureds was set in 2024 within the “Unlock the
Future” strategic plan. This objective addresses the opportunity
to develop innovative risk prevention services and solutions for
commercial insureds, increasing their resilience to the effects of
climate change protecting them against climate‑related risks.
These adaptation solutions and services include, but are not
limited to:
●

risk consulting services like flood and wind studies;

●

remote and on‑site natural catastrophe surveys;

●

climate adaptation studies and field surveys;

●

severe weather alerts with recommended actions; and

●

training, such as through engagements with local
government, authorities, and standards makers to tackle
climate change adaptation at the community level.

For example, the AXA UK team has engaged extensively with
the UK Government on flood resilience and preparedness. In
2023, following AXA’s Building for the Future report, the
then‑Government accepted our recommendations to mandate
sustainable drainage systems for new developments in England
aimed at reducing surface water and sewerage flooding. AXA
continues to support public policymakers seeking to
future‑proof the built‑environment, with the publication of a
follow up report on extreme weather risks in England in 2024.

4.2 Environmental information

Target setting and monitoring

Mitigating climate change

Own operations decarbonization ambition

AXA's operations contribute to significant GHG emissions
(Scopes 1, 2 and 3). AXA has not implemented a global
decarbonization policy for its operational activities due to its
decentralized organizational structure.

As stated in the AXA for Progress Index, AXA targets achieving a
50% reduction in its GHG emissions related to energy (Scopes 1
and 2), car fleet and business travel (Scope 3.6) between 2019
and 2030, while financing carbon credits corresponding to the
amount of the residual emissions (1). 2019 has been chosen as a
baseline year for this target in order to remove the COVID‑19
effect and to ensure a consistent geographic scope following
the integration of AXA XL. This target is science‑based and set in
accordance with SBTi guidelines (2) to be compatible with the
1.5°C pathway on Scope 1 and Scope 2, and with a well‑below
2°C pathway on Scope 3.6.

Scopes 1 & 2 | Car Fleet and Energy
To effectively track the reduction of its Scope 1 (fuel
combustion on AXA' sites and car fleet) and Scope 2 (purchased
electricity, heat, or steam consumed in buildings and data
centers) emissions, AXA has established different targets
(market‑based value (3)) with two‑time horizons:
●

●

by the end of 2025, AXA aims to reduce its Scope 1 and
Scope 2 emissions (in tons of CO2 equivalent) by
respectively 25% and 35% compared to 2019 (4);
by the end of 2030, AXA aims to reduce its Scope 1 and
Scope 2 emissions (in tons of CO2 equivalent) by 60%
compared to 2019.

These targets apply to 100% of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions.

Scope 3.6 | Business Travel
To effectively track the reduction of its GHG‑emissions related
to business travel, AXA has set two targets, each associated with
distinct time horizons:
●

●

However, depending on the categories of emissions, the Group
issues guidelines that may be transposed into local policies. To
support Group entities in reducing their own operations’
emissions, the Group has developed an operational handbook.
This document provides a non‑exhaustive list of possible
climate actions and levers to address the obstacles to the
implementation of these actions.
The decarbonization initiatives and actions have been defined
according to AXA's market‑based targets. This approach
ensures consistency across the various regions where AXA
operates.
The following section details the different actions and
initiatives implemented either globally or locally to reduce
AXA’s negative impact on climate change.
As of the date of this Sustainability Statement, AXA is not in the
position to quantify the contribution of each decarbonization
action. The Group is working to be in a position to assess these
contributions in the future.

Energy (Scopes 1 & 2)
To achieve its objective of contributing to net zero and
reducing carbon emissions related to energy Scopes 1 and 2 by
2030 compared to 2019 levels, AXA has taken the following
actions:
●

by the end of 2025, AXA aims to reduce its GHG‑emissions
related to business travel (in tons of CO2 equivalent) by 18%
compared to 2019;
by the end of 2030, AXA aims to reduce its GHG‑emissions
related to business travel (in tons of CO2 equivalent) by 40%
compared to 2019.

Please refer to “Reporting on AXA’s footprint” below for Scopes
1 & 2, and Scope 3.6 decarbonization target 2024 results. For
further information on the other decarbonization targets AXA
has set on its Scope 3 GHG emissions, please refer to the
sections 4.2.1.3 - Addressing climate change as an investor,
and 4.2.1.4 - Addressing climate change as an insurer.

●

AXA aims to reach 100% renewable electricity sourcing for
its operations by the end of 2025. In alignment with this
objective, AXA has signed a Europe‑wide Virtual Power
Purchase Agreement ('VPPA') in 2023 which is expected to
cover the electricity consumption of all the Company’s
buildings and data centers in Europe from 2025 and onward
in addition to supplying the grid with renewable energy;
additionally, AXA is dedicated to achieving high levels of
energy efficiency in all owned buildings. Regarding sites not
owned by AXA and not meeting the environmental
standards satisfactory to the Group, various measures are
being taken, including the transition to more innovative and
energy‑efficient buildings. AXA Belgium, for instance, plans
to close an energy‑inefficient site by 2025 and relocate to a
significantly more environmentally friendly building, while
also implementing sustainable practices, such as solar
panels.

4.2 Environmental information

Car fleet (Scope 1)
As part of the Group's efforts to reduce its car fleet emissions, AXA
Procurement team has taken the lead on the Request for Proposals
(RFP) for car fleets across all entities in Europe.
The RFP took into account European regulations on CO₂
emissions along with legislative changes related to ecological
penalties. Furthermore, sustainability considerations were
integrated into the supplier selection process. The GHG
emissions of the proposed vehicles and the countries of
manufacture have been assessed and included in the final
recommendations made by Group Procurement to European
entities ensuring alignment with the Group’s decarbonization
target.
Entities are also granted the flexibility to establish specific local
initiatives to reduce their car fleet’s carbon footprint to reach
the overall 2030 target set by the Group:
in anticipation of upcoming legislation related to company
car fleets, AXA Belgium has been exclusively procuring
electric vehicles since 2024, with the goal of achieving a fully
electric vehicles fleet by 2026 (1);
similarly, AXA France is implementing initiatives such as
transitioning to 100% electric vehicles for executives and
offering financial compensations to employees eligible for a
company car who choose alternative commuting options.

Business Travel (Scope 3.6)
To achieve the decarbonization target of -40% by 2030
compared to 2019 for the business travel category, the Group
revised its global travel framework in 2024. This framework
incorporates sustainability guidelines that are applicable to all
AXA entities, with the possibility for local travel policies to be
more restrictive while maintaining the established standards.
The sustainability guidelines are centered on proactively
managing travel volumes to reduce the overall carbon footprint
of the Group. These guidelines encompass measures focused
on reducing AXA’s GHG emissions, with specific
recommendations for alternative transportation options. These
recommendations include utilizing trains for trips under 3
hours instead of air travel, opting for public transport over taxis
(excluding high‑risk countries), choosing green taxis (Hybrid or
Electric Vehicles) over conventional vehicles, and prioritizing
the rental of low GHG emission cars.

Digital technologies (across Scopes 1 & 2, Scopes 3.1,
3.2 and 3.3)
AXA has the ambition to leverage data and digital technologies
to improve its operational efficiency. However, the
unsustainable environmental impact of Information and
Communications Technology (ICT) has been acknowledged by
certain global institutions, including the United Nations in their
“Digital Economy Report” and this underscores the urgent need
to “embrace a new mindset that considers sustainability at
every stage of the digital life cycle” (2).
This observation led Group IT to launch the “Digital
Sustainability” program in 2020. This program aims to measure
the carbon footprint of AXA’s digital activities within a scope
that includes data centers, workplace equipment and digital
services purchases like cloud computing and network services
from main AXA's providers (3). It considers both the impact of
hardware manufacturing phase and of energy consumption
linked to its usage. The program's goal is to identify levers to
reduce this environmental footprint and to support the
transformation of AXA's organization to better manage its
emissions.
Combining the Group's ambitious Tech, Data & Operations
strategy while setting environmental targets is a challenge,
which AXA aims at answering with the following actions:
●

●

●

●

validate its strategy by the Digital Sustainability program
Steering Committee chaired by the Group Chief Information
Officer and composed of entity Chief Information Officers
with the support of Digital Sustainability Leaders in AXA
entities;
set internal GHG digital targets for the Group Information
Technology Department and cascade them across AXA
entities;
further reduce the demand for new equipment by extending
its lifespan and minimizing the number of devices per
employee;
secure timely cloud migration, decommissioning replaced
servers and assess the environmental impact of new
projects, services and technologies, such as Generative
Artificial Intelligence (4);

Supporting the transition
Supply chain decarbonization program
AXA has developed an internal program for supply chain
decarbonization to address the adverse impact of AXA’s
operations on climate change. The primary objectives of this
program are:
●

●

to enhance the precision of GHG emissions measurement
from goods and services procured from suppliers; and
to promote wider adoption of carbon reduction strategies
across the supply chain.

Through this program, AXA is expecting a reduction in its own
emissions related to the procurement of goods and services.

This program specifically focuses on the General Expenses
("GenEx") and IT supply chain, excluding Insurance
Procurement (Scope 3, category 1).
Through the implementation of this program, AXA aims to meet
the GHG Protocol standards for the emissions measurement
objective. This program is accessible to all stakeholders,
including the procurement and sustainability community.
Furthermore, it has been communicated to top suppliers
during executive reviews and/or webinars (e.g. joint webinar
with EcoVadis on AXA supply chain decarbonization on October
8, 2024).
Key actions that are being implemented on the procurement
side include:
●

●

●

●

a pre- and post‑contractual assessment of suppliers by a
third party on ESG topics, with a specific focus on
carbon‑related issues;
inclusion of carbon‑related considerations in the
procurement process, including sustainability criteria in
requests for proposals ('RFPs') regarding suppliers’ carbon
data and their commitment to reducing emissions with
credible transition plans, as well as the inclusion of
sustainability clauses in procurement contracts;
strengthening of ESG performance monitoring for key
suppliers with notably the implementation of action plans
to enhance their contribution to AXA’s sustainability
strategy;
training of AXA procurement associates to raise awareness
and promote action within the supply chain.

Target set on Purchased goods and services (Scope
3.1)
On purchased goods and services, AXA has set a target of
achieving 66% of General Expenses ('GenEx') and IT suppliers
(in spend) having committed to a credible transition plan.
Suppliers with credible transition plans have been defined as
those that have science‑based targets with the most
far‑reaching and credible transition plans, based on a case‑by
case review that aligns with the latest and most ambitious
climate science recommendations. For instance, some
initiatives could be the SBTi, Exponential Roadmap Initiative, or
The Race to Zero.

Reporting on AXA’s carbon footprint
Revised comparative figures
Given 2024 was the first year in which CSRD applied to AXA, it
has reviewed the calculation of the carbon footprint related to
its own operations. The main changes relate to the removal of

entities that are not in the scope of the CSRD but that were
previously considered (notably entities not controlled), as well
as the refinement of extrapolation methodology (applied for
estimating consumption data from AXA's sites of less than 50
FTEs) that is applied at entity level.
Additionally, Scope 3 GHG emissions relating to emissions of
AXA agencies (reported in downstream transportation and
distribution) have been included in the calculation for 2024.
The Scope 3.1 GHG emissions related to purchased goods and
services was extended in 2024 to cover emissions related to all
GenEx and IT categories (and not solely cloud and network
services on the main providers). Due to lack of data, the
retroactive impact on 2019 and 2023 results was assumed to be
equal to the additional 2024 GHG emissions in this category.
The Scope 3.2 category related to capital goods also includes
the emissions from additional equipment such as headsets,
keyboards, mice and docking stations.
Consequently, the GHG emissions data for 2019 and 2023
reported in the previous annual reports have been restated for
the purpose of this Sustainability Statement.

Sustainability
4.2 Environmental information

GHG emissions related to energy (Scopes 1 and 2), car fleet and
business travel decreased by 38% between 2019 and 2024, and
amounted to 101,033 tons equivalent CO2 (tCO2 eq) in 2024.
Those emissions remained flat as compared to 2023, as the
resumption of business travel has been offset by a decrease in
vehicle fleet and energy emissions.
The target of decrease by 20% between 2025 and 2019 on the
GHG emissions related to energy, car fleet, business travel and
IT was already reached in 2024 with a reduction of 30%.

Analysis by Scope
GHG emissions related to Scope 1 was 21,054 tCO2 eq (1) in
2024, decreasing by 4% as compared to 2023 mainly due to the
switch to hybrid and electrical vehicles in several countries this
year. In 2024, 22% of the km travelled by AXA's Group's vehicle
fleet were covered by hybrid and electric cars versus 11% last
year. The decrease in GHG emissions from vehicle fleet reach
26% versus 2019 this year.
GHG emissions from Scope 2 Market‑based was 23,146 tCO2
eq (2) in 2024, decreasing by 11% as compared to 2023 driven by
a lower energy consumption and an increase in the share of
renewable energy.
GHG emissions from Scope 3.6‑Business travelling increased by
7%. Despite the measures taken at entity level to reduce their
impacts, several inter‑continent events occurred in 2024,
leading to an increase in the number of km travelled this year.
Yet, the emissions associated to business travel decreased by
29% compared to 2019, on track regarding the 2030 target of
40% reduction and well beyond the 2025 target of 18%
reduction, confirming sustained changes of habit.
GHG emission from Scope 3.1‑Purchased goods and services
remained stable, however the portion related to cloud
computing and data centers services increased by 23% due to
the transfer of services from AXA data centers to the cloud
purchased services, and to the organic growth. AXA expect
better performance from cloud hyperscalers compared to data
centers it operates directly. While progress has already been

made, more transparency from cloud services providers is
needed to confirm this assumption, for instance in electricity
and water consumption, manufacturing footprint of digital
equipment, digital waste and equipment lifecycle policy.
GHG emissions from Scope 3.2‑Capital goods increased by 5%
as compared to 2023, due to the increase in number of
terminals tracked (+7%) that is partly compensated by the
lifespan extension levers activated by AXA entities. Furthermore
the latest hardware generation used in AXA's data centers,
though more energy‑efficient, happened to have a higher
manufacturing footprint.
GHG emissions from Scope 3.3‑Fuel and energy related
activities decreased by 10%, due to the decrease of energy
consumption and the decrease in the life cycle upstream
emissions factor provided by the International Energy Agency.
GHG emissions from Scope 3.9 - Downstream transportation
and distribution related to the emissions from energy used by
AXA Agencies. The measurement has been introduced this year,
retroactively since 2019, with no material difference versus 2023
due to a stable number of agencies.
GHG emissions from Scope 3.7 employee commuting
decreased by 29% as compared to 2023, due to lower number
of kilometers travelled for commuting reported by AXA
employees that answer to the AXA's Transport Survey in 2024.
The transport survey has been simplified to improve the data
quality, however there is still high volatility due to low level of
answers collected (around 20% of employees).
GHG emissions from digital increased by 4% market based
compared to 2023, from the increase in emissions of capital
goods (explained above) and the emissions from electricity of
terminal due to higher number in inventories and the
consequence of the winter 2023 European energy crisis, who
caused the IEA’s electricity emission factors to inflate in 2024.
This result is to compare to the global IT sector GHG footprint
that grows at an average rate of 6% per year according to The
Shift Project 2021 report (3).

In addition to the emissions associated with its own
operations, the overall Scope 3 GHG emissions of AXA include
the financed emissions, which correspond to the carbon
footprint of General Account assets, including all real estate
asset categories. For further details, please refer to
paragraphs 4.2.1.3 - Addressing climate change as an investor Target setting and monitoring.
On top of the Scope 3 categories disclosed above, AXA also
analyzed the carbon footprint of its insurance underwriting
portfolios through the evaluation of its Insurance‑Associated
Emissions (IAE) as well as the carbon footprint related to third
party assets managed by AXA IM. For further details, please
refer respectively to Sections 4.2.1.4 - Addressing climate

to its insurance portfolio and 4.2.1.3 - Addressing climate
change as an investor - Monitoring financed GHG emissions.

Contributing to net zero
As provided in its AXA for Progress Index 2024‑2026, AXA targets
achieving a 50% reduction in its GHG emissions related to
energy Scopes 1 and 2, car fleet and business travel, between
2019 and 2030, while financing GHG emission reduction
projects outside the value chain by purchasing carbon
credits (1), corresponding to the amount of residual
emissions (2). AXA's selection process is based on specific
criteria, such as: (i) projects must have a significant positive
environmental impact; (ii) they must be located in countries
where AXA operates; and (iii) they must meet high quality
standards through certification (including Gold Standard for the
Global Goals, Verified Carbon Standard - Verra, Climate Action
Reserve Standard, ISO 14064‑2 standard and CERCARBONO
Certified Carbon Standard).
For 2024, the GHG emissions considered were aligned with the
scope covered by the 2025 targets (3). As a result, AXA has
financed the equivalent of 154,461 tCO2 eq carbon credits
generated by the following projects:
●

Restoring the Mayan Jungle of Calakmul in Conhu’as:
This project, located in Mexico, focuses on the restoration
and protection of 47,400 hectares of tropical forest in a rural
community. It seeks to conserve local biodiversity and
strengthen resilience to climate change and natural
disturbances while also addressing fires and illegal logging.
(Climate Action Reserve);

●

●

Biogas Development Sichuan: This project, located in
China, helps avoid carbon emissions and aims at supporting
low‑income rural Households in Sichuan with advanced
biogas digesters and smoke‑free biogas cookstoves. After
switching to biogas, each participating smallholder farmer
family saves about 2 tCO2 eq of methane and carbon
dioxide emissions every year. This project substantially
affects nearly 400,000 rural Households and avoids
approximately 800,000 tCO2 eq per year. (Gold Standard for
the Global Goals);
REDD+ Colombia: This project is a forest conservation
initiative in the Amazon region of Colombia, aimed at
protecting 130,777 hectares from the threat of unplanned
deforestation. It protects around 60,000 hectares of
threatened forest in the Mesoamerican Biological Corridor.
The project has avoided 5.3 million tCO2 eq. (CERCARBONO
Certified Carbon Standard);
Solar Power Project Ouarzazate: This project, situated
200km southeast of Marrakesh, is part of the world's largest
concentrated solar power project. It is expected to feed an
annual average of 698 MWh of clean electricity to the
Moroccan power grid, thereby improving national energy
supply. With the provision of clean energy, the project
reduces the amount of power that would otherwise have
been generated by fossil‑fueled plants. It contributes to a
reduction of approximately 400,000 tCO2 eq per year.
(Verified Carbon Standard - Verra);
San José del Rincón: This project, located in the Monarch
Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in the State of Mexico, aims at
improving forest management and promoting reforestation,
restoration of degraded areas, fire protection as well as
project monitoring. Through improved forest management,
reforestation, protection and conservation of 4,839 hectares
of forest, this project helps capture approximately 24,101
tCO2 eq per year (Climate Action Reserve standard) (4);
Improved Forest Management in Durango: This project,
located in Mexico, is a forest carbon capture initiative
aiming at mitigating climate change through enhanced
forest management practices. Spanning over 8,918
hectares, it involves several key interventions including
thinning, selective logging, reforestation and soil and water
conservation. These activities are designed to enhance
carbon removal while promoting sustainable land use.
(Climate Action Reserve Standard);

Addressing climate change risks

Two risks related to AXA’s investment and insurance activities
were identified as part of the DMA: (i) the risks to hold assets
with unrealized losses and (ii) increasing costs of claims paid
out to AXA's policyholders due to higher frequency and
intensity of climate‑related perils. It is necessary to keep
monitoring these risks to identify material changes in
underlying trends whose magnitude may challenge the
insurance business model over the medium and long term. The
material risks together with other IROs outlined in the context
of CSR are consistent with the priorities of AXA's sustainability
strategy as presented in the Group's strategic plan “Unlock the
Future” and in the 2024 AXA Group Climate and Biodiversity

176

182,000

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

Report. These publications detail AXA's objectives and
commitments to address both risks and opportunities in
relation to climate change but also illustrate how the climate
risk analysis requests inputs from various expert teams to
better gauge physical and transition risks. The key elements of
this analysis are further investigated in the context of the Own
Risk & Solvency Assessment (“ORSA”) which is prepared in line
with the Solvency II directive guidelines and discussed with the
Autorité de contrôle prudentiel et de résolution (“ACPR”). This
assessment is also complemented by the stress test exercises
which are launched by ACPR (e.g.: Climate Pilot Stress test in
2020, Climate Stress Test in 2023).

Sustainability
4.2 Environmental information

The exchanges with the ACPR (or other supervisors) around
climate‑related physical and transition risks are opportunities
to evaluate the impact of long‑term stressed scenarios on AXA's
profitability and financial strength (e.g.: adverse impact on
reserves and claim payments, deterioration of combined ratio,
loss in fair value of real assets) and more generally speaking to
consider challenges such as insurability issues and the
resilience of insurers’ business model.
AXA also conducted a resilience analysis in 2024 whose main
steps and outcomes are summarized below.

Scenario analysis
The quantitative estimate of the financial impact of the main
ESG risks are evaluated based on available climate change
scenarios offering high‑level narratives to illustrate the
potential trajectories of the economy under different
assumptions. The scenarios employed in the Group’s ORSA are
as follow:

The Group built its business resilience analysis based on
reference scenarios released by the Intergovernmental Panel on
Climate Change (“IPCC”) and the Network for Greening the
Financial System (“NGFS”) which are widely used by economic
players across the insurance industry and sectors.
As part of the ORSA and the stress‑tests exercises, AXA conducts
an analysis of its physical risk and adopts different time
horizons depending on the nature of the considered business
or underlying risk factors. These exercises typically include a
short‑term time horizon (3‑5 years) but may also cover a
medium (10 years) or longer‑term view (30‑50 years).
Regarding the transition risk assessment, it was decided to
follow the scenario selected by the European Insurance and
Occupational Pensions Authority (“EIOPA”) in the context of the
2022 climate stress test required by the Institutions for
Occupational Retirement Provision (“IORP II”) Directive. This
scenario assumes that new climate policies are not introduced
until 2030 and assesses the impact of a delayed and yet, firm
policy action towards transition to a low‑carbon economy so
that the global temperature remains below 2°C by 2100. This
scenario aims at showing the shocks that would suddenly
impact financial markets, across asset classes and sectors.

Lastly, AXA uses the Climate Value at Risk (CVaR) developed by
MSCI to analyze the physical and transition risks (see dedicated
sub‑section below) under two temperature rise scenarios
including one limiting global warming to +1.5°C.

Physical risks to AXA’s insurance businesses
As identified in the DMA, the risk for AXA of having an insurance
portfolio not adapted to more frequent extreme natural events
and more impactful climate related perils is reflected through
the physical risks to AXA’s Property & Casualty (“P&C”) business
and AXA’s Life and Health business.

Physical risks to AXA’s P&C businesses
Over the past risk assessment exercises (1), P&C physical risks
have been evaluated through modular approaches (from
sophisticated to simple modeling were used to represent the
three drivers of natural risks (changes in hazard, exposure, and
vulnerability) and model the evolution of Average Annual
Losses (2) (“AAL”) according to forward‑looking scenarios
(pessimistic versus optimistic views).

(1) ACPR 2020 Pilot and 2023 Stress test exercises, Group ORSA report
(2) AAL represent our expected incurred losses resulting from modeled hazards over a one‑year time horizon as per current climate parameters.

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

177

4

Sustainability
4.2 Environmental information

The materiality assessment highlighted that for the P&C
business, the most significant physical risks from climate
change by 2050, under a pessimistic scenario (RCP 8.5), would
be rising temperatures, increasing sea levels, and extreme
precipitation. The assessment also reviewed risks such as
extra‑tropical cyclones, severe convective storms, droughts,
hail, or wildfires focusing on the perils that could primarily
impact AXA’s financial indicators through its insurance
business. In this perspective, there is either limited claim
experience in the Group's past business exposure or insufficient
scientific consensus on other hazards mentioned in the EU
Taxonomy to adequately assess these risks.
Due to the Group’s worldwide exposure, which affords a high
level of intrinsic diversification, the possible evolution of future
P&C natural catastrophe (“NatCat”) claims remains driven
mainly by changes in future exposure (demographic changes
and wealth growth), rather than an increase in the climate
hazard itself.
Based on the 2020 ACPR Climate Pilot Stress test which
provided more details on the French market, the Group’s
current studies show that the fluvial and pluvial flood risk
would increase by 1.5% per year up to 2050 in France (80% due
to evolving exposure and 20% due to changing physical flood
characteristics) under a pessimistic climate scenario (RCP 8.5).
Such a change could be managed in a timely manner with no
significant impact on AXA by adapting AXA’s underwriting,
pricing, reserving or reinsurance strategy and fostering
prevention initiatives.
The findings of the 2023 ACPR climate stress test align with
previously identified trends: the overall impacts are limited and
primarily result from the combined effects of inflation and
changes in exposure, outweighing the isolated impact of
climate change on natural disasters.

Physical risks to AXA’s Life and Health businesses
The potential physical risks to the Life and Health business are
related to indirect effects of global warming temperature and
primarily impacts Protection & Health products.
Generally speaking for Life business, climate change could
impact the underlying trend of the future mortality and
morbidity rates. This risk is relevant for insurance products
which pay out contingent on death of the insured person
(Protection business) or on survival (for example, “annuities”) of
the insured person. The risk of increased morbidity and
medical expenses is limited given that Health policies are often
renewed annually. The Group participated in recent ACPR
stress tests and launched its own study to further investigate on
the potential impacts by 2050.

During the 2020 Climate Pilot Exercise and the 2023 Climate
Stress test, the ACPR focused on two physical scenarios
(vector‑borne diseases and pollution in urban areas) and
provided data for metropolitan France with shocks by age‑band
– the elderly being the most affected population.
In 2020, based on the results of ACPR Pilot exercise, AXA
estimated that AXA’s Protection & Health business had the
potential to withstand climate change impacts over a 30‑year
period. The timing of the impact depends on the pace of the
temperature increase, which remains highly uncertain. The
main financial impact would come from the deaths induced by
the pollution scenario that would mainly hit the largest
metropoles, although expected to be limited under a
conservative approach.
In 2023, the conclusions of the most recent ACPR Climate Stress
test were derived from a less pessimistic scenario (RCP 4.5
instead of RCP 8.5 (1), and confirmed the limited impacts
observed during the ACPR Pilot Exercise.
In 2021, AXA also conducted a six‑month study on the impact of
climate change on its health and protection business by
deriving AXA’s own air pollution mortality shocks more adapted
to its portfolio. Without applying any reactive management
actions such as repricing, AXA’s internal study further evidenced
the relative resilience of the AXA Protection & Health business
to climate change in general and the air pollution scenario in
particular.
The results of these studies and stress tests support the
conclusion that climate change physical risks may have a
long‑term financial impact on Life & Health businesses,
although with low materiality and not in an abrupt way. AXA
current assessment is that potential changes would occur at a
speed that would allow for adequate management actions
such as repricing.

Physical and transition risks to
AXA’s investments
As identified in the DMA, the risk for AXA of having an
investment portfolio not adapted to climate‑change and
exposed to both physical and transition risks (with the risk of
holding stranded assets in its investment portfolio) is reflected
through physical risks to the Group’s real estate assets and
transition risks to the Group’s investments.

(1) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) have been defined by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) experts and used

activities). The median temperature corresponding to scenarios RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 are shown in the table above which summarizes the scenarios
covered in the Group ORSA.

Physical risks to AXA’s real estate assets
Extreme weather events may impact the Group’s direct
property assets, which are subject to both physical and
transition risks in TCFD terminology. AXA has a significant
amount of claims‑related data to conduct a physical risks
analysis of its real estate portfolio. The underlying climate
mechanisms overlap with property insurance and reinsurance,
but the impacts differ significantly when looking at such assets
from an investor’s perspective.
AXA studies the effects of climate change on its real‑estate
holdings and provides an updated estimate of the Average
Annual losses ("AAL") on a yearly basis (1). This analysis covered
a range of direct property investments totaling c. €46billion in
2023 General Account. AXA’s Responsible Investment and Risk
Management teams analyzed the financial impact of floods,
windstorms and hail on these properties in a selection of 20
nations that make up close to 85% of its portfolio.
According to AXA's research on the 2023 real‑estate portfolio,
the total AAL were estimated at €5.4 million which is small in
comparison to the value of all assets. The AXA Group’s
real‑estate exposure is global, with the majority of its portfolio
located in Europe (80%). The portfolio’s highest risk exposure
was to floodings (36% of the AAL), followed by windstorm (35%)
and hail (29%). This figure was calculated in proportion with
AXA’s stake in each property. Furthermore, Germany led the AAL
in terms of the risk of flooding (44%), followed by the United
States and Switzerland (20%). Japan, the United States and
France accounted for 61% of the average annual loss due to
windstorms. The United States, France and Australia make up
75% of the AAL for hail hazards.

Transition risks to AXA’s investments
The ORSA or the stress‑tests exercises illustrated that most of
the Group's transition risk may stem from its invested assets
which AXA assesses with a sectorial approach - summarized in
the next two paragraphs below - to limit its exposures to
potential stranded assets.
Based on the CPRS classification (2), AXA assessed the corporate
bond (3) and listed equities that are part of its General Account
and exposed to industries potentially affected by transition risk.
The CPRS‑related assets represented 23% of the overall

considered invested assets portfolio as end of 2023 (4). Of note,
67% of AXA’s investments in corporate bonds and exposed to a
CPRS sector were expected to mature by 2030.
As part of the 2022 climate stress test required by the IORP II
Directive, the EIOPA provided market shocks reflecting a
sudden, disorderly transition to carbon neutrality due to
delayed policy action. This scenario explores high transition
risks compared to an orderly transition scenario and provided
sectoral shocks based on NACE codes. For its annual ORSA, the
Group simplified the EIOPA IORP scenario by focusing its
analysis on corporate bonds and listed equities in General
Account to assess how portfolios could be exposed to and
impacted by the most penalized sectors and stranded assets.
For this purpose, AXA considered the credit spread shocks and
equity price changes by sector (5), while ignoring the other
shocks on interest rates and other asset classes. The overall
impact at the Group level of transition risks based on this EIOPA
scenario (IORP) is equivalent to approximately -9% of the
shocked assets’ market value as end of 2023.

Forecasting future climate‑related
financial impacts
AXA uses the Climate Value at Risk (“CVaR”) metric to assess the
potential future financial impacts of climate change on its
investments in listed corporate assets. This metric, different
from the traditional Value‑at‑Risk ("VaR") used in Risk
Management, covers the physical risk by providing an estimate
of the impact of extreme climate events on company valuation,
according to various climate change scenarios. The result is
expressed as a percentage of the current company valuation.
For more information on CVaR methodology, please refer to
Section 4.5.2.
AXA has been analyzing the Physical CVaR for its listed corporate
debt and listed equities portfolios (6) since 2021. In the +1.5°C
Orderly and 3°C NGFS scenarios, the physical CVaR reduced
compared to 2023 levels. The physical CVaR went from -2.5 % in
2023 to -1.7% in 2024 under the 1.5°C Orderly scenario. This
reduction is mainly a consequence of updates made to the
underlying model, particularly the flooding model, with improved
flood hazard data.
