AXA’s business resilience
to climate‑related risks
Based on AXA’s resilience analysis to climate related risks
presented above, there is no significant risk of a material
financial effect within the next annual reporting period to the
carrying amounts of assets and liabilities reported in the
related financial statements.
The strategic plan and capital allocation exercises involve all
professional families and particularly business, finance and risk
functions to ensure the consistency of the projections. These
financial projections are regularly presented to the Board of
Directors as well as to AXA's investors and tend to focus on
shorter‑term time horizons. For medium- and longer‑term
horizons, AXA has a dedicated Emerging Risks Steering Board
attended by Group and local senior management members
which meets bi‑annually to follow‑up on the Emerging Risks
action plan.
AXA’s Climate Transition Plan (2) illustrates the Group's
commitment to accelerating the transition of the energy sector
towards a more sustainable model, consistent with net‑zero
trajectories. AXA has implemented actions to address physical
or transition risks. On the one hand, restrictions on certain
activities are defined by AXA’s Energy Policy, and on the other
hand business objectives toward a more sustainable and less

carbon‑intensive economy (3) were communicated to external
stakeholders (4). Lastly, AXA is also committed to initiatives
intended to upskill and develop all AXA’s employees with
training material on transition matters notably via the AXA
Climate Academy.
AXA uses natural hazard models that rely on data obtained
from models driven by current climate conditions, the
frequency and severity they capture are characteristic of
current climate. These models simulate a large set of climate
events over a typical period of 10,000 years that could occur in
the year following the current one. The climate variations over
a 3–5‑year horizon are expected to be covered in the
10,000‑year simulation set. The natural catastrophe models are
typically revised every 5 years to remain representative of
current climate conditions. For longer‑term horizons such
models are not suitable to accurately assess climate change
and require further developments. Going forward, AXA will keep
monitoring developments in the climate science as well as in
the modelling of the climate‑related perils to progressively
better account for their specificities and derive financial
impacts at a more granular level.
AXA will continue to analyze its resilience to climate‑related
risks by taking a more comprehensive approach notably in
terms of underwriting, investment, or risk management and
thus addressing concerns from customers, regulators and
governments. The adoption of new competencies in areas such
as engineering and green technologies is also embedded in the
Group's strategic plan “Unlock the Future” with specific
objectives shared with external stakeholders. Lastly, AXA is also
committed to fostering a multidisciplinary approach notably
through the AXA Research Fund or partnerships with public
authorities which further strengthens its ability to anticipate
future risks.

4.2.2 Other environmental issues
AXA views the need to address other environmental issues as
an extension of its climate efforts (1). Biodiversity loss
endangers ecosystem services and poses risks to society and
businesses that depend on them, and in turn investors and
insurers that rely on a well‑functioning economy. Furthermore,
the Intergovernmental Science‑Policy Platform on Biodiversity
and Ecosystem Services (“IPBES”), the Intergovernmental Panel
on Climate Change (“IPCC”) and the Taskforce on
Nature‑related Financial Disclosures (“TNFD”) all identify
climate change as a key driver of changes to nature and by
extension, biodiversity. As a result, the Group implemented a
series of initiatives designed to contribute positively to the
protection of ecosystems and to act on the nexus between
climate and nature, along with ongoing efforts to improve
quantitative analyses relevant to nature‑related issues to
support future target setting.

As a result of the DMA, AXA has identified the material impact of
its investment and insurance activities on nature and
ecosystem services (including issues related to biodiversity,
water and marine resources, and pollutions). Additionally, the
impact on the use of resources through claims management on
circular economy and underwriting activities is also seen as
material and actions have been initiated to develop products
and services to support the transition to a more sustainable
and a less resource‑intensive economy.
AXA's policies, actions, and targets regarding other
environmental issues are presented in relation to each activity
for which the topics are material, i.e. investment activities and
insurance activities. The potential impact related to the
investment activity is presented in Section 4.2.2.2 and the
impact related to the insurance activity is presented in
Section 4.2.2.3.
Definitions, methodologies and, where applicable, the
associated margins of uncertainty are specified for the
concerned indicators in Section 4.5.2.1 - Environmental
methodologies.

impacts related to invasive alien species has not been assessed

Identification of
nature‑related impacts
‑
and dependencies
AXA has screened its assets and activities to identify actual and
potential pressures and dependencies on nature and
ecosystem services in own operations, as well as upstream and
downstream value chains. The analysis specifically considered
the impacts and dependencies related to own sites, insurance
clients and investee companies. It was informed by previous
initiatives, notably the findings of a study concluded in early
2024 to better assess the impacts and dependencies of AXA
France's activities (i.e., as a company, an insurer and an
investor) on nature and ecosystem services.
Two initiatives with distinct approaches have enabled an initial
assessment of the impacts and dependencies of AXA's own
operations on nature and ecosystem services.
In 2022, the Group determined a Global Biodiversity Score,
which focused on purchased goods, notably office furniture
and supplies, IT equipment, corporate car fleet, catering food.
The study assessed the indirect impacts of the sectors that are
producing such goods.
According to its results, the main impacts are linked to food
supply and car fleet production, with pressures on land use,
water consumption and pollution, but these indirect impacts
remain limited in their scale. Dependencies in AXA’s own
operations have been evaluated as limited, as they are not
directly relying on natural resources, while activities within its
value chain that are exposed to significant dependencies are
not critical to its functioning and perturbation of these
activities would not result in significant financial risks for AXA.

182

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

In addition, a study conducted by AXA France and concluded in
early 2024 analyzed more than 3,000 sites in France to
determine their proximity to biodiversity issues and their
possible contribution to biodiversity erosion. This
macro‑analysis of AXA France's portfolio of sites revealed
limited risks of impact on nature or dependence on ecosystem
services.
Consequently, no material impacts or dependencies have been
identified in AXA's own operations and sites.
However, through the companies it finances or insures, AXA
contributes to impacts on terrestrial, freshwater and marine
resources and can indirectly accentuate the decline of nature,
which ensure the functioning of ecosystem services.
The assessment of the potential impact on nature through the
activities of its investees and policyholders was based on
geographical data to specify the interfaces between nature and
financed or insured assets, on a sectoral materiality of the
impacts and dependencies, and on the weight of the financed
or insured assets in the overall activity portfolio. It was
supported by scientific publications review, sectoral research
and interviews with internal experts. While no external
consultation was planned as part of this analysis, information
sources included the Global Biodiversity Information Facility
(GBIF), the World Resources Institute, the Biodiversity Risk Filter
and others.
The absence of precise geographical data and the lack of
transparency regarding the activities ultimately financed make
it impossible to carry out an in‑depth diagnosis of the physical
and transition risks. Consideration to these risks in insurance
activities was also challenged by the access to detailed
information at asset level. Nevertheless, this analysis has
enabled AXA to identify sectors, such as construction and real
estate, which are associated with major impacts on nature and
highly dependent on ecosystem services. Farming has also
been identified as a high‑stakes sector, given its dependence
on and interaction with nature.
Accurate quantification of impacts and risks in Personal lines
remains also a challenge, but the manufacturing of insured
vehicles has an impact on biodiversity, insured homes have an
impact on land artificialization, and biodiversity loss can lead
to increase in claims from extreme events on insured
properties.
AXA's analysis has confirmed that potential impacts on nature
and dependencies on ecosystem services through investment
and insurance activities are indirect, but material. They have
encouraged the Group to implement policies and actions to
mitigate or prevent their adverse effects.

4.2 Environmental information

Finally, AXA did not identify systemic risks related to the
impacts and dependencies on nature and ecosystem services.
The transition and physical risks are generally indirect and
limited but opportunities have also been identified, such as
investments in natural capital, insurance products to restore
biodiversity damages, or the development of circular practices
in claims management.
AXA's own operations have no material impact or dependency
on nature and ecosystem services, and do not currently
generate any significant risk for its strategy or business model.
Nevertheless, a better understanding of impacts and
dependencies in its various value chains enables AXA to better
assess their risks and opportunities, and to begin to better
integrate these issues into its investment activities or its
insurance offering by mobilizing internal expertise in various
workstreams. By progressively enhancing its assessment of
impacts and dependencies, AXA will then be able to appreciate
the actual and anticipated effects of its impacts on its value
chains, and the need to further embed these issues into its
strategy and business model.

4.2.2.2

Addressing other environmental
issues as an investor

Nature plays a fundamental role for human well‑being and
economic activities through the provision of a range of
ecosystem services, including food and water production. Many
policy makers, central banks, financial supervisors are starting
to recognize the risks biodiversity loss poses to economic
activities and financial systems. AXA has also introduced
consideration to nature‑related issues into its investment
activities.

Measuring AXA’s

Acting for biodiversity and ecosystems
preservation
Ecosystem Conversion and Deforestation Policy
Deforestation leads to severe consequences, including climate
change, biodiversity loss, and the destruction of carbon sinks,
further contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. Recognizing
the urgency of these challenges, AXA has adopted a
comprehensive approach to address deforestation and
promote sustainable practices. To tackle the key drivers of
deforestation and ecosystem conversion linked to commodities
within the Group's activities, AXA introduced a Group Ecosystem
Conversion and Deforestation Policy (2) in 2021. Building on
previous efforts to mitigate deforestation, this policy reflects
AXA’s objective of protecting forests. It incorporates three
screening methods: assessing exposure to high‑risk
commodities, monitoring controversies related to biodiversity
and land use, and evaluating the impact of corporate activities
on forests.
The Deforestation Policy is reviewed annually by the RISSC and
monitored by the RIC, ensuring an integration across all
investment‑related
activities.
Stakeholders,
including
investment managers, are informed through AXA’s investment
guidelines, regular meetings, and AXA’s website.
As part of this policy, AXA bans investment in companies linked
to unsustainable palm oil production, those facing “high” or
“severe” biodiversity and land‑use controversies, or those with

activities posing a “critical” impact on forests by the Carbon
Disclosure Project (“CDP”). These exclusions apply to AXA’s
General Account and Unit‑Linked assets in fully controlled
mandates. Additionally, AXA engages with companies through
direct dialogue and coalitions.

Biodiversity actions for mitigation and adaptation
In December 2022 at the Conference of the Parties (“COP15”) in
Montreal, parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity
adopted the Kunming Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
This framework includes 23 new targets. Not all of them are
quantitative, and ongoing work is necessary to translate them
into quantifiable and standardized objectives for
implementation by governments and eventually voluntary
adoption by non‑state actors, including the private sector.
AXA has started taking concrete actions to meet the above
targets, with a focus on:
●

●

●

contributing to target 1: Loss of highly important biodiverse
areas close to zero by 2030;
contributing to target 10: Sustainable management of
agriculture;
contributing to target 11: Restore and enhance ecosystems
through nature‑based solutions.

In this context and to mitigate the negative impacts on nature
and ecosystems, the Group has taken concrete actions:

Natural Capital Fund
Launched at the end of 2022, AXA IM Alts’ Natural Capital Fund,
with a size of $400 million, will principally finance projects that
aim to protect and restore natural capital, for example in
forests, mangroves and peatlands. In addition, the fund will
invest in project developers to enhance their capacity to
develop and deliver natural capital projects, solutions that
enable faster and more accurate measurement of nature‑based
projects, and marketplace solutions for carbon.
Sustainable forestry investments
Forests are virtuous invested assets due to their high
biodiversity value and role in capturing carbon, while offering
sustainable long‑term returns resilient to economic cycles.
Therefore, AXA is engaged in responsible forestry, working to
ensure that its investments foster both environmental
preservation and sustainable growth, aligning with AXA's
broader sustainability objectives.

4.2.2.3

Addressing other environmental
issues as an insurer

Maintaining the integrity of nature is fundamental to the
stability of terrestrial and marine ecosystems, and its
degradation threatens all life and ecological balance. AXA is
engaged in the protection and restoration of nature – from
incorporating nature risk into underwriting, by developing
specific environmental risks insurance coverages, to insuring
natural assets such as mangrove forests and coral reefs. As it is
crucial that while AXA builds collective awareness and
willingness to act the Group also engage with its clients and
increases biodiversity awareness via dedicated training to put
nature at the heart of their plans.
In the context of its new 2024‑2026 “Unlock the future” strategic
plan, and to deliver on its ambitions to support the climate
transition through its insurance activities, AXA set up a global
underwriting sustainability expert network involving major P&C
markets and key Group functions. This expert network, called
PlanNet as in “plan to Net Zero”, is key in delivering the
ambition as detailed below.

Understanding AXA’s impacts
and dependencies on nature
As contextualized by the EIOPA, the dependency or impact on
nature of the insurance and reinsurance sector itself is limited:
from its direct operations, the insurance and reinsurance industry
neither has a significant impact on nature nor consumes
significant natural resources compared to other sectors (1).
AXA could experience indirect nature‑related risks by providing
coverage to companies that are not adapted to the transition to
a low impact on the environment or that are already or
increasingly, at risk from reduced biodiversity and ecosystem
services. Therefore, AXA is exposed to indirect nature‑related
transition or physical risks.
AXA initiated a project to map biodiversity impacts and
dependencies with WWF between 2019 and 2021. AXA's largest
entities, such as AXA France and AXA XL that insure organizations
across many sectors have also assessed their portfolio to identify
relevant nature impacts and dependencies (2).

Action 1 | Avoid and reduce AXA's impact on biodiversity

“what is being insured” (focusing on high‑impact industries and

the continuous enforcement of the rules already established by

have through its insurance activities to the erosion of nature
and ecosystem services.

AXA Group Natural World Heritage Sites policy
In line with the UN PSI‑UNESCO classification, AXA supports the
protection of Natural World Heritage Sites (“NWHS”) by
ensuring it does not support, through Property and
Construction insurance underwriting, businesses in sensitive
sectors that are developing activities incompatible with
ecosystem preservation in these vital sites. NWHS are classified
by UNESCO as containing both “exceptional natural beauty”
and “the most important and significant natural habitats for
conservation.” Examples include the Galapagos Islands of
Ecuador, and the Ivindo National Park in Gabon. They provide
both key biodiversity benefits, such as fauna and flora
protection, and environmental benefits, including soil
stabilization, flood prevention, and carbon capture. They also
contribute to economies through jobs, ecotourism and
recreation.
To date, there are 266 natural sites inscribed on the UNESCO
World Heritage List and NWHS account for around 8% of the
total surface area covered by all 280,000+ terrestrial and marine
protected areas worldwide. Yet they are under increasing
pressure. (1) AXA has identified the insured assets located in
NWHS.
The NWHS policy restricts project‑specific construction and
property covers for oil and gas, mining, large scale hydropower
and large‑scale infrastructure projects located in NWHS. This
policy has been implemented by all AXA entities.

Full details of the current AXA Group Natural World Heritage
Sites policy are available at https://www.axa.com/en/
commitments/axa‑and‑forests.
A specific questionnaire has been developed for high‑risk
projects (e.g. hydropower projects) on biodiversity and natural
capital, to engage with clients and ensure that appropriate due
diligence, prevention, and mitigation measures are in place to
avoid impacts on nature and biodiversity. Specific questions
address the rights of indigenous people and local communities
to Free, Prior and Informed Consent (“FPIC”) in accordance
with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of
Indigenous Peoples.
With a particular focus on water and oceans, and as a signatory
to the Poseidon Principles for Marine Insurance, AXA XL has
implemented since 2022 a framework for measuring and
reporting alignment of insurers’ shipping portfolios with
climate goals. The aim of this framework is to promote
environmental stewardship throughout the maritime value
chain, foster collaboration with clients and gain insights to
enhance strategic decision‑making.
AXA XL has also put in place additional safeguards to support
the detection of Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated (“IUU”)
fishing by requiring International Maritime Organization (“IMO”)
numbers for all fishing vessels and refrigerated cargo vessels
that it insures and adding further explicit checks on IUU fishing
to its Marine Underwriting Rules and Guidelines.
The monitoring of those policies is presented along with the
referral process in Section 4.2.1.4 - Addressing climate change
as an insurer.

Those insurance products include the environmental risks

pollution incidents and support restoration efforts, but also,
nature‑based solutions insurance such as mangroves forests
and coral reefs parametric insurance provided by AXA Climate
or AXA XL’s Political Risk, Credit and Bond offer that helps

bonds”. Thanks to this innovative development finance
approach (1), expansion of marine protected areas (“MPAs”) and
fund conservation trusts in the Seychelles, Belize (2), Barbados,
Ecuador (3), and in Gabon have been successfully issued.
In addition to insurance products, AXA seeks to extend the
provision of prevention services. For instance, AXA XL
developed an “Environmental Sensitivity assessment” enabling
companies to identify and mitigate pollution and
environmental risks in Europe and in the UK. The tool uses
comprehensive datasets and applies machine learning
algorithms to assess the environmental liability risks of
individual sites and facilities. The outputs include
environmental sensitivities scores and high‑resolution maps for
each location. When combined with customer‑specific
information like site location, industry type, and occupancy,
companies can use this tool to assess their environmental risks
exposures at individual facilities or across an entire portfolio of
sites. The overall goal is to prevent and mitigate environmental
risks including impacts on biodiversity. Currently the tool is
being used by clients and underwriters in Europe and the UK,
with expansion to more markets in 2025.
AXA XL and AXA France have also partnered with emergency
pollution response specialists to offer companies with
environmental risk insurance policies access to tailored
recommendations through a 24/7 hotline when an incident
occurs.

trainings
AXA is increasingly learning how biodiversity loss and climate
change compound and reinforce each other. This is the reason
why the Group has enriched its original engagement strategy
focused on climate mitigation (i.e. decarbonization) and
broaden these engagements to include nature and biodiversity.

AXA Climate has also developed specific trainings on nature
and biodiversity in addition to climate change mitigation,
climate change adaptation via the Climate school (4) and
Climate briefs (5).

Action 1 | Enhance AXA's understanding of risks
associated with the use of reclaimed and
bio‑sourced
‑
materials in the build environment
Since reclaimed materials may come from various sources and
have a history that is not easily traceable, there is a higher risk
of potential defects compared to new materials. This
uncertainty around quality and risk levels can potentially lead
to higher premiums or even lack of insurance coverage.
Therefore, a dedicated workstream, gathering representatives
of the “Construction” and “Property” lines of business in the
entities, aims at enhancing AXA's understanding of the unique
risks associated with these materials in order to facilitate their
insurability.

Action 3 | Develop circular practices in motor claims
management
The workstream will prioritize the delivery of the +10%
“sustainable claims” target (1) set for retail motor (see below
metrics and target). The workstream will leverage existing
initiatives already in place in several European countries, to
promote (i) the use of remote expertise for claims adjusting, (ii)
the repair of damaged parts rather than their replacement, and
(iii) whenever replacement is necessary, the use of
second‑hand parts, to limit the use of raw material and prevent
waste generation in downstream value chain. This action will
be implemented over the 2024‑2026 plan period.

Action 2 | Enhance AXA's understanding of risks
associated with the insurance of recycling plants
Some recycling companies, especially smaller operators,
struggle having insurance coverage due to their higher risk
exposure to fire, thus triggering multiple adverse effects: their
financials are affected by higher insurance costs (if any),
investors cannot finance recyclers as too risky, companies
struggle to source recycled materials since unavailable and/or
too expensive. On the other hand, insurers – particularly in
Property business - seek opportunities to improve their
performance on this market. The aim of the workstream is to
develop guidelines and prevention measures and engage with
clients and partners (e.g. reinsurance) on innovative solutions.

With respect to AXA’s potential negative impact on resources
use and circular economy, which could occur through claims
management, AXA has set a voluntary target to increase its
“green and sustainable claims” (2) by 10% for its retail
motor business by 2026 (compared to the 2021 baseline).
“Green and Sustainable Claims” correspond to claims involving
(i) repair over replace (incl. windscreen repair, paintless dent
repair for hail, smart repairs), (ii) replacement with
second‑hand spare parts, or (iii) remote assessments. Note
that it is possible for a claim event to have more than one
sustainable claim solution used, for example the use of both
remote assessment and a second hand part, such that the
sustainable claims utilization could be higher than the number
of claims overall.

The workstream dedicated to “sustainable claims” aims at
developing practices with reduced environmental impacts.

The geographical scope of this target covers AXA France, AXA
Germany, AXA Switzerland, and AXA UK, and the target has
been defined by involving claims experts from those entities.

4.2.3 EU Taxonomy disclosures
General information
The following provides information with respect to the
requirements of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 of the European
Parliament and of the Council of June 18, 2020 on the
establishment of a framework to facilitate sustainable
investment, and amending Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 (the EU
Taxonomy Regulation) and the five supplementing Commission
Delegated Regulations that have been published as of June 27,
2023.
The EU Taxonomy Regulation and the Commission Delegated
Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 of July 6, 2021 (the “Disclosure
Delegated Act”) require companies such as AXA to disclose how
and to what extent their activities are associated with economic
activities that qualify as “environmentally sustainable" under
articles 3 and 9 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation.
Pursuant to Article 3 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation, an
economic activity must meet the following conditions to be
considered
“environmentally
sustainable” (i.e.
a
Taxonomy‑aligned economic activity):
●

●

it contributes substantially to at least one of the six
environmental objectives laid down in Article 9 of the EU
Taxonomy Regulation;
it complies with the technical screening criteria (“TSC”)
established by the Commission for each eligible activity;

4.2.3.1

it meets the “do no significant harm” (“DNSH") criteria,
having no negative effect on any of the other five
environmental objectives; and

●

it complies with the minimum safeguards (“MS”) laid down
in Article 18 relating primarily to human rights and social
and labor standards.

●

non‑Life insurance and reinsurance GWP. Under the Climate
Delegated Act Non‑Life insurance activities through the
underwriting of climate‑related perils can indeed qualify as
contributing substantially to climate change adaptation.
AXA also separately discloses the KPI related to investments by
insurance or reinsurance undertakings, which present the
weighted average of those investments that are directed at
funding or are associated with Taxonomy‑aligned economic
activities. Such indicators measure the extent to which
investments by financial undertakings, such as insurers and
reinsurers, contribute to reorient capital flows towards

Taxonomy‑aligned economic activities
The methodology deployed in the Group to identify premiums
eligible or aligned to EU Taxonomy is described in detail in
Appendices in Section 4.5.3.5 - Additional information related
to the EU Taxonomy.
Based on the criteria set out in Article 3 of the EU Taxonomy
Regulation, AXA recognizes only 1% of its Non‑Life GWP as
being Taxonomy‑aligned.
For now, the Taxonomy‑aligned share of Non‑Life GWP only
covers the following policies underwritten by AXA France and
AXA XL:
●

●

insurance policies covering natural catastrophes for cars
and homes underwritten by AXA France;
insurance policies covering commercial property damage
underwritten by AXA XL, where pricing and
recommendations offered to the clients are dependent on
the assessment of a loss prevention report analysis which is
influenced by the degrees of prevention against
climate‑related events.

Non‑Life insurance products covering climate‑related perils
distributed by AXA entities generally contain features that help
customers to better adapt to the consequences of climate
change, including incentives to prevent its effects on property
and people. However, as they do not strictly meet all the
conditions in order to qualify as “environmentally sustainable”,
under Articles 3 and 9 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation, these
products cannot technically be considered as a
Taxonomy‑aligned economic activity.
AXA considers that the complex and restrictive framework
defined by the EU Taxonomy Regulation does not reflect
appropriately the role that Non‑Life insurance sector in general
should have in helping its clients to adapt to climate change.

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

Integration of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
in the business strategy and product design process
Insurance products and features are developed locally at
market or entity level. All new P&C insurance products and any
major product feature changes must follow the guidelines of an
approval process, which includes instructions for the
consideration of sustainability features in the design of a new
insurance product. If an insurance coverage or service delivers
a positive impact on the environment by contributing to at
least one of the following objectives: climate change
mitigation; climate change adaptation; transition to circular
economy; protection of biodiversity and nature (that includes
water and marine resource) and pollution prevention, Group
entities should fill in the “Insuring the Transition Index”
template.
Regarding the climate change adaptation objective, the
“Insuring the Transition Index” template enquires as to the
availability of risk prevention services within the new product.
Such risk prevention services may encompass two dimensions:
(i) impact of an insured’s activity on the environment or
climate, and how to reduce any negative impacts, and (ii) the
risks to the insured related to the consequences of climate
change and advice or encouragement to reduce their
vulnerability. The features of the service are described and
scored with the relative significance the service has on the
climate change adaptation dimension, either minor or
significant. The final score will classify whether this new
product may be classified as a “sustainability value added
product”, “standard product”, or “not recommended as a
sustainable classified product”.
To further support the development of Taxonomy‑aligned
products, a network across entities covering all P&C product
lines has been set at Group level to support and set clear
sustainability underwriting objectives. This network should
facilitate the development and introduction of additional
products and/or features which align to the EU Taxonomy
Regulation insurance product criteria for climate change
adaptation. At this stage, AXA has not made any global
commitment regarding Taxonomy regulation alignment for its
insurance portfolio.

The proportion of exposures to Taxonomy‑aligned activities
represents the weighted average value of invested assets
directed at funding, or associated with, Taxonomy‑aligned
economic activities relative to the value of total invested assets
included for the purpose of the calculation of the KPI (the
“Covered Assets”).
The Covered Assets correspond to all assets invested, including
cash and excluding exposures to central governments, central
banks, and supranational issuers. The Covered Assets thus
include exposures to investments in properties, equity
securities, debt instruments (excluding sovereign exposures),
non‑consolidated investments funds, derivatives, loans, cash
and cash equivalents. Assets backing contracts where the
financial risk is borne by policyholders are also included. In
2024, the Covered assets represented 74.6% of the total
investments.

the reporting requirement under the EU Taxonomy Regulation
and collected through ESG data provider, AXA has identified

equity instruments in European non‑financial companies held
directly by AXA.

employees enables AXA to adjust at local or global levels
actions and policies by Partners, Human Resources Directors,
and the Culture, Inclusion, and Diversity community. Further
work is required to appreciate more precisely the actual and
anticipated effects of these impacts on AXA's workforce, and
the need to further embed these issues into its strategy and
business model.
The workforce that could be materially impacted by AXA,
through its own operations or through its value chain, products
and services are:

●

AXA’s employees who are physically working on‑site or

non‑salaried workforce corresponds to the staff physically

AXA has not identified any business partnerships at significant

capacity to address own workforce impacts.

Policies supporting AXA’s culture
and strategy
In order to be a sustainable organization, AXA has implemented
Group policies, disclosed in the next Sections, that have a
positive impact on employees and contractors and mitigate
potential disparities in treatments or opportunities by
promoting inclusion and diversity.
The policies and actions described in this section can be
grouped into two major priorities:
●

supporting inclusion and diversity; and

●

taking care of its own workforce.

In this way, the policies are expressions of AXA’s people strategy
and culture. A good example of such a policy is the “We Care
and Dare for Progress” strategy, launched in 2024. “Care”
reflects our commitment to protect & demonstrate empathy for
our customers and employees. “Dare” is our call to action to
confront challenges and foster a growth mindset.
AXA's culture is based on four core values of (i) Customer First,
(ii) Integrity, (iii) Courage and (iv) ONE AXA. Care and Dare lies
at the heart of the Group's people strategy, driving a strong
focus on the behaviors and mindsets of collaboration,
feedback, agility and innovation.
AXA’s policies apply to all employees. AXA operates under a
decentralized framework, where each entity applies the Group
policies according to local specificities and is encouraged to adapt
the Group policies to their unique context. The responsibility for
implementing these Group policies ultimately belongs to AXA’s
Chief Executive Officers at entity‑level. Progress is monitored at the
Group level by the Group HR team - comprising Group Culture,
Inclusion and Diversity team, Group Compensation and Benefits
team and Group Talent and Learning team.
Two Pulse surveys and one Inclusion survey are conducted
annually to track the impact of Group policies' and gather
insights from employees about their experiences. These
insights are used by leaders to develop plans at both local and
global levels. Other yearly reports describe the reach of AXA’s
programs. The Group measures the utilization and adoption of
policies and standards that derive from the Healthy You and We
Care programs.
Results from the Pulse and Inclusion surveys are recorded
anonymously. They are aggregated before they are shared, and
that output goes to Partners, Human Resources Directors, and
the Culture, Inclusion, and Diversity community. Local entities
access their own results and share them as needed. Local
actions plans are developed according to these insights, taking
global recommendations into account. This approach ensures
that feedback influences decisions at both global and local
levels.
At Group level, specific targets for material IROs are not set, as
they are often best determined at local level, enabling a more
tailored and effective approach. The policies and actions
outlined below are already in place and, while AXA keeps
enhancing its understanding of and response to social issues,
they do not require material expenditure as yet.

Supporting inclusion and diversity

Building the right culture

Preventing human rights abuses

AXA fosters a culture of inclusion

AXA adheres to international standards

The Group Inclusion and Diversity Policy ensures that every
part of the organization contributes to a welcoming, diverse
environment, reflecting AXA’s values and its dedication to
positive change. The policy sets standards for the workforce,
emphasizing the organization's expectation that every
employee and contractor will treat their colleagues, customers,
and partners with respect. The policy also commits AXA to
fairness and equal access for employees to opportunity. To
accelerate progress, AXA focuses on key areas like gender,
sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (LGBT+),
disability, origins, different age groups, and mental health.

AXA has adopted the “Group Human Rights Policy” (1) to
manage the “negative impact on workers’ human rights and
critical work‑related rights in investee companies” and address
the “negative impact on own workforce from unequal
treatment or opportunities linked to the lack of diversity or
inclusion” (i.e. work‑life balance, health and safety, gender
equality, training, diversity)”. The general objective of this policy
is to prevent human rights abuses and reflect AXA’s adherence
to general and sectoral international standards. This policy
covers the AXA Group’s activities as an employer, business
partner, insurer, and investor. The policy applies to all AXA
entities, with the aim of ensuring that human rights are
respected in all regions where AXA operates.
As an employer, AXA promotes inclusion and diversity. All
employees should be treated with dignity and respect, so AXA
aims to offer equal opportunities, and prohibits discrimination.
In this regard, AXA is guided by the Group Human Rights Policy,
which also includes ambitions to:

Rewarding people fairly
AXA’s employees must be paid equitably
The AXA Group Remuneration Policy addresses equitable
remuneration. Pay should be based on roles, skills,
contributions and impact and remuneration must not be
influenced by gender or other personal characteristics. The
guiding principles of the policy are competitiveness, fairness,
internal equity, and achievement. The policy ties remuneration
to performance over the short, medium and long term. By
adhering to this policy, AXA seeks to comply with regulations,
offer competitive compensation, and avoid conflicts of interest.
The way remuneration is calculated drives sustainable business
performance without encouraging excessive risk‑taking.

AXA employees are paid at or above
the adequate wage
For reporting purposes, AXA uses the terms “adequate wage”
and “living wage” interchangeably. A living wage goes beyond
any current statutory minimum wage: it is more comprehensive
and defined as the wage needed for employees and their
families to cover basic needs including decent housing, food,
and access to healthcare and education (depending on their
working location).
AXA’s Fair Pay Framework includes the “We Care” program next
to other local benefits and forms of remuneration. The
organization has reinforced its approach by considering that
employees’ pay should not only be fair and competitive, but
also at a level determined sufficient for the location they work
in.
In preparation, AXA contracted with the Fair Wage Network to
conduct an analysis in all of the Group’s countries of operation
to assess employees’ pay against local living wages. Since 2023,
AXA has been certified as a Living Wage employer by the
provider Fair Wage Network.
The living wage assessment at AXA is done annually. The local
living wage thresholds provided by the Fair Wage Network may
vary year on year depending on the local socio‑economic and/
or inflationary environment which may lead to a few
employees identified below these ever‑evolving local living
wage thresholds, for which AXA entities commit to close any
gap to local living wage in the subsequent pay review cycle.
Across the Group, AXA aims to offer all employees a total target
cash remuneration of at least 110% of local living wage by the
end of 2026.
In addition, and in respect of the living wage, representatives
from AXA have signed the B4IG pledge, part of the UN Global
Compact “Forward Faster” initiative.

4.3 Social information

Pay equity is a strong requirement of AXA inclusion policy
AXA monitors through regression analysis its adjusted pay gap
which compares the average pay of the women with that of the
men after accounting for a selected set of professional
characteristics (role, seniority, level, or location). The residual
gap may still be justifiable based on other relevant professional
characteristics – at AXA, the global residual adjusted pay gap is
currently assessed at 1.3% on fixed pay and 1.4% on total
compensation i.e. below the 5% threshold set by the European
Union Pay Transparency Directive (1). Entities are committed to
ensuring that unjustified pay gaps are not recreated.

The unadjusted pay gap (also called Gender Pay Gap) measures
the difference between the average pay of all women and all
men regardless of their professional characteristics, and mainly
reflects gender balance within the organization. At AXA, the
unadjusted pay gap is currently assessed at 24% on fixed pay
and 29% on total compensation.

4.3.1.3

Taking care of AXA’s workforce

Engaging with our workforce and workers’
representatives
AXA considers social dialogue at local and global level
to be essential
At Group level, the European Works Council (“EWC”) serves in
accordance with the agreement signed in 2009 as a crucial forum,
encompassing information, consultation, and participation, with
structured discussions held twice a year through plenary sessions
chaired by the Group CEO, along with seven EWC Bureau meetings
per year (comprising 12 elected EWC members plus a permanent
guest from UNI Union Network International‑Europa). More than
half of Group’s employees are covered by the EWC’s framework.
Considering the legal scheme and the social model of France and
Germany, all AXA employees are covered by a collective bargaining
(convention collective) and/or by collective agreements negotiated
in these countries. Additionally, the German and French
employment law ensures a regulated framework for workers
councils.
In 2024, several topics around the 2024‑2026 Strategic Plan, Tech
& Data transformation, Smart Working, Managerial Culture, etc.
were openly discussed and specific joint learning sessions on key
HR topics such as Domestic Violence and Daring is Ageless
(focusing on people aged 50+ and multi‑generations on the work
floor) were held. In the second half of 2024, specific attention was
given to the social consultation process regarding the sale of AXA
IM.
All discussions within the European Works Council (EWC) are
systematically documented through formal meeting reports.
These records ensure that key takeaways, employee concerns,
and management responses are accurately captured and made
available for reference and follow‑up actions. In addition to
official
reports,
employee
representatives
actively
communicate key discussion points through social media and
internal communication channels. This approach enhances
transparency and ensures that a broader segment of the
workforce remains informed about ongoing dialogue and
decisions affecting them. Direct interactions between
employee representatives and senior leadership are highly
valuable, as they provide with real‑time insights into
employees' concerns, expectations, and overall sentiment.
These discussions allow AXA to gain awareness of emerging
workplace issues and, where necessary, take appropriate
action to address them.

Looking after health and wellbeing
Policies promote positive action
Another set of policies relate to the positive impact of AXA on its
employees through benefits exceeding minimum legal
requirements worldwide and initiatives promoting progress on
social issues.

The fundamentals are covered by AXA’s Health,
Wellbeing and Safety Policy
By following this policy, AXA improves the wellbeing of
employees, and protects the health and safety of employees,
contractors, customers and visitors. The policy sets standards
for:

●

identifying risks related to safety in each local AXA entities;

●

addressing risks, proactively and reactively;

●

measuring performance.

Chief Executive Officers have overall responsibility for ensuring
that the correct policies, instructions, and safeguards are put
into practice. That includes making sure every member of the
workforce has access to appropriate information, instruction
and training.

“We Care” program
In 2024, AXA deployed the “We Care” program, announced at
the end of 2023. The “We Care” program established a
minimum level of protection and support for all AXA employees
worldwide. The program is based on four central pillars:
Parent Policy;
Caregiver Policy;
● Domestic and Sexual Violence Policy;
● “Healthy You” program.

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

The program aims to provide AXA’s employees with the time,
support and resources to make personal and professional
decisions with confidence.
Each entity is responsible for providing the services and
benefits established under “We Care” whilst working with AXA’s
in‑house teams and strategic partners; and seeking to comply
with local practices and laws; and protecting employee data.

Pillar 1: Parent Policy
Employees who are primary parents are awarded sixteen weeks
of fully paid leave. Co‑parents get eight weeks of fully paid
leave. Beyond those allowances, AXA offers leave and flexible
working arrangements to employees who have undergone
in‑vitro fertilization or experienced a pregnancy loss, including
spouses and partners.

Pillar 2: Caregiver Policy
Caregivers are employees who look after an immediate family
member who needs eldercare or care due to a serious health
condition or disability. Under AXA’s policy, they get five days of
fully paid leave each calendar year. In addition to caregiver
leave, employees are to be supported through flexible working

arrangements in line with our Smart Working policy and any
other locally relevant policies and practices.

Pillar 3: Domestic and Sexual Violence Policy
AXA has a policy of supporting employees who experience
domestic, intra‑familial or sexual violence. Employees can
expect access to psychological support, specialist support
services, flexible working arrangements, and five days of fully
paid leave. Every entity has a trusted primary contact for
employees to approach.

●

4.3.2 Workers in the value chain
AXA recognizes that respect for social and human rights
extends beyond its own workforce, and therefore considers to
which extent the workers in the supply chain, including workers
in outsourced services, and the workers in downstream
companies purchasing products and services from AXA could
potentially or actually have their social and human rights

4.3.2.1

severely affected by its activities. In addition, workers in
investee companies may also be exposed to actual and
potential adverse social and human rights impacts. The
policies and actions associated with the impact of AXA on
workers in its value chain are detailed below.

AXA's material IROs associated to workers in the value chain

The Group Vigilance Plan (see Section 4.7) and the human
rights risks assessment are the due diligence processes by
which AXA identifies, prevents, mitigates and accounts for
material actual and potential negative impacts on people with
AXA’s own operations and value chain, including through its
products or services, as well as through its business
relationships.
AXA does not publish metrics in relation to workers in the value
chain and has not set any target to drive its progress in
addressing material negative impacts related to workers in the
value chain. Nonetheless, the above due diligence processes
allow AXA to actively monitor the actual and potential impacts
that could materially affect all types of workers in the value
chain, including the workers in the investment value chain of
the Group or the employees of joint‑ventures involving AXA.
AXA considers unlikely that its operations and suppliers have
direct business relationships with companies causing or
contributing to severe human rights impacts and incidents,
particularly those in the most at‑risk sectors or countries. For
instance, AXA’s operations and suppliers are deemed not at

significant risk of incidents of child, forced or compulsory labor.
Conversely, exposure to potential negative social and human
rights impacts, including previously mentioned incidents, is
more likely through investment activities, even if limited to
individual relationships with specific investees.
AXA's impacts related to workers in the value chain do not
currently generate any significant risk for its strategy or
business model. Nevertheless, a better understanding of the
Group's relationship with investee companies through
stewardship and engagement with our investees, enables AXA
to encourage high standards of corporate governance as well
as effective management of environmental and social risks. By
progressively enhancing its assessment of impacts, AXA will
then be able to appreciate the actual and anticipated effects of
this impact, and the need to further integrate these issues into
its strategy and business model. Additionally, AXA has not
conducted a resilience analysis of its strategy and business
model regarding its capacity to address workers in value chain
impact.

4.3.2.2

AXA's impact as an investor

Consideration of social criteria through
the ESG credit assessment and investment
processes
Since 2015, AXA has made ESG a cornerstone of its investment
policy by incorporating ESG considerations into its credit
assessment and investment processes. AXA’s Credit Research
Team assesses which issuers are eligible for Fixed Income
investments and assigns internal credit ratings (ICRs) along
with investment maturity constraints. In addition to the Credit
Research Team’s assessment of creditworthiness, all
investments must comply with AXA's Responsible Investment
("RI") policies.
AXA’s credit review combines top‑down and bottom‑up
approaches - which are essential for assessing credit risk - and
helps to identify and capture ESG risks and opportunities at
both the industry and issuer levels.
During a credit review, several factors related to an issuer’s
business and financial profiles are assessed. This includes E, S
and G factors that may impact credit performance, expressed
through the “Resilience & Transparency” factor. The relevance
of this factor depends on the nature of the industry and is also
often implicitly considered in various other aspects of the
business risk profile such as the issuer’s strategy and the
competitive position.
AXA’s Credit Research Team classifies industries into three
Resilience categories - high, medium, or low - based on an
overall assessment of the materiality of E, S and G factors. For
each industry, AXA defines the credit material E and S factors,

while considering Governance as crucial and core to the credit
assessment across all sectors. Governance is an overriding
factor; poor governance - such as inadequate reporting,
inappropriate company structure or weak Risk Management can significantly impact credit performance, although all
companies remain exposed to idiosyncratic events.
Social factors, such as labor management can also be credit
material, especially for business segments facing labor
shortage and/or whose workforce is exposed to challenging
working conditions. Inadequate health and safety practices can
negatively impact a company's operating performance (e.g.
accidents, injuries, operational disruptions) and may damage
its license to operate, leading to legal liabilities.
The impact of the Resilience and Transparency factor may vary
from short term to long term. It can be credit material within
the typical Credit rating horizon (approximatively 2 years) and
thus affect the issuer’s Internal Credit Rating ("ICR"). The risk
may also have a longer time horizon, for instance, when
integrating transition risks into credit assessment. In such
cases, AXA’s Credit Research Team may use other levers, such
as proposing to cease investing or imposing maturity
constraints. These decisions are then implemented by asset
managers investing on behalf of AXA in fully controlled
mandates.

AXA’s Human Rights Policy as an investor
As an investor, with respect to human rights risks, AXA has
implemented various responsible investment policies
(including, as an example, a policy on controversial weapons)
and built an analytical framework to identify potential indirect
impacts on human rights.
In its General Account, AXA seeks to avoid any adverse human
rights impact that might be associated with its investments
activities by applying the exclusion list derived from the AXA
Human Rights policy. AXA Human Rights Policy aims at
preventing Human Rights abuses and reflects AXA's
commitment to general and sectoral international standards by
incorporating the following human rights‑related inputs: (i)
fundamental principles such as those of the United Nations
Global Compact, the International Labor Organization (ILO) as
well as OECD recommendations, and (ii) the reputation and
potential controversies regarding these companies.
The Human Rights Policy is reviewed and updated on a regular
basis and applied in respect of the AXA’s General Account. AXA
does not disclose, if any, the cases of non‑respect of human
rights in investee companies but addresses the questionable
human‑rights practices during engagement meetings.

4.3 Social information

For instance, the content of the POG Policy focuses on several
aspects with a view to preserving customer trust and financial
well‑being by offering our customers suitable products and
delivering them the right information:
offering suitable products to our consumers: the POG Policy
requires entities in scope to define a target market for
products that are designed or reviewed. This includes
considering vulnerable customers when relevant. Once the
target market is defined, AXA entities need to test whether
the product is suitable for the defined target market and
adapt it if necessary. Products are also reviewed regularly to
ensure that the product stays suitable for its target market
during its whole lifecycle. During product design or review,
AXA entities should also aim to ensure that the
remuneration of the distributor does not create any conflict
of interests between the distributor and its customers;
delivering the right information to our customers: the POG
Policy requires AXA entities to check that the distribution
channel selected for the product is adequate, including that
distributors are themselves suitable to sell the products.
AXA entities should also provide distributors with all the
relevant information to be able to sell the product in a right
manner to ultimately provide customers with clear,
understandable, accurate and non‑misleading information
on the product they are buying.
Accountability for the implementation of the POG Policy is with
a first line business teams, to ensure that conduct and
customer protection is well embedded. Second line of defense,
both at Group and local levels, are responsible for monitoring
its implementation and compliance through appropriate
second line controls.
Additionally, AXA is committed to promoting the respect and
protection of human rights of consumers and end‑users
through its comprehensive Human Rights Policy. This policy is
embedded within AXA's wider Risk Management framework
and is supported by various processes to ensure its
implementation across all business activities, including
insurance and investment operations. The AXA Group's Human
Rights Policy takes into account several internationally
recognized instruments that can be seen in the Vigilance
Plan 4.7.2.2 - Human Rights Risk Assessment. AXA regularly
conducts Human Rights risk assessments to identify and
address potential risks. The most recent assessment,
conducted in 2022 by an independent third party, identified
risks in areas such as forced labor, discrimination, and inclusion
of vulnerable populations. The Group monitors compliance
with its Human Rights Policy and follows up on any issues of
non‑compliance through active engagement with the relevant
entities or individuals. Specific cases of non‑respect of the UN
Guiding Principles, ILO Declaration, or OECD Guidelines
involving consumers and/or end‑users are addressed through
corrective action plans and continuous monitoring to ensure
resolution and improvement.

AXA's general approach to promoting respect for the human
rights of consumers and end‑users includes:
●

●

●

●

●

As an insurer, AXA engages with customers throughout the

aims at treating our customers fairly and professionally.
To do so, AXA has several processes that detail this principle:
●

●

●

●

●

at product design phase: AXA designs products aligned with
the demands and needs of its customers. In some cases,
specific measures are taken to test the product with, for
instance, groups of customers. This can be organized
internally or by an independent firm. The principle is
reflected in the Group POG Policy and completed by
entities' local practices.
when selling our products: AXA checks that its distributors
have the professional ability to sell products. AXA provides
its distributors with all the relevant information, notably
through documentation or training, that they need to
distribute AXA's products and respect the customers’
interests. This is notably ensured by the Group POG policy.
after‑sales: AXA has standards and norms, in addition to
local regulatory requirements, to endeavor to ensure AXA's
customers claims and complaints are handled in a way that
allow the Group's customers to express their concerns. AXA
informs its customers of available channels to file claims
and complaints. This is notably reflected in the Group
Advisory on Complaints Handling.
product follow‑up: products may be monitored after launch
notably through the follow‑up of specific indicators. Those
indicators along with external events, evolving needs, trends
of complaints, could trigger a review of the product. In
addition, these may be complemented by any relevant local
initiatives, such as aftersales follow‑up calls with customers
for specific products.
continuous improvement: AXA periodically review its
products in line with the Group POG Policy and regulatory
requirements and make improvements based on
customers' feedback (e.g. analysis of complaints' root
causes, other entities' initiatives such as post‑sales calls,

other relevant information.

INCLUSIVE INSURANCE
Contribute to closing the global protection gap for populations
that are un‑or under served by insurance products and services.
I- Negative impacts I+ Positive impacts O Opportunities R Risks

According to the Geneva Association, the insurance protection
gap is defined as “the difference between the amount of
insurance that is economically beneficial, and the amount of
coverage actually purchased”. Under this definition, lack of
insurance among financially vulnerable populations might lead
to negative coping mechanisms (e.g., recurring to emergency
loans, selling productive assets).

Inclusive insurance by AXA EssentiALL

Recognizing the importance of insurance in economic
empowerment and progress, AXA has identified actions to
address the global protection gap, by extending the reach of
insurance to financially vulnerable populations, i.e.
low‑income to mass‑market customers in emerging markets
and modest income customers in mature markets, that are not
served or under‑served by traditional insurance. In turn, this
represents a business opportunity to strengthen AXA's
positioning as a universal brand and build trust and insurance
awareness among relevant interest groups.

The AXA EssentiALL business unit is composed of 17 FTEs with
diverse backgrounds in insurance, financial inclusion, and
international development. The multidisciplinary nature of this
business unit aims to respond to the multiple barriers behind
the protection gap that underserved communities and small
businesses in the low‑income to mass‑market segments in
emerging markets, and modest income segments in mature
markets face daily. The end goal is that, taking a
customer‑centric approach, AXA EssentiALL drives the
development of new, or adaptation of existing, insurance
products and services that address the unmet needs of the
target population (attractiveness), at a price they can
sustainably pay over time (affordability), and that can be
bought through convenient means (accessibility).

These actions include:
●

●

●

the creation of a dedicated business unit to deliver on AXA’s
Inclusive Insurance strategy, AXA EssentiALL (formerly
known as AXA Emerging Customers)- reporting to the
Deputy CEO of AXA;
the creation of the AXA EssentiALL community of practice to
ensure implementation across key markets;
oversight by the Inclusive Insurance Steering Committee
composed of -among others members of AXA’s
Management Committee. In addition, the Compensation,
Governance & Sustainability Committee reviews, at least
once a year, the Group’s sustainability strategy including
AXA EssentiALL’s ambition and performance.

AXA EssentiALL, the Inclusive Insurance business of AXA, was
founded with the mission of “providing affordable, accessible
and attractive products (insurance and services) that reach
underserved communities, enabling better risk mitigation and
overall financial health.”

This business unit has the mandate to:
●

define AXA’s Inclusive Insurance strategy encompassing
emerging and mature markets, including the principles of
inclusive insurance underpinning the target set for 2026 in

define the target segments for inclusive insurance and
conduct relevant market research to gather relevant
customer insights around their needs from an insurance
perspective;
define, in collaboration with relevant AXA’s entities, their

establish and manage the financial and social performance
framework for the business, as well as conduct frequent
business reviews on each market, to make sure that the
delivery of AXA EssentiALL's 2026 ambition takes place
successfully.

Business conduct and corporate culture
at AXA
Compliance and Ethics Code
AXA has implemented a Group Compliance & Ethics Code to
address the following IROs: “the positive impact on society and
business environment through a corporate culture that fosters
ethical behavior and trust, notably by protecting
whistleblowers”.
This Code seeks to establish Group‑wide rules to ensure that all
AXA employees worldwide share a common understanding of
the compliance, corporate culture and ethical standards the
Group requires. It applies to all AXA directors, officers, and
employees, as well as other personnel with employee status
(i.e. trainees, temporary employees and other personnel who
are considered employees for purposes of applicable
employment laws and regulations and/or for tax purposes) and
tied agents.
The Code is focused on AXA's core values: Customer First,
Integrity, Courage and One AXA. The Code also covers a variety
of matters and topics, such as specific rules concerning
conflicts of interest, anti‑bribery and corruption, insider
trading, management of confidential information, etc. The
Code is available on the Group’s website. Further information
on corporate culture can also be found on AXA's websites on
Our vision, purpose and values (1) and on AXA's Adventure (2).
In 2024, AXA launched its revised Compliance and Ethics Code.
The Code offers clear guidance on what employees should
focus on and also includes concrete examples designed to help
employees apply it to their daily professional activities.

Anti‑Bribery and Corruption prevention
‑
In order to prevent and mitigate the risk of bribery and
corruption, AXA has a Group Anti‑Bribery and Corruption
(“ABC”) Policy that establishes the minimum standards for
anti‑bribery and corruption that must be implemented by AXA
entities. This policy is updated annually, notably to incorporate
applicable regulations (for example Sapin II Law and FCPA). A
Group anti‑bribery officer sets up the Global ABC Policy
including the Group requirements and monitors its
implementation across AXA entities.
The objective is to achieve a consistent anti‑bribery and
anti‑corruption program across the Group’s entities, which
includes the necessary requirements under international
standards (including Sapin II Law) and prevent corruption risks

through trainings, policies, processes and associated controls.
A local ABC program must be reviewed and updated annually.
The program must cover, as a minimum, the following five
requirements: (i) actions to mitigate risks identified during the
ABC Risk Assessment exercise, (ii) a communication /
awareness / training plan, (iii) actions to mitigate any
recommendations raised during Group ABC Technical Reviews,
(iv) major ABC activities and projects, and (v) the local control
testing plan for the ABC program.
Regarding training, the AXA companies must formalize and
implement a training and awareness plan regarding their
Anti‑Corruption Code of Conduct and anti‑bribery policies and
procedures. Specific training must be given to staff identified in
their Anti‑Bribery and Corruption Risk Assessment as being
most exposed to ABC risk (such as procurement functions,
distribution functions, claims functions, underwriting
functions, and finance functions) and Senior Management.
Training must be conducted on a periodic basis and can be
included in other compliance and/or ethics training.
AXA employs a multi‑channel approach to communicate its
anti‑corruption policies, including intranet publications,
internal newsletters, and employee workshops.
In addition, AXA Group Standards set out a certification by
entities’ CEOs that includes an “anti‑bribery and fight against
corruption” section. As a result, for all the entities in scope of
the AXA Group Standards, CEOs are required to certify annually
to the Group CEO that their entities comply with the Standards.

Monitoring corruption and bribery
AXA aims to ensure that investigations related to corruption or
bribery are conducted by independent teams ultimately
reporting to or supervised by Internal Audit. This structure
minimizes conflicts of interest and maintains the impartiality of
the investigation process.

Whistleblowing procedure
AXA has zero tolerance to any misconduct relate to a behavior
or a process believed to be inappropriate, unethical or illegal
which may cause detriment to (an) individual(s) or AXA. Group
Standards set out that Whistleblowing is dealt with, reported,
and investigated in a consistent and appropriate manner
across the Group.
All entities must have a documented Whistleblowing procedure
that defines Whistleblowing, associated protections, as well as
roles and responsibilities, aligns with local legal and regulatory
requirements and allows any suspicion of inappropriate,
unethical or illegal behavior by a member of staff or an external
party to be escalated either locally or to the Group.
Allegations can be raised through various channels, for
example line management, a trusted colleague, the dedicated
local Whistleblowing hotline, local Audit, or Group Audit
directly. Speak‑up@axa.com is accessible internally via local
intranets and externally via “axa.com” that is globally reachable
to employees, suppliers, business partners, and external
stakeholders.
Whatever the channels, when a concern is submitted, its
content is evaluated and triaged by independent Investigations
teams, based on pre‑established criteria, including categories
and impact severity of the reported concern.
All allegations received will be acknowledged to the
whistleblower promptly (target response time is within 7
working days from receipt) and monitored either by the
relevant professional family or directly by the Investigation
teams. An update to the whistleblower will be provided within 3
months.
All allegations which fall within AXA’s Whistleblowing &
Investigations Policy must be logged in AXA’s global internal
audit tool. If at any point it becomes clear that the allegation is
not admissible under the Whistleblowing & Investigations
Policy, the reasons will be provided in writing to the
whistleblower.
Independent Investigation teams across the Group, ultimately
reporting to or supervised by Internal Audit, investigate the
allegations. All Investigation outcomes are presented and

218

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

discussed with the CEO and/or Top Executive management.
The chair of the relevant Audit Committee(s) will be made
aware of “very high” (material) founded cases.
The investigative procedures follow strict protocols outlined in
the Investigation Manual which sets out the methodology to
respond to allegations. The investigation is intended to confirm
or refute each element of the allegation, through interviews,
documentary evidence reviews and could also involve
advanced tools for data analysis. Investigations teams can also
engage external specialists for forensic investigations where
specific expertise is required.
To maintain the integrity and effectiveness of these policies,
AXA regularly checks its alignment to local regulations,
ensuring the process evolve and are updated in line with
regulatory requirements. Periodic audits and reviews are
conducted to identify and address any weaknesses.
AXA supplements these efforts with regular internal
communication campaigns and an e‑learning module to raise
awareness about the importance of reporting unethical
conduct. The Group's commitment to transparency is reflected
in its public disclosures about the number of allegations
received, the types of outcomes of investigations, and the
corrective actions taken.
AXA does not tolerate retaliation against whistleblowers and
any such incidents should be reported. Retaliation may lead to
disciplinary action, up to and including termination. In
addition, malicious allegations made in bad faith are
considered a disciplinary offence.
Whistleblowing and investigations are confidential.

Legal Requirements for Protection of Whistleblowers
In Whistleblowing, everyone, anonymous or otherwise, can be
confident that they will be treated fairly. Any disclosure made to
Investigation teams will be taken seriously and handled
confidentially, with strict adherence to data privacy regulations.
Any leakage of confidential information will be subject to
appropriate disciplinary action.
The whistleblower’s identity will be known only to those
involved in the independent investigation unless there is a
specific legal requirement, or the whistleblower decides
otherwise. In addition, any person facilitating the reporting of a
Whistleblowing is protected under the AXA’s Whistleblowing
and Investigations policy.
Retaliation against whistleblowers or anyone who is part of the
process, or reporting allegations in bad faith, are not tolerated
by AXA and will be subject to appropriate disciplinary action.
Wording in employment contracts and settlement agreements
for employees leaving AXA must not prohibit those employees
from reporting a Whistleblowing disclosure, regardless of
whether such a prohibition is permitted by local law.

transposing Directive (EU) 2019/1937.

Payment practices at AXA
Translating AXA’s sustainability strategy and commitments into
its management of vendors is a key issue for the Group.
Policies, description of approaches in relation with

relationships with suppliers, supply chain risks, inclusion of
social criteria in the selection of contractual partners, and key
performance indicators on sustainable procurement are
presented in the Group’s Vigilance Plan (Section 4.7 - Vigilance
Plan).
This IRO is mainly addressed at local entity level. For example,
payment practices to manage negative impact on suppliers are
managed locally by entities to better fit the regulations and
best practices. However, due to the identification of this
material risk, AXA's Finance and Procurement Department will
collaborate with entities to confirm the feasibility of a Group
policy. Moreover, following the potential implementation of this
policy, AXA will aim to plan actions to reduce the negative
impact as well as define potential targets to measure those
actions.
However, in order to monitor the negative impact on suppliers,
AXA started to measure in 2024 metrics regarding payment
practice. AXA Group Procurement is working with a third‑party
provider to get a classification of suppliers, in order to report
indicators by main category of suppliers identified, i.e. SMEs
and large undertaking.

include but are not limited to: ecosystem cleanups, meals
preparation and distribution for people in need, clothes or
hygiene products collections, tree planting, charity sport

for the AWfG is €673,838 in 2024 (this figure includes the
salaries, benefits and other overheads of community affairs
staff along with research/communications spend if used to
help the community engage with the company).
Each year, AXA expects to on‑board more employees in
volunteering thanks to the AWfG and local programs. In 2024,
23,433 AXA employees took part in at least one volunteering
activity of more than 30 minutes during the AWfG. In 2024, 573
volunteering activities have been organized in 36 AXA entities
for a total of 90,000 hours of volunteering. The actions take
place during office hours but also during evenings or the
weekend depending on the activity. The common point is that
all the actions are organized by AXA even when it is not during
the office hours.

Monitoring employee volunteering

committed to volunteering from which progress is measured.
This target covers 2024 to 2026. This target, which is a
component of the strategic plan, is monitored and reviewed
annually. AXA has not involved stakeholders in setting this

4.4.1.5

Data privacy, responsible data use
and data security

Data privacy is an existing subtopic in social standards,
however, since data security and data privacy are managed
together at AXA, the Group has included its disclosure on data
security/privacy in the governance section below rather than
the associated social standards.
Following the DMA, AXA has identified as material IROs, the
potential impact on individuals’ privacy and trust in data
systems due to unaccountable or insecure use of data through:
●

●

a potential negative impact on individuals and society due
to non‑responsible use of data (e.g. privacy breaches,
potential for discrimination, risk of misuse for harmful
purposes);
a potential negative impact on individuals and society due
to non‑secure use of data (e.g. data leakage, identity theft,
financial fraud, privacy violations).

The below policies, actions, targets and metrics refers to these
IROs.

Data privacy and data security at AXA
Group data privacy policy
AXA adopted a Group Data Privacy Policy to manage negative
impact on individuals and society due to non‑responsible use
of data (e.g. privacy breaches, potential for discrimination, risk
of misuse for harmful purposes). The policy's primary
objectives are to ensure that AXA entities adequately protect
the personal and sensitive data of customers and other
persons obtained during their business activities, in order to
minimize the risk of AXA entities breaching applicable data
privacy and protection laws (e.g. EU General Data Protection
Regulation - GDPR) and reducing the potential for penalties or
reputational damage. The Group Data Privacy Officer (GDPO)
monitors the policy, while the Group Chief Compliance Officer
approves it to ensure alignment with regulatory requirements
and Group requirements.
This policy applies to all AXA companies. While it sets the
minimum requirements for all AXA entities, many entities may
need to exceed these standards to comply with local legal and
regulatory requirements and incorporate local market best
practices.

The CEO of each AXA entity, is ultimately responsible for
ensuring that the entity establishes policies and procedures
consistent with the Group Data Privacy Policy within their
business and that the entity aims to meet applicable legal,
regulatory, or contractual requirements.
Through the implementation of this policy, AXA aims to respect
EU GDPR and other applicable Data Protection laws and
considering the recommendations and guidelines provided by
the European Data Protection Board and the relevant
authorities responsible for the protection of personal data.
This policy objective is to ensure that AXA entities adequately
protect the personal and sensitive data of clients, employees
and other persons obtained during their business activities. It is
communicated to AXA entities and their DPOs through the AXA
Standard communication process and the Binding Corporate
Rules community (BCR call).

Binding Corporate Rules (BCR)
AXA has adopted Binding Corporate Rules (BCR) to manage
negative impact on individuals and society due to
non‑responsible use of data (e.g. privacy breaches, potential for
discrimination, risk of misuse for harmful purposes). These
rules represent an internationally recognized standard for
protection of personal data. They have been approved by the
French Data Protection Authority (CNIL) and 15 other European
data protection authorities. The general objective of this policy
is to set up adequate safeguards to ensure that personal data is
protected while transferred within the Group from an AXA entity
based in a regulated jurisdiction, e.g. the European Economic
Area, to an AXA Company located in another jurisdiction where
that transfer is not otherwise permitted by applicable law, and
any subsequent onward transfer of that data that is not
otherwise permitted by applicable law. These rules and the
Group’s Data Privacy Declaration, whereby the Group
undertakes not to sell the personal data of its customers, are
available on the AXA website (1).
This policy is monitored by the GDPO and the DPO Community
to ensure that it is aligned with the regulatory environment and
Group requirements. AXA’s Data Privacy Standard (including
GDPR and other regulations) implementation is monitored
notably through on‑site or on‑line assurance reviews. This
policy covers all signatory AXA local entities. This policy is
updated as local entities are integrated or sold. The CEOs of
AXA entities are accountable for the implementation of this
policy, as well as GDPR and other applicable regulations.

(1) https://www.axa.com/en/commitments/data‑privacy
