The Group has implemented regulations recently adopted in
countries outside the European Union similar to GDPR. AXA was
an early adopter of BCR, and aims to lead Data Privacy and
GDPR compliance. Furthermore, AXA has set a maturity level
questionnaire process in order to track the effectiveness of AXA
BCR.

Data security
The implementation of a Security Standard across AXA is one of
the key components in place to manage the potential negative
impact on individuals and society due to non‑secure use of
data (e.g. data leakage, identity theft, financial fraud, privacy
violations). The general objective of this policy is to describe
how entities’ security should be structured, managed and
operated, and consequently, strengthen and homogenize the
security maturity of AXA entities. This policy is monitored
through the entities’ respective Boards, Executive and Risk
Committees and non‑compliance with the policy are escalated
at Group level through the Board of Directors.
This Security Standard is to be applied by all the Group’s
entities and covers holistically the four security disciplines:
Information Security, Physical Security, Operational Resilience
and Health & Safety. Its implementation falls under the
responsibility of the entity's CEO, under the supervision of AXA’s
Board of Directors through the Group Audit Committee. This
policy is made available to all entities security officers by
communicating it through the Security Community of 1200+
people across the Group.
To support the implementation of Security Standards and to
enable a homogenous and continuous increase of security
maturity, AXA has designed a risk‑based security strategy,
reviewed, challenged and approved by the Board of Directors,
focusing on strengthening security foundations across the
Group and developing resilience capabilities. For instance, AXA
aims at strengthening its security foundations through
automation of detection and response processes, as well as
enhancing AXA's readiness to face certain attack scenarios such
as ransomware and ultimately develop faster reaction and
recovery capabilities. Underlying actions are structured under a
centrally managed program, “One Trust”, which organizes the
delivery around the strategic ambition.
One Trust program is a 3‑year program aiming to centrally
manage security activities to maximize return on investment,
while providing flexibility for reprioritization to ensure agility.
The program is organized around 7 projects, the strengthening
of security controls, data protection, new technologies such as
cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) protection, as well as the
strengthening of security expertise and people awareness. A
centralized vulnerability management system, a security shared
service center, the release of strengthened internal security
frameworks based on ISO 27001, are examples of what the
program can deliver. With these actions, AXA expects to bring

222

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

further homogenized security capabilities to its entities and
embed end‑to‑end resilience into the organization. One Trust
program represents a forecasted investment of €30 million from
2024 to 2026, with targets and budgets defined on a yearly
basis.

Monitoring data security and data privacy
and Responsible AI Usage
Data privacy
AXA has set a target regarding the reception of customers’
complaints with respect to data privacy in order to track the
effectiveness of the Group Data Privacy Policy and BCR, with
respect to the management of negative impact on individuals
and society due to non‑responsible use of data (e.g. privacy
breaches, potential for discrimination, risk of misuse for
harmful purposes). This target enables AXA to ensure that
customers’ data is used in a responsible manner that
safeguards clients’ privacy, in accordance with its Data Privacy
Declarations and internal corporate rules for the protection of
personal data.
The defined target consists of achieving a yearly target of 0,01%
of complaints received with respect to data privacy in the
Group (which means less than 9,500 complaints for 95,000,000
clients) and is absolute. This target covers all activities of AXA
with respect to Data Privacy. This target has been defined with
reference to complaints lodged by natural persons about any
unlawful or inappropriate processing of their personal data that
is incompatible with the BCR. This target covers the number of
complaints received during a calendar year.
AXA has defined this target using the number of complaints
with respect to data privacy received by the Group, compared
to the total number of AXA customers, to evaluate and
challenge the number of customers’ complaints. This target
considers and respects of the freedoms and rights of the
individuals, i.e. data subjects, thanks to close collaboration
between all the local entities’ DPOs, through the management
of complaints received in all AXA entities.
With respect to the first disclosed target, AXA has achieved the
following performance: in 2024, out of 95 million customers,
the Group received 509 customer’s complaints with respect to
data privacy, equivalent to 0.0005% customers. Compared with
what had been initially planned, the progress is as follows: the
ratio for 2023 is under the yearly target of 0.01%. In 2023, AXA
received 497 complaints, equivalent to 0.0005% of customers,
and in 2022, 471 complaints, equivalent to 0.0005% of
customers. This performance is explained by the
implementation of various initiatives to promote the
responsible use of data and AI, to address societal challenges
and to ensure the protection of customer data through a strong
security strategy.

4.4 Governance information

In addition, AXA set a target regarding the application of the
BCR in order to track the effectiveness of the Group Data
Privacy Policy and BCR with respect to the management of the
potential negative impact of not using responsibly data. This
target has the objective of enabling the Group to ensure that
the BCR are integrated into AXA’s governance structure. The
defined target consists of the Group entities that are applying
BCR and represents 99% of the Group’s revenues. It covers all
activities of the Group with respect to Data Privacy and has
been defined with reference to the revenue generated by the
number of AXA local entities that have signed the BCR. This
target covers a calendar year.
The target is defined using the revenue generated by the
number of AXA local entities that signed the BCR compared to
the percentage of the Group’s revenues to evaluate
performance and effectiveness of the Group’s Data Protection
strategy set forth in the BCR regarding the potential negative
impact of not using responsibly data.
This target considers going beyond Data Privacy minimum
requirements to comply with local legal and regulatory
requirements applicable to AXA local entities businesses and to
incorporate local market best practices. Furthermore, while AXA
local entities may (and are encouraged to) go beyond the
minimum requirements established in the BCR, they must not
adopt lower requirements than set forth in the BCR. Moreover,
the maturity level questionnaire process establishes
quantitatively measurable objectives, to achieve a level of
maturity and to ensure BCR compliance. The Group has not
involved stakeholders in setting this target.
With respect to the second disclosed target, the Group has
achieved the following performance: Group entities that were
applying BCR represented 99% of the Group’s revenues in 2024
(also 99% in 2023 and 2022) in line with the 99% target.
The target is yearly monitored and reviewed by AXA and the
metrics used are the generated revenues of AXA local entities
that have signed the BCR. The 99% target has been achieved
for the third year running.

DATA SECURITY AND DATA PRIVACY

Data security
AXA has set security maturity and security awareness targets in
order to track the effectiveness of security standards
enforcement across the Group. These targets aim to ensure
that both individuals and the organization are equipped with
tools and knowledge to anticipate and mitigate risks of a
negative impact on individuals and society due to non‑secure
use of data (e.g., data leakage, identity theft, financial fraud,
privacy violations.).
The defined targets consist of reaching a 3.0 ISO Maturity score,
and 100% of staff trained about security and data privacy
across the Group. As part of One Trust program described in the
previous section, AXA is currently designing an internal
framework, based on several security norms (ISO 27001, NIST,
…) to better drive the improvement of entities’ security
posture. This framework aims at evaluating the entities via a
security score considering entity’s maturity with both technical
standards (called Minimum Technical Security Baseline) and
controls maturity (called the Security Assurance Framework). In
this framework, this security score, illustrating the Group
strengthened requirements against its entities, becomes the
main indicator to drive security within AXA, and entities are
split into two groups (Tier A and Tier B) and are provided with
specific targets based on their size, branding and connection.
The security and data privacy training are updated on a yearly
basis, always with a target to reach 100% of staff trained. ISO
maturity target is defined to be reached at the end of the
strategic cycle, in 2026, and is driven and monitored on a yearly
basis through the One Trust program described before.
The maturity level of AXA entities is assessed based on the ISO
27001 norms. In 2024, AXA successfully maintained a maturity
score of 3.45 out of 5 (Scope of the Tier A entities, i.e. the
biggest and more connected entities), contributing to the goal
of remaining among the safest organizations in AXA's sector. An
external assessment, from Control Risks Group, confirmed that
those 20 entities are in the top quartile of the most mature
organizations in the financial sector. On the training side, the
mandatory training on security and data privacy deployed
across the Group in 2024, reached the 100% of salaried
employees certified.

4.4 Governance information

Responsible Usage of AI
AXA recognizes the significant potential of artificial intelligence
(AI) to provide value for customers and shareholders, but also
understands that its use requires careful governance and risk
management measures. AXA is implementing a risk‑based
approach to AI management, founded on internal AI principles,
such as Responsible AI Principles, and guided by relevant
policies and governance frameworks. These measures aim to
ensure that AI is developed and used in a human‑centered,
responsible, safe, compliant and beneficial way, with the intent
of minimizing risks and enabling the achievement of strategic
business objectives.
To ensure the implementation and adoption of AI principles
and policies across entities, AXA established the AI Governance
Forum. Its mission is to guide and support the development,
deployment, and use of responsible AI systems while
encouraging knowledge sharing and best practice
dissemination.
To support the development of skills internally and to
familiarize employees with the opportunities offered by Data &
AI, AXA launched a Data & AI Academy in 2022. This set of
learning programs offers role‑appropriate training modules for

224

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

the responsible use of data & AI, to support skills development.
In 2023, a “Generative AI for Everyone at AXA” module was
added to promote responsible usage of GenAI. A new
awareness program, “Tech Data & AI Essentials”, targeting all
employees will be rolled out in March 2025, in which the
importance of ethical and sustainable AI is reinforced.
AXA also works closely with regulators and leading research
centers (Sorbonne University, Lausanne EPFL, Stanford
University), on Responsible AI and effective AI governance in
the insurance industry. AXA has also signed a three‑year
partnership with the HAI lab in Stanford focused on six research
streams on Large Language Model agents and the business
impact of the AI revolution.
In 2024, AXA published or presented eight academic papers in
top international conferences and journals, three of which were
co‑authored through its academic partnerships with Sorbonne
University and EPFL. AXA sponsored two PhDs on Large
Language Models in collaboration with Sorbonne University.

4.5.2 Reporting methodologies
4.5.2.1

Environmental methodologies

Unless stated otherwise, all targets were set without external
stakeholders' consultation and are not based on scientific
evidence and no quantification of capital expenditures or
operational expenditures in relation to any actions plans have
been estimated.

Investments associated metrics
Carbon intensity on Listed Equities and Listed
Corporate Debt
Carbon intensity in relation to listed equities and listed
corporate debt (within AXA’s General Account investment
portfolio) takes into account Scopes 1 and 2 GHG emissions,
measured in accordance with the GHG Protocol. The targets are
expressed in tons of CO2-equivalent per € million invested
(tCO2e/ Euro millions). AXA’s carbon intensity takes into
account global GHG emissions from corporates but does not
include any avoided emissions.
In line with NZAOA’s recommended approach, AXA elected to
use a corporate’s Enterprise Value Including Cash (EVIC) as the
denominator over which to measure the carbon intensity of
AXA’s investment in that corporate. AXA uses this normalized
carbon intensity as the measure for its decarbonization targets
for 2025 and 2030. This approach, in AXA’s view, provides a
better comparison among all asset classes in its portfolio and
facilitates comparability with peers, as EVIC remains a
commonly used denominator among AXA’s peers. However,
this methodology is applied only to the extent the relevant
corporate data is available (i.e. both GHG emissions and EVIC
available).
Scope 3 emissions are not taken into account by the
calculation of carbon intensity, mostly because of the lack of
reported information pertaining to these kinds of emissions.
AXA continues to engage with its data provider to obtain the
Scope 3 emissions (upstream and downstream) in all regions,
with a high corporate coverage, and with a high‑quality
confidence level.
The formula to derive the carbon intensity at the portfolio level
is:
Carbon_emission_company
*Market_Value
EVIC_company
Market_Value

Evic is defined as the sum of market capitalization of ordinary
shares at fiscal year‑end, the market capitalization of preferred
shares at fiscal year‑end, and the book values of total debt and
minorities’ interests. No deductions of cash or cash equivalents
are made to avoid the possibility of negative enterprise values.

Financed carbon emissions
In addition, AXA monitors GHG emissions financed by assets
held in its portfolio. It is defined as the carbon intensity
(normalized by EVIC) multiplied by the assets under
management covered by the carbon intensity. The scope and
limitations applicable to this methodology mirrors those
applicable to the methodology used to measure carbon
intensity of listed equity and listed corporate debt. No specific
target has been set on financed emissions as AXA has chosen
the carbon intensity as the measure for its decarbonization
targets.
The formula to derive the financed emissions at the portfolio
level is:
Carbon_emission_company
*Market_Value
EVIC_company

Market_Value = Market Value of the positions covered by a

Carbon intensity on sovereign debt
In 2023, AXA reshaped its methodology to compute the carbon
intensity of its sovereign debt (1) portfolio in accordance with
the accounting methodology recommended by NZAOA, which
is based on the current version of the PCAF’s Global GHG
Accounting and Reporting Standard (2). The GHG emissions and
GDP data sources used by AXA are public (PRIMAP and World
Bank datasets respectively). Based on this approach, the
carbon intensity of AXA’s sovereign assets is defined as the
production emissions (tCO2e) per Purchase Power
Parity (3) (PPP) - adjusted GDP (million €). Carbon intensity of a
sovereign issuer cannot be directly compared with the carbon
intensity of other asset classes due to differences in the
calculation approach (EVIC vs. GDP‑PPP).

Carbon_emission_country = GHG Scope 1 emissions of the
country expressed in tons of CO2-equivalent (tCO2e);
GDP_PPP_country = PPP‑adjusted GDP of the country
expressed in million €;
Market_Value = Market Value of the positions held in the
portfolio expressed in million €.

AXA uses the latest publicly available data of carbon emissions,
usually with a 1‑year lag versus the portfolio valuations, and the
GDP‑PPP date is aligned with the GHG emissions.

Oil & Gas exposure
AXA is tracking its exposure, without any explicit target to the
Oil & Gas sector by identifying the portion of its portfolio
invested in corporates classified under the following
Bloomberg sectors: Oil & Gas, Oil & Gas Services, and Pipelines.
The total exposure to the Oil & Gas sector is calculated as the
total AUM for this subset of corporates. AXA reports this figure in
absolute terms (Euro billion) and relative to the total AUM of its
General Account.
To further analyze its exposure to unconventional oil and gas
activities, AXA uses the Global Oil & Gas Exit List (GOGEL 2024)
from Urgewald, which provides data on the share of
unconventional production for each company. The exposure to
unconventional activities is then determined by multiplying the
AUM invested in each corporate by its corresponding share of
unconventional production, as reported in the GOGEL dataset.
The global exposure to these industries covers both listed and
private assets from the General Account.

Physical Climate Value at Risk

Physical Risk Climate VaR metric assesses the level of exposure
and vulnerability of companies to increasingly frequent and
severe extreme weather events. This metric combines chronic
climate risks, which refer to long‑term shifts in climate patterns
such as extreme heat, extreme cold, heavy precipitation, heavy
snowfall and strong winds, and acute climate risks, which refer
to event‑driven physical risks such as coastal flooding, river
flooding, tropical cyclones, low river flows and wildfires. This
metric thus evaluates the potential economic losses in a
changing climate environment based on a given climate
scenario. The main challenge when applying the Physical Risk
metric lies in capturing all possible extreme weather events. In
addition, this metric focuses only on the assets owned by a
particular company, as identified by MSCI, and does not
account for the sustainability of the infrastructure, grids or
other necessary components that enable the assets to operate
and generate revenue for the Company.

Climate VaR (CVaR) is the ratio between the net present value of
future cash flows and the current company valuation. It is
expressed as a negative number, representing the potential
maximum loss for a company under a specific climate scenario.

SCENARIO NAME

MSCI NAME

COMMENTS

Net Zero by 2050

1.5°C REMIND NGFS Orderly

Divergent Net Zero

1.5°C REMIND NGFS Disorderly

The two REMIND NGFS 1.5°C scenarios are very similar in
terms of emissions pathways and temperature warming.
Where they differ is in the use of low-carbon technologies,
with the disorderly scenario using more low-carbon
sources of technology in various sectors and the orderly
scenario using slightly more carbon sequestration.

Below 2°C

2°C REMIND NGFS Orderly

Delayed Transition

2°C REMIND NGFS Disorderly

NDC

3°C REMIND NGFS

The REMIND NGFS 2°C scenarios are similar to the 1.5°C
scenarios in terms of electricity generation fuel mix in 2050
and, for the Orderly 2°C scenario, in terms of carbon
sequestration use. Where they differ is how fast the
transition happens, the year emissions reach net-zero
emissions and the projected carbon prices needed to reach
the temperature target.

The 3°C scenario assumes a slower pace of decarbonization
than more ambitious scenarios and is based solely on
current nationally determined contributions (NDC) of each
country.

These scenarios are derived from the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) research. The NGFS scenarios are recognized
by central banks and supervisors, making them a credible reference in the field. A selection of five NGFS scenarios has been made to
cover a spectrum of temperature increases ranging from +1.5°C to +3°C by 2100. These NGFS scenarios also consider two distinct
approaches to transitioning to a lower‑carbon economy: an orderly transition and a disorderly transition.

Potential impacts and dependencies on biodiversity
from ENCORE
AXA uses data from the publicly available ENCORE database to
assess biodiversity‑related impacts and dependencies (ID) at
an economic activity level (and not individual company level).
ENCORE assigns a materiality rating to each identified
dependency link between an economic activity (of which there
are 271) and an ecosystem service (of which there are 25).
Additionally, a materiality rating is assigned for each identified
link between an economic activity and pressure (or impact
drivers, of which there are 13). AXA mapped the 271 economic
activities to its own classification (based on level 3 Bloomberg
Industry Classification Standard).

1. sustainability dialogue: bespoke meetings, training/

normalizing across portfolios of differing sizes.

2. engagement with objectives, such as engagement with
incentives to encourage behavioral change or requests for
additional climate disclosures (such as emissions
information);

The absolute IAE measurement is appropriate for underwriting

their GHGs. AXA has therefore applied the IAE measurement

3. engagement with objectives linked with AXA's sustainability
underwriting policies, such as a reduction in non‑compliant

Climate adaptation solutions and services
AXA defines the number of climate adaptation solutions and
services delivered to commercial clients as the number of
trainings, risk assessment or awareness, gap analysis
prevention or solution, crisis management or remediation
response provided to commercial clients that create awareness
on climate adaptation or that are specifically related to climate

Sustainable claims
A sustainable claim solution is a claim service or solution that
involves less CO2 equivalent emissions or makes use of circular
economy to minimize waste. For the purposes of reporting, AXA
categorizes sustainable claims within the three below
categories:
●

Remote assessment, when a claim adjustment process
involves the application of technology or video usage to
assess and remediate the claims;

●

●

Repair (versus replace), when a damage claim is adjusted by
fixing or correcting the damage instead of replacing the
damaged piece (for example windshield reparation); and
Secondhand parts, when a replacement component is from
an after‑market provider versus from an original equipment
manufacturer.

A claim can benefit one or several of the above solutions, but a
claim can only count for one solution in each category. The
percentage of sustainable retail motor claims versus all motor
claims is calculated as the ratio of claims providing sustainable
solution by the total number of retail motor claims of entities in
scope of the target.
Data for the sustainable claims solutions is sourced from the
repair garages in the case of the use of the repair and
secondhand parts solutions, and from AXA Assistance or
external suppliers regarding the remote assessment.
Deforestation policy
The Deforestation policy incorporates three screening
methods: assessing exposure to high‑risk commodities,
monitoring controversies related to biodiversity and land use,
and evaluating the impact of corporate activities on forests.
AXA uses external data providers such as Sustainalytics and
CDP Forest.
The Deforestation policy works with the “Sustainalytics
Controversies” database and focuses on biodiversity and land
use category, levels 3, 4 and 5 corresponding to “Significant”,
“High” and "Severe".

Calculation methodology
AXA's calculation methodology applies GHG protocol, namely
the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance and the GHG Protocol
Corporate Value Chain. In respect of Scope 3 emissions, the
methodology does not take into account any removals,
purchases, sales or transfers of carbon credits or GHG
allowances.
GHG emissions related to own operations are calculated using
third‑party software (from Tennaxia) that collects data from
entities within scope including distance travelled and electricity
purchased.
GHG emissions related to primary energy consumption for
buildings are calculated using consumption in kilowatt‑hours
(kWh) multiplied by ADEME emission factors or those
communicated by the supplier for renewable energies such as
biogas. AXA does not have Scope 1 GHG emissions from
regulated emission trading schemes neither biogenic
emissions from the combustion or bio‑degradation of biomass.

For car fleet emissions, an emission factor per kilometer is
applied based on the vehicle’s emission range. To consider
regulatory changes, vehicles acquired or leased from 2020
onwards are classified according to the WLTP (World
harmonized Light‑duty vehicles Test Procedure) standard. The
WLTP is a global harmonized standard for determining the
levels of pollutants, GHG emissions and fuel consumption of
traditional and hybrid cars, as well as the range of fully electric
vehicles.
GHG emissions related to electricity consumption are
calculated on the basis of consumption in kWh which is based
on two different methods (1):
●

●

a market‑based method which reflects emissions from
electricity that companies have purposefully chosen and
where certification of origin can be used. This method is the
one used in the target; and
a location‑based method which reflects the average
emissions intensity of grids on which energy consumption
occurs (using mostly grid‑average emission factor data).

Market‑based GHG emissions for Scope 2 use
ADEME (2) emissions factors when the primary source of energy
is known. If unavailable, AXA uses either the emission factor
provided by the electricity suppliers, or the average emission
factor for residual electricity in the country or region concerned
(sourced from AIB for European countries, Green‑e for United
States and production mix of IEA for others).
Location‑based emissions use IEA production mix in relation to
electricity consumption.
For other secondary energy sources (heating and cooling
networks), consumption is multiplied by the emission factors
provided by ADEME or directly by the supplier when the energy
is produced from a renewable primary source.
Scope 3 emissions in category 3 (energy‑related) are calculated
based on the location‑based methodology.
GHG emissions related to business travel are calculated
multiplying the distance travelled by AXA's employees for the
different transport category by emission factors. For planes, AXA
uses emission factors provided by the UK Department for
Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA), including contrails
impacts and the upstream emissions. For business travels by
train, AXA uses emission factors provided by ADEME.

(1) See Scope 2 methodology defined by the Greenhouse Gas Protocol https://ghgprotocol.org/
(2) ADEME is the French Agency for Ecological Transition. It is a French public agency under the joint authority of the Ministry for an Ecological Transition,
Ministry of Energy and Ministry for Higher Education and Research.

4.5.2.2

Social methodologies

AXA's workforce
Social data reporting
The social data provided in Section 4.3.1 “AXA's workforce” of
this Sustainability Statement are collected through a reporting
process defined by procedures associated with a list of
indicators shared with all entities of the Group. Reporting
Scope covers all AXA entities under the CSRD scope. SDR
process is updated and communicated to each entity on a
yearly basis. Social data are provided by local correspondents
using an IT tool dedicated to the social data reporting process.
Consistency checks and quality controls are carried out before
and during the data collection process. A validation process of
this reporting is also performed locally by the Human
Resources Director or legal entity representative. No estimation
or extrapolation is applied to the data provided. For ratios and
percentages, the numerator and denominator are adjusted for
each calculation to exclude entities with missing data points.
Precision on temporary employees reporting
Temporary employees are salaried employees of AXA but with a
limited duration of employment. They are usually hired when:
●

●

●

there is an increase in activity (limited in duration);
there is a need to replace an open‑ended contract that has
to take days off (such as health; maternity, paternity and
parental absence; personal matters);
there is a specific mission/project (limited in duration).

Renewal of fixed‑term contracts is not included in the count of
external recruitments of salaried workforce under fixed‑term
contracts and not reported as the end of fixed‑term contract.
If an employee’s contract is converted from a fixed‑term to an
open‑ended contract, then it is not counted as the termination
of a fixed‑term contract or an external recruitment on an
open‑ended contract.

non‑guaranteed hours
‑

very limited number of cases.

salaried employees with open‑ended contracts for the same

Work‑related accidents
‑

Remuneration (gender pay gap and total remuneration)

Work‑related accidents are not uniformly defined across
jurisdictions, but generally comprise the following: an
unexpected event that occurs in the working environment
(accident in the building: e.g. falling down the stairs) or during a
work‑related activity (journey from home to work/work to
home; business trip), which may cause an injury/illness and
require medical treatment or lead to a disability. All the
indicators of this category are measured on contractual
working days and not calendar days. Employees who were
considered absent due to injury/illness during the reporting
year are included, even if they are no longer employed as of
December 31, 2024, are included.

The assessment is based on Annual Target Total Direct
Compensation which includes the Fixed Pay, Target Cash
Variable Pay and Target LTI. Assessing pay gaps on a target
basis ensures monitoring of our progress in closing the gaps
year on year and avoids potential volatility linked to AXA’s
business. For the vast majority of AXA entities, compensation
data is only available on an annual basis and not hourly basis
due to the nature of financial services activities.

The absenteeism rate (based on absences due to sickness and
work‑related accidents) provide AXA with a measure that
evaluates the impact of the Group’s local health & wellbeing
initiatives, together with SDR indicators, taking into account
short‑term / long‑term absences.
The absenteeism rate of salaried workforce
The absenteeism rate of salaried workforce is the sum of the
number of absence days in a year due to work‑related
accidents and illness, divided by the number of days worked
per year per employee, the result of which is multiplied by the
average FTE of salaried workforce. Only open‑ended contracts
are included. This rate does not take into account non‑salaried
workforce.
Pulse and Inclusion surveys
In 2024, AXA transitioned from an 11‑point eNPS measurement
scale (promoters minus detractors) to a 5‑point favorability
scale for measuring its employee engagement. The answer
options are: Strongly Agree, Agree, Neither Agree Nor Disagree,
Disagree, Strongly Disagree. Engagement (Advocacy) question
is “I would recommend AXA as a great place to work.” Inclusion
Advocacy question: “I would recommend AXA as an inclusive
and diverse workplace”. The Engagement favorability score is
the percentage of the number of respondents who answered
“Strongly Agree or Agree”, out of the number of respondents
who answered to this question.
AXA’s gender parity amongst Top Senior Executives (women
representation): represents the share of women who are part
of the Global Leadership Network (GLN), which comprises the
CEO and Executive Committees of AXA’s largest markets and
major transversal entities, as well as senior leaders from the
corporate functions, markets, and some country CEOs. The
numerator for this calculation is the number of women, while
the denominator is the number of women plus the number of
men. The scope for this calculation concerns all entities having
GLN members. The GLN definition is used as the definition of
AXA's top management.

Gender Pay Gap is calculated as the difference between the
average Target Total Direct Compensation of men and women.
The Remuneration Ratio measures the pay gap between the
highest‑paid individual and the median employee in terms of
annual total remuneration, excluding the highest‑paid
individual from the calculation of the median.
The reporting scope covers all AXA entities under the CSRD
scope and excludes AXA TianPing (China) due to data transfer
restrictions, and Roland (Germany) as it lacked adequate
preparation time for the assessment due to its recent inclusion
in the scope. Other excluded entities (missed from reporting)
are GACM SEGUROS GENERALES COMPAÑÍA DE SEGUROS Y
REASEGUROS , S.A.U. and EMERMEDICA S.A. SERVICIOS DE
AMBULANCIA PREPAGADOS which will be included from the
upcoming year’s assessment.
Adequate Wages
The wage analysis is based on Actual Total Cash Compensation
which includes the Fixed Pay and Actual Cash variable pay.
AXA's wage analysis is conducted to ensure that employees are
paid at or above adequate wages, which are defined as living
wage thresholds obtained from the external provider, Fairwage
Network. These living wage thresholds are based on a robust
methodology of the provider, whereby the living wage is
defined as a level of income that allows an individual worker to
meet his/her basic needs and those of his/her family at decent
standards (in terms of food, housing, education, health, etc.).
The living wage thresholds used by AXA take into account the
statistical number of income earners per household (average
income earners) and family size according to the national
fertility rate in each country. The analysis is conducted annually
by the Fairwage Network, and this reporting is based on full
year 2023 data to meet the reporting timeline.
The reporting scope is the same as for the section
"Remuneration (gender pay gap and total remuneration)"
above.

Definitions of social indicators
An employee is an individual who is in an employment
relationship with the undertaking according to national laws or
practices. It includes active employees who have a labor
contract with permanent and temporary, full and part‑time
contract. It excludes employees on "suspended or unpaid”
leave, employees with a “garden leave” status/contract and
people not having labor contract with (trainees on internship
without labor contract, third party agency people, contractors
and subcontractors).
A permanent employee is a permanent workforce under
open‑ended employment contract with AXA, full‑time or
part‑time. In some countries (e.g. China), renewable contracts
planned for a long period (several years) are considered as
open‑ended contracts. This indicator is reported in headcount
as of December 31 of the reporting year.
A temporary employee is a temporary workforce under
fixed‑term employment contract with AXA, full‑time or
part‑time. They are salaried employees but with a limited
duration of employment. This indicator is reported in
headcount as of December 31 of the reporting year.
The percentage of entitled employees that took
family‑related leave is calculated as the percentage of salaried
workforce, corresponding to the ratio of number of headcounts
of salaried workforce who took family‑related leaves (including
maternity, paternity, parental leaves) during the reporting year
divided by the average headcount of salaried workforce during
the reporting year. Salaried workforce who took family‑related
leave during the reporting year but left AXA and no longer are
part of the workforce as of December 31 are included. It
concerns only salaried workforce with open‑ended contract.
The contingent labor or temporary non‑salaried workforce
includes contractors, consultants or those having a contract
with a job agency and freelancers. It excludes trainees, interns,
apprentices, outsourcing agreements, third‑party suppliers or
Strategic Consulting specific services. This indicator is reported
in Average Full Time Equivalent as of December 31 of the
reporting year.

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

In 2024, the strategic decision to enlarge the scope of AXA
EssentiALL was made in recognition of the global nature of the
protection gap. In that regard, AXA EssentiALL is now working
on developing inclusive insurance solutions across mature
European Markets, with the objective of better serving modest
income households and small businesses with insurance
solutions.
As a consequence of this enlarged geographic scope with
increased rates of insurance penetration (compared to the
initial scope covering emerging markets), the methodology has
been adjusted to reflect the possibility of multiple contracts per
customer. As a consequence a customer adjustment factor has
been incorporated into the formula in an effort to eliminate
double counting. The formula is as follow:
No. of Customers = (A + B)/C
(A) Number of individual contracts in‑force at the end of the
period
(B) Number of certificates within a group contract in‑force at
the end of the period
(C) The customer adjustment factor
The primary assumptions are:
1. that in Emerging Markets the customer adjustment factor is
equal to “1” to reflect the low‑insurance penetration
environment and the low likelihood that customers have
more than one contract with AXA;
2. that in Mature Markets, the customer adjustment factor is
computed by each contributing entity based on its own
local customer data, and is applied to avoid double
counting of customers,
3. that a majority of policyholders or insurance beneficiaries
(i.e. the customers having bought or receiving an inclusive
insurance product from AXA EssentiALL) will belong to the
defined segments in the local inclusive insurance strategy
(i.e., low‑income to mass‑market customers in emerging
markets and modest‑income customers in mature markets).
Reported data is collected from AXA entities as part of the AXA
EssentiALL Performance Management Process or, in cases
where the AXA EssentiALL solutions are distributed through
partners or third parties, data is collected directly from these
business partners, which is then reviewed for consistency with
local reporting by AXA entities and submitted to AXA Group (the
AXA EssentiALL business unit) for consolidation purposes.

4.5.2.3

Governance methodologies

Volunteering
The percentage of employees engaged in volunteering
activities is calculated as the number of employees
(headcount) that participate at least to a volunteering activity
during the year divided by the total average headcount of AXA’s
salaried workforce. A volunteering activity is an active
participation in an activity with a charitable purpose/for the
benefit of a charitable organization, of at least 30 minutes.

Data‑privacy and data security
‑
Data privacy
The number of complaints with respect to data privacy
received by the Group, compared to the total number of AXA
customers, is used to evaluate the potential negative impact on
individuals' privacy and trust in data systems resulting from
unaccountable or insecure use of data.
The percentage of the Group’s revenues represented by the
Group entities that apply the Binding Corporate Rules is used
to evaluate performance and effectiveness of the Group’s Data
Protection strategy. It is calculated based on previous year
Group’s revenues and list of entities that have signed the
Binding Corporate Rules.

Data security
The One Trust Program yearly progress is used to evaluate
performance and effectiveness of One Trust Program regarding
the potential negative impact on individuals' privacy and trust
in data systems due to unaccountable or insecure use of data.
It is calculated based on the individual progress of the
underlying program initiatives in an effort to ensure they
remain on time, on scope and on budget.

Management and relationships with suppliers
The average standard time of payment in number of days
according to contractual terms is calculated as the average
across all the invoices paid during the reporting year.
The average time of payment is calculated as the average time,
in number of days, the undertaking takes to pay an invoice
from the date when the contractual or statutory term of
payment starts to be calculated. For most countries the
contractual or statutory term of payment starts when the
invoice has been issued by the vendor. Under some regulation,
the contractual term of payment starts to when the invoice is
received. In that case the entity uses the invoice receiving date
as starting point for the calculation of time of payment.

Business conduct and Anti Bribery
and Corruption metrics
The different cases of violation of anti‑corruption and
anti‑bribery laws occurring at local entity level during the year
is reported at Group level through the Group Audit Department.

4.5.3.4

Unaddressed topics and limitations

List of
non‑material topics
‑
Standard

S3 Affected communities

Assumptions, limitations and omissions
Specific assumptions based on current market practice or
limitations have been used by AXA as part of the first publication
of this Sustainability Statement under CSRD. In addition, some
data points required by the ESRS standards are missing in this first
Sustainability Statement due to unavailability of data. This
information is presented below.

●

Assumptions and limitations
●

●

●

GHG emissions of the Group's investments: AXA has faced
limitations in the scope of the metrics published in terms of
asset classes covered and data availability (Scope 3). For more
information on the asset classes covered, please refer to
Section 4.2.1.3 - Addressing climate change as an investor.
For more information on availability of scope 3 related data,
please refer to Section 4.5.2.1 - Environmental
methodologies - Investments associated metrics.

Taxonomy disclosure: The information has been prepared
acknowledging the regulatory uncertainties unaddressed or
introduced by European Commission's FAQs (including: the
relevance of the templates on Gas & Nuclear activities for
underwriting, the granularity in the application of minimum
safeguards requirements, guidance on the calculation of the
combined and consolidated Group‑level KPIs possibly
impairing the qualitative characteristics of the information),
the issues to obtain data from issuers or data providers, and
progressive improvement of the process to determine the
non‑life insurance eligibility / alignment.
●

GHG emissions of the Group's insurance activities: AXA has
faced limitations in the scope of the metric in terms of
insurance portfolio in connection with methodologies that are
not mature, unavailability of data (Scope 3) and in terms of the
maturity of the process (not all eligible policies are subject to
the calculation of the metric; only a reduced scope has been
considered for the first year and which will be extended
progressively). For more information, please refer to
Section 4.2.1.4 - Addressing climate change as an insurer,
and to Section 4.5.2.1 - Environmental methodologies Insurance associated metrics.

●

●

GHG emissions related to real estate investments (Scope 3 vs
Scopes 1‑2): Uncertainties in standards interpretations led AXA
to choose to categorize real estate investments in category 15
of the Group's carbon footprint related to Scope 3, although
this includes invested properties over which AXA has

Additional information related
to the EU Taxonomy

Contextual information for Non‑Life
Underwriting KPI
Eligibility analysis
In accordance with the Climate Delegated Act, as amended,
insurance services classified in eight of the non‑Life insurance
and reinsurance Solvency II lines of business are considered as
EU Taxonomy‑eligible, to the extent that they include policy
terms related to the underwriting of climate‑related perils.
In this regard, AXA has identified three lines of business
composed of insurance or reinsurance products generally
including coverage of risks related to climate‑related perils:
(i) motor insurance (other than third party liability insurance);
(ii) marine, aviation and transport insurance; and (iii) fire and
other property damage insurance.

254

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

The share of gross written premiums covering climate‑related
events reported in those three lines of business have been
recognized as EU Taxonomy‑eligible, excluding premiums of
products for which climate‑related perils are explicitly excluded
from the insurance policy terms or for which climate‑related
perils cannot trigger any claims.
On other potentially eligible lines of business (i.e. medical
expense insurance, income protection insurance, workers’
compensation insurance, motor vehicle liability insurance and
assistance), only the share of the gross written premiums
covering climate‑related perils in products for which such cover
is explicitly mentioned in the insurance policy terms could also
be considered as EU Taxonomy‑eligible.
The analysis has been done on direct lines of business, and
reinsurance assumed.
In the case of insurance coverage for natural disasters, the full
premium was considered eligible. In other cases, the share of
premium covering climate‑related perils can be determined in
the pricing tool at the time of the subscription; otherwise it was
estimated generally through historical losses recorded in
respect of climate‑related perils.
Alignment analysis
To determine the amount of premiums related to Non‑Life
insurance and reinsurance underwriting EU Taxonomy‑aligned
activities, AXA analyzed the EU Taxonomy‑eligible products and
identified those that satisfied each of the substantial
contribution criteria of the Technical Screening Criteria (TSC)
for insurance and reinsurance activities: leadership in
modelling and pricing of climate risks, product design,
innovative insurance coverage solutions, data sharing and high
level of service in post‑disaster situations.
Some criteria were covered at Group level and considered as
satisfied for all portfolios. It notably concerns the fact that AXA
uses state‑of‑the‑art climate risks modelling techniques (TSC
1.1), using Natural Hazard models to estimate the damage and
losses to individual risks or insured and reinsured portfolios.
Natural Hazards comprise geoscience‑based models for hazard
intensity and frequency in formation, adding in engineering
(vulnerability) and economic (financial) modules, along with
reinsurance terms. Future climate risk is also assessed through
forward‑looking scenarios analysis performed by Risk
Management. For details relating to how the climate change
risk is considered in the insurance activity (TSC 1.2), refer to
Section 4.2.1 - Climate change - 4.2.1.4 - Addressing climate
change as an insurer.

The criteria providing for risk‑based rewards for preventative

and AXA XL:
insurance policies covering damage to cars and homes from
natural catastrophes underwritten by AXA France, given the
following characteristics:
●

compulsory and regulated, including in respect of the

risk reduction and risk‑based reward are de facto
complied with due to this legal restriction. The
compulsory requirement also satisfies TSC 1.4 and TSC
3.1 on renewal condition and coverage for climate
related premiums,
preventive measures takes the form of alerts sent to
policyholders' mobile phone in case of extreme weather
events (TSC 2.1),
some specific solutions are included in commercial

high level of service in post‑disaster situation (TSC 5) is
ensured by the activation of specific measures in the
event of large‑scale events, such as the systematic
deployment of a national crisis unit to support
policyholders in securing their property, speeding up
processing times and adapting responses to individual
situations, or the provision of emergency funds for the
payment of upfront advances;

insurance policies covering commercial property damage
underwritten by AXA XL, where pricing and
recommendations offered to the clients are dependent of
the assessment of a loss prevention report analysis which is
influenced by the degrees of prevention against
climate‑related events, aligned due to the following
characteristics:
●

●

●

assessments but more importantly risk prevention
actions that could be taken to reduce the risk and
ultimately reduce their insurance premiums (TSC 1.1, TSC
2.1 and TSC 2.2);
the insurance coverage solution is client specific, and the
various needs of the insured are established through a

●

high level of service in post‑disaster situation (TSC 5),
characterized by adapting responses to individual
situations, and evidenced by the absence of complaints.

Regarding the data sharing criteria (TSC 4), AXA France already
shares loss data with the CCR (Caisse centrale de réassurance),
a public‑sector reinsurer wholly owned by the French State. In
addition, if a public authority or non‑profit research
organization is carrying out analyses related to natural hazards,
AXA will make available to them, free of charge, a significant
portion of loss data related to climate‑related event. Any
authority or research organization must submit a written
request to AXA, specifying the purpose of the research and the
scope of the data requested. Where appropriate, the data will
be provided in a granular manner to enable analytical research
but aggregated and anonymized, in order to comply with the
provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/679.
In order to comply with the DNSH criteria, the premiums from
policies covering extraction, storage, transport or manufacture
of fossil fuels or vehicles, property or other assets dedicated to
such purposes, were excluded from the scope of EU
Taxonomy‑aligned premiums.
In order to qualify as “environmentally sustainable” in
compliance with the EU Taxonomy Regulation, an economic
activity must also comply with the minimum safeguards, laid
down in article 18 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation. According to
the European Commission, the central requirement is the
implementation of appropriate procedures to identify, prevent,
mitigate or remedy, on an ongoing basis, actual or potential
negative impacts related to its operations, value chain and
contractual relationships. This ensures that the entity’s
activities are carried out in compliance with such minimum
safeguards. In France, the market consensus among French
insurance companies is that the Loi de vigilance is based, at a
high‑level, on the principles and standards mentioned in
article 18 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation. To comply with the
Loi de vigilance, AXA publishes a vigilance plan that covers AXA’s
activities and subsidiaries controlled directly or indirectly by
AXA as well as the activities of subcontractors and suppliers
with whom the group maintains an established business
relationship, insofar as the activities are linked to that
relationship. AXA's vigilance plan covers insurance activities
and details how risks are identified, analyzed and prioritized
(see 4.7.2.2). It also explains the procedures for regular
assessment (see 4.7.3.3), the actions to reduce risks and
prevent serious damage (see 4.7.4.2), and the monitoring of
their effective implementation (see 4.7.6.3).

after a climate‑risk peril, the AXA XL provides information

renewed or maintained, either with its in‑house claims

Exposures to central governments, central banks, and
supranational issuers, are excluded from the numerator and
denominator of the indicator. This exclusion is explained by the
absence of a methodology for determining their alignment with
the EU Taxonomy.

This regulatory constraint explains why the information above
only presents the share of investments in Taxonomy‑aligned
economic activities under the first two environmental
objectives set forth in article 9 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
(i.e. climate mitigation and climate adaptation).

Exposures to undertakings not subject to articles 19a and 29a
of Directive 2013/34/EU and derivatives, cannot be assessed for
Taxonomy eligibility purposes to date. Similarly, exposure to
non‑EU companies, cannot be considered in the formal
assessment of assets eligible for or aligned with the EU
Taxonomy regulation.

The share of exposures to Taxonomy‑eligible economic
activities under the four environmental objectives set forth in
article 9 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation (i.e. sustainable use
and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a
circular economy, pollution prevention and control and
protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems) are
presented for the first time in 2024.

In accordance with regulatory requirements, the information
published by financial undertakings must be based on actual
data published by non‑financial or financial undertakings. The
use of estimates or approximations is therefore not possible in
the context of mandatory reporting.

exclusion is not likely to significantly affect the KPI.

Taxonomy alignment and eligibility of nuclear
and fossil gas related activities
AXA has taken into consideration the additional requirements
of the Delegated Act 2022/1214 pertaining to Taxonomy
eligibility of nuclear and fossil gas related activities, as well as
guidance published by the European Commission (1).
On the basis of information provided by the relevant investees
concerning the levels of safety, innovation and waste

production from the fuel cycle and collected through an ESG
data provider, AXA considers that it is exposed through its
investments to all activities related to the production of
electricity, heat or cold from gaseous fossil fuels (2) nuclear
energy (3), as presented in Template 1 in Annex XII of Disclosure
Delegated Act, as amended by the First Complementary
Climate Delegated Act.
The following tables present information on exposure to fossil
gas and nuclear energy activities in accordance with templates
1 to 5 of Annex XII of Disclosure Delegated Act, as amended by
the First Complementary Climate Delegated Act. However, in
the interests of readability, as the six economic activities
covered in this section are by definition recognized as
Taxonomy‑eligible, no Taxonomy non‑eligible amounts are
attributable to them and the table corresponding to template 5
would not provide any additional information other than the
Total taxonomy‑non‑eligible economic activities in the
denominator of the investment KPI, already presented in the
table 'Investments directed at funding Taxonomy‑aligned
activities‑Breakdown of denominator' above. It was
intentionally decided not to disclose it.
In some instances, the exposure to economic activities that
have been reported as either Taxonomy‑aligned or
Taxonomy‑eligible but not Taxonomy‑aligned, could not be
allocated to either of the two climate change objectives, which
explains why amounts reported in the total columns do not
systematically reconcile with the sum of the amounts for
climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation.
These differences are not significant, in AXA's view.
The Delegated Regulation on fossil gas and nuclear energy
specifies in its Recital 15 the need for non‑financial and
financial undertakings to provide investors with a high degree
of transparency concerning their investments in fossil gas and
nuclear energy generation activities. AXA's interpretation is that
the fossil gas and nuclear energy exposure only apply to
investments (meaning the Taxonomy investment KPI). As such,
the tables intentionally do not present the Taxonomy
underwriting KPI.

Other methodological considerations
and limitations

The EU Taxonomy's regulatory framework identifies the dual
role of insurers in the environmental transition, i.e.:

To assist companies, the European Commission regularly
publishes Taxonomy FAQs and notices that aim at further
clarifying the disclosure requirements under the EU Taxonomy
Regulation and the Disclosures Delegated Act. AXA
acknowledges the interpretative and implementation guidance
provided by the EU Commission, notably the specific guidance
to financial undertakings in the Third Commission Notice
released on November 8, 2024.
Given that the legal framework for the EU Taxonomy reporting
is new and still in the process of development, the
requirements are subject to uncertainty in interpretation and
the underlying data that are necessary to produce the KPIs may
not always be immediately available. Against this background,
AXA has opted for a prudent approach and will progressively
enhance the completeness and quality of the Taxonomy
reporting.
Furthermore, the information included in the section on EU
Taxonomy Disclosures provides only a partial view of how AXA
contributes to climate‑change adaptation and should be read
in conjunction with all other information provided in Section 4
that gives further examples of such contribution.

4.5.3.6

●

●

Non‑Life insurance and reinsurance activities can contribute
to the adaptation of their policyholders to climate change,
this contribution being measured on the basis of insurance
revenues;
and insurers are also asked to demonstrate the extent to
which the invested assets on their balance sheet are
effectively redirected towards activities that contribute to
the various environmental objectives, this aspect being
measured on the basis of their invested assets.

Given that these two roles are measured on a different basis,
applying the current definition and supporting guidance to
calculate the combined KPI for insurance undertakings and the
consolidated Group‑level KPI would lead to blurred
information. Therefore, AXA intentionally decided not to
disclose these indicators.
Finally, the KPIs applicable to AXA presented in
Sections 4.2.3 and 4.5.3.5, in accordance with the EU
Taxonomy Regulation and the supplementing Commission
Delegated Regulations, for the purpose of the financial year
ended December 31, 2024, were based on financial data
available as of December 31, 2024.

4.6 Sustainability information certification report

4.6

Sustainability information certification report

This is a free translation into English of the statutory auditors’ report on the certification of sustainability information and
verification of the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 issued in French and it is provided solely
for the convenience of English‑speaking users.
This report should be read in conjunction with, and construed in accordance with, French law and the H2A guidelines on Limited
assurance engagement - Certification of sustainability reporting and verification of disclosure requirements set out in Article 8 of
Regulation (EU) 2020/852.

Report on the certification of sustainability information and
verification of the disclosure requirements under Article 8
of Regulation (EU) 2020/852, relating to the year ended
December 31, 2024
To the Annual General Meeting of AXA,
This report is issued in our capacity as statutory auditors of
AXA. It covers the sustainability information and the
information required by Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852,
relating to the year ended December 31, 2024 and included in
the Group management report and presented in sections 4.1 to
4.5 of the universal registration document (called “the
Sustainability Statement” hereafter).
Pursuant to Article L. 233‑28‑4 of the French Commercial Code,
AXA is required to include the above‑mentioned information in
a separate section of the Group management report. This
information has been prepared in the context of the first‑time
application of the aforementioned Articles, a context
characterized by uncertainties regarding the interpretation of
the laws and regulations, the use of significant estimates, the
absence of established practices and frameworks in particular
for the double‑materiality assessment, and an evolving internal
control system. This information enables an understanding of
the impact of the activity of the Group on sustainability matters,
as well as the way in which these matters influence the
development of the business of the Group, its performance and
position. Sustainability matters include environmental, social
and corporate governance matters.
Pursuant
to
Article L. 821‑54
paragraph II
of
the
aforementioned Code our responsibility is to carry out the
procedures necessary to issue a conclusion, expressing limited
assurance, on:
●

compliance with the sustainability reporting standards
adopted pursuant to Article 29 b of Directive (EU) 2013/34 of
the European Parliament and of the Council of
14 December 2022 (hereinafter ESRS for European
Sustainability Reporting Standards) of the process
implemented by AXA to determine the information
reported;

●

●

compliance of the sustainability information included in the
Sustainability Statement with the requirements of
Article L. 233‑28‑4 of the French Commercial Code,
including the ESRS; and
compliance with the reporting requirements set out in
Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852.

This engagement is carried out in compliance with the ethical
rules, including independence, and quality control rules
prescribed by the French Commercial Code.
It is also governed by the H2A guidelines on Limited assurance
engagement - Certification of sustainability reporting and
verification of disclosure requirements set out in Article 8 of
Regulation (EU) 2020/852.
In the three separate sections of the report that follow, we
present, for each of the sections of our engagement, the nature
of the procedures that we carried out, the conclusions that we
drew from these procedures and, in support of these
conclusions, the elements to which we paid particular attention
and the procedures that we carried out with regard to these
elements. We draw your attention to the fact that we do not
express a conclusion on any of these elements taken
individually and that the procedures described should be
considered in the overall context of the formation of the
conclusions issued in respect of each of the three sections of
our engagement.
Finally, where deemed necessary to draw your attention to one
or more disclosures of sustainability information provided by
AXA in the Sustainability Statement, we have included
emphasis of matter paragraphs hereafter.

Limits of our engagement
As the purpose of our engagement is to express limited
assurance, the nature (choice of techniques), extent (scope)
and timing of the procedures are less than those required to
obtain reasonable assurance.

As part of our verifications on the eligibility of activities, our
procedures mainly consisted in:
●

analysing, on a selection, the elements on which the
management based its judgement when assessing whether
the eligible economic activities met the cumulative
conditions expected by the EU Taxonomy Framework in
order to be qualified as aligned, in particular the principle of
"Do Not Significant Harm" to any of the other environmental
objectives;

●

with regard to the denominators presented in the regulatory
tables, examining the reconciliations made by the entity
with the accounting data used for the preparation of the

with regard to the numerators (eligible and/or aligned

these amounts on the basis of a selection of non‑life
underwriting activities and investments, which we
determined based on their contribution to the KPIs and a
risk analysis;
evaluating the appropriateness of the accompanying
contextual information of disclosed KPIs.

Finally, we evaluated the consistency of the information in
sections 4.2.3 “EU Taxonomy disclosures” and 4.5.3.5
“Additional information related to the EU Taxonomy” of the
Sustainability Statement with the other sustainability
information in that report.

4.7 Vigilance Plan

Vigilance Plan

To comply with applicable French law requirements (1), AXA has (i) adopted a vigilance plan that sets out the measures established
and implemented by the Group in order to identify the risks relating to, and prevent, violations of human rights, fundamental
freedoms and health and safety of persons and adverse impacts on the environment resulting from the Group’s activities and from its
own operations (the “Vigilance Plan”), and (ii) prepared a report, included in this section, on the application of the Vigilance Plan
during the financial year 2024.
For the avoidance of doubt, “ESG” and “sustainability”, as used in the context of describing criteria, risks, impacts or objectives, refer
to environmental, social (including human rights and fundamental freedoms as well as health and safety) and governance matters;
and “suppliers and subcontractors” mean the Group’s direct suppliers and subcontractors for its procurement activities.

4.7.1 Scope
In accordance with the requirements of French law on the duty of vigilance, the Group’s Vigilance Plan, covers the activities of AXA and
those of the companies controlled, directly or indirectly, by AXA within the meaning of article L.233‑16 II of the French Commercial
Code, as well as the activities of subcontractors and suppliers with whom the Group maintains an established business relationship,
insofar as the activities are linked to that relationship. The Vigilance Plan includes:
●

●

●

●

●

a risk mapping to identify, analyze and prioritize risks;
procedures for the regular assessment of subsidiaries as well as of subcontractors and suppliers with whom an established
business relationship is maintained;
appropriate actions to mitigate risks and prevent serious harm;
an alert mechanism (“Whistleblowing”) to report potential violations established in consultation with representative trade
unions; and
a system for monitoring the implementation of measures and assessing their effectiveness.

Given the diversity of the activities of AXA’s subsidiaries and the Group’s subcontractors and suppliers, the Vigilance Plan sets forth the
Group’s guiding principles and policies designed to ensure that they have a common understanding of, and operate in accordance
with, the Group’s standards in terms of sustainability, Whistleblowing and personal data protection.

(1) Law No. 2017‑399 of March 27, 2017, relating to the duty of care of parent companies and instructing companies (devoir de vigilance des sociétés mères et

4.7.2 Identification, analysis and prioritization of risks
4.7.2.1

Risk mapping of material
sustainability risks

The Group carries out three levels of risk assessment to
identify, analyze and prioritize risks:
●

●

●

firstly, the double‑materiality assessment (“DMA”), which
became applicable to the Group from 2024 following the
transposition of Directive (EU) 2022/2464 of the European
Parliament and of the Council of December 14, 2022 as
regards corporate sustainability reporting (the “Corporate
Sustainability Reporting Directive” or “CSRD”) into French
law (1), as described in the section “Double Materiality
Assessment” below;
secondly, a human rights risk assessment which identifies
and prioritizes the human rights risks for the Group and its
stakeholders, across all its activities, as described in the
section “Human Rights Risk Assessment” below; and
thirdly, an annual ESG assessment campaign for screening
general expenses and IT suppliers and subcontractors in
respect of the Group’s own operations, as described in the
section “Risk mapping of AXA’s supply chain through ESG
screening” below.

Double materiality assessment
In 2024, for the first time, AXA carried out its DMA to identify and
assess the sustainability matters which are most material to the
Group’s activities and its own operations. This involved a
comprehensive understanding of its business activities and
value chain.
The DMA extends beyond identifying sustainability risks to also
include material impacts (i.e. negative and positive impacts)
and opportunities related to sustainability matters (Risks,
Impacts and Opportunities - “IROs”). It adopts a dual
perspective: (1) examining how the Group’s activities affect the
environment and society (“impact materiality”) and (2)
assessing how sustainability issues influence the Group’s
development, performance, and position (“financial
materiality”). The focus of the Vigilance Plan is on the “impact
materiality” perspective. The full list of material IROs and
further details on the process of the DMA performed in 2024 are
presented in Section 4.1.3.2 - AXA’s material impacts, risks and
opportunities.

AXA adopts the following key steps to identify the material IROs
as part of its DMA:

Identifying Relevant Sustainability Topics
IRO identification combines stakeholder engagement, analysis
of business activities and relationships and the mapping of
material sustainability matters across the value chain.
This begins with the ten sustainability topics identified which
are based on the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU)
2023/2772 of July 31, 2023 as regards sustainability reporting
standards (the “European Sustainability Reporting
Standards” or “ESRS”) which were then refined through
stakeholder consultations and insurance sector‑specific
considerations.
The identification process also considers prior risk assessments
notably, AXA’s internal sustainability risk assessment
(performed in 2023) and the human rights risk assessment
(performed in 2022). The process resulted in a list of 16
sustainability topics, giving rise to 98 sub‑topics for further
analysis, with the end result of 27 IROs. The process of
prioritization of the IROs is described in detail in Section 4.1.3.2
- AXA’s material impacts, risks and opportunities.

Mapping Actual and Potential IROs
The actual and potential IROs were then mapped, connecting
them with the Group’s activities and stakeholders.
For the purpose of identifying risks under the French law on the
duty of vigilance (2), AXA considers the concept of risk to include
both the risks and the negative impacts derived from the DMA
exercise.

Analyzing material IROs
For the purposes of the “impact materiality” assessment,
materiality was determined using a threshold matrix combining
severity (e.g. scale, scope, irreversibility) and likelihood (e.g.
probability of occurrence across time horizons).

(1) Mainly Articles L. 232‑6‑3, R. 232‑8‑4 et seq., L. 233‑28‑4 and R. 233‑16‑3 et seq. of the French Commercial Code regarding the requirement to publish a
sustainability report.
(2) Law No. 2017‑399 of March 27, 2017, relating to the duty of care of parent companies and instructing companies (devoir de vigilance des sociétés mères et
des entreprises donneuses d’ordre) and Article L.225‑102‑4 of the French Commercial Code.

4.7.2.2

Human Rights Risk Assessment

The Group recognizes that its activities and own operations
may have direct and indirect impacts on human rights,
including those of its employees, customers and suppliers, as
well as individuals affected through the Group’s relations with
corporate customers or investments in companies which are
active in sectors and/or countries with increased risks of
human rights violations.
To address these specific issues, the Group conducts a human
rights risk assessment every three years to identify its key
human rights risks in conducting its business, as an insurer, an
investor, a business partner and a company (in respect of its
own operations).

benchmark the supplier’s performance against industry and
global sustainability standards to determine its rating (by
EcoVadis). This assessment process helps companies
demonstrate their commitment to sustainability and gain
valuable insights for ongoing improvement efforts.
In 2024, the Group's Sustainability Procurement Guidelines

contracts. From 2025, it is the aim that insurance procurement
contracts will be risk assessed at entity level. This risk
assessment is undertaken and monitored at entity level due to
the varying differences in insurance procurement needs across
businesses and different geographies.

4.7.3.3

As an insurer

In respect of underwriting activities, Group underwriting
entities are expected to comply not only with applicable legal
and regulatory requirements relating to sustainability but also
with the Group’s sustainability underwriting commitments
which are detailed in the Sustainability Underwriting
Guidelines, described below. These include limiting or
declining to offer or renew insurance coverage for risks and
customers which fail (or are likely to fail) to meet the Group’s
sustainability criteria.
The Sustainability Underwriting Guidelines, implemented in
2022 and last updated in 2024, provide detailed requirements
for P&C underwriters across the Group. The Sustainability

Underwriting Guidelines integrate the Group’s sustainability
commitments derived from the Group Sustainability Standards
and sustainability policies into its P&C underwriting
governance framework. The Sustainability Underwriting
Guidelines set out the risks and types of customer which AXA is
prohibited from, or restricted in, underwriting, as well as
applicable assessment criteria, while outlining an escalation
framework for issues and sensitive cases encountered in the
underwriting process which might otherwise result in a breach
of the Group’s sustainability underwriting commitments. Local
entities are required to notify escalations to the Group
Underwriting Office if they have any questions or potential
breaches in respect of the Sustainability Underwriting
Guidelines. The Group Underwriting Office will then escalate to
the Group Standards Committee that might further escalate to
the Audit Risk and Compliance Committee (ARCC), depending
on the nature and materiality of the breach.

Energy, Ecosystem Conversion and Deforestation, Derivative
Investments in Food Commodities, Tobacco, Human Rights,

framework.

Protection of Employee Safety, Health
and Security
As a company, AXA aims to be a “responsible employer” with
respect to health and safety, which means creating a workplace
that fosters diversity and equal opportunity for all, promotes
engagement, encourages professional development and
supports employee well‑being by providing a safe environment
to work.
The Group’s Safety Management System requires AXA entities
to regularly, and in the case of a serious incident or changes in
regulation, conduct risk assessments in accordance with
applicable local laws. The assessment involves evaluating risk
based on severity (potential harm or impact) and probability
(likelihood of occurrence) of a particular job or task and
prioritizing the risk accordingly. This approach enables Group
entities to address critical hazards effectively and efficiently,
ultimately improving overall health and safety.
Group training programs, hazard identification workshops and
template checklists are also available to employees for
conducting risk assessments to ensure a safe working
environment and consistent standards of protection of health
and safety in the workplace.
“We Care & Dare for Progress” is the flagship of AXA’s 2024‑26
People Strategy in respect of employee well‑being. “Care”
reflects our commitment to protect and demonstrate empathy
for our customers and employees. “Dare” is our call to action to
confront challenges and foster a growth mindset.
The “Care & Dare” people ambition lies at the heart of the
Group's people strategy, driving a strong focus on the behaviors
and mindsets of collaboration, feedback, agility and
innovation; it is built around three key pillars:
reinforcing our culture DNA of “Caring” for individuals,
customers and society while “daring” to challenge ourselves
and our business to grow. We rely on our teams and people
managers to drive a “daring” and “growth” mindset,
empowering individuals to take responsibility and lead
initiatives to grow our business;
developing the capabilities of our teams, prioritizing
technical excellence and preparing our multigeneration
workforce for the future through learning, mobility and
career opportunities; and
placing care and inclusion as the cornerstone of what we
do and how we do it, delivering caring support for our
people and driving progress in diversity and inclusion to
endeavor to ensure that everyone feels they belong.

As regards employee health, the “Healthy You” innovative
global program which was launched by the Group in November
2020 to improve the health and wellbeing of its employees
around the world, continued running in 2024 within all AXA
entities globally. To further care for employees, AXA also
launched a financial wellbeing program named “Invest in You”
focusing on educating employees to better manage their
finances and leveraging the opportunities existing at AXA. As a
result, AXA UK received an award for inclusion through financial
education.
In 2023, the AXA Group announced the launch of its “We Care”
program as part of AXA’s 2024‑26 People Strategy, which is also
one of the Group’s key milestones under the current “Unlock
the future” strategic plan. This program aims to provide all
employees with the time, support, and resources to make
personal and professional decisions with confidence and
enables further progress on its long‑term commitment towards
an inclusive and supportive global workplace culture. In
addition, the “We Care” program provides support to its
workforce particularly where health and safety is at issue
through the implementation of policies focused on providing
support and protection to caregivers, parents and victims of
domestic and sexual violence.
The “We Care” program was deployed across all AXA entities in
2024 through four main pillars: (i) parental leave, including
support for employees receiving and recovering from in‑vitro
fertilization or pregnancy loss, (ii) caregiver leave, (iii) support
for employees if they experience domestic and/or sexual
violence and (iv) an expansion of the “Healthy You” program to
include a supportive working environment for employees
experiencing menstrual health conditions, menopause or
andropause.
In 2024, to reinforce the third pillar of the “We Care” program,
AXA formed a working group on domestic and sexual violence.
The group was comprised of diverse employees and an
independent researcher/expert. Through this working group,
AXA's entities now have additional policies, commitments, and
partnerships in place to strengthen this pillar, which are further
elaborated in Section 4.3.1.3 - Taking care of AXA’s workforce Looking after health and wellbeing.
