Protection of Personal Data
AXA adopts privacy‑related Binding Corporate Rules for
customer, employee and other stakeholder personal data
processing. These rules are approved by European data
protection authorities and embedded into AXA’s internal
governance structure to ensure compliance. AXA entities
applying Binding Corporate Rules represented 99% of the
Group’s revenues in 2024 (the same coverage was achieved in
2022 and 2023) in line with the 99% target set by Group Data
Privacy team. These rules and the Group Data Privacy
Declaration, under which the Group undertakes not to sell the
personal data of its customers, are available on AXA’s
website (1).
In addition, and in response to the cyber risk threat, the Group
has developed a risk‑based security strategy to strengthen its
business resilience. For instance, AXA aims at strengthening its
security foundations through automation of detection and
response processes, as well as enhancing its readiness to face
certain attack scenarios such as ransomware and ultimately
develop faster reaction and recovery capabilities. For further
details on the security strategy, refer to Section 4.4.1.5 - Data
privacy, responsible data use and data security.

4.7 Vigilance Plan

4.7.5 Alert mechanism
AXA is committed to upholding its vigilance law, requirements
which necessitate the establishment of a risk reporting and
alert mechanism. In 2018, AXA established an alert mechanism
to respond to the specific requirements of the loi de vigilance
for its French entities in consultation with the trade unions. This
alert mechanism is known internally as the Group’s
Whistleblowing procedure.
AXA’s Whistleblowing and Investigations Policy mandate that all
Whistleblowing incidents be handled, reported, and
investigated consistently and appropriately across the Group.
Every entity is required to have a documented Whistleblowing
procedure that defines Whistleblowing, provides associated
protections, outlines roles and responsibilities, and complies
with local legal and regulatory requirements. This procedure
enables any suspicion of inappropriate, unethical, or illegal
behavior by a staff member or external party to be escalated,
either locally or to the Group, as AXA maintains a zero‑tolerance
policy towards any misconduct deemed inappropriate,
unethical, or illegal that could potentially harm individuals or
AXA.
Concerns can be reported through various channels, including
line management, trusted colleagues, the dedicated
whistleblowing hotline, local Audit or Group Audit directly
(speak‑up@axa.com). Once a concern is submitted, its content
is evaluated and triaged by independent Investigations teams
based on pre‑established criteria. All allegations are
acknowledged promptly to the whistleblower, with a target
response time of seven working days from receipt. An update to
the whistleblower is provided within three months.
All allegations falling under AXA’s Whistleblowing &
Investigations Policy are logged in AXA’s global internal audit
tool. If at any point it becomes clear that the allegation is not
admissible under this policy, the reasons will be communicated
to the whistleblower in writing.

Independent Investigation teams, ultimately reporting to or
supervised by Internal Audit, investigate the allegations. The
outcomes of these investigations are presented and discussed
with the CEO and/or top Executive Management. In "very high"
founded (material) cases, the chair of the relevant Audit
Committee(s) is made aware.
All AXA investigations adhere to the strict protocols and
procedures for conducting the investigation which are outlined
in an Investigation Manual. Global compliance with these
procedures across all AXA entities is mandated in the
Whistleblowing and Investigations Policy. Each investigation
aims to confirm or refute each element of the allegation, using
methods such as interviews, documentary evidence reviews,
and advanced data analysis tools. External specialists may be
engaged for forensic investigations where specific expertise is
required.
To ensure the effectiveness and integrity of these policies, AXA
regularly checks its alignment with local regulations and
evolves its policies and protocols in line with regulatory
requirements. Periodic audits and reviews are conducted to
address any weaknesses.
AXA promotes awareness about reporting unethical conduct
through internal communication campaigns and e‑learning
modules. The Group's commitment to transparency is reflected
in its public disclosures about the number of reports received,
the types of investigation outcomes, and corrective actions
taken.
AXA does not tolerate retaliation against whistleblowers, and
any such incidents should be reported. Making malicious
allegations in bad faith is a disciplinary offence. Whistleblowing
and investigations are confidential, and any disclosure made to
Investigation teams will be handled confidentially, with strict
adherence to data privacy regulations. The whistleblower’s
identity will be known only to those involved in the
independent investigation unless there is a specific legal
requirement or the whistleblower chooses otherwise. Any
person facilitating the reporting of a Whistleblowing incident is
also protected under AXA’s Whistleblowing & Investigations
Policy.

4.7.6 Monitoring the effective implementation

4.7.6.1

As a company

Reporting process
AXA has put in place a comprehensive system of internal
control and risk management (please refer to Section 4.1.4.3 Risk Management and Internal Control over sustainability
reporting) to support the enforcement of Group standards and
policies across its operating entities. This system aims to
ensure compliance with applicable regulations and to monitor
the implementation of vigilance measures (such as sustainable
procurement and fair treatment of customers) to ensure
effectiveness.
In addition, AXA relies on the Group’s Sustainability team’s
annual review and reporting process for AXA entities, known as
the AXA Entities Sustainability Index (the “AESI”). Conducted
each year, the AESI is an internal questionnaire which assists in
promoting and assessing the implementation of the Group’s
Sustainability guidelines and standards. Evaluation criteria are
shared in June allowing entities to focus on any required
remediation actions prior to year‑end.
In 2024, the AESI was completed by 32 AXA entities (compared
to 29 in 2023). The AESI questionnaire was reviewed and
enhanced in 2024 based on the improvements identified in
2023, with questions focused on the Group's sustainability
strategy implementation. Regarding the French duty of
vigilance in particular, questions were included this year which
allowed entities to self‑assess their compliance against the 27
requirements split across the themes below:

described in more detail at Section 4.2.1.3 - Addressing climate
change as an investor.
In respect of underwriting, AXA monitors its Insurance
Associated Emissions and the respective trajectories to meet
2030 targets as described in more detail at Section 4.2.1.4 Addressing climate change as an insurer.

In respect of underwriting
The Group P&C Underwriting Sustainability Guidelines
mandates the application of an underwriting sustainability
restriction list, which, following the Group Energy Policy, the
Group Ecosystem Conversion and Deforestation Policy, the
Natural World Heritage Sites Policy and the Group
Controversial Weapons Policy, applies underwriting restrictions
on certain lines of business or activities. This restriction list
is regularly updated and disseminated by the Group
Underwriting Office (GUO) to all local underwriting teams and
their respective CEOs.
These sustainability exclusions apply to all new business and
renewals comprising "P&C Commercial lines" for direct
insurance and assumed facultative business, which comprises
all policies written for legal entities.
Local CEOs must ensure timely escalation of any breaches of
the
restriction
list
and/or Group P&C
Underwriting
Sustainability Guidelines to the Group Chief Risk Officer, Group
Chief Underwriting Officer and Group Sustainability Officer as
soon as possible.
A business referral process is in place to monitor and control
the implementation by AXA entities of both the restriction list
and the Sustainability Underwriting Guidelines. This requires

any sensitive business risks identified being escalated to the
GUO to the attention of the Head of Sustainability
Underwriting. Such sensitive business risks are assessed by
sustainability underwriting experts. Each case that is referred
requires a prior engagement with the broker and the client to
gather all information necessary to prove that the case is not in
breach of the controls referred to above. Specific engagement
meetings can be organized together with the local entity
involved, the underwriting sustainability experts at the GUO,
the client and broker. In 2024, 94 business cases were referred
and/or escalated to the GUO, compared to 100 in 2023.

In respect of investments
The Group Sustainability Standards mandate compliance with
a responsible investment restriction list, which is regularly
updated by the Group Investment and Asset and Liability
Management teams and disseminated by the Financial Risk
Management teams to all local investment teams and their
respective CFOs/CEOs.
These restrictions apply to all investments made by local
entities as principal and, with respect to General Account assets
and Unit‑Linked assets in fully dedicated mandates,
notwithstanding the asset manager. To monitor our General
Account investments and ensure compliance with these
restrictions, AXA has developed a dedicated monitoring tool.
This tool tracks the Group's General Account investments and
provides timely alerts regarding potential breaches.
Local CEOs/CFOs of AXA entities must ensure timely escalation
of any potential or actual breach of the Group Sustainability
Standard to the Group Chief Risk Officer and Group
Sustainability Officer as soon as possible.

Risk factors and risk management
5.1 Risk factors

Risk factors

You should carefully consider the following risk factors together
with other information contained in this Document. Any of
these risks could materially affect our business, financial
condition, or results of operations, cause the trading price of
our ordinary shares to decline materially or cause our actual
results to differ materially from those expected or those
expressed in any forward‑looking statements made by or on
behalf of the Company.
Management believes that these are the significant risks to
which the AXA Group is exposed as of the filing date of this
Document with the AMF, based on Management’s assessment
of their materiality and specificity to the AXA Group. These risks
are presented below in order of their materiality according to
that assessment, which takes into account the likelihood that
they may materialize and the expected magnitude of their
negative impact on the Group. The primary categories of
risk are:
●

market‑related risks;

●

credit and liquidity‑related risks;

●

insurance and reinsurance pricing, underwriting and
reserve‑related risks;

●

operational risks;

●

regulatory and litigation‑related risks; and

●

risks related to the ownership of the Company’s shares.

The risks faced by the Group are increasingly interconnected.
For example, risks related to climate change may affect our
claims experience through increased natural catastrophe
frequency and severity, while also increasing legal, regulatory
and compliance risk.

The risks identified in this Document are not the only risks the
Group faces, and new information may change Management’s
assessment of these risks. In particular, Management’s
assessment may be impacted by the most significant risks
identified in AXA’s most recent Future Risks Report, including
climate change, cyber‑security risks, geopolitical instability,
risks related to artificial intelligence (“AI”) and big data, and
energy risks. Other risks that are currently unknown to us, not
specific to us, or currently assessed as immaterial, may also
materially adversely affect us.
Management devotes substantial resources to risk
management, but the Group’s risk management activities, like
all control systems, are inherently limited and cannot provide
absolute protection from risks or losses.
Where the risks herein have had quantifiable and material
financial impacts on the Group and/or resulted in material
contingent liabilities, that information is reflected in the
Consolidated Financial Statements, in accordance with
applicable accounting principles. The Company’s risk
management processes, procedures and controls are
described in Section 5.2 - Internal control and Risk
Management of this Document, which should be read together
with this Section. You should also refer to Section 5.3 - Market
risks, and the subsequent sections of this Document, for
quantitative information on the material risks to which the
Group is exposed (1).

(1) References to insurance, reinsurance, Life, and Property & Casualty in this Section also include Health activities and/or business, as applicable.

5.1.1.1

Market‑related risks

Negative developments in economic and
financial market conditions, whether on a
national, continental or global basis, may
materially and adversely affect our business
and profitability
Our businesses, financial condition, results of operations and
solvency are impacted by global financial market fluctuations
and economic conditions generally.
A wide variety of factors have adversely affected, and could
negatively impact in the future, economic growth prospects
and contribute to volatility in financial markets, including:
adverse geopolitical events/conflicts and rising geopolitical
tensions in various regions and countries, which may cause
spikes in asset prices (such as oil) or inflationary pressures,
impact supply and value chains, or otherwise destabilize
financial markets;
political conditions and volatility that may threaten or
create heightened unpredictability in major economies and
key financial markets;
trade‑related disputes, protective measures or tensions
between major economies (whether existing or anticipated),
changes in existing trade and tariff policies, related
disruption to global supply and value chains, and any
further “de‑coupling” of China from the global economy;
concerns over slowdowns or reversals in economic growth
and levels of consumer confidence;
conditions around asset valuations and credit risks and
volatility of asset prices, which may lead to an abrupt and
significant repricing in financial markets, disruptions in the
global supply chain and elevated and volatile energy and
raw material prices;
interest rate levels and actual or expected volatility in
interest rates;
the strengthening or weakening of foreign currencies
against the Euro;
the availability and cost of credit;

●

●

●

●

●

the stability and solvency of financial institutions and other
companies, including related systemic credit risk concerns
and/or central bank intervention in financial markets;
inflation or deflation in certain markets;
risks of market manipulation and lack of transparency in
AI‑powered trading activity, which may result in large losses
and a loss of investor confidence;
a downturn in real estate markets (either one or more
specific significant markets or the global market) or the
broader private asset markets; and
tight labor markets or lower employment.

Investment income from our large investment portfolio is
crucial to our profitability and may be impacted by any of the
foregoing factors. These factors also impact demand for
insurance and Asset Management products that we sell, as well
as their performance, which could reduce those sales and/or
increase product surrenders and lapses. Moreover, our profits
from insurance and investment products depend in part on the
returns on investments supporting our obligations under those
products.
In addition, certain types of insurance and investment products
that we offer expose us to risks from financial market
fluctuations. These products include certain interest‑sensitive
or variable products, such as guaranteed or variable annuities,
which have crediting or other guaranteed rates that are not
necessarily related to prevailing market interest rates or
investment returns on underlying assets. Our hedging
techniques to help mitigate such exposures cannot protect us
against all such risks or volatility in the financial markets.
Furthermore, financial market conditions such as those
described above could have a material adverse effect on our
solvency position, and any of the foregoing factors or their
impact on our income or sales could have a material adverse
effect on our business, results of operations and financial
condition.

Risk factors and risk management
5.1 Risk factors

Changes in interest rates and credit spreads
may adversely affect the value of our
investments, as well as our business,
results of operations, solvency, liquidity
and financial condition
Fluctuations in interest rates directly impact (i) the value of our
assets (particularly fixed‑income investments) and (ii) our
ability to realize gains or avoid losses from asset sales,
ultimately affecting our earnings. Increased volatility in these
fluctuations reduces the predictability of our investment
valuations and earnings.

Asset Management business. In addition, we may be required
to pay higher interest rates on our debt securities, debt, and
bank facilities. We may also face an increase in the costs of our
repurchase agreements and derivative hedging transactions,
increasing our interest expenses.
Our exposure to changes in credit spreads (both corporate and
sovereign) primarily relates to the impact of such changes on
market prices and cash flow variability. Widening credit spreads
will generally reduce the value of the fixed‑income securities we
hold (including credit derivatives where we assume credit
exposure) and increase investment income from purchases of
new fixed‑income securities in our investment portfolios.
Tightening credit spreads generally increase the value of
fixed‑income securities we hold and reduce our investment
income from new purchases of fixed‑income securities in our
investment portfolios.

Periods of declining or low interest rates may negatively impact
our net investment income and the profitability of our Life &
Health and Property & Casualty businesses, as well as our
Solvency II ratio. Earnings from fixed income investments
entered into in a low‑rate environment compared to the rates
we pay to policyholders and annuity contract owners may
result in reduced profitability. In‑force life insurance and
annuity products may become comparatively more attractive
to customers when interest rates decline, increasing our
liabilities (for both flexible- and regular‑premium products),
asset‑liability duration mismatches (as more policies and
contracts remain in‑force from year to year), and an increase in
provisions for guarantees in life insurance and annuity
products. Our Property & Casualty business profitability may
also be negatively impacted, as periods of lower rates and
corresponding reduced investment returns put pressure on
underwriting margins and may result in a higher combined
ratio for our Property & Casualty business. In addition, an
extended period of low interest rates may increase the
regulatory capital and amount of assets required to cover
provisions, which could adversely impact our Solvency II ratio.

Fluctuations in currency exchange rates
may significantly affect our results
of operations, financial condition, liquidity,
and solvency position

During periods of increasing interest rates, the fair value of
certain of our fixed‑income investments may decrease, which
could negatively impact our shareholders’ equity and
Solvency II ratio, or could impact our net income in the event
our fixed‑income assets were sold. Furthermore, surrenders
and lapses of life insurance policies and fixed annuity contracts
may accelerate as policyholders seek higher returns, which may
cause us to liquidate fixed maturity investments to obtain
liquidity to satisfy such obligations. This, in turn, may result in
liquidity strains and realized investment losses. Lower assets
under management would reduce the management fees of our

The geographical diversity of our businesses and the location
of significant Group subsidiaries in the United States, the
United Kingdom, Switzerland, Japan, Hong Kong, and other
international markets exposes us to exchange rate fluctuations.
A significant portion of our shareholdings and investments,
revenues and expenses are denominated in non‑Euro
currencies, while our Consolidated Financial Statements are
published in Euros. Likewise, the portion of our debt and other
obligations (including certain of our reinsurance treaties and
retrocession agreements) denominated in non‑Euro currencies
is exposed to exchange rate fluctuations.

Although we try to manage interest rate and credit spread risk,
including hedging through derivative instruments, this may not
mitigate effects of volatility in interest rates or credit spreads,
which could have a material adverse effect on our solvency
position, results of operations, financial condition or cash flows
through realized losses, impairments and changes in
unrealized gains and loss positions. For additional information
on the sensitivity of our Eligible Own Funds (“EOF”) and
Solvency II ratio to changes in interest rates and credit spreads,
please refer to Section 6.6 - Note 4.2 - Market risks (including
sensitivity analysis) of this Document and the AXA Group’s
SFCR, available on AXA’s website (www.axa.com) (1).

Risk factors and risk management
5.1 Risk factors

Equity of Group entities is expressed primarily in the Euro, US
Dollar, British Pound Sterling, Swiss Franc, Japanese Yen and
Hong Kong Dollar. Fluctuations in Euro exchange rates have
had, and may again have, a negative impact on the Group's
shareholders’ equity and underlying earnings. We do not fully
hedge the changes in the value of the equity of our subsidiaries
with equity denominated in foreign currencies.
Similarly, exchange rate fluctuations may impact the Group’s
net income (through the translation of foreign currency
transactions, the settlement of foreign currency balances and
discrepancies between foreign currency liabilities and assets),
cash flows, gearing ratio and solvency position. In addition, our
currency hedges to manage foreign exchange rate risk may in
themselves impact our cash and liquidity position. For more
information about exchange rate fluctuations and AXA SA’s
foreign currency hedging, please refer to Section 5.3 - Market
risks of this Document.

Inflation or deflation in our principal markets
would have multiple impacts on the Group
and may negatively affect our business,
solvency position and results of operations
We are exposed to inflation risk in certain of our principal
markets (i) through our holdings of fixed interest rate and other
instruments, and (ii) as a result of the potential for claim
payments and expenses to rise faster than anticipated in our
reserving and pricing assumptions.
Elevated inflation could impact our assets via increases in
interest rates by central banks, leading to a decrease in the
market value of bonds held in our investment portfolio, which
could adversely affect the profitability of our investment
portfolio and our revenues. Increases in inflation could also
have an impact on the creditworthiness of bond issuers and
could result in an increase in credit spreads (see “Changes in
interest rates and credit spreads may adversely affect the value
of our investments, as well as our business, results of
operations, solvency, liquidity and financial condition” above).
Depending on the macroeconomic context, increases in

inflation could also have a negative impact on risk premiums
and share prices, which could cause a decline in the market
value of the Group’s equity portfolio.
Both our Property & Casualty and Life & Health businesses are
impacted by claims cost inflation, the size of damage awards
resulting from litigation, labor costs, costs of energy and raw
materials, medical costs, new/replacement parts and materials,
construction costs and/or inflation due to disruptions in the
global supply chain. The impact of inflation on claims costs
could be more pronounced on claims indexed to inflation and
long‑tail Property & Casualty lines of business, such as general
Liability, Workers’ Compensation and professional Liability, and
other specialty lines of our AXA XL business, where finalizing
and settling claims for a given accident year takes a relatively
long time. In addition, lags in re‑pricing in our Property &
Casualty business, when combined with inflation, could reduce
our profitability, and our customers may refuse pricing actions
to counteract inflation. Inflation driven in the short term by
supply chain disruptions and shortages affecting raw materials
and goods may negatively impact our results, especially for our
short‑tail lines of business. Changes in the level of inflation
could also result in an increased level of uncertainty in our
estimation of claims reserves, particularly for long‑tail lines of
business, which could have a significant adverse effect on our
solvency, results, financial position or cash flows. Moreover,
inflation may negatively impact the value of Life & Savings
products (for example, those with fixed future payments),
which may reduce new business and increase lapse rates,
including as a result of policyholders being attracted to other
financial products with comparatively higher rates of return.
A significant decline in the market value of the Group’s asset
portfolio and an increase in claims costs could also lead to a
decrease in the Group’s shareholders’ equity.
We are also exposed to deflation risk, which has materialized in
the Eurozone and parts of Asia in prior periods. Deflation may
erode collateral values and diminish the quality of certain
invested assets, and may otherwise negatively affect our
business and results of operations.

Risk factors and risk management
5.1 Risk factors

Adverse experience relative to the
methodologies, estimates and assumptions
used by Management in valuing investments
and determining allowances and impairments
may adversely affect our results of operations
Certain of our invested assets do not have an active trading
market or other observable market data and are valued using
methodologies involving estimates, assumptions and
significant Management judgment. During periods of market
disruption, more of our invested assets may be valued using
these methodologies as a result of reduced trading or
observable market data for certain asset classes. Our resulting
valuations may not represent the price for which a security may
ultimately be sold or the effect on such valuations of external
factors, including but not limited to climate‑related transition
risks. These transition risks may cause the market and prices for
certain investments with a high carbon footprint (also known as
“stranded assets”) to decrease over time. More generally, the
foregoing risks may materially impact fair value amounts, with
potential material adverse effects on our results of operations
and financial condition.
The determination of the allowances and impairments that we
recognize for invested assets varies by investment type, and is
based upon our periodic assessment of known and inherent
risks associated with the respective asset class. Such
assessments are revised as in light of changes to relevant
conditions and available information. Management considers a
wide range of factors for impairments, including those
described in Section 6.6 - Note 1.9.2 - Financial investments of
this Document, and uses its best judgment in evaluating the
cause of the decline in the fair value of the invested assets and
the prospects for near‑term recovery. For certain asset classes,
particularly debt instruments, Management’s evaluation
involves various assumptions and estimates about the relevant
issuer and its earnings potential. Management updates its

292

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

evaluations regularly and makes any corresponding
adjustments to allowances and impairments. However,
Management may not have accurately assessed the level of
impairments taken and allowances reflected in our financial
statements. The need for and timing of any additional
impairments and/or allowances may have a material adverse
effect on our results of operations and financial condition.

5.1.1.2

Credit and liquidity‑related risks

Adverse capital and credit market conditions
may significantly affect our ability to meet
liquidity needs, our access to capital and
increase our cost of capital
Capital and credit markets may experience high levels of
volatility and disruption which, during certain periods of acute
stress, limit the availability of additional market liquidity and
credit capacity of issuers, including the Company.
The Group needs liquidity to pay our operating expenses
(including claims and surrenders) and dividends, buy back
shares, pay interest on our debts, refinance certain maturing
debts, meet collateral or margin calls and cover other liabilities.
The availability of additional financing depends on market
conditions, the availability of credit, our credit ratings and
credit capacity. It also depends on customers’ or lenders’
perception of our long- or short‑term financial prospects. Our
Liquidity Risk Management framework includes active
monitoring of the Group’s liquidity position and contingency
plans for accessing liquidity, but prolonged liquidity constraints
may have a material adverse effect on our business, results of
operations and financial condition.
For information about the contractual maturities of debt
instruments held by the Group, please refer to Section 6.6 Note 7.4.3 - Debt instruments and loans by contractual
maturity and exposure to interest rate risk of this Document.

5.1 Risk factors

Downgrades in our insurer and reinsurer
financial strength and credit ratings could
adversely impact our competitive position
and damage our relationships with creditors
or trading counterparties
Insurer and reinsurer financial strength and credit ratings are
important factors used by the market and customers in
establishing the competitive position of these companies and
in assessing claims‑paying ability. Rating agencies review their
ratings and rating criteria and methodologies on a recurring
basis, and they may change or withdraw their ratings at any
time, based on relevant factors that may not be entirely within
our control. Consequently, our current ratings may not be
maintained in the future and undue reliance should not be
placed on such ratings, which should not be considered as
recommendations to purchase, sell or hold any securities we
have issued.
A downgrade or potential downgrade in our ratings could have
adverse effects including (i) damaging our competitive
position, (ii) negatively impacting our ability to underwrite new
insurance policies, (iii) increasing the levels of surrenders and
termination rates of our in‑force policies, (iv) increasing our
reinsurance costs, (v) triggering termination provisions or
collateral delivery requirements, or requiring us to return
unearned premiums to cedants under certain of our
reinsurance and retrocessional agreements, (vi) negatively
impacting our ability to obtain financing and/or increasing our
cost of financing, (vii) harming our relationships with creditors
or trading counterparties and/or (viii) adversely affecting
public confidence. Any of these developments could have a
material adverse effect on our business, liquidity position,
results of operations, revenues and financial condition.

5.1.2 Risks related to the Company and its business
5.1.2.1

Insurance and reinsurance pricing, underwriting and reserve‑related risks

Adverse experience relative to the
assumptions and judgment used in setting
reserves, developing and pricing products and
calculating industry measures of value may
significantly affect our results of operations or
performance indicators, which may have an
adverse impact on the price of our securities
The profitability of our businesses depends on a variety of
factors including social, economic and demographic trends,
natural catastrophe forecasts and budgeting for large losses,
policyholder behavior, dispute/litigation settlements or court
decisions, changes in laws and regulations, inflation,
investment returns, the cost and availability of reinsurance, and
underwriting expenses. We make assumptions about these
factors in estimating our risk exposures, determining the
pricing of our products, establishing our technical provisions
and employee benefits reserves and reporting capital levels
and business results. These assumptions are based on various
modeling techniques (e.g., scenarios, predictive, stochastic
and/or forecasting), using both proprietary and third‑party
models, data analytics and related analyses. The model
outputs and related analyses are subject to various
assumptions, uncertainties, model errors and the inherent
limitations of any statistical analysis (including the existence,
availability, use, accuracy and relevance of historical, internal
and industry data). In addition, they incorporate numerous
assumptions and forecasts about market conditions (such as
interest rates, inflation and currency exchange rates), capital
requirements, loss frequency and severity and policyholder
behavior. The use of such models can also be affected by
operational risks, including cyber risks impacting us directly or
indirectly via third parties, as well as input, data and human
errors. Adverse experience relative to such assumptions (in
particular in the context of the occurrence or timing of major
natural and man‑made catastrophic events, pandemics,
systemic risks, cyber risks, the use of and reliance on inaccurate
or incomplete models and data, the inability to accurately
model risks because of a lack of historical data, or inherent
product defects) may result in an increase in the pricing of our

294

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

insurance products and, as a consequence, an increased need
to further strengthen our product reserves. This may in turn
have an adverse effect on our results of operations and
financial condition, or lead to litigation.
In our businesses and for the Group’s reinsurance activities, we
establish reserves for claims (reported and unreported) and
claims expenses in accordance with industry practices, as well
as accounting, actuarial and regulatory requirements. Reserves
do not represent an exact calculation of liability, but instead
represent expectations of what the ultimate settlement and
administration of claims would cost based on our assessment
of available facts and circumstances, review of historical
settlement patterns (if any), estimates of trends in claims
severity and frequency, actuarial experience with respect to
past events, legal liability and other factors. The amount of
reserves net of reinsurance also depends on the availability and
loss coverage of reinsurance/retrocessions, including, for
example, our ability to aggregate losses in accordance with the
relevant policy terms and recoverability of reinsurance
receivables. In establishing such reserves, there is also a risk
related to discounting, which may turn out to be erroneous or
need updating, and which may in turn impact the Group’s
assessments and/or require that they be revised.
Furthermore, given that our New Business Value (“NBV”) and
Contractual Service Margin (“CSM”) calculations are done on a
market‑consistent basis, changes in assumptions used in
calculating these measures may have a material adverse effect
on the level of our NBV and/or CSM. For example, our NBV is
sensitive to interest rate movements and, consequently, an
adverse evolution of interest rates may significantly impact our
NBV and impact the trading price of our securities.
In both our Property & Casualty and Life & Health businesses,
we are exposed to primary insurance risks and our earnings
depend significantly on our actual claims experience being
consistent with our assumptions in pricing our products and
establishing the liabilities for obligations for technical
provisions and claims. Certain risks for each of those business,
relating to actual claims experience, reserving and related
potential losses, are set out below.

Property & Casualty reserve risk, resulting from fluctuations in

During Property & Casualty loss settlement periods, which can
last several years for certain of our businesses, new information

Other factors, such as social inflation (increased litigation,
expanded theories of liability, higher jury awards and
settlement expectations), as well as mass litigation claims
concerning harmful products or substances (e.g., asbestos,

ultimate costs of claims in our Property & Casualty business in
ways that are difficult to assess for reserve estimate purposes
and could be material. For example, it may be difficult to
estimate the losses resulting from major litigation claims due to
uncertainties in the timing of claims, damage awards, or
settlements. Our estimates may also be more difficult during
times of adverse economic conditions due to unexpected
changes in behavior of claimants and policyholders, increased
fraudulent reporting of exposures and/or losses, reduced
maintenance of insured properties or increased small claims
frequency. Because establishing claims reserves is inherently
uncertain and complex and involves numerous estimates and
assumptions, ultimately losses may materially exceed our

claims reserves and have a material adverse effect on our
results of operations and solvency position.
Life & Health. In certain cases, product features may result in
higher than anticipated realized losses. While we use our

estimate future policy benefits, including information used in
pricing insurance products and establishing the related
actuarial liabilities, actual experience may not match these
estimates.
This may be due to a variety of factors, including changes in
morbidity and longevity patterns/data that we have not
anticipated or modeled with sufficient accuracy, or a lack of
historical data for the relevant pricing of products and
estimation of liabilities.
The above risks may result in loss experience that is
inconsistent with our pricing and reserve assumptions, with
resulting Life & Health reserve risks that may have a material

We employ risk management strategies, including reinsurance
for our own account and capital markets solutions (such as
catastrophe bonds), to avoid or limit losses and liabilities. A
failure or inadequacy of any of our risk management strategies
could result in significant losses and have a material adverse
impact on our financial condition, results of operations, and
cash flows.
We use hedging to mitigate risks under guarantees provided to
our clients or stemming from our assets. We hedge a portion of
those risks via derivatives (including equity futures, treasury
bond futures, interest rate swaps and swaptions, equity options
and foreign currency derivatives). In particular, to hedge against
significant widening of credit spreads, we use credit swaps to
mitigate our exposure to significant deterioration of the credit

quality of our asset portfolio. Our hedging program is modeled
using numerous estimates and Management judgments,
including, among others, judgments about volatility and
interest rates, and correlation among various market
movements.
However, we may not use (or be able to use) our hedging
program to hedge our risks as intended or expected, for any
number of reasons, which may result in higher realized losses
and unanticipated cash needs to collateralize or settle
transactions. Our hedging models or their underlying estimates
and assumptions could prove inadequate for certain market
environments, especially when financial markets experience
high volatility. These models may also fail to function as
expected for reasons including: the size or liquidity of the
derivative markets in question; the financial cost of hedging; or
the nature of the relevant risks themselves, which may limit our
ability to effectively hedge them. Hedging counterparties may
also fail to perform their obligations, creating unhedged
exposures and losses on uncollateralized positions. Any such
failure of our hedging strategies or models to perform as
intended or expected may adversely affect our results of
operations, financial position, liquidity and solvency.

Operational risk is part of the business environment in which

Risk factors and risk management
5.1 Risk factors

We rely on these systems to perform necessary business
functions, including providing insurance quotes, processing
applications and claims, providing information and support to
customers and distributors, administering complex products,
conducting actuarial analyses and keeping financial records.
We also use computer systems to store, retrieve, evaluate and

company data and information, including proprietary and
confidential information. Some of these systems are, or rely on,
third‑party systems, such as cloud computing infrastructure.
System failures or the failure by third‑party technology

obligations (including under significant outsourcing
arrangements), could result in business interruptions or
compromise our ability to perform necessary business
functions in a timely manner, which could harm our business
and hurt our relationships with our customers and business
partners. The risk of such failures and/or their overall impact
may be increased to the extent services are concentrated with

interruption, whether direct or indirect, our systems may be
inaccessible, and our employees unable to perform their
duties, for an extended period of time. Such incidents may also
result in losses, impacts on our liquidity, legal claims,
regulatory sanctions or damage to our reputation.
In addition to protecting, maintaining, and effectively operating
our existing systems, we face an ongoing challenge of
effectively adapting to a constantly changing technological
landscape.
There has been in particular a rapid increase in the nature,
volume and availability of data in recent years, as well as tools
and innovations for its collection, storage, use and
management, which impact us and our industry. These tools
and innovations include, among others, AI, connected
customers, “big data”, “blockchain”, cloud computing,
increased mobile Internet access, personalization of genetic
data and asymmetric information with respect to genetic
testing. If we are not able to invest, develop and deploy these
tools as quickly and effectively as our competitors, our
competitive position and profitability may be adversely
impacted. We may also be adversely impacted, or our business
may be impaired, if we do not effectively anticipate the impact
on our business of such technologies.
We are working, in particular, to expand our use of data tools
and AI to streamline administrative processes, improve
customer experience, make efficiency gains and enhance
decision‑making capabilities. As with many technological
innovations, these tools offer significant promise, but also
present a number of potential challenges. There is a significant

risk that AI systems could produce inaccurate or misleading
content or other discriminatory or unexpected results or
behaviors that could harm our reputation, business or
customers. In addition, the use of AI involves significant
technical complexity and requires specialized expertise, and its
development and our use of it in our business and operations
may have unanticipated impacts on us as an insurance
provider. The energy demands of AI capacity may also be

Regulations for underwriting syndicates and related risks.
We manage, through AXA XL Underwriting Agencies Limited,
Syndicate 2003, a large underwriting syndicate at Lloyd’s and,

risks. For instance, the Council of Lloyd’s has wide discretionary

through Lloyd’s. A downgrading of the Lloyd’s market could
also impair Syndicate 2003’s ability to trade in certain classes of
business at current levels. As a Lloyd’s syndicate providing
coverage to US policyholders and covering US risks, we could
also be required by US regulators to increase the level of
funding required as minimum deposits for the protection of US
policyholders. Any Lloyd’s‑related risks could have an adverse
effect on our business, financial condition and results of
operations.

The evolving and complex regulatory
environment surrounding data and artificial
intelligence could increase our costs and

Collection, transfer, and protection of significant amounts of
sensitive data are critical to the operation of our business.
Regulations in this area are evolving rapidly around the world,
which could adversely affect our business if we fail to adapt our
rules, internal controls, and strategy to the emerging regulatory
environment.
In the European Union, we are subject to GDPR restrictions on
data usage/processing (including profiling) and requirements
regarding disclosure to customers, as well as an enforcement
regime under which competent data protection authorities are
able to fine companies that do not comply with EU rules up to
4% of their global annual turnover. Similar data protection
regulations to GDPR have entered into force in many other
jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom, certain US states,
China, Brazil, Algeria, Egypt, and Thailand.
There is a risk that data collected by the Group and its
third‑party service providers is not processed in accordance
with notices provided to, or obligations imposed by, data
subjects, regulators or other counterparties, or in compliance
with applicable data‑privacy laws. Negligence or failure to
implement and follow internal Group policies, in particular
regarding encryption of data, or to fail to perform adequate
internal data collection/processing controls, may also facilitate
hacking and other intrusions and result in breaches of GDPR
and other applicable laws. In addition, data transfer practices
and mechanisms for data transfer may be subject to future
challenge or to stricter regulatory scrutiny.
Regulation with respect to AI is also at various stages of
evolution around the world. In the European Union, the AI Act
aims to foster responsible AI development and deployment,
and establishes obligations for AI systems based on their
potential risks and impact. Competent authorities may impose
large fines for infringement of the AI Act requirements (e.g., up
to 7% of the global annual turnover for infringements related to
prohibited AI practices). AI regulations have entered into force,
or will likely enter into force, in many other jurisdictions,
including China. In the meantime, competent authorities may
apply stringent GDPR or other data privacy laws to the use of AI
involving personal data.

5.1 Risk factors

We have been and may become in the future
subject to lawsuits, regulatory investigations
and/or other proceedings which may affect
our business, brand, reputation, relations
with regulators and/or results of operations
We are a party to numerous lawsuits (both class actions and
individual lawsuits) in our corporate capacity and in our
capacity as a (re)insurer and involved in various regulatory
investigations and examinations and other actions arising in
the jurisdictions where we and our subsidiaries do business.
We may be involved in similar proceedings in the future.
Certain of these lawsuits, investigations, and other proceedings
seek significant or unspecified amounts of damages, including
punitive damages (notably in the United States), and may
involve allegations of bad‑faith denials of coverage, which
could potentially increase the overall amounts due, if any, in
connection with such matters. The amount of damages and
penalties claimed in litigation and regulatory proceedings, as
well as the volume of claims, against global financial
institutions remains high and may increase. These lawsuits also
have the potential to impose interpretative judgements on
insurance policy wordings and therefore increase our liabilities
under these policies. Certain of the regulatory authorities
involved in these proceedings have substantial powers over the
conduct and operations of our business. The class action
system in France and similar litigation mechanisms in certain
other European jurisdictions, including EU laws and regulations
on consumer representative actions, have increased, and are
likely to continue to increase, litigation risks and costs.
Furthermore, the increasing number of legislative and
regulatory requirements, including tighter controls and higher
capital requirements, consumer protection, enhancement of
regulatory requirements for the oversight and disclosure of
climate, ESG and sustainable finance‑related initiatives as well
as social and reputational trends may expose us to additional
civil, criminal or regulatory actions, investigations, proceedings
or sanctions, which could restrict business or have an adverse
effect on the Group. For additional information, please refer to
the paragraph above “Increasing scrutiny and evolving
expectations from investors, customers, regulators and other
stakeholders regarding climate change and other
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) matters, as well
as geopolitical matters, may result in increased litigation and
may impact our business and results of operations”.

In addition, in connection with the recent COVID‑19 pandemic,
as well as the opioids crisis in the United States, attention to
PFAS and the ongoing war in Ukraine, coverage lawsuits have
been brought against insurers, including the AXA Group or its
subsidiaries in multiple jurisdictions, many of which are
ongoing. The extent of reinsurance coverage on these claims
may vary depending, among other things, on the resolution of
the coverage issues under the primary policies. We may also be
involved in proceedings with our reinsurers regarding coverage.
For additional information, please refer to the paragraph above
in Section 5.1.2.1 - Insurance and reinsurance pricing,
underwriting and reserve‑related risks “Reinsurance may be
unavailable or too expensive and may not be adequate to
protect us against losses, in particular in the context of cyclical
Property & Casualty insurance and reinsurance businesses”.
For additional information on our litigation and investigation
matters, please refer to Section 6.6 - Note 28 - Litigations of this
Document.

As a global company operating in numerous jurisdictions, we

Uncertainties in the interpretation or future developments of

interpretations of tax laws and/or regulations (including but not

tax audits, reassessments and investigations may result in
adverse consequences, including penalties and sanctions. Our
business operations, results, financial condition, liquidity,
outlook or reputation could be materially affected if one or
more of the aforementioned risks materialized.

Developments adversely impacting the

The valuation of our intangible assets (such as goodwill) is

concerning inherently uncertain items. Adverse changes to
those assumptions and judgements could reduce the value of
our assets, which could in turn reduce shareholders’ equity.

The recognition of deferred tax assets depends on entity
performance and relevant tax laws, regulatory requirements
and accounting methods, as well as the interpretation of tax
laws and regulations by regulatory authorities, which may
change, including with retroactive effect. Certain events, such
as actual operating earnings being lower than projections,
losses continuing for a longer than anticipated, or changes in
tax laws, regulatory requirements, regulatory interpretations of
tax regimes, or accounting methods, could lead to write‑downs
of deferred tax assets for regulatory or accounting purposes.

5.1.3 Risks related to the ownership of the Company’s shares
In order to raise capital to fund future growth or for solvency
purposes, we may, in the future, offer rights, warrants or similar
securities at prices below the then‑current market price which
may adversely affect the market price of our ordinary shares
and dilute the positions of existing shareholders.

The Mutuelles AXA, which comprise two French mutual

The Group has implemented a comprehensive Internal control
and Risk Management system to ensure timely awareness and
management of significant risks, maintaining the accuracy of
Consolidated Financial Statements and market disclosures.
The Solvency II regime mandates that the Group maintains an
effective governance system for sound and prudent Risk
Management, based on a clear separation of responsibilities
and proportionate to the nature, extent, and complexity of the
Group's operations.
AXA has established a control framework with three lines of
defense, each with clearly defined boundaries, and appointed
four key functions.

The control framework with three lines of defense ensures that
the AXA Group’s risks are systematically identified, measured,
managed, and controlled.

First line of defense: management and staff

(i) establishing and maintaining an effective control
environment; (ii) identifying and managing the risks inherent in
the products, services, and activities in their scope; and
(iii) designing, implementing, maintaining, monitoring,
evaluating, and reporting on the Group’s internal control
system in accordance with the risk strategy and policies on
internal control as approved by the Board of Directors.

Group Risk Management (GRM) function
GRM is led by the Group Chief Risk Officer, reporting to the

allocation. GRM is responsible for defining and implementing
the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework within the
AXA Group.

5.2 Internal control and Risk Management

Group Compliance function
The Group Compliance function is responsible for advising
Executive Management and the Board of Directors on
applicable compliance laws, regulations, and administrative
provisions, and on the impact of regulatory change on the AXA
Group’s operations. The Group Compliance function provides
expertise, advice, and support to AXA entities to assess
significant compliance matters, analyzes the major compliance
risks and contributes to designing solutions to mitigate the
risks to which the Group is exposed. The Group Compliance
function manages a wide range of compliance related matters
including (i) financial crime (which includes anti‑bribery and
corruption, anti‑money laundering and international
sanctions/embargo compliance), (ii) data privacy and artificial
intelligence (AI) compliance, (iii) conduct and customer
protection, (iv) compliance & ethics, (v) the monitoring of other
major compliance and regulatory risks, and (vi) regular
reporting of significant compliance and regulatory matters to
Executive Management, the Board of Directors and regulators.
The Group Chief Compliance Officer reports to the Group
Deputy Chief Executive Officer & Group General Secretary.
Compliance activities within the Group are set out in a number
of standards and policies which set the minimum requirements
expected to be achieved by AXA entities and their Compliance
functions.
The compliance section of the Group Standards contains
standards and policies on significant risk areas affecting
compliance activities and sets out the high‑level controls and
monitoring principles to which the entities must adhere.
Adherence to the Standards and Policies (Compliance
Governance, Anti‑Money Laundering, Sanctions, Anti‑Bribery,
Cross Border, Data Privacy, Conduct & Customer Protection) is
mandatory.
In 2024, the AXA Group Compliance and Ethics Code was
updated to reinforce existing ethical and compliance
commitments in various areas such as customer protection, the
prevention of conflicts of interest as well as anti‑bribery and
corruption. A new section around the environment and human
rights has also been introduced. The new Code, applicable to
all AXA employees was launched in November 2024.
The Group Compliance function undertakes an annual
Compliance Risk Assessment exercise which requires entities to
identify the most significant compliance risks to which they are
exposed. Based on this assessment an Annual Compliance
Plan is developed for the following year. Using the same
methodology and to comply with the French extraterritorial law
(Sapin II) and ACPR requirements, separate Anti‑Bribery and
Corruption Risk Assessment and Anti‑Money Laundering Risk
Assessment were also implemented across AXA entities. These
risk assessments enable entities to identify in a more granular
manner the associated risks.

316

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

The Group Compliance function has implemented a number of
oversight and monitoring processes to assess AXA entities
against the Group Compliance framework and regulatory
requirements. For example, the Compliance In‑Depth Review
(CIDR) which is an ongoing program of structured on‑site
Compliance reviews conducted by the Group Compliance
Department to AXA Group Companies worldwide. The main
purpose of these reviews is to measure adherence to the Group
Standards and Policies, to define improvement action plans, to
provide experienced advice, including on compliance technical
aspects, and to rate the entity’s maturity level against other
Group companies. This program was introduced in 2009 using
a risk‑based approach.
On a regular basis, the Group Compliance function reports to
the Group Audit Risk & Compliance Committee, the Audit
Committee, and the Board of Directors (as required) on
significant compliance matters. These include major regulatory
changes that have compliance implications, results of the
Group oversight activities and the Compliance Risk
Assessment, and any other significant issues that require
escalation.

Group Internal Control function
To further strengthen its control environment, the AXA Group
established in 2017 a centralized Internal Control function
within the second line of defense independent from business
operations. The Group Internal Control Department is
responsible for the development of a standardized
methodology and framework for internal control and for
oversight of its implementation in the AXA Group’s subsidiaries.
The Internal Control framework of the AXA Group:
●

●

●

●

●

is based on the principle of proportionality and takes into
account the nature, scale, and complexity of the entities’
operations;
is aligned with the “Internal Control – Integrated
Framework” of the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations
of the Treadway Commission (COSO);
is an integral part of the Risk Management thus providing
Executive Management with a view of the risk and control
environment;
is underpinned by the Group Risk Management Standard
and Group Solvency II Internal Control and Operational Risk
Policy, first approved by the Audit Committee and the Board
of Directors of AXA SA in December 2017;
encompasses Internal Financial Control, implemented since
2010 to provide reasonable assurance regarding the
reliability of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
(ICOFR), and extended to Solvency II in 2014 to contribute to
the Internal Model validation process.

The Group Internal Control function regularly reports to the
Group Audit Risk & Compliance Committee and to the Audit
Committee of the Board of Directors.

5.2 Internal control and Risk Management

Third line of defense: Group Internal
Audit function
The Group Internal Audit function provides the Group Audit
Committee and the Group Management Committee with
independent and objective assurance on the effectiveness of
Risk Management and the overall control environment across
the Group to help protect the assets and reputation of the
organization and help improve its operations.
Group Internal Audit sets an annual plan of work, approved and
monitored by the Audit Committee, based on an assessment of
both the inherent risk and the adequacy of controls as well as
consideration of cyclical coverage.
A report is issued at the conclusion of each audit assignment to
relevant senior management, with the results and resolution
status of internal audit issues presented regularly to the Audit
Committee and Management.
Organizational independence and objectivity are ensured
through the Group Head of Internal Audit reporting to the Chair
of the AXA Group Audit Committee and to the Group Deputy
Chief Executive Officer & General Secretary.
All Internal Audit teams across the Group report to the Group
Head of Internal Audit and have a direct reporting line to their
local Audit Committee Chair and an administrative reporting
line within their local management structure.

Risk Management, Internal Control,
Compliance and Actuarial function
at local level
Governance: The Group Governance Standards mandate the
establishment of an Audit Committee by the Boards of AXA’s
main subsidiaries. The Audit Committees are responsible for
reviewing financial results, financial reporting and control
processes, critical accounting policies, specific accounting
issues, key risks, and systems of internal control.
The Group has established Standards that apply to AXA SA and
entities where AXA has the majority of the voting rights or
exercises control. These Standards are mandatory for all
entities within the scope and focus on critical requirements as
part of the overall Risk Management framework, enabling a
clear understanding of risks both locally and Group‑wide.
Chief Executive Officers must annually certify to the Group Chief
Executive Officer that their entities comply with the Standards.
Entity Boards should be informed of the annual certifications,
material breaches, non‑compliance areas, and mitigation plans
to monitor remedial action progress.
Please note that in the following paragraphs AXA SA is included
within the scope of local entities.

Risk Management: Local entities are responsible for Risk
Management, following GRM standards and guidelines. The
roles of local Risk Management teams are validated by both the
Executive Committees of local entities and the Group Chief Risk
Officer, ensuring alignment between central and local interests.
The minimum responsibilities of local Risk Management teams
are:
●

●

●

●

●

coordinating the second line of defense locally through a
specific governance framework;
maintaining local written policies aligned with Group

ensuring the risk appetite is implemented consistently with

providing a second opinion on key processes including

checking the adequacy of the local risk profile with respect

Local Chief Risk Officers head the local Risk Management teams

which meets on a quarterly basis.

5.2.1.4

Conclusion

The Group has established a comprehensive system of internal
control procedures and mechanisms that are appropriate and
adapted to its business and the global scale of its operations.
However, all internal control systems have inherent limitations
and cannot provide absolute certainty against the
materialization of risks and control failures. They can provide
only reasonable assurance.

5.2 Internal control and Risk Management

5.2.3 Internal Model (1)
For more information on regulatory capital and solvency
requirements applicable to the Group, including Solvency II,
please refer to Section 7.3 “General information - regulation
and supervision” of this Document.
The Group has developed a robust economic capital model
since 2007, which is utilized in its Risk Management systems
and decision‑making processes. The ACPR has approved the
Group’s use of its Internal Model for calculating its SCR under
Solvency II regulations. This Internal Model incorporates the
use of the AXA Group’s economic capital model across all
material entities.
AXA regularly reviews the scope, methodologies, and
assumptions of its Internal Model and adjusts its Solvency
Capital Requirement (SCR) accordingly. The model may be
revised to comply with regulations, and any significant changes
require college of supervisors’ approval, potentially affecting
the SCR level. Additionally, the Group monitors EIOPA’s work
program which, through its objectives, is also expected to
continue to review the consistency of European insurers’
internal models. This could lead to regulatory changes
enhancing convergence and oversight, impacting internal
models and Solvency II capital requirements.
The Group’s primary objective in utilizing its Internal Model
over the Solvency II standard formula is to more accurately
represent its risk profile in the SCR. This goal is achieved by
taking into account local specificities, allowing for a tailored
approach to risk calibration and benefiting from diversification
across various markets and products. Additionally, it addresses
the limitations of the standard formula by leveraging the
Group’s expertise to develop models that more closely match
local specificities and risk exposures. Furthermore, the
flexibility of the internal model supports ongoing adaptation
and improvement, reflecting the Group’s expanding experience,
entry into new markets, and the introduction of innovative
products with new risk considerations.
The Internal Model is based on a common definition of risks
used consistently throughout the Group, aiming to ensure
comprehensive risk mapping across the Company. It
establishes efficient procedures and reporting, with clearly
allocated roles and responsibilities for identifying, measuring,
monitoring, managing, and reporting key risks.

The Group risk grid (2) aims to identify all material risks
applicable to the Company’s insurance businesses, using the
Internal Model to capture all material risks to which the Group
is exposed. This process includes risk assessment at the
sub‑risk level and the overall aggregation of risk categories.
The underlying methodologies and assumptions used in the
economic capital model are regularly reviewed to ensure they
accurately reflect the AXA Group’s risk profile, with new
methods regularly developed and integrated in accordance
with the Internal Model change policy.
The Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR), calculated using the
Internal Model, represents the capital necessary to withstand
an extreme shock, occurring with a 0.5% probability (equivalent
to a 1 in 200 years event), ensuring the Group’s Eligible Own
Funds (EOF) are protected at the 99.5th percentile over a
one‑year horizon. This requirement encompasses all material
quantifiable risks, including market, credit, insurance, and
operational risks, and accounts for the Group’s diversified risk
profile.
In addition to monitoring risks that impact the Solvency Capital
Requirement (SCR) through the Internal Model calculation, the
Group also oversees its liquidity risk, reputation risk, strategic
risk, regulatory risks, and emerging threats.

5.2.3.1

AXA Group Solvency II ratio

The AXA Group conducts sensitivity analyses of its Solvency II
ratio to material risks and events, in addition to the SCR
assessment that covers all quantifiable risks (insurance,
financial, and operational risks) to which the Group is exposed.
These analyses quantify the potential impact on the AXA
Group’s Solvency II ratio of financial shocks on corporate bond
and sovereign spreads, interest rates, equity, and credit
migration, a wide range of shocks reflecting historical stress
events (such as the 2008‑2009 financial crisis and the 2011
financial crisis), and standardized shocks such as 1‑in‑200‑year
pandemic spread on mortality exposures, a vicennial natural
catastrophes shock, or a vicennial operational risk.

(1) This information is not required under IFRS and as such is not part of the Consolidated Financial Statements. Therefore, it is not covered by the report of
the Statutory Auditors on the Consolidated Financial Statements.
(2) The Group risk grid is designed to identify all risks applicable to AXA businesses. Risk categories are further split into sub‑risks. The risk assessment is
performed at the sub‑risk level. The risk grid is regularly reviewed and validated at Group level.

These sensitivity analyses are designed to demonstrate that the

5.2.3.2

Internal Model governance

At the Group level, the governance bodies involved in the
Internal Model governance include the Board of Directors,
which reviews the Internal Model and authorizes the
application to the ACPR for approval of major changes, the
Audit, Risk and Compliance Committee, and the Solvency II
Committee.
At the Group level, the Internal Model undergoes continuous
review, testing, and approval by the Solvency II Committee,
which is aided by risk technical working groups. These groups
assess proposed changes to the Internal Model and present
their findings to the Solvency II Committee. Additionally, the
Committee oversees the Internal Model validation and model
change processes, coordinates with local governance, and
evaluates the outcomes of regular validation activities.

5.2.3.3

Internal Model validation

The Group has implemented and documented a validation
process for its Internal Model to monitor performance and
continued adequacy, with the process and governance detailed
in the Group validation policy, endorsed by the ARCC.
The Group validation policy is supplemented by local
validation policies that specify the local validation activities
and responsibilities.
Validation encompasses both the quantitative aspects of the
model, including input data quality and lineage, theory and
methodology, parameters and assumptions, and results, and
the qualitative aspects such as expert judgment,
documentation, model governance, use test, and systems/IT.

Risk Management conducts integrated validation activities as
outlined in the Internal Model validation policy, focusing on the
validation of the model structure, modeling choices,
parameters, and assumptions, as well as the validation of the
Solvency Capital Requirement calculation and results.
The tasks are primarily conducted by the Risk Management
Departments responsible for the model, using validation tools
like sensitivity tests, back testing, scenario testing, and stability
analysis, along with any other pertinent activities, to perform
controls and validation.
These validation procedures are complemented by
independent challenge and validation of assumptions, key
parameters, and results through Committees intended to
provide an adequate level of expertise and seniority.
Group Risk Management teams conduct independent testing of
local model choices, parameters, assumptions, calibration, and
results.
Apart from this fully integrated validation, sanctioned by the
Group Chief Risk Officer’s review and sign‑off, a comprehensive
independent review process has been defined and
implemented to provide adequate comfort to the AXA Group
Management and Board of Directors that the model and its
outputs meet a “fit for purpose” standard.
The independent reviews are performed by the following two
internal teams:
●

●

IFC teams, at local and Group level, responsible for
assessing the effectiveness of the Internal Control
framework over Solvency II, based on the testing of
processes and controls relating to EOF and the SCR, at least
annually; and
Internal Model Review (IMR) team, a Group team
responsible for the in‑depth actuarial review of the model
under local teams’ responsibility, the design and
methodology when locally developed, and the local
implementation of Group principles where relevant. IMR
controls are performed on a three‑year rolling basis,
independently from the Group's year‑end procedures. Both
IMR and IFC are fully independent from the development,
the governance, and the processing of the Internal Model.

(1) The Solvency II ratio is estimated primarily using AXA’s Internal Model calibrated based on an adverse 1/200 years shock. For additional information,
please refer to Section 5.2 “Internal Control and Risk Management - Internal Model” of this Annual Report. For more information on the Solvency II ratio,
please refer to the publication of the AXA Group’s Solvency and Financial Condition Report (SFCR).

5.2.4 Governance of investment strategy and Asset Liability
Management (ALM)
The AXA Group’s investment strategy is primarily guided by
Asset Liability Management (ALM) with the key objectives of
fulfilling its commitments to policyholders, safeguarding the
solvency of its entities, and achieving superior returns over
time.

These Committees are tasked with defining the entity’s
strategic asset allocation, approving and monitoring
investments, ensuring compliance with local regulations, and
evaluating both syndicated investment proposals from the
Group and local investment proposals.

5.2.4.1

5.2.4.3

General investment governance

The Group Chief Investment Officer (Group CIO) leads the
community of local insurance companies’ CIOs and the central
Investment & ALM Department, reporting to the Group Chief
Financial Officer. He is tasked with aligning AXA’s investment
strategy with the Group’s overall strategy and its commitments
to responsible investment. This includes fostering better
cooperation between entities, enhancing investment strategies
and methodologies, and guiding investment decisions.
Local investment & ALM activities are steered by local CIOs who
manage local portfolios with the goal of optimizing the
risk‑return ratio. They maintain reporting lines to the Group
and manage close relationships with asset managers and local
stakeholders. Additionally, they are responsible for investment
performance and for implementing and executing sound ALM.

5.2.4.2

Group and local governance bodies

To efficiently coordinate local and global investment processes,
decisions within the Group’s investment community are made
by two main governance bodies: the Group Investment
Committee, chaired by the Group Chief Financial Officer, which
defines the Group’s investment strategy, steers asset allocation,
evaluates new investment opportunities, and monitors the
Group’s investment performance; and the Group Financial Risk
Committee, co‑chaired by the Group Chief Financial Officer and
the Group Chief Risk Officer, with the Group Chief Investment
Officer also a member.
At entity level, each insurance company has a local Investment
and ALM Committee, with terms of reference approved by the
local Executive Committees.

ALM studies and strategic
asset allocation

ALM focuses on matching assets with the liabilities from
insurance policy sales, aiming to optimize asset allocation. This
ensures liabilities can be met confidently while maximizing
expected investment returns.
ALM studies are conducted by the Investment & ALM
Department, utilizing internal asset managers when suitable,
and are reviewed for a second opinion by the Risk Management
Department. These studies are based on methodologies and
modeling tools to create deterministic and stochastic scenarios
that take into account policyholders’ behavior for liabilities and
financial market evolution for assets, while also acknowledging
the interaction between them. The aim is to maximize expected
returns within a defined risk level, incorporating considerations
such as the Solvency II economic capital model, earnings
stability, solvency margin protection, liquidity preservation, and
adherence to local and consolidated capital adequacy
requirements.
ALM constraints are taken into account during the design of
new insurance products as part of the product approval
process, as detailed in Section 5.6 “Insurance risks - Product
approval” of this Document.
At entity level, the strategic asset allocation resulting from the
ALM study is reviewed by local Risk Management and verified
against predefined risk appetite limits before approval by the
local Investment and ALM Committee.

5.2.4.5

Governance framework
for derivatives

Products involving hedging programs based on derivative
instruments are designed and implemented with the support
of dedicated teams at AXA Investment Managers and AXA SA. In
a similar way, this set‑up ensures that all entities benefit from
technical expertise, legal protection, and proper execution of
such transactions within the following governance framework
for derivatives.
Derivative strategies are reviewed by local Investment and ALM
Committees. In addition, there is a segregation of duties
between those responsible for making investment decisions,
executing transactions, processing trades, and instructing the
custodian. This segregation of duties is aimed in particular at
avoiding conflicts of interest.
The market risks arising from derivatives are regularly
monitored, taking into account the Group’s various constraints
(such as risk appetite and internal model).
Monitoring is designed to ensure that market risks arising on
cash or derivative instruments are properly controlled and
remain within approved limits.

324

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

Legal risk is managed through the establishment of a
standardized master agreement, ensuring that derivatives
trading by the Group’s business units is conducted under legal
documentation that adheres to Group standards. Changes to
specific mandatory provisions within these standards require
approval from the Group Risk Management (GRM).
GRM has established a centralized counterparty risk policy that
includes rules on authorized counterparties, minimum
requirements regarding collateral, and counterparty exposure
limits.
The operational risk related to derivatives is measured and
managed within the Group’s global operational risk framework.
Execution and management of derivatives are centralized
within dedicated teams, which reduces the AXA Group’s
operational risk.
Valuation risk is managed by dedicated teams within the
Group’s asset managers and banks, who independently assess
derivatives positions to ensure accurate accounting, payment,
and collateral management. These teams also scrutinize
counterparty prices for initiating, terminating, or restructuring
derivatives, relying on their expertise in market analysis and
staying current with developments in new derivatives
instruments.

5.2.4.6

Investment and Asset Management

For a significant portion of its assets, the Group employs asset
managers for market investments. Local AXA entities primarily
entrust the management of their asset portfolios to AXA’s Asset
Management branch, AXA Investment Managers, with local
CIOs actively overseeing the performance of these asset
managers. Additionally, the Group occasionally calls on
external asset managers to leverage specific asset or
geographical expertise, conducting comprehensive due
diligence and maintaining ongoing oversight at both Group and
local level.
