5.3 Market risks

5.3

Market risks

5.3.1 Market risks: definition
and exposure

5.3.2 Risk control and
risk mitigation

Information in this section should be read in conjunction with
Section 6.6 - Note 4 “Financial and insurance Risk
Management” and the paragraph “Market risks” in Section 5.1
“Risk factors” of this Document.

For more information on the AXA Group’s risk controls and Risk
Management processes, please refer to Section 5.2 “Internal
control and risk management” of this Document.

The AXA Group is exposed to financial market risks through its
core business of financial protection and through the financing
of its activities as part of its equity and debt management.
The market risks to the Property & Casualty (P&C) and Life &
Health portfolios include a decline in market returns that may
lead to accelerate amortization of intangible assets, reduced
investment margins or fees due to lower returns on assets, and
adverse impacts on the Group’s solvency or liquidity from
changes in yields on fixed‑income investments. Additionally, a
decline in the market value of investments such as equity, real
estate, or alternatives could negatively affect the Group’s
solvency position and available surplus. While changes in
foreign‑exchange rates have limited impact due to hedging,
they could affect earnings in euros. Health and P&C activities
face inflation risks, which may increase compensation payable
to policyholders, managed through regular pricing adjustments
or specific inflation protections.
The AXA Group manages market risks through policies tailored
to each product type and their related risks. The main market
risks include interest‑rate risk, spread risk, and equity risk
associated with the operating activities of Group subsidiaries,
exchange‑rate risk from these activities, and risks from the
management of holding companies’ exposure to foreign
currency exchange rate fluctuations and debt.
The AXA Group’s exposure to market risks is managed through
its Solvency Capital Requirement metric, as outlined in the
“Internal Model” paragraph of Section 5.2 “Internal control and
risk management,” and is incorporated into the Company’s
Liquidity Risk Management framework, as detailed in
Section 5.5 “Liquidity risk” of this Document.

The AXA Group’s investment strategy is primarily guided by ALM
with the objective of fulfilling the Group’s obligations to
policyholders while safeguarding the solvency of the Group
and its entities. This approach is detailed in the section entitled
“Governance of investment strategy and Asset Liability
Management (ALM)” within the “Internal control and risk
management” section of this Document.
Local operating units are primarily responsible for managing
their market risks within the risk framework defined at Group
level, which includes limits/thresholds and standards. This
strategy enables a swift, accurate, and targeted response to
changes in the financial markets, political, and economic
environments where the Group operates.
A wide variety of Risk Management techniques are used to
control and mitigate the market risks to which the Group is
exposed. These techniques include local risk appetite
governance and processes, ALM for optimal strategic asset
allocation, a disciplined investment process with formal
analysis and a second opinion by Risk Management, hedging of
financial risks exceeding tolerance levels, regular monitoring of
financial risks on the Group Solvency II ratio, and reinsurance to
mitigate certain financial risks.
Regarding the management of holding companies’ foreign
exchange and interest rate exposure, specific Risk Management
measures have been defined and implemented.
To optimize financial management and control of financial
risks linked to AXA SA and its sub‑holding companies, the
Group Corporate Finance and Treasury Department has
defined a methodology to monitor and assess financial risks.

5.3 Market risks

The policy on the management of holding companies’ interest
rate risk is designed to monitor and limit the potential variation
in interest expenses, thereby partially protecting future interest
expenses against fluctuations in interest rates. Additionally, the
policy regarding foreign exchange risk aims to partially protect
the value of AXA’s net foreign currency investments in its
subsidiaries and safeguard significant cash flows.
AXA regularly monitors its exchange rate hedging strategy,
reviewing its effectiveness and the potential need for
adaptation based on impacts on earnings, value, solvency,
gearing ratio, and liquidity.

The Group Corporate Finance and Treasury Department is
responsible for producing reporting data that consolidates
interest rate, foreign exchange, and liquidity risk exposures,
along with the interest expenses of AXA SA and its
sub‑holdings, and includes medium‑term forecasts.
Synthetic reports, including information about hedging
strategies, are sent to, and reviewed by the Finance & Risk
Committee of AXA’s Board of Directors five times a year.

5.3.3 Main market risks and sensitivity analyses
5.3.3.1

Interest rates, equity and real estate
risks related to the operating
activities of Group subsidiaries

The AXA Group conducts sensitivity analysis on the Group's Eligible
Own Funds (EOF) to assess its vulnerability to fluctuations in
interest rates, equity markets, and real estate values. These
analyses help estimate the impact of both positive and adverse
market movements. The results of these sensitivity analyses are
detailed in Section 6.6 - Note 4 “Financial and insurance Risk
Management” of this Document.

5.3.3.2

Exchange‑rate risk related
to the operating activities
of group subsidiaries

A 10% change in foreign exchange rates as of December 31,
2024 and December 31, 2023 between the euro and the main

5.4 Credit risk

Credit risk

5.4.1 Credit risk: definition
and exposure
This section should be read alongside Section 6.6 - Note 4
“Financial and insurance Risk Management” of the Annual
Report, as only the information in Note 4 is covered by the
Statutory Auditors’ report on the Consolidated Financial
Statements.
Information in this section should be read in conjunction with
the paragraph “Credit and liquidity risks” in Section 5.1 “Risk
factors” of this Document.
Credit risk is defined as the risk that a third party in a
transaction will default on its commitments. The AXA Group
monitors three major types of counterparties to manage this
risk: investment portfolios held by the Group’s insurance
operations and by banks and holding companies; receivables
from reinsurers resulting from reinsurance ceded by the AXA
Group; and credit and credit‑sensitive exposures on third‑party
obligors stemming from some Group insurance and assumed
reinsurance businesses.
The AXA Group’s exposure to credit risk is managed through its
Solvency Capital Requirement metric, as outlined in the
“Internal Model” paragraph of Section 5.2 “Internal control and
risk management,” and is incorporated into AXA’s liquidity Risk
Management framework, as detailed in Section 5.5 “Liquidity
risks” of this Document .

5.4.2 Risk control and
risk mitigation
For more information on the AXA Group’s risk controls and Risk
Management processes, please refer to Section 5.2 “Internal
control and risk management” of this Annual Report.
The AXA Group’s investment strategy is primarily guided by ALM
with the objective of fulfilling the Group’s obligations to
policyholders while safeguarding the solvency of the Group
and its entities. This approach is elaborated in the section
entitled “Governance of investment strategy and Asset Liability
Management (ALM)” within Section 5.2 “Internal Control and
Risk Management” in this Document.

A specific set of limits considers all the AXA Group's exposures
on a given ultimate shareholder through various financial
instruments and commitments, including debt securities, cash,
equity, derivatives, reinsurance receivables, insurance, and
assumed reinsurance. These limits are designed to manage the
overall default risk associated with a particular counterparty.

5.4.2.1

The AXA Group's concentration risk is monitored through
analyses at the Group level by issuer and ultimate shareholder,
complemented by local procedures, and managed within a
framework of Group and local issuer limits.
These limits are designed to manage the default risk associated
with a particular issuer, taking into account its credit rating as
well as the maturity and seniority of all bonds (corporate,
government agency, and sub‑sovereign) issued by the issuer
and held by the AXA Group.
On sovereign exposures, specific limits have also been defined
on government bonds and government‑guaranteed bonds.
Compliance with the limits is ensured by the Group through
defined governance. The Group Financial Risk Committee,
which meets monthly, is regularly updated on the main credit
risks and addresses issuer exposure breaches of the Group’s
limits and coordinates actions for excessive credit
concentrations. A Group Alternative and Credit Team, under the
Group Chief Investment Officer, conducts independent credit
analyses alongside local CIO teams.

Counterparty risk arising from
Over‑The‑Counter (OTC)

●

rules on derivative contracts (ISDA, CSA);

●

mandatory collateralization;

●

a list of authorized counterparties;

●

a limit framework and an exposure monitoring process.

based on an internal scoring system. This policy also includes
daily collateralization for the majority of the Group’s exposure.
The Group Financial Risk Committee approves changes to the
above policy and reviews the exposures every month.

5.4.2.6

Bank credit activities

As of December 31, 2024, total invested assets of banking activities
amounted to €10.1billion (€10.4 billion as of December 31, 2023).
AXA's banking operations, based in France, are mostly limited to
retail banking activities, distributing simple investment and credit
products.
AXA banks’ Risk Management policies align with their stated risk
appetite, emphasizing key principles such as dedicated
Counterparty and Credit Risk functions overseen by appropriate
Committees, close monitoring of the quality of sovereign,
international institutions, corporate, and bank counterparties
portfolio, adherence to Group risk standards, and stringent
management of market, asset and liability, foreign exchange, and
interest rate risks, underscored by a strict collateral policy.
Credit risk in banks includes retail credit risk, which arises from sales
of mortgages and loans to retail customers and small enterprises,
managed through careful risk assessment and regular monitoring
by product management and Risk Management teams.
Additionally, it encompasses non‑retail credit risk from investment
activities, controlled through stringent processes.
Credit risks are regularly reviewed by the Management Board of
each bank and are subject to regulation, with the banks aiming to
meet all regulatory capital obligations.

5.5 Liquidity risk

5.5

Liquidity risk

This section should be read in conjunction with Section 2.4 “Liquidity and capital resources” of this Document.
The liquidity risk involves uncertainty from business operations, investments, or financing activities about AXA SA and/or an AXA
entity’s capacity to fulfill payment obligations promptly in both normal and stressed conditions. This risk pertains to assets and
liabilities and their interaction.
Liquidity is a crucial aspect of the risk appetite framework for the AXA Group, aimed at ensuring that AXA SA and its local entities
maintain sufficient liquidity buffer to withstand severe shocks, on a standalone basis, over various time horizons.

5.6 Insurance risks

Insurance risks

5.6.1 Insurance risks: definition and exposure
This section should be read alongside Section 6.6 – Note 4
“Financial and Insurance Risk Management” of this Document,
as only the information in Note 4 is covered by the Statutory
Auditors’ report on the Consolidated Financial Statements.
Information in this section should be read in conjunction with
the paragraph “Pricing and underwriting‑related risks” in
Section 5.1 “Risk factors” of this Document.
The Group’s insurance subsidiaries manage their insurance
risks related to underwriting, pricing, and reserving, and take
appropriate actions in response to changes in insurance cycles
and the political and economic environments.
In the context of its Property & Casualty (P&C) and Protection &
Health businesses, the AXA Group faces several main insurance
risks as outlined in Section 1.2 “Business overview” of this
Document. These risks include premium risk, which arises from
fluctuations in the timing, frequency, and severity of insured
events and can lead to insufficient liability coverage, mispricing
of policies, and unexpected expense payments.
Additionally, there is reserve risk, which involves fluctuations in
the timing and amount of claim settlements due to failure to
accurately estimate claim costs and statistical payment
fluctuations. Catastrophe risks are also significant,

encompassing natural events such as climatic or meteorologic
phenomena (e.g., windstorms, hurricanes, floods, hailstorms),
tectonic events (earthquakes, volcanoes), and man‑made
events such as nuclear incidents, liability issues, cyber‑attacks,
conflagrations, and terrorist attacks.
Life risks encompass various factors including mortality,
longevity, lapses, disability, and pandemics. Among these, the
Life business primarily faces longevity risk, which pertains to
the overestimation of mortality rates in longevity‑contingent
business, and lapse risk. Lapse risk involves the potential for
actual lapses to deviate from expectations either by being
lower or higher on a permanent basis for businesses sensitive
to changes in lapse rates, as well as the possibility of a mass
lapse affecting all businesses in the short term. Both longevity
and lapse risks are notably sensitive to interest rate
fluctuations.
The AXA Group’s exposure to insurance risks is managed within
its Solvency Capital Requirement and is taken into account in
AXA’s liquidity Risk Management framework, as detailed in the
section entitled “Internal Model” in Section 5.2 “Internal
Control and Risk Management” and Section 5.5 “Liquidity risk”
in this Document.

5.6.2 Risk control and risk mitigation
For more information on the AXA Group’s risk controls and Risk
Management processes, please refer to Section 5.2 “Internal
Control and Risk Management” of this Document.
The AXA Group’s investment strategy is primarily guided by ALM
to fulfill its obligations to policyholders while safeguarding the
solvency of the Group and its entities, as detailed in the
“Governance of investment strategy and Asset Liability
Management (ALM)” section within Section 5.2 “Internal
Control and Risk Management” in this Document.
Insurance risks for the Life & Health and Property & Casualty
businesses are managed through four key processes at Group
level, involving both central and local teams. These include the
implementation of a product approval process that involves
risk controls and profitability analyses for new products,
optimizing reinsurance strategies to limit peak exposures and
protect solvency, reviewing insurance liabilities through roll
forward analysis, and monitoring emerging risks to leverage
shared expertise within the underwriting and risk communities.

332

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

5.6.2.1

Product approval

The AXA Group has established procedures for approving new
product launches, adapted and implemented locally to
encourage innovation while controlling risks. The validation
framework, which includes assessments based on the AXA
Group’s Internal Model and the Solvency Capital Requirement,
ensures a comprehensive approval process for new products
before market introduction.
In Life & Health insurance, the Product Approval Process for
traditional products is managed locally, adhering to the
Group’s minimum requirements to ensure swift time‑to‑market
launches. For sophisticated products, local entities must obtain
the Group’s approval before launch. This ensures that
long‑term commitments are monitored at the Group level,
leveraging the Group’s expertise on enhanced or specific
guarantees.

Risk factors and risk management
5.6 Insurance risks

In Property & Casualty, methods are tailored to risk
underwriting while upholding local decision‑making based on
a documented approval process and leveraging the internal
model’s output. The objectives are to ensure pre‑launch
business risks are thoroughly evaluated before being offered to
customers and to maintain appropriate profitability and risk
control for post‑launch business, ensuring alignment with the
Group’s risk framework.
This framework is integral to the Group’s underwriting policy,
ensuring adherence to Group tolerances and value creation
through adequate risk pricing.

5.6.2.2

Exposure analysis
and risk assessment

The AXA Group regularly reviews its exposure to ensure risks are
diversified geographically and by lines of business, managing
concentration risk and verifying the adequacy of reinsurance.
For the Life & Health and Property & Casualty activities, the AXA
Group has developed and deployed common models and
metrics to consistently measure risks throughout the Group.
This enables the Group to verify that its exposure complies with
consolidated risk appetite limits in terms of earnings, EOF,
solvency, and liquidity. These tools also contribute
substantially to monitoring the major risks, including
accumulations, claims frequency deviation, claims severity,
reinsurance, pricing consistency, natural and man‑made
catastrophes, and biometric and behavior risks deviations.
In the Life & Health businesses, the AXA Group utilizes tools for
analyzing mortality/longevity risks across multiple countries,
regularly monitoring its exposure to these risks, including
mortality, longevity, and morbidity. The insights gained from
this monitoring are used to optimize product design and
reinsurance coverage, with these exposure analyses being
supported by expert risk models in Life.
Regarding Property & Casualty exposures, ad hoc concentration
risk models, both internal and external, are used for natural and
man‑made catastrophes to ensure that yearly volatility from
events such as windstorms, earthquakes, hurricanes, typhoons,
cyber incidents, and liability issues does not exceed the Group's
set tolerance levels.
Since 2015, the Group has strategically developed strong
in‑house expertise in the collection and standardization of sum
insured and financial terms and conditions underwritten by
AXA entities and the development and validation of natural

catastrophe models to address their dynamic nature amid
global climate change. This effort has been complemented by
enhanced expertise in modelling systemic events, such as
cyber, which are not constrained by time and space.
On top of the Group risk appetite limits definition run annually
and from which entities frame their underwriting capacities,
the Group has developed a comprehensive approach to
collecting, analyzing, and leveraging concentration and
accumulation of natural catastrophes information by
centralizing in a single tool the exposure (i.e. sum insured,
deductible, (sub)limits, etc.) by geolocation and associated
type of coverage from most entities around the world.
These measures allow AXA to effectively monitor and manage
its concentration and accumulation across the Group and
enhance its decision making and reaction capabilities on a
proactive basis. The AXA Group's standardized exposure is
modelled through sophisticated stochastic physical natural
peril software to assess the risk in terms of loss.

5.6.2.3

Ceded reinsurance

The reinsurance structure responsible for Life & Health and
Property & Casualty reinsurance operates under the
supervision of the Group Chief Underwriting Officer. Its primary
role is to enhance the Group’s protection by centralizing the
purchase of reinsurance.
For the Life & Health and Property & Casualty operations,
reinsurance programs are established in accordance with
Group Standards and local risk appetite limits, based on prior
risk assessments. Risks are analyzed through comprehensive
actuarial studies. Specifically, Property & Casualty modeling
aligns with the Group’s economic capital model, utilizing both
in‑house and external models for natural perils like storms,
floods, and earthquakes, and in‑house models for man‑made
risks, including Casualty and Cyber.

Reinsurance strategy
The centralization and harmonization of treaty reinsurance
purchase follow identical procedures for both the Life & Health
and Property & Casualty activities.
To build adjusted and optimized protection, the Group’s
operating entities are reinsured by AXA SA, with exceptions for
specific cases, notably products developed in partnership with
reinsurers in Life & Health and some AXA XL treaties.

Risk factors and risk management
5.6 Insurance risks

Group Ceded Re can place a variable part of the local treaties
on the reinsurance market for regulatory reasons. A portion of
the risk exposure is retained within AXA SA and protected
through Group covers, including an internal pool mechanism
for Property, while the remaining part is ceded to external
reinsurers.

5.6.2.4

Group Ceded Re is responsible for all Group external cessions.
Since the acquisition of the XL group, AXA XL contributes to
placing directly part of its covers under Group Ceded Re’s
delegation and control, mainly quota share for specialties and
for US portfolios. The 2024 Group reinsurance protections
ensure that the risk appetite is respected as in 2023.

The additional liability calculations are performed locally
through a process based on two independent opinions.

These protections include major Group‑covers such as CAT,
Property Per Risk, International Liability, Marine Whole Account
(including Marine, Energy, etc.), Cyber, and Life, along with
various entities’ specific local covers primarily driven by AXA
XL‑dedicated protections like Aviation, Marine, Energy, US
Liability, Political risks, and retro.

They notably ensure that a sufficient number of operating
elements have been scrutinized, enough data is available and
adequate for the reserving exercise, the technical assumptions
and actuarial methodologies are in line with professional
practices with sensitivity analyses performed for significant
cases, a roll‑forward analysis of liabilities including merit‑rating
back‑tests has been performed taking into account the
regulatory and economic context with material deviations
explained, the operational losses relating to the reserving
process have been adequately quantified, and the best
estimate liabilities have been calculated in accordance with the
Solvency II Directive and Group guidelines.

The structures of Group covers are designed to protect the
Group in compliance with the Group risk appetite framework,
using specific proportional and non‑proportional covers
arranged through the traditional reinsurance market or
alternative capital markets (Insurance Linked Securities – ILS,
such as cat bonds or collateralized reinsurance) on both an
indemnity and industry loss index basis.
AXA incorporates Insurance‑Linked Securities (ILS), including
catastrophe bonds, into its reinsurance strategy. However, ILS
may not offer the same level of protection as traditional
reinsurance, with the extent of protection potentially varying by
region and the nature of the loss. Market access to ILS can be
affected by major catastrophic events, leading to disruptions or
volatility. Additionally, when AXA opts for ILS products that
provide coverage based on industry loss indexes rather than
AXA’s actual losses, the Company may face a discrepancy in
expected versus actual residual losses
The Group Security Committee regularly monitors the AXA
Group’s credit exposures to reinsurers to ensure that
consolidated exposures remain within the Group’s risk
tolerance, as detailed in Section 5.4 “Credit Risk - Receivables
from reinsurers” of this Document.

334

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

Insurance liabilities

Operational entities specifically monitor their reserve risks,
estimating and booking liability for incurred claims on a
file‑by‑file basis by the claims handlers. Additional liabilities are
also booked by the local entities.

Actuaries responsible for evaluating liabilities use a range of
statistical and actuarial techniques. These assumptions are
formulated after consultations with claims managers, pricing
actuaries, underwriters, and other specialized departments.

Risk factors and risk management
5.7 Operational risks

5.7

Operational risks

Information in this section should be read in conjunction with
the paragraph “Operational and business risks” in Section 5.1
“Risk factors” of this Document.
The AXA Group has established a unified framework to identify,
quantify, and monitor the primary operational risks stemming
from organizational failures, system malfunctions, process
inefficiencies, resource inadequacies, and external events.
Operational risks include legal risks and exclude strategic
decisions, as well as reputation risks.
The AXA Group’s operational risk framework provides a unified
system, specialized operational risk teams, and a common
operational risk typology to categorize operational risks into
seven areas: internal fraud, external fraud, employment
practices and workplace safety, customers, products and
business practices, damages to physical assets, business
disruption, and system failures and execution, delivery and
process management. This framework is applied across all AXA
entities, including insurance companies, banking activities, AXA
Investment Managers, and internal service providers, in
alignment with AXA’s policy on operational Risk Management.
Both quantitative and qualitative requirements are defined
across the Group by identifying and assessing the most
critical operational risks of each entity and a set of stress
scenarios using a forward‑looking and expert‑opinion
approach. These scenarios estimate the capital requirement
needed to cover operational risks using advanced models
based on Solvency II principles.
●

The operational Risk Management process is integrated into
local governance through senior management validation to
ensure the risk assessment is adequate, appropriate, and
comprehensive, and to define and implement corrective
and preemptive actions for the main risks. Additionally, a
loss data collection process within most Group companies
tracks and mitigates actual operational risk losses, serving
as a source to back‑test risk assessment assumptions.

and to establish a suitable risk response strategy for significant
operational risk scenarios. Profiles of operational risk at both
entity and group levels are reviewed by local and Group Risk
Committees to determine necessary decisions and actions.
In 2024, the Group Operational Risk Profile is well‑distributed
across the seven operational risk categories, with the main risks
identified as transaction capture, execution, and maintenance
risk due to process error, failure, and/or misperformance;
compliance risk, heightened by increasing legislation and
regulation, closely monitored by Group Compliance; and
external fraud & system security risk, with the AXA Group’s high
exposure to cyber risk as new technologies are integrated into
its products and services.
The AXA Group’s exposure to operational risks is included in its
Solvency Capital Requirement, as detailed in the “Internal
Model” paragraph of Section 5.2 “Internal Control and Risk
Management” in the Annual Report.
Specific actions are identified at Group and local levels to
mitigate these risks, and the implementation of the Internal
Control framework will continue to better embed controls in
activities and mitigate the risks.
AXA has developed an Information Risk Management (IRM)
framework to ensure consistent information risk decisions
throughout the organization and to establish integrated and
sustainable Risk Management capabilities. In the entities
subject to the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA),
documentation and practices against the DORA requirements
have been anchored into their IRM framework, in close
relationship with Security, IT and Procurement functions who
altogether contribute to AXA’s digital operational resilience.
AXA relies on third‑party providers for outsourcing of services at
different stages of the value chain, which is a strategic
advantage. However, onboarding a vendor requires AXA to
assess potential risks, including regulatory, compliance, and IT
security risks.

The AXA Group’s operational risk economic capital model aims
to understand and mitigate losses from operational failures

5.8 Other material risks

To protect both business and customers, AXA has established a
dedicated Vendor Risk Framework program, co‑sponsored by
Group Risk Management and Group Procurement, and
supported by Group functions such as Compliance, Data
Privacy, Information Security, Operational Resilience, Legal,
Reputation, and Internal Control, along with local stakeholders
including Chief Risk Officers, Chief Procurement Officers, and
Insurance Procurement Directors.

5.8

For more information on the AXA Group’s risk controls and Risk
Management processes, please refer to Section 5.2 “Internal
control and risk management” of this Documen

Other material risks

5.8.1 Strategic risks
A strategic risk is the risk of a negative impact on earnings or
capital at Group level due to a lack of responsiveness to
industry developments or changes in consumer needs, or
adverse business decisions. This includes significant changes in
footprint through disposals or acquisitions, changes in product
offering and client segmentation, and changes in the
distribution model, including channel mix, alliances/
partnerships, multi‑access, and digital distribution.
Given the nature of strategic risks, there is no capital charge
assessment but a strong strategic Risk Management framework
to anticipate and mitigate these risks. Group Risk Management
is involved at an early stage in major strategic projects, such as
large M&A projects. The Group governance standards require a
Risk Management second opinion on key processes, including
significant transactions and strategic plans. Additionally, the
ORSA report provides an assessment of the overall solvency
needs, which includes the Solvency II ratio projection in line
with the strategic plan timeframe and in stress scenarios, as
detailed in Section 5.2 “Internal Control and Risk Management Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA)” of this Document.

5.8.2 Reputation risk
Reputation risk is the risk that an event, internal or external, will
negatively influence stakeholders’ perception and trust in the
Company or the risk of a gap between stakeholder expectations
and the Company’s behaviors, attitudes, values, actions, or
failures to act.

336

The Vendor Risk Framework employs a risk‑based approach to
define requirements for both existing and potential new
contracts, focusing on the criticality of each relationship
through pre‑determined criteria. It ensures an appropriate level
of due diligence, minimum requirements, and oversight is
implemented for each.

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

The AXA Group has established a global framework to manage
reputation risk, focusing on both reactive protection and
proactive measures to identify, monitor, manage, and mitigate
reputational issues. This approach aims to minimize value
destruction while building and maintaining brand equity and
trust among stakeholders, without the need for a capital charge
assessment.
The AXA Group’s Global Reputation Network is designed to
implement a local Reputation Risk Management framework,
aligning with the Company’s overall Enterprise Risk
Management approach. This initiative aims to foster a culture
of reputation risk awareness and intelligence, ensuring that
Risk Management strategies are consistently applied across the
organization.
The Reputation Risk Management approach at AXA is driven by
three main objectives: to proactively manage reputation risk by
avoiding or minimizing negative issues and building trust
among all stakeholders, to define accountability for reputation
risk across the organization at both Group and local levels, and
to implement a common Reputation Risk Management
framework throughout the organization.
The AXA Group monitors potential and existing issues in near
real‑time and receives periodic top reputation risk reports from
local entities. An informational report is submitted to the Group
Audit, Risk and Compliance Committee every two months, and
an internal report analyzing the main cases of reputation risk
managed by AXA is produced annually. Regular dialogue with
the Global Reputation Network facilitates the identification and
dissemination of key topics that could negatively impact the
Group’s reputation.
The implementation of the Reputation Risk Framework
encompasses the AXA Group’s main activities including
insurance and Asset Management.

Risk factors and risk management
5.8 Other material risks

5.8.3 Emerging risks
Emerging risks are risks that may develop or already exist and
are continuously evolving, characterized by a high degree of
uncertainty, with some potentially never materializing.

The AXA Group aims to enhance the understanding and
forecasting of emerging risks and support sustainable
development by developing new solutions, advising on Risk
Management, and contributing to the broader discussion on
these issues with other key market participants.

5.8.4 Regulatory risks

The AXA Group has established processes to monitor emerging
risks, which could develop over time and become significant,
without a capital charge assessment. The emerging risk
framework includes a network of approximately 120 people
across insurance, Asset Management, and support functions
such as AXA Group Operations, facilitating expertise sharing
within the business and risk communities and ensuring the
definition of adequate underwriting policies.

For further information on the regulatory environment in which
the AXA Group operates including regulatory risks, please refer
to the paragraph “Regulatory‑related risks” in Section 5.1 “Risk
factors” of this Document.

Emerging risks surveillance is organized through a detection
process that includes regular monitoring of scientific
publications and court decisions. Risks are monitored and
classified within a risk mapping constituted of five sub‑groups:
environment & energy, society, regulation & politics, economy,
finance & business, health & medicine, and tech & data. After
prioritization by senior management or after a warning from an
entity, in‑depth internal studies are developed biannually by
GRM to review a specific risk and its potential impact in terms
of insurance.

For further information on the sustainability risks to which the
AXA Group might be exposed, either from the impacts on AXA’s
business or from the impact of AXA’s business operations,
please refer to Section 4.1 “AXA Sustainability strategy” of this
Document. Additionally, certain sustainability risks which are
material to the AXA Group are referenced in “Risk Factors” in
Section 5.1.

5.8.5 Sustainability risks

5

Since 2014, an annual Future Risks Survey collects the views of
internal and external stakeholders on the most significant
emerging risks for society.

1.1

Accounting principles

General information

AXA SA, a French Société Anonyme (the “Company” and, together
with its consolidated subsidiaries, “AXA” or the “Group”), is the
holding (parent) company and the internal reinsurer of an
international financial services group focused on financial
protection. The list of main entities included in the scope of
consolidation is provided in Note 2 to the Consolidated Financial
Statements.
AXA is listed on Euronext Paris Compartiment A.
The Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended
December 31, 2024, including all notes, were set by the Board of
Directors on March 12, 2025.

1.2

General accounting principles

AXA’s Consolidated Financial Statements are prepared as of
December 31, in compliance with International Financial Reporting
Standards (IFRS) and interpretations of the IFRS Interpretations
Committee that are endorsed by the European Union before the
end of the reporting period with a compulsory date of January 1,
2024.
Accordingly, the Group uses the option provided by the European
Union which allows not to apply the annual cohort requirement
under IFRS 17 - Insurance Contracts for determining the groups of
insurance contracts meeting some criteria (refer to
paragraph 1.14.2).

1.2.2

Standards and amendments published

Amendments to the Classification and Measurement
Requirements for Financial Instruments in IFRS 9 Financial Instruments and IFRS 7 - Financial Instruments:
Disclosures
These amendments, issued on May 30, 2024, will be effective on
January 1, 2026, with earlier application permitted. They have not
yet been endorsed by the European Union.
They result from the post‑implementation review of the
classification and measurement requirements in IFRS 9 - Financial
Instruments and related requirements in IFRS 7 - Financial
Instruments: Disclosures. These amendments notably improve the
requirements in IFRS 9 and IFRS 7 related to settling financial
liabilities using an electronic payment system as well as to assessing
contractual cash flow characteristics of financial assets with
contingent features, including those with Environmental, Social and
Governance (ESG)-linked features.
The amendments also modify disclosure requirements relating to
investments in equity instruments designated at fair value through
other comprehensive income and add disclosure requirements for
financial instruments with contingent features that do not relate
directly to basic lending risks and costs.
The assessment of their impact on the Group’s Consolidated
Financial Statements is in progress.

Statements
IFRS 18 - Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements,
published on April 9, 2024, will be effective on January 1, 2027, with
earlier application permitted. The standard has not yet been
endorsed by the European Union.
It is aimed at improving the quality and cross‑industry comparability
of financial reporting, notably by introducing defined subtotals in the
statement of profit or loss, adding new principles for aggregation
and disaggregation of information and requiring disclosures about
management‑defined performance measures. It will replace IAS 1 Presentation of Financial Statements.
The assessment of its impact on the Group’s Consolidated Financial
Statements is in progress.

Preparation of financial statements

The preparation of financial statements in accordance with IFRS
requires the use of estimates and assumptions, as well as a

principles described below. In this respect, goodwill (in particular
impairment tests described in paragraph 1.8.1), other intangible

the asset and liability items concerned where material and useful.

1.3

Principles and methods
of consolidation

1.3.1

Scope and basis of consolidation

Companies in which AXA exercises control are subsidiaries. They
are fully consolidated from the date on which control is
transferred to AXA. Under IFRS 10 - Consolidated Financial
Statements, AXA controls an investee when it is exposed, or has
rights, to variable returns from its involvement with the investee
and has the ability to affect those returns through its power over
the investee. Only substantive rights (i.e. the holder must have the
practicability to exercise them) and rights that are not protective

shall be considered. AXA can have power with less than a majority
of the voting rights of an investee, in particular through:
●

●

●

the proportion of ownership with regards to the other
investors;
potential voting rights;
a contractual arrangement between the investor and other
vote holders;

●

rights arising from other contractual arrangements; or

●

a combination of these indicators.

Under IFRS 11 - Joint Arrangements, companies over which AXA
exercises a joint control alongside one or more third parties are
joint ventures and are accounted for using the equity method.
Companies in which AXA exercises significant influence are
accounted for using the equity method. Under IAS 28 Investments in Associates and Joint Ventures, significant
influence is presumed when AXA directly or indirectly holds 20%
or more of the voting rights. Significant influence can also be
exercised through an agreement with other shareholders.
Under the equity method, AXA’s share in equity investments’
post‑acquisition profit or loss is recognized in the statement of
profit or loss, and its share in post‑acquisition movements in
reserves is stated under “Other reserves”.
Investment funds and real estate companies are either fully
consolidated or accounted for using the equity method,
depending on which conditions of IFRS 10/IFRS 11/IAS 28 listed
above they satisfy. Fees received by internal asset managers are
also taken into account in the assessment of the exposure to
variability of returns. For investment funds managed by external
asset managers, when group voting rights (including AXA
Mutuelles) are less than 99%, the presumption is that the asset
manager is not the agent of AXA only and acts on the best interest
of all investors. This presumption can be rebutted based on other
indicators such as the removal rights, the exit mechanism or
existing contractual arrangements. For fully consolidated
investment funds, non‑controlling interests are recognized at fair
value as liabilities in the consolidated statement of financial
position, if the companies’ instruments can be redeemed at any
time by the holder at fair value. Investment funds accounted for
using the equity method are shown under the caption “Financial
investments”.
Some companies in which AXA exercises control, joint control or
significant influence, are excluded from the scope of
consolidation as they are not material with respect to the Group’s
Consolidated Financial Statements. These are mainly investment
funds.

1.3.2

Business combinations and
subsequent changes in the Group
ownership interest

1.3.2.1

Consideration transferred in a business
combination

The consideration transferred in a business combination is
measured at fair value.
Purchase consideration includes any contingent element
(adjustment in the acquisition price conditional upon one or
more events). Any change to the estimate of the contingent
element between the acquisition date and the amount actually
subsequently paid is recognized in the statement of profit or
loss.
Direct transaction costs related to a business combination are
charged in the statement of profit or loss when incurred.

1.3.2.2

Valuation of assets acquired, and liabilities
assumed in a business combination

Upon first consolidation, all assets, liabilities and contingent
liabilities (unless they are not present obligations) of the
acquired company are estimated at their fair value.

Insurance and investment contracts
Insurance and investment contracts within the scope of IFRS 17
are measured as follows (refer to paragraph 1.14 relating to the
classification and measurement of insurance contracts):
●

●

●

●

the groups of contracts acquired in a business combination
are identified as if AXA had entered into the contracts at the
date of the acquisition, following the general guidance for
the level of aggregation described in paragraph 1.14.2;
these groups of contracts are measured using the
consideration received or paid for the contracts as a proxy
for the premiums received or paid;
if those groups of contracts are profitable, and unless the
premium allocation approach (PAA) for the Liability for
Remaining Coverage (LRC) applies, the contractual service
margin (CSM) is initially recognized applying the general
valuation principles described in paragraph 1.14.3. The
excess of the consideration paid or received over the
fulfilment cash flows adjusts goodwill for the contracts
measured using the PAA and the CSM for other contracts;
in case of onerous groups of contracts, the loss component
of the liability for remaining coverage is determined on

initial recognition applying the approach described in
paragraph 1.14.3, and the excess of the fulfilment cash flows
over the consideration paid or received is recognized as a
part of the goodwill;
●

an asset for insurance acquisition cash flows is recognized
as at the acquisition date.

Groups of insurance contracts acquired in their settlement
period are, if material, valuated as if they were new insurance
contracts issued by the acquirer as at the acquisition date: the

Contrary to direct participating insurance contracts and

Purchase and sale of

Restructuring costs

1.3.2.5

In the context of a business combination, only restructuring
costs that can be measured reliably and which correspond to a
liability of the acquired company existing prior to the
acquisition date are included in restructuring provisions
recognized in the statement of financial position of the
acquired company at acquisition date.

Purchase and sale transactions of non‑controlling interests in a
controlled subsidiary that do not change the conclusion of
control are recorded through shareholders’ equity (including
direct acquisition costs).

1.3.2.3

Non‑controlling interests in the acquiree
‑

According to a decision taken for each acquisition,
non‑controlling interests may be measured at fair value or at its
proportionate interest in the acquiree’s identifiable net assets.

If control in a subsidiary is lost, any gain or loss is recognized in
profit or loss. Furthermore, if an investment in the entity is
retained by the Group, it is re‑measured to its fair value and any
gain or loss is also recognized in profit or loss.

1.3.2.6

Intra‑group transactions
‑

In step acquisitions, previous non‑controlling interests held by
the Group are measured at fair value and the resulting
adjustment is recognized through profit or loss. Similarly, when
an additional purchase changes the status from significant
influence or joint control to control, any investment
pre‑existing in a former associate/joint venture is re‑measured
to its fair value with the gain or loss recognized through other
comprehensive income (OCI) or profit or loss, depending on the
previous classification (consequently also resulting in a new
goodwill).

Intra‑group transactions, including internal dividends,
payables/receivables and gains/losses pertaining to these
transactions, are eliminated in full for controlled subsidiaries
and to the extent of AXA’s interest for entities accounted for
using the equity method.

1.3.2.4

In the event of an internal sale of an asset that is not intended
to be held on the long term by the Group, a deferred tax is
recognized as the current tax calculated on the realized gain or
loss is eliminated.

Goodwill

Goodwill is measured as the excess of (i) the aggregate of the
consideration transferred, the amount of any non‑controlling
interest in the acquiree and, in a business combination
achieved in stages, the fair value of the Group’s previously held
equity interest in the acquiree over (ii) the net amounts of the
identifiable assets acquired and the liabilities assumed, as of
the acquisition date.
If the cost of acquisition is lower than the net amounts of the
identifiable assets acquired and the liabilities assumed as of
the acquisition date, the difference is directly recorded in the
consolidated statement of profit or loss.
Adjustments can be made to goodwill within twelve months of
the acquisition date if new information becomes available to
complete the initial accounting and relates to a situation
existed on the acquisition date.
Goodwill is allocated to cash generating units corresponding to
(i) the companies acquired or portfolios of business acquired
according to their expected profitability, and (ii) the entities
already within the AXA Group that will benefit from the
synergies of the combination with the activities acquired. This
allocation of goodwill is used for impairment testing (refer to
paragraph 1.8.1).

The effect on profit or loss of transactions between
consolidated entities is always eliminated. However, in case of
a loss, an impairment test is performed, in order to assess
whether an impairment of the underlying item has to be
booked.

In addition, the transfer of shares of a consolidated entity
between two consolidated entities held with different
ownership percentages should not impact the profit or loss.
The only exception would be any related tax recorded in
connection to the transaction, which is maintained in the
Consolidated Financial Statements. Such a transfer also has an
impact on Group shareholders’ equity (with a balancing entry
recorded in non‑controlling interests). This impact is identified
in the “other” changes of the consolidated statement of
changes in equity.

assets and liabilities of entities in a functional currency
different from Euro are translated at the closing exchange

revenue and expenses are translated at the average

At the local entity level, foreign currency transactions are

When currency risk relating to such monetary items is hedged
using derivative instruments as described in paragraph 1.10,
changes in fair value of those derivative instruments are
recognized in profit or loss and therefore offset most of the
translation difference relating to monetary items.
Foreign exchange differences arising from monetary financial

are recognized as income or expense for the period in respect
of the portion corresponding to amortized cost. The residual
translation differences relating to fair value changes are
recorded in OCI, like for non‑monetary items such as equity
securities designated at fair value through OCI without
recycling.
The groups of insurance contracts that generate cash flows in
one or several foreign currencies are treated as monetary items,
which requires translating their carrying amounts at the end of
the reporting period into the functional currency using the
closing rate.
When measuring a multi‑currency group of contracts (including
the contractual service margin – refer to paragraph 1.14.3.5),
the entities determine on initial recognition whether the group
is denominated in a single currency or in the multiple
currencies of the cash flows within the group, the methodology
having to be applied consistently for similar transactions:
●

under a single‑currency denomination policy, the changes
in exchange rates between the currencies of the cash flows
and the currency of the group of contracts correspond to a
financial risk accounted for applying IFRS 17 whereas the
changes in exchange rates between the currency of the
group of contracts and the functional currency are
accounted for applying IAS 21 - The Effects of Changes in
Foreign Exchange Rates;

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

●

under a multi‑currency denomination policy, all changes in
exchange rates are exchange differences that are accounted
for applying IAS 21.

Goodwill arising on the acquisition of a foreign entity is
recorded in the functional currency of the acquired entity and
is translated into Euro at the closing date.
Foreign exchange differences arising from the translation of a
net investment in a foreign subsidiary, borrowings and other
currency instruments qualifying for hedge accounting of such
investment are recorded in shareholders’ equity under
translation differences and are recycled in the statement of
profit or loss as part of the realized gain and losses on disposal
of the hedged net investment.
Regarding the cumulative amount of the exchange differences
related to disposed business, the Group applies the
step‑by‑step consolidation method (IFRIC 16.17).

1.5

Hyperinflation accounting

In accordance with IAS 29 - Financial Reporting in
Hyperinflationary Economy, financial statements of the entities
operating in hyperinflationary economies are adjusted to
reflect the changes in the general purchasing power of their
functional currency. Thus, non‑monetary assets and liabilities
of these entities which are not already expressed in terms of the
measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period are
restated to reflect the change in the consumer price index (CPI).
The effect of inflation on monetary assets and liabilities relating
to the reporting period is included in the consolidated
statement of profit or loss of the reporting period as a gain or
loss on net monetary position. The cumulated gains and losses
on net monetary position for previous periods are included
within the retained earnings.
All items in the consolidated statement of comprehensive
income need to be restated by applying the change in the CPI
between the dates when those items were initially recorded in
the financial statements and the end of the reporting period.
To be included in the Group’s Consolidated Financial
statements, financial statements of hyperinflationary entities,
restated for hyperinflation as described above, are translated in
Euros at the closing exchange rate.
In the consolidated statement of financial position as at the
reporting date, the restatement effects on equity items are
included in other comprehensive income, altogether with the
translation differences, to the extent that the change in the CPI
is correlated with movements in the exchange rate between the
functional currency of the entity and Euro.

Consolidated financial statements
6.6 Notes to the Consolidated financial statements

The Turkish economy is considered to be hyperinflationary in
accordance with the criteria in IAS 29. By consequence, the
financial statements of the Turkish consolidated entities are
incorporated in the Consolidated Financial Statements
applying the hyperinflation accounting. However, the
presentation of the consolidated statement of profit or loss is
not restated as the effect of the restatement is not material.

1.6

Fair value measurement

The Group applies the fair value hierarchy of IFRS 13 - Fair Value
Measurement as described below for all assets and liabilities
where another IFRS requires or permits fair value measurement
or disclosures about fair value measurement in the Notes to the
Consolidated Financial Statements. Principles below address
mostly assets given the nature of the activities of the Group.

1.6.1

Assets and liabilities quoted
in an active market

An asset or a liability is considered as being quoted in an active
market when quoted prices are readily and regularly available
from a stock exchange, dealer, broker, pricing service or
regulatory agency and those prices represent actual and
regularly occurring market transactions on an arm’s length
basis between a willing seller and a willing buyer.
The assets need to be liquid, meaning that AXA can dispose of
them in the ordinary course of business within a certain limited
time period at approximately the price at which the asset is
valued. Liquidity for debt instruments is assessed using a
multi‑criteria approach including the number of quotes
available, the place of issuance and the evolution of the
widening of bid ask spreads.
The fair value of assets and liabilities traded on active markets
is determined using quoted market prices when available. For
financial instruments traded in active markets, quotes received
from external pricing services represent consensus prices, i.e.
using similar models and inputs resulting in a very limited
dispersion.
The fair value of assets and liabilities which is determined in
whole directly by reference to an active market is disclosed as
level 1 in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements.

1.6.2

●

●

when there is a significant decline in the volume and level of
trading activity;
in case of significant illiquidity;
if observable prices cannot be considered as representing
fair value because of dislocated market conditions.

Characteristics of inactive markets can therefore be very
different in nature, inherent to the asset or the liability, or
indicative of a change in the conditions prevailing in certain
markets.
The fair value of assets and liabilities that are not traded in an
active market is estimated using:
●

external and independent pricing services; or

●

valuation techniques.

The fair value of assets and liabilities that are not traded in an
active market mainly based on observable market data is
disclosed as level 2 in the Notes to the Consolidated Financial
Statements. The fair value of assets and liabilities which is
mainly not based on observable market data is disclosed as
level 3.

1.6.2.1

No active market: use of external
pricing services

External pricing services may be fund asset managers in the
case of non‑consolidated investments in funds or brokers. To
the extent possible, the Group collects quotes from external
pricing providers as inputs to measure fair value. Prices
received may form tight clusters or dispersed quotes which
may then lead to the use of valuation techniques. The
dispersion of quotes received may be an indication of the large
range of assumptions used by external pricing providers given
the limited number of transactions to be observed or reflect the
existence of distress transactions.

1.6.2.2

No active market: use
of valuation techniques

The objective of valuation techniques is to arrive at the price at
which an orderly transaction would take place between market
participants (a willing buyer and a willing seller) at the
measurement date. Valuation techniques include:
●

Assets and liabilities not quoted
in an active market

An asset or a liability is regarded as not quoted in an active
market:
●

●

●

if there is little observation of transaction prices as an
inherent characteristic of the asset or the liability;
●

market approach: the consideration of recent prices and
other relevant information generated by market
transactions involving substantially similar assets or
liabilities;
income approach: use of discounted cash flow analysis,
option pricing models, and other present value techniques
to convert future amounts to a single current (i.e.
discounted) amount;
cost approach: the consideration of amounts that would
currently be required to construct or replace the service
capacity of an asset.

6.6 Notes to the Consolidated financial statements

Valuation techniques are subjective in nature and significant
judgment is involved in establishing fair values. They include
recent arm’s length transactions between knowledgeable
willing parties on similar assets if available and representative
of fair value and involve various assumptions regarding the
underlying price, yield curve, correlations, volatility, default
rates and other factors. Unlisted equity instruments valuation is
based on cross checks using different methodologies such as
discounted cash flows techniques, price‑earnings ratio
multiples, adjusted net asset values, taking into account recent
transactions on instruments which are substantially the same if
concluded at arm’s length between knowledgeable willing
parties, if any. The use of valuation techniques and
assumptions could produce different estimates of fair value.
However, valuations are determined using generally accepted
models (discounted cash flows, Black & Scholes models, etc.)
based on quoted market prices for similar instruments or
underlyings (index, credit spread, etc.) whenever such directly
observable data are available, and valuations are adjusted for
liquidity and credit risk.
Valuation techniques may be used when there is little
observation of transaction prices as an inherent characteristic
of the instrument, when quotes made available by external
pricing providers are too dispersed or when market conditions
are so dislocated that observed data cannot be used or need
significant adjustments. Therefore, internal mark to model
valuations is either normal market practices for certain assets
and liabilities inherently scarcely traded or exceptional
processes implemented due to specific market conditions.
When valuation techniques are used, the classification between
levels 2 and 3 depends on the proportion of assumptions
supported by observable market data used by external pricing
services or, in very limited cases, by the Group.

1.6.2.3

Use of valuation techniques
in dislocated markets

The dislocation of certain markets may be evidenced by various
factors. For example, a very large widening of bid ask spreads
may be a helpful indicator in understanding whether market
participants are willing to transact. The dislocation of markets
may also be suspected in case of wide dispersion in the prices
(over time or among market participants), small number of
transactions, closing down of primary and/or secondary
markets, forced transactions motivated by needs of liquidity or
other difficult financial conditions with insufficient time to
market the assets to be sold, and large bulk sales to exit such
markets at all costs that may involve side arrangements (such
as sellers providing finance for a sale to a buyer).

(1) Europe – Middle East – Latin America.

354

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

In such cases, the Group uses valuation techniques including
observable data whenever possible and relevant, adjusted if
needed to develop the best estimate of fair value, including
adequate risk premiums, or develops a valuation model based
on unobservable data representing estimates of assumptions
that willing market participants would use when prices are not
current, relevant or available without undue costs and efforts:
in inactive markets, transactions may be inputs when
measuring fair value, but would likely not be determinative and
unobservable data may be more appropriate than observable
inputs.

1.8

Intangible assets

1.8.1

Goodwill and impairment
of goodwill

Goodwill is considered to have an indefinite useful life and is
therefore not amortized but subject to a regular test for
impairment, performed at least annually. Impairment of
goodwill is not reversible.
AXA performs an impairment test of goodwill by cash
generating unit, using valuation approaches that rely on
parameters such as market indicators, market value of assets
and liabilities, and future operating profits derived on the basis
of operational and economic assumptions in order to
determine any significant adverse changes that might lead to
impair the goodwill. In compliance with IAS 36 - Impairment of
Assets, within each cash generating unit, a comparison is made
between the net book value and the recoverable value (equal
to the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use).
An impairment loss is recognized for a cash generating unit if,
and only if, the recoverable amount of the unit or group of units
is lower than the carrying amount of the unit or group of units.

Consolidated financial statements
6.6 Notes to the Consolidated financial statements

Value in use consists of the net assets and the value placed on
expected future earnings from existing and new business. Fair
value less costs to sell is determined in compliance with IFRS 13
(refer to paragraph 1.6).
For Life business, the fair value approach is based on risk‑free
rate valuation techniques applied to future cash flows. The fair
value is made of:
●

●

●

the net asset carrying value (excluding intangible assets net
of taxes and subordinated debts);
the profitability of the business in force, represented by the
contractual service margin (CSM), net of tax, determined by
projecting the expected margins from the in force portfolio
of insurance contracts until the end of their coverage
period; and
the profitability of future new business, computed on the
basis of multiples of the new business value (IFRS 17 NBV)
which corresponds to a standardized year of new business
contribution (present value of net projected future
distributable profits generated from the business written in
the current year). The determination of the future earnings
arising from the new business relies upon the use of
operational, technical and economic assumptions, all of
which are compliant with the requirements of the different
regulatory frameworks and regularly reviewed by
independent parties.

The recoverable value of Life business is first assessed on a
risk‑free rate basis (consistent with fair value), then on the basis
of market assumptions aligned with a real world valuation
(value in use) if the recoverable value determined on a risk‑free
rate basis is lower than the carrying amount.
For Property & Casualty business, the recoverable value is built
upon cash flow projections, based on the business plans (using
IFRS principles) approved by AXA management and discounted
using a risk adjusted rate (value in use). Cash flows beyond that
period are extrapolated using a steady growth rate and a
terminal value.

In case of unrealized loss over 15%, an impairment is
recognized for the difference between the net book value of the
investment property and its fair value (determined as described
below) based on an independent valuation. Furthermore, at a
geographical segmentation level that generally corresponds to
a country, if the cumulated amount of unrealized losses under
15% (without offsetting with unrealized gains) represents more
than 10% of the cumulated net cost of real estate assets,
additional impairment is booked on a line‑by‑line approach
until the 10% threshold is reached.
If, in subsequent periods, the appraisal value rises to at least
15% more than the net carrying value, previously recorded
impairment is reversed to the extent of the difference between
(i) the net carrying value and (ii) the lower of the appraisal
value and the depreciated cost (before impairment).
The fair value of investments in real estate properties generally
cannot be determined via reference to quotes of an active
market from an exchange market or a service provider. Instead,
AXA real estate properties are valued by independent
appraisers with relevant professional qualification and
experience in the locations and segments of the properties to
be valued. These external real estate valuation experts are
members of one of the professional organizations composing
the Internal Valuation Standard Council (IVSC).
External valuations are performed at least annually except for
Switzerland, where 20% of real estate properties a revaluated
externally each year, internal valuations being however
performed for the remaining 80%; hence, the entire real estate
portfolio is covered by external valuation over a 5‑year cycle.
External real estate valuation experts generally use a primary
valuation method to value real estate properties held by AXA,
and additionally provide a value derived from a second method
for verification. When relevant, an average value between the
two valuation methods is retained. As the primary valuation
method has to be applied consistently from one period to
another, any change needs to be justified.
Three main valuation methods may apply to determine the fair
value of AXA real estate assets (the first two ones being the
most used):
●

the discounted cash flow method determines the value of
the real estate property from its potential to generate future
income. Thus, the value is estimated by compiling the net
present value of the future cash flows. Main inputs for the
valuation are: projected rental income, projected operating

356

AXA | Universal Registration Document 2024

expenses, capital expenditures requirements, discount rate
and exit yield which corresponds to the rate used to
capitalize the exit rent to determine the exit value of an
asset. The Group provides external appraisers with all
relevant information (notably detailed rent rolls,
budget, etc.) to enable them to determine future cash flows,
to which they also apply their own assumptions. The
discount rate and exit yield applied vary from one property
to another since they are combination of the risk‑free rate
and the risk premium attached to each property due to its
location, quality, size, and technical specificities;
●

●

the income capitalization method determines the value of
the real estate property by applying a capitalization rate at
the net operating income at perpetuity. The income
capitalization method can notably be used when cash flows
are stable and relatively certain, mainly where the real
estate asset is fully leased (with limited number of tenants)
and/or no occupancy changes are expected. In that case, it
may not be necessary to consider an explicit forecast period
such as used under the discounted cash flow methodology
and a terminal value may form the only basis for value;
the Hardcore method is a variation of the income
capitalization method and determines the value of the real
estate property by applying a different capitalization rate at
the net operating income depending on the type of income.

Specific risks (such as climate, regulatory, legal risks...) on real
estate property are reflected in the exit yield or discount rate
used in the modelling by the external appraiser.

1.9.2

Financial investments

1.9.2.1

Classification of financial assets

Financial assets held by AXA include notably debt instruments,
equity instruments, loans, receivables and investments in
non‑consolidated investments funds. These instruments are
held directly or through controlled investment funds.
The classification of financial assets reflects the way those
assets are subsequently measured in the statement of financial
position and how gains and losses generated by those assets
are reported. The classification of financial assets (including the
application of classification options) is assessed at initial
recognition applying the guidance below and cannot be
modified afterwards, unless if, in extremely rare cases, the
business model in which those financial assets are held
changes.

Consolidated financial statements
6.6 Notes to the Consolidated financial statements

Financial assets held directly
Financial assets are classified in the three following
measurement categories, based on the business model in
which those financial assets are held and on the characteristics
of their contractual cash flows:
●

●

●

a financial asset is measured at amortized cost if both (i) the
asset is held within a business model whose objective is
achieved by collecting contractual cash flows from the
assets held, and (ii) the contractual terms of the financial
asset give rise on specified dates to cash flows that are
Solely Payments of Principal and Interest (SPPI) on the
principal amount outstanding;
if both (i) the asset is held within a business model whose
objective is achieved by collecting contractual cash flows
and selling financial assets (which is the major business
model for AXA’s investments in debt instruments), and
(ii) the contractual terms of cash flows are SPPI, the
financial asset is measured at Fair Value through Other
Comprehensive Income (FV OCI) and realized gains and
losses are recycled through profit or loss upon sale;
assets not fitting either of these categories are measured at
Fair Value through Profit or Loss (FV P&L).

In addition to the general classification guidance above, the
Group uses the following classification options:
●

●

optional FV OCI designation for investments in equity
instruments (other than those held for trading), also referred
to as “FV OCI without recycling”. When applying this option,
all subsequent changes in fair value on concerned equity
instruments are presented in OCI and never recycled to
profit or loss; however, the corresponding cumulative gains
or losses are transferred to retained earnings on
derecognition. Dividends received on those instruments are
recognized in profit or loss. AXA applies this optional
designation for most of equity securities held, except those
backing contracts where the financial risk is borne by
policyholders, measured at a FV P&L basis;
optional FV P&L designation (Fair Value Option for financial
assets). AXA applies this option for some financial assets
that otherwise meet the requirements to be measured at
amortized cost or at FV OCI, if doing so eliminates or
significantly reduces an accounting mismatch in profit or
loss, for example, for some loans backing insurance
contracts measured using the Variable Fee Approach
described in paragraph 1.14.5.

Financial assets held through consolidated
investment funds
Assets held through consolidated investment funds are
classified:
●

●

either as assets of the “Core Investment Portfolios” which
include assets backing liabilities arising from insurance and
investment contracts, managed in accordance with the
AXA’s Assets and Liabilities Management (ALM) strategy;
or as assets of the “Satellite Investment Portfolios”,
reflecting the strategic asset allocation based on a dynamic
asset management aiming at maximizing returns. Those
portfolios are managed, and their performance is evaluated
on a fair value basis.

Financial assets held in the “Core Investment Portfolios” are
classified on a line‑by‑line basis as if they were held directly.
Debt instruments held in those funds are managed within a
business model whose objective is achieved by collecting
contractual cash flows and selling financial assets and, by
consequence, are measured at FV OCI to the extent that their
contractual cash flows are SPPI on the principal amount
outstanding.
Financial assets held in the “Satellite Investment Portfolios” are
held within a business model whose objective is achieved
neither by collecting contractual cash flows nor collecting
contractual cash flows and selling financial assets and are,
therefore, accounted for at FV P&L.

1.9.2.2

Impairment of financial investments

The impairment applies to debt instruments, loans and
receivables measured at amortized cost or at FV OCI and
reflects Expected Credit Losses (ECL) on those financial assets.
The Group measures ECL allowances at an amount equal to:
●

●

12‑month ECL resulting from default events that are
possible within the 12 months after the reporting date and
recognized for financial assets for which the credit risk has
not increased significantly since initial recognition (it is also
assumed that the credit risk has not increased significantly
since initial recognition if the financial asset has low credit
risk at the reporting date); or
lifetime ECL resulting from all possible default events over
the expected life of the financial asset and calculated for
financial assets for which there have been significant
increases in credit risk since initial recognition, as well as for
financial assets for which a credit event has occurred since
their initial recognition.

a qualitative assessment based on expert judgment, carried

ECL is defined at each financial reporting date based on the key

closing date.
The amount of ECL is updated at each reporting date to reflect
changes in credit risk on the concerned financial assets. Any
